Euro Truck Simulator 2 is that rare thing, a strong sim tethered to a strong game. Where other vehicle-obsessed devs seem to take player motivation for granted, Czech studio SCS understand that a pleasingly modelled steed needs a pleasingly modelled environment to shine.
On this occasion that environment is a swathe of Europe stretching from Plymouth in the west to Wroclaw in the east, from Aberdeen in the north to Milan in the South. The tangle of motorways and major roads is stylised and condensed, but feels massive. After a splendid week of non-stop trucking the stats screen tells me I've still only seen 50% of it.
There's satisfaction in exploring new routes, seeing new golden been-there-done-that squiggles appearing on the in-game map, but it tends to be the promise of cold, hard cash that gets you out of bed in the morning. Like Farming Simulator, ETS2 has a simple yet resonant economic sandbox at its centre

Hm, now, what to say about this game? This game is just absolutely adorable, and definitely worth your money. It is by no means complete, but what they got so far is perfect for those that love management-type games. The basics of the gameplay is that you are a Rancher on a far-off planet. The things you ranch are Slimes, which are adorable blobs, and to make the muns you need, you need to collect their plorps, which is their poops. There isn't too much story, but trying to find what your Slimes like, fulfilling orders, and following the poop market makes this game so much fun. For some basic tips, you cannot suck up Largo's (When a slime eats another slime's plorts, it becomes a combo of the two), the Tarr's are bad, and the super-big slimes, you basically feed until they explode.
0.5.1 edit: Alright, after returning to the game, and playing it for a bit longer, they have added a LOT. There are 4 new kinds of slimes, Slime Science­™, and all new area's to explore. There are small story signposts dotted along the world, so I still recommend Pooper Scooper Simulator!

TLDR: Game is too repetitive, slow and has very bad UX, further exacerbating the slowness.
I've completed Xenonauts on veteran today. And Xenonauts is NOT a good game. The user experience is horrible. ***Mild spoilers ahead***
2 main points to illustrate, strategically and tactically:
1)Strategically, this game pointlessly drags on for many, many hours more than necessary because the UFOs that contain necessary tech just simply DO NOT arrive until VERY LONG time into the game. Case in point: First Battleship for me? UFO-199... You have to go through like 100+ tactical mission drudgery just to advance the game... And you sort of HAVE TO play the tactical part because Airstrike (option to quickly destroy downed UFO for a very small amount of money) doesn't give enough resources. Then, even when you have some end game aircraft like Marauders (but not a lot of them yet), you still have to play each air combat mini-game out, and it's exactly the same, you patiently click and wait, click and wait, until you are tailing UFO for comfortable Cannon takedown to avoid taking damage... And you will have to play 10s of air battles, which you solved 10+ hours ago, just to farm enough money to afford 10+ Marauders so you can autoresolve.
2)Tactically the game is also really bad. The maps are too goddamn large and Industrial map is the biggest nightmare of them all - you will have to advance at a REALLY SLOW pace, or else you will get killed. That is not difficulty, that is just boring. And 90% of deaths I had was because I got so bored of advancing a few tiles a turn I just rush in with all TUs spent.
Late game things get even more messed up - Once you got Sentinel Armor (aka Flying Suit), you cannot simply order a soldier to move to a point, and then do it with the next one - The camera will FORCEFULLY center on a soldier who's flying MULTIPLE times and will break your control of someone in a Predator armor because your previous soldier is flying at a DIFFERENT ALTITUDE LEVEL... And thus you are forced to watch EACH of 12 soldiers SLOWLY move one by one to the target point. The same bull$hit happens on UFOs with multiple levels.
I think the developers didn't play this game themselves. I do not know how they could subject anyone to this mindless boring repetitive piece of krap.
What's the difference between old school UFO Defense of 1994 and this?
1)Turns resolve momentarily. In Xenonauts they take 5-15 seconds on I5-3570K. The simple AI logic doesn't warrant this amount of computation.
2)The animation was instantaneous. Courtesy of DOSBox speedup, but still. In Xenonauts. you have to watch people fly for like 7-10 seconds each in Sentinel armor for NO good reason. And you have 10+ of them, imagine spending a minute each turn just to move.
3)The UFOD does not swarm you with pointless spam of UFOs. Maybe it should have, but you should NOT have to capture EACH of them in order to barely have enough money for anything. I've had 10 Colonels by mission 30-35. Then what? Nothing - you still play 100 more combats with them, with barely any progress at all once TimeUnits and Accuracy are maxed out.
4)Game pace in UFOD is much better, you do not have to trudge through 50+ UFOs to advance to next tech level.
5)With late game tech you can own small UFOs no problem. Not true in Xenonauts. Due to best armor in the game being unable to stop the very wild 50-150% damage fluctuation, you still have to be wary of a lucky burst from a simple Caesan.
6)UFOD had Psi. Xenonauts? Only aliens do.
Would I play this game again? Hell no. Too much time wasted NOT playing or making decisions, but watching unit animation, and waiting turns.

Storytime - very mild game mechanics spoilers;
It was my first base assault. It got called in the middle east, and I'd been putting the raid on hold for a geoscape week. The team was led by Lieutenant Jennifer Miller, a strong shieldwoman previously of the American Navy Seals. She was the one who I could count on to open doors and have the Reflexes to not take reaction fire, and "shock-jock" with a stun baton to take alien scum in alive.
The firefights were long and daunting, fending off aliens in their own sprawl, and constantly keeping an eye on my rear-guard. Reapers and assault sebilians made me pay for every corridor in blood, to the point when it came to the alien base's command center being the last room, Lieutenant Miller was the only one remaining. A sebilian officer geared for war charged my team of three, killing the sniper who failed to hold down the kill zone corridor before the command room, and mauling a rifleman on its way.
Lieutenant Miller retreated and bunkered down with just a laser pistol and a broken riot shield, ready for a last stand, but the sebilian officer withdrew back to the command room to hold the fort confidently. Lieutenant Miller fell back herself desperately, over the gore of firefights that happened a half hour ago. But among her dead allies, one had a RPG launcher still loaded, and some rockets on their belt. It was enough munitions to seek out the base's power core and destroy the base, but Lieutenant Miller wanted blood. Personally. She gathered up all the grenades she could find, and went back to the corridor, knocking on the command room's blast door with an RPG.
They flooded through the smoke and fire of the blast, three sebilians, and opened fire as Miller was hunkering down and putting in another rocket. She took a graze, but responded with a stun grenade that culled the weaker ones unconscious, then filling the command room with two more rockets. To much relief, the mission became a success. The base was captured.
On the lonely carrier back to home, it was shot down by a very, very angry squadron of alien fighters over the Atlantic. Yet fortune would have it that the local navy would find Lieutenant Miller barely alive out at sea, and ushered back to HQ to receive decoration and promotion to Captain for her legendary service.

With only 5 hrs into the game I can say that it plays how I remember the original XCOM - UFO Defense back in '94.
It is funny how those "great vga graphics" could pull you into a whole new world!
Xenonauts captures what was great about that game, but with a nice new high res graphics environment that although basic is more than enough for this kind of gameplay.
So far the good, that is more than enough to warrant my purchase.
The only things I find disappointing (minor) is the choice of uniforms, the early troopers look like sewage workers with old piz pans on their head. Even in the late seventies early eighties, special forces looked like special forces. In Xenonauts they look like early James Bond baddies...
Also there are too few conventional weapons, like SMGs etc.
Although minor, I'd like to have some variation.
The troops should look like the bad asses they are supposed to be, with the variety of weapons that Spec Ops use.
Being relatively basic in the graphics department (and weapons modeling) it should not be too difficult to address these matters (like the modding community is doing at the moment).
Also the maps seem to lack variety, even with my few hours of game play, that might become an issue in the long run. The way the maps are generate, might lead to the game becoming too repetitive.
Aliens have a tendency to pop in and out of their UFO, shooting when it is their turn and going back when it is the player's turn. Tedious and very gamey, of course a rocket or heavy weapon can remove the door and solve that issue. Still some AI tweaking seems to be in place, including interaction with the environment.
Still I like the game and it earns a solid 7/10, which could easily get above 8 if the developer gives it a little more attention, even if it is done through DLC.

(I do love this game so don't hate me for my critisisms...please? If you feel offended skip ahead past the disclaimer)
Now, I haven't finished this game yet but nothing that happens could really change what I'm about to write. Is the game perfect as some people say? Ha ha ha...no. If I were writing this review based on the constant praise this game gets from some people then I'd be pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥while writing this.
So just to leave you with a sense of where this game shines, I'm going to start with the bad stuff.
Optimization: Yes, you read that right. I don't usually write about optimization in my reviews but the reason I've taken so long to even play this game is because I originally gave up on starting it. The game crashes a lot when I try to start it and I have to cross my fingers as to whether or not it'll work. Thankfully, it's only crashed once DURING play so while the crashing is frustrating (and time-consuming) it doesn't affect overall gameplay.
Story: If I were to go by my version of the so-called "perfect game" I'd say that there are much better stories out there in games. Don't play this game for any meaningful story because the one it has is so generic and unoriginal. We all know how it goes, girl gets kidnapped, hero goes off to save her. However even me and my cynicism have to admit that I did laugh a bit at the cutscenes it has and almost feels like a bit of a parady of some of these generic tropes. Basically, I enjoyed it but it didn't kick me right in the feels as Life Is Strange or the KOTOR series have.
Disclaimer: this is where what I say begins to actually matter as to whether or not you'll enjoy the game
Gameplay: Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing god, as much as I hate the game (for being a rage inducing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) I loved (almost) every minute of it. Yes, I didn't enjoy some of the bosses as much as I'd like but honestly, the gameplay is tight and responsive, the levels are properly challenging and everything feels as though it's meant to keep you determined like no need to keep playing. The gameplay is seriously addicting and feels skillful rather than luck-based. This is the type of game where you know the developers knew what they were doing (you monsters). I genuinely cannot describe the feeling you get after you finally A+ a level you've spent 15 minutes on. I love the gameplay. It's ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant.
Music: The music was actually very well done, while some would argue that I'm underplaying it but I felt like the music just fit. It wasn't some distracting rock album or some tear-jerking country soundtrack but rather a well-done arcade-like OST which fit well with the constant focus you feel while playing. I won't remember the music and in a way that's a good thing, if I remembered the music then it would have been distracting and I wouldn't have been able to focus the way I wanted to.
Overall: If you're reading this to decide whether or not to buy the game just go buy it. The game is rage-inducing and yet extremely satisfying to play and (almost) everything fits together perfectly. If you're afraid that it won't work on your computer (it probably will) then buy it for almost nothing during a sale. My only regret in review is not seeing a sequel to this masterpiece.
If, like me, you don't enjoy playing the same goddamn level 250 ♥♥♥♥ing times until you finally get it right, this game might not be for you.

An awesome, highly-polished game with great progression and fun gameplay mechanics.  Plays very smoothly w/ Xbox360 controller.  Sound design and direction in general are dramatically better than in most indie/budget games.
The billing of "hybrid of Super Metroid and Terria" is fair and accurate, though it lacks the vastness and complexity of those titles.  Not that it matters, in my opinion, as what IS here is handled exceptionally well and captivates throughout.
The only knock against this game, in my book, is the length.  Exploring the vast majority of nooks and crannies, as well as backtracking regulary (more on this after the review) put me at 6h11m for completion.  Others are reporting clear times of around 3 hours, and knowing what I know now, I would assume that those people are enjoying the game even more than I did (and are probably even more upset about the game's brevity).
Overall I'd give this game an 8/10.  If the game were dramatically longer or lower-priced, I'd probably be calling it 9/10.  On a day when I had nothing important to do, and was really dying for a timekiller, this absolutely hit the spot and was worth the money.
(spoilers ahead, read at own risk)
I hate spoilers and I hate spoiling things for people, but there is one thing I reallllllly wish I knew before starting the game:
Relatively early-on, you'll get a chance to buy a consumable item that allows faster travel to/from town.  Because the currency required for this item is very rare in the beginning, I was hesitant to use them.  In retrospect, I regret the additional time spent backtracking in lieu using these items.
If you're fairly thorough in your search, you'll find enough currency to buy at least a dozen of these items and still have enough left-over to buy all of the upgrades.  This will obviously cut your playtime down a bit, likely to the range of 3-5 hours, but you'll probably get a bit more enjoyment out of the game than I did!
If you enjoyed playing games like Motherlode and Terraria, youll love this

Do not let my short time with this version mislead you; whereas, I have destroyed the 3DS version of this game and found myself surprisingly hooked for hours.  I was pleasantly surprised to notice this on sale today, and purchased it immediately - it's that good.  After only 15 minute on the Steam/PC version, rest assured, the transition is everything it should be.  Here's an actual review of the game itself.  Last, I apologize now for spelling, grammatical, or contextual errors, i.e., I am typing quickly in a dark room~
This game is fresh, imaginitive, visually stylish, and is easy to pickup, but requires elements of strategy as you dig and rewards you with progress often.  It delivers a perfect balance; whereas, it is far from super easy, though never hits impossibile or the bang your head against the wall to end it all 'frustration rage' (we've all seen this, be it controllers, walls, friends, etc).  You start casually, but there are no long drawn out tutorials, cut scenses, or credits.  Shorrtly after hitting the start button, you are playing - a feature that is more uncommon than is often noted.  Its apparent almost immediately that the game possesses visually asthetic fluidity.   As you continue to explore, the pacing set by the game is consistently maitained and develops respective to the depths you traverse, and keeps you balanced by means of progressive upgrades, powerups, the twon's growth, purchasable items, and increased value of the loot you find. This game constantly rewards you and creates the sense of wanting to play just a bit longer.  I found myself setting aside some of lifes responaibilities simply because I enjoyed the time I spent playing, e.g., foolhardily making the wife wait longer than any wife prefers to wait...multiple times (Protip: AVOID this mistake).  Additionally, the balance feels very natural and honestly has a rare bit of brillance that you never really think about, probably because it does play so well.  The time you spend jmping through the air, punching, digging, upgrading your items, treking back to town, while thinking about how youre going to get all the way back to the pipe/teleporter as you make some questionable wall jumps never really got old; rather, it did feel as though you accomplished and understand the game more.  As the game tosses new dynamics this feeling continued to evolve... and I found myself enjoying it as I evolved as a player.  Despite the hollistic theme of digging, digging, digging, the gameplay never really got old.  It all comes together in a package that delivers an experience that really ends up complimeting the multiple componets of its own gameplay; therfore, bringing itself together delivering syle, balance, exploration, while provinding a (gamer's) sense of accomplishment, excitment, and fun -> a feeling often associated with video games; however, is all too often replaced with a sense of obligation to finish simply becasue we started or have put so much into it.  This gam never created a sense of obligation, and if your a gamer you know the feeling I am referring to.  This game transcends that dynamic and sccomplishes the ever more difficult task of creating the fundemtntial elements of enjoyment.  This game is appropriate for gamers of all ages, styles, and skill level(s).  The constant rewards will develop younger players, yet can offer old school gamers (the one's who grew up on arcades/atari/nes/collecovison) an experience that is a often more difficult to find in a game.  Buy it.  You will literally find yourself digging in~

This is the most polished Alpha game I have ever played. More so then most full releases. The video above regarding first day / first week in Rust really does give a good indication of the kind of game it is. It's survival, farming, building, exploring, looting, raiding, hunting, playing accoustic guitar, making traps, setting up trading shops/vending machines... it's whatever you make it. A classic adventure VN that is likely published by amateur developers. This will be explained more in depth, starting with the story.
Based on the brief description, the story sounds promising. It had a nice mystery to it that would entice the player. Any game that involves survival as well as a good cast of characters would grasp my interest, and this game did a well job at executing this. The story was well made, and (without stating my spoilers) all had it wrapped up to a satisfying ending.
However, this was the only pro to what all other aspects turned out to be. The controls were pretty basic, and with limited actions in even the combat system. In the introduction, you are notified of how the combat system works as RNG.I could only ask: Why would the developers deny a feature that could have been a plus?
So in the end, we, as the player do not have much option but to skim through the masses of dialogues and scenes - which, if I may add, are just as a much disappointment to the gameplay. The dialogues have nothing new or memorable other than common quotes such as “knowledge is power”. A lot of it was just cheesy.
The scenes were more developed however, and had its detail. There were depth in shading towards areas with a thick environment such as the forest and in Mech-City. The wallpaper patterns in certain bedrooms were also nice and they almost felt real. But, too many of the graphics were repetitive and the characters were … undeveloped. Their actions were rigid and limited. They’re basically statues, much like those figurines you’d see from Thomas the Tank Train (T.V show). This destroyed much of the overall arts, as one of the main basis of the game. It’s in the category title itself, a “Visual” novel. If a VN is created with graphics that are neither neat, dynamic nor polished – especially at this age of game design – expect many criticism on the Visuals.
I’ll say the BGM was appropriate at scenes that would suit the mood and environment. You do get a feel of the environment too with some of the audio: the sounds of people and hustling about in Mech-City, the barking from your pet dog Snoopy to the sounds of splashing when you reach the lake in the game.
In conclusion, Wild Island Quest had a great plot going. But, it was hard to follow with the story, when both the visuals and dialogues are as dull as wall paint that is still drying. I’ll have to give a thumb down to this game.

Well,
is an indie "choose your own adventure" game with not much visual, nor literary appeal. Yet, it is a short and somewhat disturbing trial coming from the Russian three-person developer team. Acquired in a bundle, or on a semi-decent discount, it is to present you an hour to kill with achievements. Other than that, there is not much positive to say about it.
We are a young boy, hailing from a setting where people live in obscure flying islands, and apparently a place called "the Wild Island" is about to float really close to our primary settlement, the Mech City. It is a mysterious and rare event which we'd like to observe, so before the island appears, we are presented with limited time to gather our friends and resources which might be useful in exploration. As we approach to the island though, our spastic puppy called Snoopy - yeah, that's the name, really creative - decides to chase an odd animal, jumping on to the alien place to disappear from view. As young, brave and stupid we can be, we hurry after it, only to get trapped in the unknown wilderness, forced to spend the night. Depending on our prior choices of item and companions, we are to face some events and somehow survive through the experience, also hoping to find our idiotic pet on the way.
Now the core story is established, we can take a look on various aspects of the game. I must declare that the display qualities are horrendous. I do not know, it might just be me, but there is something really disturbing about the character models and how they look. They look exaggeratedly plastic, even creepy to a degree. The developer states that "the game's engine is created on the basis of C and Lua which easily allows to make changes and create your own modifications." in their website. They also declare that they use a free and open source cross platform visual interactive fiction editor which can be used by other developers. Uhm... I'd pass this kind offer if I would be a developer though, since they really look disturbing rather than interesting or appealing. The soundtrack and added sound effects are equally annoying, all being quite repetitive and intrusively loud.
The gameplay requires you to make a dice roll at the start of the story to determine your luck. Developers claim that since our protagonists are all children, they cannot have actual stats to determine the results of their action. They mostly rely on luck. Hımmm... I won't challenge that idea since this may turn into a debate concerning whether children have the ability to affect their environment or not, yet the theory's various flaws should be noted. Later, you'll be given limited time to choose your companions and items before going to the island, mostly determining the path you may take. Later on the island, you either immediately solve things if you have the proper item + companion combination, or make a dice roll to add with your luck to see if the event ended in your favor or not. Quite simple. Making 3-4 choices to live through some vaguely dangerous encounters, you come to the end of a gameplay anyhow.
Here, I must state that even though the concept and the setting has some spark and potential, with the way it’s been presented, it ends up being tedious and mediocre. Events are really scarce, and your actions rarely actually danger the children. They mostly somehow always end up being saved by adults if you screw up enough. Aside that, some choice actions and the resulting reactions from our characters are surreal. This might be considered a spoiler, so please skip the rest of this paragraph, but what kind of mentally healthy kid decides to shoot a village of natives with a rifle to save his puppy before even trying to communicate and returns home happily, without being even slightly traumatized? Sure there are some vague scenes concerning a trial at empathy, but they end up being pathetically unrealistic, thus eventually just disturbing.
The narrative itself is an issue altogether. Clearly, the English narrative is a direct translation from the original Russian version, but it really is a subpar translation. As if the display isn't robotically artificial enough, narrative reactions stand to be similarly artificial, with inappropriate choices of words all around. Grammar itself is vaguely correct, yet it fails to present any kind of elegance or even excitement.

I'm pretty sure, most critics talk about gameplay so i'm not gonna bother giving you another copy of them. Yes the gameplay is great, also the truck physics are well implemented and in general words it's a good simulator. Good for teaching kids the traffic code. Now to the point.
The best part of ETS2 is the multiplayer part. If you're not aware of it, there is the multiplayer MOD. Just google TRUCKERSMP and you'll get it. That's the real fun of Eurotruck. I'm the kind of player that gets bored way too easy, but i never lost my interest for the multiplayer part. Cause in my opinion, the singleplayer repeats itself after a while, you drive and drive and drive to get money, pay your bills, create a good company etc.
In the multiplayer, the real achievement is to create a successfull company. It's much harder than it sounds cause you'll have to pay most of your earnings for repairs to your truck. Why? Because laws exists but not applied by most drivers. In most two lanes roads, you'll find yourself at some point having two trucks coming towards you (Overtaking) or you'll try overtake a slow truck only to realise halfway that another truck is coming fast towards you. The right of way is not a thing and if you think for a moment that you shouldn't look both ways when crossing a road then you're probably gonna end up in the service station. Some people are bothered by these things, but not me. It's these little things that make the game great. And that's why i never get bored of it.
And in my opinion the 5 euros (current offer -75%) are money very well spent.

This game is one of the most masterfully designed games I have ever seen, at least in terms of what it wanted to achieve. I'm surprised at the pretty lukewarm response the general gaming industry seems to have towards it at this point. It's not the most technically or graphically impressive tiltes out there, but this games ability to make you truly feel like you are your character can't be overstated. Sure, some flaws are there, but this level of interesting game design should be applauded. Slithering between platforms, sliding up poles, and desperately lashing out after wrapping myself around a stray piece of bamboo to grab a small, golden coin completely encompass everything I would want from a current-gen, innovative Rare platforming title while providing enough modern day shine and polish to hopefully lead the new age of entertaining, physics-based platforming. All I can say is that I hope this, and games like it, will receive some more spotlight so the companies who produce them can keep pushing the genre forward.

With its bright colors, cute characters, and bouncy soundtrack, this might the perfect game to play with your kids if you want them to learn the F-word. No, not due to any spoken dialogue by the characters, but because
will likely repeatedly desecrate the charming ruins of Snake Pass with some downright salty language as you'll often struggle to get Noodle, the snake you'll play as, to do what you're trying to get him to do.
That's not to say there is anything wrong with the controls. They're actually quite ingenious/enjoyable, once you get the hang of it. The difficulty lies in the fact that the inherent complexity of even the
controls (a stick for direction, a button to "constrict," a button to propel yourself forward, and a button to raise your head up) are, if not
complicated, certainly in the same ballpark as
and
in the sense that they're the equivalent of the proverbial "walking while chewing gum while patting your head while rubbing your belly." There will be times when you'll need four of your fingers to work perfectly in concert together, but instead of skillfully nabbing a shiny gold coin while hanging impressively from a bamboo shoot, you'll find yourself nabbing a gold coin as you fall stupidly to your death. Again.
Of course, as you watch Noodle fall into that endless void, his mouth open in terror, some part of your brain may actually feel relief at the thought that that's one less huge snake in the world. You know, silver linings, and all that! Because for all his cuteness, he's still a big♥♥♥♥♥ heavy snake who will, with your help, demonstrate his ability to get absolutely EVERYWHERE. If this game was set in a suburban neighborhood instead of floating ruins, with a slightly-different soundtrack, it could have easily been in the horror genre. Maybe that's an idea for the sequel, actually. "Snake Pass 2: Baby Eater."
In all seriousness, though, this is a well-constructed platformer that feels both familiar (particularly for those feeling nostalgic for bright, 90's-era collect-a-thons) and refreshingly unique. You've probably never played anything quite like it, and for that reason it's worth a look. The controls are unique and the visuals and audio are well-executed. My only real complaint so far is the inability to skip cutscenes on your second playthrough, when you go back to hunt for collectables you missed on your first run, but that's an easy fix that I fully expect will be addressed in a patch, so depending on when you're reading this review it might actually no longer be a problem. And, assuming you have more control over your language than I do, sure, your kids would probably really enjoy watching you play.

So I first wrote a review for this game on it's intial alpha release. I'm now scrapping that review and starting from scratch because the game has evolved so much between 1.0 and 1.5 that my original review became largely irrelevant.
I'll keep this much more succinct than last time. The Orion Project (Previously called Guardians of Orion) is a highly ambitious game coming from a relatively small indie developer. The game began as a top-down arcade shooter with not much depth to it, but has evolved and will continue to evolve into a massive and expansive title.
Since launch, The Orion Project has added a 3rd person and 1st person perspective in addition to retaining its top-down perspective as an option. You can switch perspectives in real-time seamlessly during gameplay to suit your combat needs. This is a pretty revolutionary concept for a shooter. I love it. My biggest issue as of right now is that because the maps were intially designed around a top-down orientation, there is little to no verticality in any of the maps. I'm sure this will be fixed given time, but as of right now the world seems a bit too flat in 1st/3rd person view.
As of right now the game is still in its VERY early stages, and much of the content is still in development. The developers have been working tirelessly to pump out consistent updates and I've watched the game grow before my eyes. Given another year of development, this could very well be the next big thing. It's only $1 as of right now and I cannot stress enough how much of a steal that price is. Think about the things that cost $1 in your everyday life, and then compare those things to AN ENTIRE VIDEO GAME. I think you'll find that this is the most cost efficient use of $1 you'll ever find. Just buy the damn thing. It doesn't matter if you don't touch it for a year, come back to it months or years down the road when you forgot you even bought the game and it'll be 50 times better than when you bought it. It's like investing in a penny stock, except you literally can't lose. Just buy it. Stop reading and buy it. Right. Now.
I'm a big fan of Orion: Prelude. I initially played it when it was called Orion: Dino Horde, so I never experienced the horror that was Orion: Dino Beatdown. Guardians of Orion is a completely different game from its predecessors. Prelude was a true FPS, whereas Guardians is a top-down arcade style shooter with a wonky 3rd person option. Guardians was clearly built and balanced around the top-down camera angle, and 3rd person was thrown in as an afterthought due to popular demand.
The best way to describe the difference between Prelude and Guardians is this: Prelude is to Call of Duty's Nazi Zombies as Guardians is to CoD's Dead Ops Arcade. I hope this clarifys for everyone exactly what kind of game Guardians is.
Now, some people are going to be disappointed that Guardians isn't an FPS, but others will prefer the arcade style shooter. That's just up to your individual tastes.
Guardians of Orion will be featuring a first-person mode in the near future. (Spring 2016)
The core gameplay or Guardians is fun after playing a few matches, but I can imagine it getting very boring and repetitive after a short while. There are currently only 5 maps, 2 game modes, and a day/night option. Considering it is still in early access, I'm sure they will gradually release new maps and game modes, but as of now that is it.
Something I really enjoy about Guardians is the addition of a skill tree and crafting system. This helps make each class (Assault, Support, Recon. Tech, Pyro) feel much more unique, as they each level up individually and have their own unique skill trees. I have no experience with the crafting system yet, however I think that it will give players an incentive to grind the somewhat limited content in order to craft super cool weapons and items.
I'm honestly a little confused and disappointed as to why they chose not to include either a campaign or a competitive versus game mode in Guardians. Most games draw success either from a compelling story mode, or an intense and addicting competitive scene. It is very difficult to retain player interest with only a co-op surivival arcade game. Perhaps those features are in the works, but if not I can't see myself spending more than 10 hours on this game, unless the crafting ends up being highly addicting!
The graphics are beautiful when you enter 3rd person mode, so again I'm a little confused as to why they chose a top-down camera angle to build the game around. I'd rather enjoy the graphics froms 3rd person, but it puts you at a massive disadvantage because you can't see flying enemies very well, and the tiny dinos are impossible to spot in the tall grass. Not to mention it is much harder to turn around in 3rd person quickly due to low sensitivity relative to top-down sensitivity.

Overall, I give Guardians a 7/10 because the core gameplay is fun, but replay value is just not there at this point in time. It is on sale right now for $2 and I HIGHLY recommend buying it. However, when it returns to it's normal price of $20, I'd wait until they release more maps and game modes before spending that much on it.

Slime Rancher is one of the cutest, most fun games I've ever played. I wanted to buy it so bad after watching Jacksepticeye play it. I really hope it gets updated soon, because I've done almost everything so far. So please update!

Slime Rancher is a really fun game with a cute aesthetic and a lot of time and care put into its presentation. It uses polished VFX and sound to craft a playful and fun atmosphere that creates satisfying interaction with in-game elements. Everything from sucking up slimes, selling plorts (slime poop, essentially), and feeding your tiny slime flock is perfectly calibrted to feel fun, satisfying, and cute.
The physics in this game aren't always consistent, however, and sometimes collision and force glitches shoot the player up into the air, but such problems are to be expected with early access games. The major flaw of this game comes with its early access label, in fact, as most of the content can be seen, explored, and farmed within the first 5 hours of gameplay. There are plenty of planned and hinted-at additions to the game, however, so the future seems bright for your tiny slime business.
Overall, this game is a fantastic, fun experience that feels satisfying and cute through the entirity of its relatively short jaunt through slimespace.

I knew this game by reputation going in, and I assumed that it wouldn't have anything to it besides the curveball it's most known for, but it's a well-crafted puzzle-platformer with functional controls and clever level design. It may be short, but considering how simple it is, I think it's the perfect length for its kind.
Each eversion level has its own rules of what's solid and what isn't, and you'll have to jump back and forth between 3+ levels per stage to collect all of the gems and reach the end. The final gem stage in particular requires you to put all of your knowledge of what each eversion level entails to good use if you want all of the gems, and it was easily my favorite part of the game for how much it makes you think.
Some of the jumps later on are a pain, especially on the path to the true ending, and I wish the game would be clearer on what to do once you have all of the gems, but those are my only complaints. Well worth your money, even if you're spoiled.

Gosh do I love this game. The way I see it, this game has the potential to be literally the best game fathomable. Here's why:
-It has soo much variety in playstyles, guns,environments and enemies
-It's creative as hell
-Tons of hilarious writing
-It's very atmospheric at times
-Very unique mechanics; I especially love the badass rank mechanic
-Tons of content when you get the DLC
-It's infinitely replayable and you WANT to play it again
However, every game has its problems, and boy does this game have a lot
-First of all, the story is very mediocre. There was clearly more effort and thought put into other elements of the game than the story. It can feel like a more colorful version of COD at times sadly
-Second, the game CAN be boring depending on the person. I personally can't stand playing as Axton But others might find that Gaige is lame or that Krieg isn't fun. So, depending on who you are, you won't be able to get the most out of the 6 total characters available.
-3rd, the game has a clear bias on coop. It definitely supports single-player but it's the kind of game that's meant to be played with friends, and I personally like to play alone.
-4th, and this is by far the biggest problem, the game can be relentlessly frustrating at times. While the variety is nice and certainly makes it more interesting than other shooters, you are limited by the variety in a way. For example, You won't be able to rely purely on sniping or corrosive damage weapons because some enemies flat out say no to those type of playstyles. Another thing is UVHM. UVHM, when you start it right after TVHM, is an absolute NIGHTMARE. It flat out requires you to have the very best weapons your class can utilize, and sadly healing weapons are not given much variety in terms of where you can get them. It's either Moxxi or the grog nozzle, you HAVE to have one item from them at all times in UVHM or your build isn't viable. There are other things like the AI on enemies being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when you're trying to get a kill in FFYL mode, any flying enemies being stupendously difficult to hit (except Rakk), and sometimes, out of nowhere, you find that your build simply isn't viable against a certain boss. It's also annoying when you have to farm for certain items because it can take considerable time for them to drop. Yeah, as you can see, I have a lot of complaints about stuff I personally believe is rather BS.
Overall though, this game is a blast at normal mode, TVHM, and to some extent, UVHM. Get it and you will love it

I love this game! I recently bought both Borderlands GoTY and Borderlands 2 GoTY when they were on sale on Steam, and  they were well worth the sale prices. I have played all the way through the game twice as the commando, and partway through once as the gunzerker. I've only played single player.
Borderlands 2 picks up some years after the original. The characters you play in Borderlands all play significant roles as NPCs here who provide the major story missions and even many of the side-quests. This game deals with the aftermath of opening the Vault at the end of the first game and its impact on the planet of Pandora. It really does a good job of building organically on the story begun in Borderlands, and building on characters players are already familiar with if they played the orginal. The writing is very good. In terms of quality, I describe it as "Mass Effect with a sense of humor." Just like with the original, the writing and graphic feel work very well together to create a cohesive environmental experience.
The controls with Borderlands 2, just like with the original, are basic FPS (WASD+Mouse), so they are easy to pick up. Driving is again quite easy (turn and shoot with mouse; forward, back, and boost with keyboard). If you like FPS and their mechanics, Borderlands 2 may be right up your alley.
My one big complaint about the GoTY edition of Borderlands 2 is that it doesn't come with even half the DLC. A bunch of character customizations, missions, and areas show up in-game with asteriks next to them, and when you click one of those, it takes you to the Steam store to purchase the missing content. For a game this old, I wish there was a complete edition available (ala Skyrim: Legendary Edition), where I know I've got the whole package. As it stands, it would cost me more to purchase the missing DLC than it cost for the Borderlands 2: GoTY. Just a gripe on my part, but you should be aware that you will be missing significant DLC content if you just purcase the GoTY.

If you're looking for an old-school (but also new at the same time) collectathon with bright environments and peaceful music, Snake Pass is definitely one of the best modern options I've played so far. This game is up there with Ubisoft's
& its sequel
in terms of being fun adventure games with no combat and unique yet satisfying movement mechanics. In Ubisoft's Grow games, climbing was done by alternating hand grips. In Snake Pass, climbing is done by literally slithering around bamboo and using that grip to pull the snake upwards. All three games are definitely worth playing, but enough comparisons.
Snake Pass stars a snake named Noodle who, with the help of his hummingbird friend Doodle, must restore the gates linking the different realms of Haven Tor together. Haven Tor consists of 15 levels spread across 4 realms, each with a different visual theme (and slightly more challenging obstacles than the last) and song. Yes, this means there are only a handful of original music compositions through the entire game, but the ones that are here fit perfectly and never seem repetitive.
The physics are really solid here, with Noodle mostly reacting the way you would want him to, and Doodle's ability to lift Noodle's tail is pretty well thought out. Use it right and Noodle can scale obstacles easier, but bad timing may send Noodle to his doom. Either way, most of the time spent in Snake Pass is spent climbing up and around bamboo to navigate each level.
Every level has 3 keystones (the main objective) and side collectibles consisting of 5 coins, 20 wisps, and some of those idols I mentioned earlier. Each level took me around 30 minutes as an average, with some of the later levels taking slightly longer, and there are some achievements that encourage replayability, such as playing every level without dying or finding hidden idols that are otherwise unmentioned.
My only real criticism of Snake Pass is that sometimes, the camera can get stuck on the scenery, which can make some of the coins a real nuisance to collect. Also, if you die you reset at the last checkpoint and any collectibles you acquired since have to be grabbed again. The latter, in and of itself, isn't a problem really (I kinda like that design decision to be quite honest) but the camera makes this a minor issue. Here's a pro tip to reduce frustration: When you grab something tricky, find the closest checkpoint you can and tag it. Better safe than sorry.
If you played Yooka-Laylee (which I haven't yet as of writing this review) and found it disappointing, or if you're looking for a modern twist on the old-school collectathons of the N64/PlayStation era, give Snake Pass a shot. As far as I'm concerned, this is one of the best collectathons on Steam.

A fresh take in an otherwise, incredibly nostalgia entrenched genre. First I would like to list the features and things Snake Pass does right, and then list some of the issues that come from an extension of playing for a while. The first, and best, feature of this game in comparison to other 3D platforming games is the incredibly unique feeling of control, which I can only compare to games like Octodad, but those games are made in such a way for comedic effect, rather than for intuitively enhancing the challenge. In Snake Pass, as the name implies, you play as a snake named Noodle, and goal is to complete a relatively open ended, but somewhat tightly designed level. You collect 3 objects or so (usually found in difficult to reach vantage points) and then proceed to the end of the level. Pretty basic fundamentals to a game, you will have seen this kind of work in games like Banjo-Kazooie, but what Snake Pass does best is how you CONTROL the game itself.
I have played both with keyboard & mouse, plus using a controller, and both seem to work virtually in both ways efficiently, whether you choose between will typically be preference, and I went with the controller on this one. The game does an amazing job at how well it controls, as you meander around a deep-grass jungle looking environment, attempting to wind up bamboo-looking structures and traverising the environment using simple puzzles. The real meat and challenge of the game comes with mastering the controls, and with this, makes you feel like you are having a truly unique experience with the game, as you become the snake.
Visually, the game is gorgeous, using the Unreal 4 engine, and really showcasing excellent lighting, and just the right tinge of bloom and an effective colour pallette. You will more than likely get that trademark feeling of "Rareware" from playing this, with its cartoony and friendly look. The soundtrack is also very enjoyable, composed by the extremely talented David Wise, known for his works on Rare titles in the past (Battletoads, DK Country) and fits perfectly with the game's aesthetic.
Unfortunately, unlike Snake Pass, this review isn't all sunshine and rainbows, and there is an issue that arises the longer you play the game. One of my biggest complaints would honestly be the somewhat repetitive nature of the game overall; as the objective does not change, and eventually assets from the previous levels will be reused again, and again, and again. Unlike some other 3D platformers which would have suffered from this, they would have broke up the monotony with minigames like in Banjo Kazooie or other titles of similar nature. This game lacks some variety, and it is a shame, considering how much potential there was for variety with their physics engine and how the controls functioned. The novelty runs thins after a while, and this personally, makes me question the price tag at its current level. Currently I have clocked around 6 hours of gameplay, and I am honestly not sure how long this monotony continues throughout, however at this point it does admittedly get tedious.
Overall, if you are not put off the repetitious nature, and instead can focus on the music, aesthetic, challenging controls and FEEL of a classic Rareware title, I would highly recommend the game, though I would still be relatively cautious of its current price tag at £15. I hope to see more of these types of games that attempt to spice up the formula of 3D platformers.

Where do I even begin with this game... Wild Island Quest follows the story of a group of guys who are going from their home island (Mech-City Island) to Wild Island while it's on a rare pass-by. While you can go it alone, you can also gather up your friends to go with you. What choices you make determine how many of your friends you can recruit (I did the path with recruiting Conan only).
Interesting idea, right? That's what got me initially interested. Unfortunately, everything goes wrong in Wild Island Quest quite fast. If you're able to even follow the story, you'll find a a lot of English mistakes in terms of grammar and odd word choices. This pretty much tells you that this was translated with a Russian to English dictionary and in quite a few places it seemed they didn't quite know which word to use so they just picked a random one. Of course, this "random one" makes very little sense to a native English speaker, and in several cases I actually had to go search up words that were used to try and figure out what word/meaning they were going for.
The horrendous English coupled with the pretty poor graphics (the models just look awful) make Wild Island Quest fall very short of what it could have been. As it stands, unless some drastic improvements are made, this game gets a gigantic pass. There are better visual novels/choose your own adventures out there. Oh and no, there isn't really a "combat system". You just choose if you were lucky or unlucky in an outcome.

The emotional response garnered by the plot was much better than many other games out there, and the characters had a good amount of depth, especially after playing through the first game.  However, the lack of satisfactory animations during any sort of interaction hurt the depth of character interplay. The new characters were less developed and much shallower than legacy characters, but this was a problem with the original as well.
As far as actual gameplay goes, the guns are not so frustrating in the early game as the original's were. There is always something viscerally satisfying about shooting an enemy in Gearbox games, and this one did not disappoint. Unfortuntely, the combat is quite repetitive, and the enemies in later modes (TVH, UVH) become meatshields with ridiculous damage output more than they become legitimate strategic challenges. this detracts from the fun of replaying the game. After all, why not just use a worse gun and shield in normal mode if that's all the challenge it gives you. The combat is fairly bland, and seems to attempt to repeat the success of the original's quite innovative feeling. It falls short, and ends up with something that feels derivative, and doesn't really bring anything new to the table.
Overall rating: 7/10. A great game to play through in a very casual setting, but I would not consider it worth the original asking price. Now that it's on sale, buy away and blow up some bandits.

I played this game with an Xbox 360 controller and on max graphics settings.
I thought this game was fun, but it is far from perfect. The original game mechanics are really fun and unique, it's fun to climb stuff acting like a real snake, but there is a lot of bad game design that can't be ignored. I have played through the whole game.
Pros:
- Fun
- Original mechanics
- Vibrant (yet monotone...) world
- Length is good for $20 game
- Snake vision after you complete the game is a good idea in finding the collectables, as a lot of people after finishing the game may have just looked at a guide anyway.
- Checkpoints mostly fair
Cons:
- IT'S ALWAYS SO DAMN LOUD ON LAUNCH, until you click the A button your sound setting don't kick in. rip headphone users.
- Camera gets bad in some close-up sections.
- There is basically no story, and the story that is there is very weak and doesn't add anything to the game.
- The soundtrack is bad in my opinion, I've seen some reviews on here that say it's good, but for me it was too repetitive and annoying.
- The environments are all the same, even between different 'worlds'. Just because they changed the lighting and changed spikes to lava, doesn't make it feel unique enough. For example, in the lava world, they use the same grass from all the worlds, where they could of made it a bit more barren or ashy. All world environments feel the same and the slight changes they have made shouldn't justify the different worlds.
- No enemies, having the addition of enemies in some areas would have given a lot to the game, the ending of the game sucked so bad, having a boss fight or a massive epic challenge to overcome would of been great, but there wasn't any. It's not like having colourful enemies would change the atmosphere of the game as there is already spikes that impale the noodle and kill him.
- There isn't much aim for the collectables, I haven't 100% the game yet so there might be something after that, but there is no game aspect that motivates you to collect all the collectables.
- Can't skip the bad cutscenes.
So, if the developers created a sequel to snake pass, I would suggest working on a story that makes sense, it doesn't have to be long. look at spyro 1 or crash bandicoot for inspiration. I would also suggest working on the camera more and the environments. In addition to a better soundtrack, hopefully unique songs for each level? I'm not even sure how many songs are in the game right now, they were all so similar which made listening to them for hours annoying. MORE UNIQUENESS BETWEEN LEVELS.
In saying all this bad, it's still great and I would recommend it! 6.5/10~ I hope these developers improve on their next game!

A clever and innovative puzzle/platformer game that allows you to take control of an adorable corn snake named "Noodles" and challenges you to slither around bamboo, through water, and across dangerous clifftops. The game has 4 stages with several levels in each stage that all increase in difficulty, with main objective keys to collect, basic collectable bubbles, and difficult to obtain medals.
The game's graphics look fantastic and Sumo Digital makes good use of the Unreal 4 engine, with depth of field, advanced shaders, and an overall great presentation. I encountered no technical issues and had flawless performance throughout my playthrough. The game allows you to adjust a few settings along with resolution, brightness, and you can tweak a few of the graphical settings like the depth of field effect.
Overall, I highly recommend this game, especially for the low asking price of $20. It's a lot of fun and it's rare to see a creative and innovative platformer game in the market nowadays. Be sure to check out my video for a more detailed look at the game and stay tuned to my channel for more game reviews if you're interested.

Eversion is simply a 2d platformer where you move from left to right, collect items, defeats enemies, and utilize the "eversion" mechanic to travel between different versions of levels. On the surface, this seems rather simplistic, and it is, but the eversion mechanic is surprisingly in-depth, with each object having different properties in each version of a level. These differing properties allow for a variety of intricate puzzles. The game also excels at teaching its mechanics through shear level design as opposed to a text-based tutorial, something that I'm always happy to see. Through in a great soundtrack and some - er - shocking visuals, and you've got yourself a fun little platformer that I'd definitely recommend.

Eversion plays quick and pretends to be innocuous, but don't be lulled by its innocent look: this is one mean puzzle-platformer. The game's seeming simplicity makes the mechanics by which its world works immediately apparent, but the levels become demanding faster than you'd expect. First you'll find yourself working out the logic by which many of the more out-of-reach gems can be collected, but as you gain proficiency with Eversion's particular style of platforming, you'll soon find yourself tested on your ability to execute precise leaps and on your persistence in the face of intense opposition. This game is pretty difficult to master, but play through to the end at least once and you'll see why it's one of the all-time classics.

This game was a pleasant surprise for me.  It's a short but sweet little platformer with clever puzzles, pretty neat atmosphere, and very solid controls.  I think the only real complaint I have is how there's no leeway when you're jumping up through gaps, where if even one pixel of a block is above you, it will bump you back down.  But that's a very minor gripe and I can't think of anything else negative to say.  It was a fun short romp that didn't overstay its welcome and I would jump at the chance to buy more games from the dev if they put more on Steam.

Eversion is a game best suited for diehard platformer lovers who enjoy redoing puzzle aspects over and over again or any player who can brave those aspects to enjoy the effect of the player's actions on the world.  Anyone else should probably watch someone else play this game instead.
The game does not mess around after the third level: if you can't jump at the exact height in the exact arc at the exact time the game wants you to, you're not going to be able to complete the level any time soon.  The game has a checkpoint system and an infinite amount of lives so there's no pentalty for starting over, but it takes a ton of time to memorize the level design and master the timing to pull a lot of the jumps off.  This is a great time if you love challenges and dying a ton, not great if you don't enjoy replaying the same parts of a level 30+ times over.
If you like the idea behind the game but can't spend the 3+ hours it takes to master a level's layout, buy it for your hardcore platformer friend and watch them play it for you.  It's a worthwhile game for those who like hard as balls platformers, but super hard to reccomend to anyone else.

(I know there is a big blue banner reminding my readers that this is an early access game so take what I say seriously but with the understanding that it's still a work in progress. )
Guardians of Orion provides for some FPS arcade fun while giving the player some neat abilities to work with. I especially like it's concept as you can go from a top-down view to a first person view (which I think is a great addition). Although the game can be immersive (especially with friends), it can be redundant after a bit.
The game's structure is either a survival mode or slaughter mode. In survival mode you defend your harvester. It can defend itself but will need your help in maintaining it's health. In slaughter mode, the harvester is on the move! Unlike survival, you'll have to keep moving with the machine in order to keep it alive. If the machine becomes damaged, the player may repair it with a special weapon (that is given to the player). Any player of any class may repair the machine. All classes come with one main weapon and a side arm. On top of having basic abilities including roll, teleport, and grenade, each class has their own unique ability. There are four classes available at the moment : assault, support, tech and recon.
Assault class is my favorite as they are given jet packs as their special ability and have an automatic weapon at their disposal. Support class has a shotgun instead of an automatic rifle and can deploy a healing bubble as his specialty. The tech can deploy a machine turret as their ability and the recon can turn invisible for a time being. This last class is given an EMP grenade to tackle robot type units. The grenade function isn't extremely effective at the moment and it's physics aren't exactly right. Imagine running then throwing, there isn't an extra "umph" and the trajectory feel isn't quite as right. Every class has an ability to upgrade their skill tree (this can be seen in the screenshots). Players can upgrade their melee ability or choose to be faster. There are three trees in total with usually two options to choose from. I believe adding this into the game can really make it stand out. As mentioned, the player can cycle through a top-down view or a first person view. I like to stick with a first person view when I'm engaging flying type units (to shoot in the air) but the overview helps when you're being swarmed by enemies. Small enemy dinosaurs, for example are difficult to see in first person as they can mask their movements through the grass.
The enemies themselves are pretty varied (even for early access) and some enemies will have you running for your life while you're trying to shoot at them. I really like the variety and the choice of enemies. Players are able to sprint in game while crouching is not available (I couldn't imagine what you would use it for anyway). I think they did a pretty good job allocating the controls and given the player a good feel of control over their unit.
The
are OK at the moment. Their neither extremely good, or bad, rather in between. You'll notice anything green or some rock edges not being exactly smooth (but this is okay because there is time to touch this up)! This also won't effect your game play experience.
are pretty good but I would recommend adding some sort of scream when a big enemy starts charging at you. Make the player scared and excited to play! Although sounds do not directly effect game play, they can change how the player is feeling in any moment of the game. The first Splinter Cell did it with one note being played hard on a piano, I'm sure GofO can do something similar or even better.
Overall, not a bad game. It feels like a mix between Halo, Turok and some defense FPS's out there. There is no campaign at the moment (I hope there is one) and multiplayer servers aren't exactly full. It will be tough finding a game. I would highly recommend getting this game on the premise that either you like it for what it is, or that you'll be playing it with a friend. I really hope as well they make it so you can burn the grass as you fire through it or some sort of effects along those lines. The game sort of lacks in this department regarding effects.
Early access RATING : 6.95/10

Anyone looking for a fun hoard-mode style game to play with friends, this is definitely one to consider. Don't let the "Early Access" tag inlfuence your opinion too much, however, as it is surprisingly smooth for such a game. Guardians of Orion is simple and easy to jump into, but has an endless amount of replayability. The class-based gameplay system, skill trees, and ability to swap between a top-down or third person perspective adds a good amount of variety to the actual gameplay, and is accomomdating of personal play-style. Perhaps the driving factor of the game is that the main antagonistic forces are dinosaurs (everyone loves dinosaurs).
If there is one thing I would like to see added to the game, it would be a weapon/character customization system that allows people to slightly alter the functionality of their class. While the skill trees for each class are nice, being able to physically change weapons and armor would be only help to improve the game, in my opinion.
All things considered, it's a really enjoyable game.

Slime Rancher is a really fun game with a cute aesthetic and a lot of time and care put into its presentation. It uses polished VFX and sound to craft a playful and fun atmosphere that creates satisfying interaction with in-game elements. Everything from sucking up slimes, selling plorts (slime poop, essentially), and feeding your tiny slime flock is perfectly calibrted to feel fun, satisfying, and cute.
The physics in this game aren't always consistent, however, and sometimes collision and force glitches shoot the player up into the air, but such problems are to be expected with early access games. The major flaw of this game comes with its early access label, in fact, as most of the content can be seen, explored, and farmed within the first 5 hours of gameplay. There are plenty of planned and hinted-at additions to the game, however, so the future seems bright for your tiny slime business.
Overall, this game is a fantastic, fun experience that feels satisfying and cute through the entirity of its relatively short jaunt through slimespace.

In Wild Island Quest, you play as a boy who lives on a floating island with his friends, whom each have different skills. In the game, another island has collided with your island, and when your dog runs onto the new island, you chase after him and get lost in the jungle. Depending on the choices you make, you will get different endings.
+
- This adds some extra replayability to the game.
+
- I enjoyed the music in this game, even if there wasn't very much of it.
+
- The concept was good, though the execution was poor.
-
- It will take you a maximum of 15 minutes to beat this game for the first time. Any playthroughs afterwards will be a breeze since you'll already know the correct choices to progress.
-
- Just a glance at this game will show you that very little of the budget was spent on how the game would look. The humans are frankly terrifying and the rest is mediocre at best.
-
- Some parts of the plot seem either very forced or simply make no sense. For example, in the very beginning of the game, you see your dog in your yard, but by the time you get to the place where you will watch the island, he's somehow raced all the way over there without you noticing and randomly jumps onto Wild Island for seemingly no reason. The ening makes even less sense, but I'll let you see for yourself.
-
- Past a certain point, it becomes very repetitive trying to get all the achievements and trying out the different options. You have to click through the same dialogue over and over again just for some slight variation on what happened in your previous playthrough. Most of the time, there are a few "wrong" choices that lead to death and one "right" choice that lets you progress. Going with different friends or using different items had very little impact on the game in the long run.
If you got this game in a giveaway, then yeah, go ahead and play it. The game's short and only takes about 10 minutes to beat, and it's not
. But don't consider spending even a penny on this, it's just not worth the $2. Go buy a better game instead.

I hesitate to call Xenonauts a spiritial successor to one of the greatest games of all time - UFO: Enemy Unknown (X-COM: UFO Defense in the USA) - rather instead, it's purely a spiritual
.
The earth has come under attack from aliens, and you manage a PMC tasked with fighting them. The nations of the world fund the company, and based on how you defend each country the funding can rise or fall. This is done from a map view of the earth, showing your base, and craft as they start to appear. To begin, just a few small scout craft arrive, easily shot down. If you intercept the craft over land, sometimes it crash lands, forming a crash site you can investigate. Alternatively, the craft sometimes lands and you can send a dropship to the location. Once the dropship arrives at the site you enter an isometric view where you can move your units, and shoot at any aliens you encounter. This section is turn based, and the amount of movement you can make is determined by how many Time Units each unit has. Once you have cleared the site, you can recover alien technologies and take them back to your base to research, leading to the ability to manafacture new items. There are many other elements to both the management and tactical section of the game, which I won't spoil here.
If you're looking for a modern take or an evolution on this forumla, look instead into the excellent 2012 Fixaris reboot, XCOM: Enemy Unknown. This is a very different experience however, and I'd still throughly recommend trying the original. However Xenonauts now presents an interesting new third option. I've recommended the original to people, only to see them never really get into it thanks largely to the outdated interface. Xenonauts allows you to experiece the brilliance of the original, but tuned to remove those frustrations.
For example, one of the least enjoyable parts of the original was surely the inventory management. While I love the base management overall, manually replacing every last clip, medkit, rocket, grenade wore thin pretty quickly, especially when most of the items were cheap enough to never really be a concern. In Xenonauts, this is thankfully gone for most of the mundane consumables. Other areas which have been simplified include reloading, and using grenades. In X-COM, using a grenade was a series of actions, removing it from your belt, putting it in your hand, pulling the pin/setting the timer, throwing it. Each took a small amount of time units, and it was entirely possible to pull the pin, only to realise you didn't have enough time units left to throw it. While this did invoke exactly the feeling of panic it was no doubt supposed to, it was largely just frustrating. In Xenonauts all of this is just replaced with a single action with a single time unit cost. To my tastes, they developers have thankfully only simplified elements which probably needed it - it certainly doesn't feel dumbed down.
It might just be me, but Xenonauts does feel a little easier than UFO was. However, this really is no bad thing - UFO was punishingly difficult, and it wasn't unusual for newcomers to be in real trouble before even their first funding review. In Xenonauts, easy mode should allow new players to get a good long feel for the game before they start ramping up the difficulty.
If you loved UFO, or you enjoy classic tactical games, if you like retro graphics style, you'll most likely enjoy this greatly. It's such a closely tied remake of UFO it almost feels like I'm reviewing that, rather than Xenonauts - either way, I cannot recommend either one highly enough.

For those of you who have played L4D2, you will most likely have come across the realism mode. The difference between realism mode and the normal co-op mode in L4D2 is that in realism mode you cannot see the silhouette of your teammates, items, and you cannot come out of the closet (respawn) when you are dead. Most players take the realism mode as an additional challenge as it adds a certain amount of difficulty to the already challenging expert co-op mode. The aim of L4D2's realism mode is to make the game real so that you can have a taste of reality in L4D2. It works well, though when L4D2's realism mode is pitted against No More Room in Hell, L4D2 looses out in almost all aspects of realism.
The first thing you need to know about No More Room in Hell (NMRH from here on) is that it is a Mod for Source games (Half-Life 2, Portal 2, Counter-Strike: Source, Left 4 Dead 2 ... etc). Meaning, you will need at least one copy of such games installed before you can play it. The game (or mod) itself is free, so don't worry about that. Since NMRH is a mod, you can basically expect graphics and controls very similar to that of Half-Life 2 and other games based upon the source engine. There really isn't anything spectacular about the graphics and controls, so I'll leave it for you t decide for yourself.
After installing NMRH (and maybe a source based game if you have not already done so), you are ready for your first game. You go in, choose a server in a very Counter-Strike manner (opening a server list and clicking on a server you like, which most likely will be a server with the lowest ping and an empty slot), and you wait for your game to load. You will be curious how the game will be. Finally, after somewhat less than a minute (on my gear), the game is finally loaded and ...
... four empty walls.
Well, to be fair, there are some run down furnitures and the environment is decorated with cracks and dust, but the point is, where are the HUDs (Head-Up Display)? In a typical first-person shooter, there will be numbers representing your health and the amount of ammunition you are currently holding on to. Alright, I was not holding a gun so maybe I don't get to see any numbers representing any bullets. Fine. But what about my health? What I have found out, later on, is that there are no in-game HUDs that represents your health value. On the other hand, health is represented by the colour saturation of your in game graphics - the lower the value of your health is, the lower the colour saturation will be and your screen will look pretty much grayscale-ish before you fall on your face. Also, your screen will be highlighted red if you are injured or infected (the highlight for each condition differs from each other).
After walking around for a bit, triggering green silhouettes whenever you look at items lying around (or red when your backpack is full) and picking them up, I soon come to realize that there actually are HUDs in the game. One is your Fallout-3-like compass (remember, you don't have a map). Another is the item and ammo screen (1, 2). The third are the instructions given, which will pop out in the middle of your screen when you've triggered them. The last one is the number of ammunition you have (at least you get to see how much ammo you have left, phew!).
Speaking about guns, the game tries to make its item system as realistic as possible, just like many other aspects of the game. In order to do so, the game uses something similar to a "weight system" for its item system (something like Killing Floor, I guess). Larger, heavier and, more importantly, higher dammage items takes up more weight, while lighter, weaker and, generally speaking, more useless items take up less weight. For example, a fire axe, something that can split the skull of the zombies with one charged swing, will take up more space then a torchligh, a little black stick which you can use to shine the places on the zombies where sun don't shine or simply whack them so that they can whack you back and infect you. The same applies for large weapons, such as M4A1, which is definitely much heavier than little hammers used for nailing boards (where do the nails come from, I always wonder). Ammunitions take up space too, so becareful not to take up too many unwanted ammunition types.
What's next after picking up your utensils ... I mean, weapons? Your dinner... I mean, enemy. There are 2 distinctive types of zombies in general: slow and fast. Most of them are slow ones, so you can pretty much blow their head up with a well aimed melee strike with a fire axe or sledge hammer. Melee is always recommended, especially when you have quite a number of temmates to back you up, as ammunitions are highly scarce in game (reality, duh!). Of course, you better not get hit by your enemy. Even if you do get hit by an enemy, which will happen at least once in every game, you better not get infested, as you will definitely and inevitably die, with your corpse rising as a fast zombie, running towards your living comrades and trying to kill them. Well, its actually kind of nice watching your comrades trying to fight your zombified self. Maybe it's because you get kind of envy of them for being alive, and they can't hear you on chat once you are dead.
For the general picture, this game is bleak, barren and aims to be highly realistic. As a matter of fact, it is actually succeeding in terms of realism because when I first played it, the realism bores me to tears (I was playing alone). Whacking zombie after zombie, trying to meet the objectives which is to whack more zombies is not as entertaining as it seems, so much so that I initially have removed the game from my list (it's free anyway). But then, a Korean friend of mine started playing, so I reinstalled the game and picked it up again and, to be honest, playing NMRH with friends has a type of peculiar yet interesting taste to it. It is actually fun when you sit back, strode through the zombified garden with your friend, help each other out when in need, laugh at your peers that fell in battle, and get laughed at when your zombified peers start tearing you apart. Yeah, that is how some of my nights are spent.
NMRH is an interesting game when you play with a bunch of people. It will amaze you how barren and inconvenient reality is, and how a tiny little mistake can amplify and manifest into a giant globe of chaos. It's not a complicated game, so anyone can go in, shoot a few, get killed, and watch your zombified self run wild and get killed again. It's free anyway. Still, be warned that you should have your mobile phone or tablet or a book with you, as you might have to wait for a long long while before you can play again once you are dead. Reality, yeah?
P.S. [Easter Egg] If you ever play the map Chinatown, look out for a blue sign saying "按摩你的屁股". It literally means "massage your backside".

By now, everyone probably knows that this is a very good game. So I'm just going to state what I personally like about it over the other 3D titles and why it's a personal favorite of mine to come back to play.
- Levels that encourage exploration similar to Genesis titles, rather then linearity with getting through a level like SA2
- Every character plays differently, unlike SA2 where one playstyle played virtually the same as another
- All of the side characters have short stories with a small amount of levels, meaning that even if someone didn't like a certain playstyle, they wouldn't have to worry about playing it for very long
- Story is fairly simple
- Emerald Hunting missions are at their best here, the hints in DX allow the player to know exactly where an emerald is where as in Adventure 2 it's completely vague, this was a big problem from me with Adventure 2
- Almost every boss (with the sole exception of Chaos 4) is fun to fight against
- Missions only need to be completed three times to gain all the emblems, where as in Adventure 2 it takes five times
Honestly, this might be my favorite out of the 3D titles. Adventure 2 had a lot more polish, but DX for me is the prime example of how to make a 3D title from a gameplay perspective and overall turns out to be a better game. It's got some buggy physics and occasionally the camera will freak out, but otherwise it is a very fun, simple title that never leaves the player bored with at least 20+ hours worth of content to gain out of it. I'd definetly reccomend it with or without a sale.
