Orignally released in 1999 for the Sega Dreamcast, Sonic Adventure was Sonic's first real venture into 3D. In 2003 the game was re-released for the Nintendo Gamecube under the title "Sonic Adventure DX Director's Cut" that improved the graphics and added some new features. This version came out in 2010, part of the Sega Dreamcast collection on steam and consoles.
In Sonic Adventure, you have six characters (plus a final story) each with a unique style of play.
: Fast pased 3D Platfroming gameplay, the main attraction of the game. Sonic has the most stages and most of them are fun to play (Speed Highway, Emerald Coast to name a few).
: In the Tails stages you race Sonic or Eggman to the end of the stage, its pretty simple, and its pretty fun.
: The game kind of goes downhill from here, but its not quite there yet... Knuckles has treasure hunting stages where you find three peices of the Master Emerald, I can see why someone may not enjoy this in a Sonic game but these stages aren't that bad in my opinion. Once you figure out the locations the peices can spawn its fun seeing how quickly you can finish the stage.
: Amy has slow 3D platfroming stages. These aren't fun at all. A robot named "Zero" chases Amy through her stages and you have to work at avoiding and stunning it to progress. I thought these stages where quite annoying because that dang robot. On a good note, Amy only has three stages in her story, and getting through her doesn't take long at all.
: Oh dear, Big the Cat is kind of famous for his stages in Sonic Adventure... They are the most out of place. Big has fishing stages, the main objective is to fish for his friend "Froggy". If you enjoy games like Sega Bass Fishing (Also part of the Dreamcast Collection) you may like Big's gameplay. I personally don't hate it, even though I agree it doesn't fit well in a sonic game.
: Eggman Ex-Machina ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°). E-102 has shooting stages, the objective is to save your friends after you betray eggman. I love E-102's gameplay, its just really entertaining shooting up as much as you can.
The story is really simple. Eggman wants to distory Station Square, you gotta stop him. What more could you need in a Sonic game.
One of the best parts of this title is the "Chao Garden", where you get to raise little pets called "Chao". Playing with these adorable little creatures becomes quite addicting and give the game some replay value as you gain items to level up your Chao in the action stages.
Like most Sonic games, Adventure has a nice soundtrack, and you can access every track in the game through the sound test mode.
The game really hasn't aged well from 1999-2003, so its not exactly eye candy. The biggest issue arguably  is the pi*s poor camera, it will likely be the main cause of death in this game.
In the end, the game plays alright(when the camera doesn't scew you over)  and for the first 3D sonic game it was a pretty dang good first try.
I recommend it.

Writing this review is a bummer, because if you're reading this, there's a good chance that Eversion's secret has already been spoiled for you. It had technically been spoiled for me, too, but I only knew that the game was "different." That, despite the cutesy screenshots, there was more to it.
That's definitely true. I don't know if I'd necessarily call Eversion an outstanding game. It is very, very simple; even more simple than the games it is clearly trying to reference. But it's the hook that makes it interesting, and in spite of its simplicity, Eversion works within its mechanics extremely well. If you do end up playing this game, don't just finish it once and then move on -- for as short and as basic as it is, you really need to get a full, 100% clear to truly appreciate it.
And appreciate it I did. What Eversion lacks in complexity, fidelity, and length, it more than makes up for in everything else. It's definitely worth checking out.

I'm not sure quite how to feel about this game yet. Right now I'm neutral. Snake Pass is a brighly colored, physics based platforming collect-a-thon.  The core objective of each level is to find 3 gems to open a portal to the next level of "Haven". There is some light puzzle solving involving switches or pressure plates, etc., but the most substatial challenge seems to come from the optional collect-a-thon in each level.  Finding the 20 optional bubble crystal things (I'm just going to call them "snake charms") is fairly easy, but collecing the 5 coins can be brutal.

Your enjoyment of the game comes down to how quickly you master the controls.  Although vastly different, this game shares a similarity with Surgeon Simulator, such that most of your frustration will be due to your inability to effectively perform a task you think should be so easily performed.  So far this really only seems to be a major issue If you are trying to collect everything in a given level.
Control learning curve:
It took quite a while for me to get the hang of movement controls. This is because they are based off of the camera position and not the snakes head.  Therefore to climb corkscrew style up bamboo, you can't just hold left or right on the analog stick and slither your way up. You must instead rotate the analog stick clockwise or anti-clockwise as you ascend.  This is generally fine, but if you start to shift the camera as you move, you can quickly become unraveled.  Even after you've master those controls, you may find that Climbing upwards is fairly straight forward and sometimes suspicously easy, whereas climbing down things safely can be a huge pain.
I've died so many times trying to get the 5th coin on just the first level, I'm starting to make an  "Asp" of myself.

So, I played the original game, ORION: Prelude, and I love that game. So much so, that I've probably purchased copies of it for about 20 of my friends (although I'll admit, the $1 price tag was also a big factor in doing that) because it was so much fun. And when I heard about the planned follow up, I was expecting more of the same.
Sadly, this isn't what we have here, at least not at this point. Instead of a first person shooter, we have an isometric, top down shooter, which is not what I signed up for. Maybe it's partially my fault, but it's not easily noticed anywhere on the store page that this game is NOT a first person shooter. It's there, sure, but you have to click on the tags rather than just look at them. Maybe it's just me, but if you're gonna completely change the genre of your game, that should be something that is put front and center on the page, unless the intent is to try and trick people into spending money on the game before they realize what is going on. I don't think that's the case here, as the developers seem to genuinely care about their player base, as evidenced by the huge amount of support and work they put into Prelude, but I'm still glad Steam offers refunds now, because this isn't what I expected or wanted from this game.
All that said, I still like and will support the developers, and will be watching this game. Should it develop an option for first person, or should the mod community make one that is good, I may be back. But for now, this one isn't for me, and if you were expecting more of the same as was offered in Prelude, you won't find it here, at least not yet, so for now, stay away. If you're more open to change than I am though, feel free to check it out. What little I played of it seemed well made, but I didn't play long, as isometrics aren't my thing.
TL;DR version: Not an FPS like the game before it. If that's what you're expecting, stay away, at least for now. If you're open to isometric shooters though, check it out. Solid developers who will surprise you.

As a huge fan of X-Com/UFO: Enemy Unknown (and Terror From the Deep) I felt let down by the path of  the modern remake of "XCOM" with its smaller squad sizes, missions that took a fraction of the time, and the overall feel of its base management system.
Well what have we here? "Xenonauts"? I have NOT been disappointed. Touted as the spiritual successor to the original X-Com games and it really does live up to the hype.
PROs:
- Base management: Way more in tune with the original, building hangars, labs, living quarters, workshops.
- Research: Still figuring out the order in which I should be researching but loving it so far, trying to improve the classic stuff (weapons, armor, aircraft, etc).
- That classic feel! Guess what? Your prize Lieutenant is going to get shot by an alien in the dark, your recruits (Privates) are going to panic, and that frustration of combat missions is really recaptured. You hate it, but you LOVE it!
- Computer AI: Very very good. The aliens don't just walk around shooting you as they see you. They can be quite content to know you're outside their craft from having had their pal shot to bits, and hole up in there behind some cover... waiting for your Lieutenant to say... "open the door, Private!"
- Mod community: Not looked into it, but like a lot of titles on Steam it seems to have a community for mods, and that can only be a good thing!
- Music/Atmosphere: That sometimes menacing, sometimes spooky music from the old X-Com? It's not the same, but it has that same feeling.
CONs:
- They could do more to lessen the learning curve for new players. Things like outfitting your soldiers with grenades should be done as standard. I think I did my first 4-5 missions wondering why grenades weren't on Xenonauts because they'd be damn handy! Turns out they are, you just need to outfit your soldiers before the craft leaves the base.
- Targeting. I know this will come across as a gripe, but when you run up behind an alien within touching distance, with a shotgun, get a 95% chance to hit and MISS... well, part of the charm? Or outright unrealistic? ;)
OTHER THINGS:
- Civilians are present on some of these missions, some of them are armed (most of them panic and crouch with their hands over their heads), but the armed ones  WILL fire at the aliens!
- "Normal" difficulty. Damn hard! As it was in the original, and I'd recommend jumping in at this level for nostalgia's sake ;)
Overall then... if you're looking to play an updated version of the old 90s X-Coms then I would HIGHLY recommend this. As always, check out some YouTube footage before purchasing, but I'm having a blast! Sadly, so are the aliens!

I did not play the old X-com games, but I did play the new one, so that will be my frame of reference in this.
To me, this game feels like XCOM:EU bashed together artfully with Jagged Alliance 2 - it's got the depth, graphic style, and sometimes gameplay of JA, with the basic concepts and more modern feel of XCOM. The UI is also somewhat JA style, but has been streamlined enough that it reminds me more of Fallout 2's UI. Like XCOM, it has managed to do away with the tedious, forced micromanagement of JA and other games of that period, but does also seem to reward it a bit if you want to take the time to mess with the details, and has made doing so much easier than games from the period this one is trying to emulate.
Yeah, reading that sure makes this game sound derivative, doesn't it?
That's because it is, and proudly so. And what's wrong with that? Why wouldn't I want a game that looks good enough. lets me tweak things as much or as little as I want, and plays and feels like some of the best games ever?
If you are into shiney graphics and found hard difficulty XCOM:EU to be fun and challenging enough, then don't bother with this - the normal difficulty is generally a little more difficult than hard EU.  If you thought it was a great game, but just lacking something to make it a real 700 hour monster time eater, then you should really check this out. If you liked Jagged Alliance or it's modern clone, then you'll love this - it plays very similarly, and the RNG, LOS, and other mechanics are less broken. If liked the quirky gameplay of Fallout 1 and 2 and the darkly comical world, then you'll probably like this, but if you found the combat there overwhelmingly hard, then you might not.
One more quick little note: If you haven't played any of the above, but want to get into this sort of games, this is a good place to start. Unlike most of them, the easy mode is actually easy enough fora brand new player to get the swing of things, but becomes challenging enough to be worth playing through to the late game.

Game requires some 60 hours to finish, depending on play style/difficulty. XCOM:EU and Xenonauts are both very good games but from different reasons. XCOM:EU has graphics and Xenonauts has sandbox and somewhat larger scale.
Positives and negatives:
+ Tactical battles. No spawnpoints, larger number  of troops, every alien type requires different tactics by you.
+ Tactical battle AI. There seems to be random element and thus AI reactions are hard to predict, I saw no stupid behaviour during 60 hour gameplay. Do not think you are safe behind closed doors!
+ Normal difficulty level is hard already (I savescummed the hell out of this)
+ Balance!! Game is and feels absolutely and fantastically balanced. Every weapon has it's purpose, credits are hard to come by but not too hard, items get obsolete very slowly etc etc.
+ Almost buggyless. Only one minor bug encountered during 60 hours (One soldier got stuck to wall)
+ Immersion.
- Lesser graphics (especially 2D images, like the generals around the table)
- Area effect weapons in tactical battles. Be prepared to blow yourself up. It is way too likely to hit the table in front of you with a rocket.
I know that after Xenonauts there is no longer need for me to play the original XCOM. That is the best indicator of excellence this game could have.

APB has a lot of really good ideas. Like, really damn good. Don't let the MMO dressing fool you, APB is 100% a competitive team-based shooter, but the genius of it is that the matches take place in a non-instanced overworld; with players being assigned to teams by skill. This game would have been absolutely revolutionary if it were any good at all.
The game is simply not a fun shooter, and a lot of this has to do with the MMO central server based network design. Lag is unavoidable, and car driving is a nightmare, thanks to a completely inescapable one-second input lag due to the driving being server-side. And even when the lag isn't an issue, the weapon design got screwed hard by the pay-to-win overhaul of the game. Yes, this game is very much pay-to-win.
On a fundamental level, though, the gameplay just isn't satisfying even when it works and the teams are balanced. Characters are floaty and odd to control, and the guns have very little weight or impact. Imagine Loadout but without the custom guns, and you'll get why combat in APB is not very fun.
Also, the neat ideas I mentioned? Not very well implemented. The team selection algorithm isn't very good, so teams are almost always imbalanced. And not many places in the overworld were designed for interesting firefights, making nearly every mission generic and confusing.
And finally, for the record, this is not in any meaningful way an MMO. There is no PvE, none whatsoever. There's an auction house, but TF2 has that too. There's clans, but those are pretty standard in any modern shooter. APB is not an MMO.
In conclusion, the only reason to be at all interested in APB is that 1) it's free to try anyway, and 2) to see the interesting ideas it tries out, to see a failed revolution in shooter design. Actually trying to approach it as a game will only end in misery.

When this game came out, 2 things happened. Sonic's fanbase got turned into a warzone, and Sonic made his true jump to 3D. Yes, I know about Sonic 3D Blast and Sonic Jam, but Jam was a compilation with a 3D mode and 3D Blast was isometric. Anyway, this game proves that games can still work well in 3D.
Story: Chaos has arrived! Literally! A new entity named Chaos comes and causes mayhem, but thankfully, our heroes go and try to stop him. Chaos gets more power by the Chaos Emeralds, which Eggman is trying to do so he can take over the world. It's up to Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy, E-102 Gamma, and Big the Cat to stop Eggman and Chaos before it's too late.
Gameplay: as the most important part of any game, the gameplay feels solid. Every character plays in their own way. Sonic has the speed and spindash, Tails can fly, Knuckles can glide and climb walls, Amy is slower, but can use a hammer, Gamma is basically the mechs from SA2, and Big is just Big (who is voiced by the guy who voiced Duke Nukem). It all works too with solid level design and you won't want to stop unless the awful camera gets you mad.
Music: Crush 40 started doing Sonic songs with this game and it shows. Their first game OST to my knowledge was of all things, a NASCAR arcade game that SEGA developed in 2000. I know, strange, but this OST is amazing. When Crush 40 sends their lyrics, you are in music heaven. Even the non-Crush 40 sings are pretty neat, including a remix of Green Grove Act 1 from Sonic 3D Blast Genesis! Now that's quality.
Graphics: Sonic Adventure DX was also on Gamecube, this is just a port of that, just without the Game Gear games for some reason. Anyway, the graphics are.... subpar. They just scream of old 3D platformer, but they have some charm in them, and hey, it looks fine too with some references including a NiGHTS section in a pinball area, and sometimes Cream can be found just flying around after you beat a stage. I approve of that one because Cream is my favorite Sonic character (just look at my avatar).
Chao Garden: I haven't played it yet, but the Chao Garden feels like it's own game with mingames, different uses, and much more that I can't explain well. In the Gamecube version, you could even connect to the Advance games to transfer Chao. That is cool!
Conclusion: despite what I said, this game is said to not have aged well. It's an old game, it came out first in 1998 and the remake came out in 2001. That being said, I still recommend this to any Sonic or 3D platformer fan as it has enough content to keep you interested. EVERSION REVIEW
Type of game: Platformer with light puzzle elements
Controls: Supports keyboard and 360 controller. Other controllers I tried required something like XPadder.
Gameplay: The gimmick behind this game is that your character has to switch between dimensions at "Evert" point in order to complete levels. There are a certain number of collectable gems in each level. All of them must be collected in order to get what appears to be the game's true ending.
Visuals: Very basic visual design, although not to the point of coming off as amateurish.
Sound: Certain dimensions have pleasantly distorted remixes of tracks from earlier dimensions, but overall the music and sound design are also very basic.
Amount of content: Frankly, this game is over in the blink of an eye. I spent a little over 2.5 hours with it, but that was getting 100% and cleaning up the achievements. If one is concerned about simply beating the game, I'm unsure if it would even take an hour.
Final impression: It's not worth the $5 price it normally goes at, but if it goes below $2, it might be worth picking up just to waste a bit of time.

Eversion HD is an updated re-release of Eversion. It's important to note some things before coming in. First of all, this version of Eversion is 16 bit, unlike the original 8 bit version you can download for free on the internet. This version also has some bonus content, and extra unlockables, but; I'll cover them as we go.
Eversion for what it is, is a very short game; it's got 7 stages, and a secret unlockable 8th stage. In order to unlock the 8th stage, you have to collect 240 jewels scattered among the stages. Why are you doing this? Because the main character needs to rescue a princess. Yeah, Eversion's not one for story; and it doesn't need it at all. But it is interesting to note; that Eversion is based off the writings of H.P. Lovecraft.
That of course means, that the game is scary.. But not "Jumpscare in your face" scary like so many games attempt. Eversion is scary because the entire tone of the game is dictated by the signature ability; Eversion. When you use it, the world around you changes; and that's the key gameplay element. There are 8 layers of Eversion that you cycle through as the game progresses, and each layer has it's own rules; so the majority of the game is learning how each layer affects your platforming. Aside from this feature; the game plays as a Mario style collectathon with you gathering 240 jewels.
There are 3 Unlockable endings, and after unlocking the "True" ending, you unlock Time Attack which allows you to race the scoreboard to see who can beat the game the fastest. The Time Attack mode also includes the original Stages 4 and 8, as the HD remake made new versions of those stages to replace the old ones. There's also hidden letters that spell out "EVERSION" for a hidden Achievement for those who like to 100% games.
However, one thing I will warn players of, is Eversion gets hard later on. Now, difficulty in games is a good thing, and a game should gradually get harder; but the issue is, Eversion starts off too easy. The first 3 stages are pushovers, with the only challenging part being figuring out how to collect the jewels in them. Once you hit stage 4 however; the game pulls no punchs from here onward. The rest of the game can be a spiraling rage cycle of pure frustration.
-- The Good --
+ Eversion is a unique gameplay mechanic.
+ The music and atmosphere are terrific.
+ The graphics range from bright and colorful, to grim and terrifying.
+ Based on H.P. Lovecraft
+ Easy to 100%.
-- The Bad --
- Huge Difficulty spike midway through the game.
- Little to no replay value once finished.
- Extremely short. (I got 100% in 2 hours).

This is an odd one for me. Nothing about the screenshots or trailers for Boxlife interested me, but the description: “Gain abilities, find secrets and escape from the box.” peaked my interest.
I’m going to be blunt; I don’t think this is a good game. I don’t take pleasure in giving negative reviews, and I even asked my followers on Twitter if it would be worth posting an almost entirely negative review. The conclusion I came to is that it would, because it’s my responsibility as a reviewer to lay the truth bare regardless of how I think I’m going to make the developer feel if they see it.So, here’s the truth laid bare.
Boxlife is not a pretty game, especially since I’ve seen some really awesome stuff come from the Unity engine, that this game was made in. The colours don’t go well together, and there really isn’t any art. It’s all made up of shapes, and rectangles which there is nothing inherently wrong with, but it doesn’t really feel self-aware. I don’t get the impression that this was the planned look for the game, or that any real thought was put into the design. And the cheap atmosphere is made worse by the really awful sound effects in which you can hear the background noise for -- since there’s no music in the game to mask it.
The idea behind the mechanics is an old one, but not necessarily bad. You’re basically given free reign to explore wherever you want, and you're given no instructions other than the controls. What you find is that your character keeps finding new abilities that allow him/her to explore more and, in turn, acquire even more abilities. These range from jumping, to double jumping, to… being able to walk through certain blocks.. It’s not anything special, but I felt a twinge of satisfaction when I found a new ability that allowed me to progress further, but that’s no different to, say, any Zelda game.
The real deal breaker here is that the game is only 15 minutes long. Or, at least, that’s how long it took me to complete it. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with that, because a 15 minute story, if told well, can be extremely compelling. For $3, a really good 15 minutes of story would totally be worth it my opinion. But you might have noticed that I didn’t include a story section in this review like I normally do. There is no story and, because of that, I think this game is nothing short of a rip off. There’s no one I could recommend this game to, unfortunately.

Snake Pass is a well-polished platforming adventure with unique character functionality. You play as a snake named Noodle. You slither around with the aid of your bird pal trying to repair the destruction to your homeland by fixing all of the gateways. The story is told through text, and there isn’t much else to say about it.
Snake Pass features character control and movement, that looks and feels as if it’s actually simulating a snake. The way you slither by moving side to side along the ground, or how you can coil your entire body around just about everything in the environment is a really great. It’s pretty awesome to have so much interaction within the environment as you scale up and around bamboo poles and other terrain to make your way through the levels. You also have a bird companion to help guide you, and he can also help you out buy lifting up your tail.
Aside from the snake simulation, the game has a large focus on exploration and collecting. There are only 3 main items that you have to collect to finish the chapter, but each level is chock-full of items to find. These collectibles are not mandatory, but trying to find and get all of them is meant to be a large portion of the game. Some will be easy to get, while others will likely have you dying several times before you succeed.
Dying causes you to lose any progress since the last checkpoint. These checkpoints can be activated as many times as you’d like, but there are times where you’ll probably wish there were a few more checkpoints available.
It took me over 8 hours to complete the game while gathering 87% of all the collectibles. The last few levels kicked my butt so hard, and I died so, so much there. After finishing the campaign, you unlock snake vision, and can go back and find any collectibles you missed earlier, or even test out your slithering skills on the timed runs.
Snake Pass is an endearing platformer with a unique game design that is executed well. Don’t be fooled by the overwhelming cuteness though, because behind the relaxed demeanor, some parts are sure to challenge you. If you’re looking for something with fresh mechanics to try, and enjoy exploring and collecting, you might want to check out Snake Pass.

This game is amazing.  It's a tight package that has completely unique controls; cheerful art and environments; beautiful music; and cute characters.  This game feels very new, both in terms of graphical fidelity, where it really makes Unreal 4 shine, as well as gameplay, where the complicated movements of a snake are reduced to simple controls that are easy to learn, but hard to master.  This really stands out in an environment of entrenched genres and safe bets.
It seems like something that would have come out on the dreamcast or gamecube as a launch title, during a more exploratory era.  With aesthetics that fall somewhere between Crash Bandicoot, Super Monkey Ball, and Banjo Kazooie, it's unmistakably a game for the sake of fun, and despite reminding me of those older classics, it has its own strong identity.  A skeleton of a story takes a back seat to a lush and inviting world filled with detail that compels you to explore it, making sure the focus is on play.
I recommend this, not just as a great game, but as a reminder that games can exist for their own sake without having to immerse us, and without having to weave a cinematic narrative.

Very very basic tips:
1) Initial party composition should have:
a) 2-3 melee fighter types (Fighter, Valkyrie, Lord, Samurai, Monk, Ninja).  I always recommend Valkyries over Lords as they are functionally the same class, but Valkyries gain levels faster.
b) a defensive caster/healer (Priest or Alchemist)
c) a thief-type (Thief, Bard, or Ranger).  I highly recommend a Bard.
d) an offensive caster (Mage, Psionic, or Alchemist)
2) Save often, and make backups of your saves.  It's easy to irreparably ♥♥♥♥ something up in a wway that will make you glad you had a save from 45 minutes prior.  Also, QUIT-NOSAVE if your friend.
3) Many skills gain points on successful use.  Important ones include Skullduggery (gain a point when you successfully pick a lock or disarm a trap) and Ninjitsu (gain a point with every X number of succesful Hide attempts).  Ninjitsu affects your Monk/Ninja's intrinsic defensive ability.
4) Crucial spells to gain access to: Heal Wounds, Cure Lesser Condition, Cure Poison, Identify.  Identify items before equipping/using them whenever possible.
5) Quest items cannot be sold, but they can be dropped.  Do not drop anything unless you're pretty sure you don't need it anymore, and drop used quest items in a safe and easy-to-remember location in case you're wrong.
6) There's a Journey Map Kit in the forest behind your initial spawn location.
7) Explore and enjoy!  The game world is huge and immersive, and the humor is perfectly tongue-in-cheek.

I bought this game on sale and then never touched it, returning to the older XCOMs even the new XCOM.
Then just after Christmas 2014, I decided to give it a try.

Awesome :-)

The best modern remake of X-com: UFO Defense and Terror From The Deep. It's the one most faithful to the old games.
+ Improved interface/GUI, e.g. aiming interface is more like Jagged Alliance: right-click to improve accuracy.
+ New air combat system that's much more fun.
+ Eerie/Horror soundtrack similar to original games.
+ Ground combat requires new tactics, e.g. grenades were nerfed, there is a suppression system.
+ As in X-Com Apocalypse, you need to require live aliens and explosives destroy aliens bodies and equipment. So, it's more challenging to get live aliens.
+ Improved graphics. Xenonauts and aliens animations are really fluid.
+ So far (3rd month in the game), you can't seem to make money by creating items like in the old games. Your main source of income are the funding from the nations. Might be a minus for you.
+ Quickstart guide and in-game tooltips lets you get started playing in no time.
+ Geoscape now shows UFO events throughout the world, so you don't need to mess around with the cumbersome UFO Activity Graph like in the older games.
+ Devs are still updating the game.
+ The story and xenopedia entries are very well written.
+ You can now air strike a UFO crash site for money, if you don't want/can't do the mission at the moment.
+ Soundtrack and other goodies are included in the extras folder.
+ Game is easily moddable.
+/- Some parts of the game were simplified, but overall it still retains the essence of the original X-Com games. Some of those simplifications were: unlimited *basic* ammo/weapons, a single warehouse holds unlimited items, unlimited flares for night missions, buildings like missile defenses and some items like medkits are auto upgraded after research is done, alien items are sold/destroyed/stored automatically after a ground mission, soldiers don't have an energy meter.
- Can't throw equipment to teammates. Have to drop it on the ground and have the other one pick it up.
- I found the machinegun to be really useless.
- Downed UFOs can only be entered through main door. You can't blow up any part of the hull, however you can still blow up the door.
- Apparently, there is no incendiary ammo, particle disturbance grenade and particle sensor.
Overall, the game is great! A must buy for X-Com fans.

Certainly an interesting experience, and certainly not the worst in terms of value-for-money, but unless you are interested in the old XCOM I found that the mechanics can get quite grating towards the end of my playthrough:
There is a lot of UFOs, and thus crashsites to clear, and this doesn't exectly hide the fact that there is a VERY limited number of maps - about 8, so you can expect to have to clear EACH map about 30 times if you were to manually do every mission.
A related issue is that the game doesn't handle multiple levels very well - e.g. so move a soldier from the first floor to the ground floor you need to press tab once, select the soldier, then press tab about four times to cycle back to the ground floor before issuing a move order. Enemies on higher elevation can hide in spots not visible from the ground, occasionally annoyingly prolonging combat.
And sadly, there is not a huge amount of gear to choose from - e.g. you end up with two choices for armour (heavy armour limiting the user to machine guns, and light armour with a jetpack that makes the character FLY nearly every time you give him a move order and also makes checking corners redundant due to 360 degree vision), which ultimately contributed to me rushing towards the end; having everyone in the annoying jetpack armour was just too damn annoying.
If this review had been for the first half of the game I'd have recommended it, but with the 2nd half I don't think I can recommend the game overall UNLESS you are already into what I assume old school XCOM was like; I, at least, won't be playing it without looking very hard at mods to fix the above.

I've had huge fun testing this game, and later playing the current early release (1.0.1)
This is a birds eye view perspective twin stick shooter, where both mouse/keyboard and controller work very well.
You will have a blast learning to use the varied arsenal of each class and learning how to effectively take down every dinosaur and machine that crosses your path.  The main online mode challenges you to survive ten increasingly difficult waves while you protect and repair the harvester.  You will shoot, stab, throw grenades, jetpack, cloak, mini teleport and regen your way to victory.
The current waves are quicker to blast through than what you remember from Orion Prelude and the action is more constant on these smaller maps.  It took me two or three rounds to get used to the game enough to master normal mode, but I had fun doing it, and eventually challenging hard, and even ridikulous modes with friends (spoiler: you won't survive round 1 of redik with a 4-person team.
After you have played a few matches online you'll have built up a few points to spend on customising each of the three classes to your personal play-style.  This starts with simple options like do you want to move faster, while sprinting or aiming?  Or even faster recharging grenades?
Later you will get more class specific perks, but these are likely to change.  A fully levelled up recon class could share cloaking with friends, but I believe now that they just suffer less damage if hit while cloaked.
There is fun to be had playing by yourself, working your way up the ranks to beating hard mode by yourself for the first time.  However the best of the game is having fun against increasing numbers of dinos in a larger team online.
All fighting for survival and trying to keep the squad and harvester alive.
Numbers of dinos increase depending on how many players are on the server.  Best example of this was a friend bragging the he and a mate beat the game on highest redik difficulty in 2-player mode.  Then he attempted it in four-player with some n00bs (me!) and... it did not go well haha.
I highly recommend this game.  The enemies are great to fight, and you will have a blast online no matter who you are playing with.  Definitely jump on board the GoO band wagon!

I'd like to do a Completionist-style review for this game. Because his reviews are awesome.
Foreword, Eversion is a quick Mario-style platformer and also a Lovecraftian game meaning the game starts out cute and bright, but as you progress through, it gets darker and darker. It also has achievements and trading card content to go with it! Eversion started out as a free online game, then implemented to Steam with HD graphics and new updated features.
THE STORY
Zee Tee, the cute protagonist of the game, looking like an orange star-shaped creature with legs, has to go out in the land and save the princess Nehema. Zee Tee is able to "Everse" to different layers of the world. Which get darker and scarier as he gets lower and lower in the layers. The other entities get dangerous and horrid as he gets lower. The game has three different endings based on what you do in the last few levels.
THE PRESENTATION
The game begins in the top layer, where everything is bright, colorful, and cute, just like the first few levels of a Mario game! There are flowers and blue skies. Once you cross to the first eversion layer, which is right below the top one (Not the one you started at), the first layer shows a lower saturation of visuals, and you can see several things have slowly deteriorated. In fact, if you get down into lower eversion layers, they deteriorate even more and the other creatures get more monstrous. Also blood. It's a rather disturbing game. That's why you should acknowledge the fine print at the start of the game: "not intended for children or those of a nervous disposition".
THE GAMEPLAY
The game has seven levels before the main ending. Each level is short and quick. Use the arrow keys to control your character, and press the Space bar to locate Eversion portals and flip through layers when at one. However in deeper layers, you won't be able to locate them, but you'll know when you're at them when the background partially changes. There are also gems in each level to collect and they are required for a secret eighth level and secret ending for 100%. The best part about the gems is they are ALL persistant meaning they remain collected when you die or quit the level. No need having to collect them again! Of course flipping through eversion layers is crucial for going through most levels and collecting gems. There is also a Time Attack mode after the secret ending and you can run through any level in the shortest about of time. It has worldwide leaderboards. I'm working on some good times now. I'm top 40 in the first level, but that's only the first level. Finally, the game has controller support, so grab your Xbox 360 controller if you have one!
THE FINAL LEVEL (SPOILERS!)
I'll actually talk about not only the seventh level but the secret eighth level also. The seventh level is one of the few that goes through ALL the layers. You start at a deep layer where the background is red with demonic hands in the background, and no music. Collecting all the gems is tricky work as you have to go back and fourth through the level to find the eversion portals. You don't need to shift to any layer to beat the level, but when you do. You see the ending with the princess becoming a MONSTER. Game over, then the game crashes. So if you want a better ending, you must beat the secret level. At the start of the seventh level, there is a gem count. If you get ALL the gems in the game, you're able to shift to the FINAL layer where it's the DARKEST ever, with enemies regenerating over time. Beating the level with the final layer takes you to the eighth, which is the same deal, except you need to solve puzzles, locate portals, and get to the end to get the good ending. It's similar to the endless castles in SMB. You start at the lowest layer, and work your way up to the top layer to the end of the level. Then the secret ending, it was much more screwed up, as not only has the princess became a monster again, but ZEE TEE as well. WHAT A TWIST.
So that was Eversion. It's a quick game that turns cute to HORRIFYING quick. It can really unsettle you if you're not prepared. Yesterday I started playing this game, beaten the game, got all gems, got the secret ending, and got ALL achievements. It's THAT quick. However it's $5 for a game you could play for free, but you have extra features. I suggest buying it when it's on sale. Like I did! To conclude, Eversion is a fun game with a really interesting gameplay mechanic. I find it have a nice replay value with the graphics and everything. If you're not like me, it's a game to mess around with for a short time until you go tired of it, or a game you can play to waste time on. I recommend this game. Awesome concept.

I don't recommend supporting Sega. Buying any of their games only supports their current practices.
Of their console-centric IPs, Sonic is particularly likely to be affected by Sega's worst policies for DLC and DRM. This particular release doesn't have any 3rd party DRM but if it were released more recently then there's a good chance it would.
This is a bad port whose sole saving grace is fan modding which fixes a number of issues that have existed since the Dreamcast original or were even introduced by each new revision.
The texture and audio quality is a significant step down from the 2004 PC port which was a step down from the 2003 Gamecube port which in turn was a step down from the 1998 Dreamcast original although the original had a somewhat different style.
It’s best to replace as much of the core content as possible with assets taken from either the Dreamcast or Gamecube versions, depending on preference.
There are also severe glitches exclusive to this port's audio meaning some sound effects play throughout an entire stage rather than as-intended in one small area of it & others play even if you set the game’s volume sliders to zero.
Though it fixes Lost World's "darkness" effect which seemingly not even fan mods have restored to the 2004 PC port; every single other aspect of this port is a downgrade from the fan-patched version.
None of the Dreamcast version's DLC is accessible though, via fan modding, at least some of the extra Twinkle Circuit tracks are playable.
The admittedly poor Game Gear emulation is gone unless you use a fan mod.
Sega were also too lazy to enable any trading of Chao between this port and Sonic Adventure 2, as was possible on Dreamcast and Gamecube alike. Likewise any content which required Tiny Chao is completely inaccessible without hacking.
Sega, surprisingly, patched the PC version a few years back to add native resolution switching. The port was locked at native 480P & merely upscaled previously. Great, huh? Except that Sky Chase's AI and collision detection is completely broken at higher resolutions & Sega didn’t bother fixing that.
They didn’t bother adding widescreen support either. Fans had to do that.
Unused folders added by the patch, including ones for Linux, suggest Sega were considering further patches or maybe even ports but gave up. That's our Sega!
I see no reason that a game this old couldn't have been sold on a DRM-free storefront such as GoG. Other than all the issues with the port. Considering that pirates have had access to the much better 2004 port for years they're merely turning down willing customers.
Perhaps they could have even brought in certain members of the fan community to help produce an improved port for all current platforms. Who knows.
Anything would probably be better than the port as it is now. This port & its PS3 & 360 counterparts has demonstrably caused damage to the reputation of this dated but still somewhat decent early attempt at a 3D Sonic.
I will give the port one last compliment: it's somehow more stable on my laptop than the 2004 PC port, fan patched or not. My assumption is that it somehow takes advantage of my laptop's hardware acceleration or shader support in ways the old port doesn't since the 2004 port runs far smoother than the Steam one on a friend's much older but otherwise far more powerful laptop.
If you’re in the tiny niche of having modern but extremely weak (near Chromebook level) hardware then go ahead & consider a purchase. You might be able to run the port at 30fps just like on Dreamcast.

A lovely little morsel of a roguelike. You pick one character from a selection of 3  - warrior, thief, or wizard, each with a single unique gameplay mechanic - and traverse a maze in search of a key to take you to the next level. Along the way you encounter treasure and single-use items that enhance gameplay, beacons to light up the world, traps, and enemies. There is an xp collection mechanic. Levelling up increases your hitpoints by 1. For every hit you land on an enemy, they land a hit as well, so to beat them in an encounter requires you to have more hitpoints. If a beacon is activated, the surrounding zone of the maze is lit up; traps are made visible, certain types of item-giving blocks are activated, and enemies are turned into a cute collectible. Activating beacons however become a very strategic action later on when you encounter an enemy that is actually woken up rather than eliminated by light. Most levels seem to have two exits, so it adds a meta-game exploration aspect to the game (from my experience, there is no way to go back to previous levels).
The graphics are very simple; all movement happens in a normal 2d maze - seen in a top down view - where everything is represented by blocks; you, the enemies, collectibles, items of interest,  and traps. There is a simple 8/16bit pixel-art projection/representation of your character's journey beneath the actual maze you navigate, but this projection is only 1 dimensional, so in the projection your character only seems to move left and right along a very long corridor. This I found a bit disorienting at first, but you get used to it.

As is I couldn't say this is worth $20 unless you're really enthusiastic about it, but still I recommend this game hesitantly because it's somewhat promising. It's still quite new in early access, so at the time of this review the game still feels very bare-bones and hopefully that will be fixed with future additions.
The core gameplay idea is interesting. Slimes can absorb the "plorts" other slimes make after they eat and become a larger hybrid slime of the two types. You can also collect and sell these for upgrades to both yourself and your slime corrals (and you can also build a few different buildings). Also, there's a "stock market" with different prices each day on different types of slime plorts, which forces you to diversify, since they are unique to each type of slime, and it also encourages you to make lucrative slime hybrids of two high-value types since hybrid slimes give plorts of both their constituent types.
In my opinion it could either become a really great game if they keep adding interesting things to it or a really bad game if they just take their money and run. I feel like the game could stand to use a lot more land for slimes and exploration as it is now, but being early access it could either happen or not happen at this stage.

Alright Wizardry 7. I hope you have played Wizardry 6 before thinking playing this Game. ;-)
This may have the better graphics and the sound is pretty amazing here, but rust me, play Wizardry 6 before or don't play this series at all.
You ask why?
Well it's pretty simple while Wizardry 6 is hard as hell, I feel it's still waaaaay easier than this one. Additionally if you finish Wizardry 6 you can import your Party winto W7 and continue in this adventure.
Generally the Wizardry Series tend to be much harder than other dungeon crawler games, even the older ones, so if you're new to the genre, I really suggest you try Lands of Lore 1 and then Eye of the Beholder first.
Alright, let's talk about W7.
The game is highly complex with a ton of spells, most of them useful in at least some scenarios. There are plenty of riddles in this game, a lot of them also requires to carefully read and note basically everything. A lot of information may just appear dead, but at some point, you need it.
The battles are sometimes tough and sometimes really easy. You can adjust the difficulty in some kind, that if the game gets too difficult you can change the classes of your party, which makes a lot of encounters trivial. But it may require some grinding at some point, altough I think you can make it through without senseless grinding. There are plenty of random encounters anyway.
The much harder thing in this game are the riddles and "quests". Did I mention that you don't have a quest book? Well you don't have one. The good thing is: You have a minimap. Well kind of. You have to raise the card drawing skill first and even then, it's not a full minimap.
The riddles and dungeon mechanics are so hard that I think if you play this game the first time without consultating a walkthrough you probably end up with 750 - 1000h of gameplay.
The game content is about 3 times as big as in Wizardry 6 and the map is huge. Additionally there are plenty of dungeons and they have some of the most annoying mechanics I've ever seen, which requires some map drawings even if you have the minimap.
I really suggest this game to anyone who likes dungeon crawling games and is looking for a real challenge. This is as hard as it can get.

Let's compare this to X-COM: Enemy unknown:
Enemy Unknown is for people who like their life to be more spontaneous, graphic, even if somewhat unrealistic (the traits tree).
Xenonauts is for the people who would say "That's not realistic". Fine then, this game really does a better job of you taking control of everything, even if it's far less fun. War isn't fun, and your 8-person squad being killed in the space of 3 turns isn't either

Summary: High-quality clone of the original X-Com: Enemy Unknown (1994).
Positive: Its X-Com with modern features draped in a nice Cold War setting. The geoscape and battlescape are here with almost nothing left out (see below).
The writing is actually a standout, reading the research reports was a small joy. Everything is presented in a way that is plausible in a late '70s timeline. The conclusions the science teams come away with are believable works of good fiction. I would love to provide an excerpt for your enjoyment here, but its too good to potentially spoil anything. There is also a bit of humor with a minor rivalry between the science and engineering departments.
Speaking of research, as the game progresses and the Xenonaut program continues it's scientific advance, the graphics of your base screens update with the newfound technology; its a nice touch. Non-Xenonaut friendly forces also gain some of the technology you discover over time; neat!
The game is also moddable.
Negative: A few bugs: nothing too major, but there was one glitch that locked the game. This error only happend once over a 50+ hour campaign. There are some graphical errors when minimizing the game. Further visual glitches when aliens throw grenades; sometimes doubling in size until the animation completes, or appearing to throw twice in succession.
There is a type of combat that doesn't involve traditional weaponry that is notablely missing from the game. The aliens still have it, but unlike every other X-Com clone the human forces simply cannot gain it... ever. Personally, I would have preferred for this type of combat to be rebalanced rather than removed from the game. There are only two ways to fight back against this "weapon" and neither one is reliable.
There are very few maps in the battlescape. You'll end up on the same slightly-altered variations endlessly. There is a popular mod that fixes this.
The infamous "95%-chance-to-hit-but-still-somehow-misses" RNG is still alive and well here. The aliens also get to throw grenades in some situations in which you cannot ("100% block").
Smoke Grenages are heavily nerfed, almost to the point of being useless. They were too powerful in the original for sure, but here they only last three turns (at best) and only work against a few types of aliens.
The geoscape UFO activity happens all at once instead of being spaced out. Basically, the aliens coordinate one big "assault-of-the-week" every few days without variation. It would have been better to keep the old style of individual missions rather than this approach; it feels too synthetic.
Overall: 8/10, I can't remember the last time a game has kept me playing in one sitting as long as this one. I felt like a kid again playing this wonderful game. Great job developers! With mods this is a nine out of ten game.

Knuckles, he also is great, not my favourite gameplay style, but it's good, i can play this gamemode without problem.

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
It is a Platform mini-puzzle game!
There is no audio volume or toggle available. You have to go to your speaker settings to reduce the volume of the game.
You can play this in fullscreen or window mode, It's either super small window or super zoomed view.
You can play this game with a xbox controller. No Rumble effect.
The game is based for kids, however the game contains alot of flashing. (Switching the layer screen will cause the flash.) Layer screen is changing the gameplay, Sometimes this is required to complete the level or for obtaining gems. You play as some sort of a Flower. Let me guess you have to rescue the flower princess or a Florist?  The difficulty is based on the "layer screen", some of these layers makes it very easy to move on and others makes it difficult. (Some of the background is able to hurt you while others will let you to pass through them). You will launch higher on an enemy if you time your jump.
The music changes on the current "Layer screen".
It has Retro music, (music could give you a headache after awhile).
It has Retro graphics.
The game is short but has different endings.
Hidden checkpoints.
Has Level selection with a gem counter. There are 240 gems.
You have unlimited Lives and there is no timer.
Gems will be saved no matter what. So even if you quit/die/restart the gems will not be lost.
Gems are not required to finish the game but they will reveal a secret level for an atlernative ending.
The game reminds me a little bit too much from Mario, The "Goomba" thingy and layout in the first level. It has a Mario Finish flag, Goomba looking enemies. and in ending aswell.. Even some achievements...
The Game Closes itself in the end After you have completed it.  TWICE (like a Crash).
Sometimes it is better to kill yourself after you have obtained some Gems which was required to switch some Layer Screens. Just to save your self some "travel" time (This is mainly useful for the gems that you had to obtain in the beginning of the level and was forced to switch layers"

OK where to start?
The idea of the game is simple, make it from one randomly generated dungeon to the next, collecting loot and many useful items along the way, but there are differences from this game and other similar titles which I would like to explain.

Firstly; you will notice that the screen is cut into two sections, this reminds me of old style DS games, which; I may add, this would have felt right at home on.
The bottom section of the screen displays the player at their current location within the dungeon, the items that they find and any encounters and fights that they may have,
While the top half of the screen shows the local map area, with darkness covering the unexplored sections and colored squares to represent the player, the enemies, the loot and the items.
You will likely find yourself looking mostly at the top section; as the directions on this map directly relate to the up, down, left, right keys that you will need to press as you explore the Mad King's dungeon.
The items that you find play a crucial role in being successful in your quest, you cannot simply run in and bash the enemies willy nilly, you will need to think a little about what to use and when to use it.
An example of this would be the use of teleport orbs, these are used to move from one part of the dungeon to another and in early levels this would seem to be just a formality, but on later stages it is important that they are used wisely; in order to avoid contact with the nastier denizens that lurk within the dark, dank, stench filled halls (Especially the ones that stand still and hit hard!)
In my opinion it's that the fact that this game is just as much a puzzle/brain teaser as it is a roguelike sets it apart from other games in the genre and make it a very refreshing challenge.
So to sum up:
I'll be honest with you; when I first saw this game I was unsure what to expect, there are so many games available on STEAM nowadays and I find that many of them seem to range from mediocre to terrible if I'm being truthful, so it can be a bit of a lottery as you never quite know what you are going to get, but for free I felt it would be rude not to give it a go.
Well let me tell you that I am glad that I did as I have been plesantly surprised by this game, the graphics are adorabe in all thier retro, 8-bit, pixelated beauty and the simplicty of game mechanics makes it easy to pick up, but hard to put down, with later levels sure to prove a challenge for even the most hardened RPG or rouguelike fans, I think it has enough appeal to keep most gamers coming back for more.
I highly recommend this game to one and all, why not try it for yourself?
And; as a free to play game you really have no excuses not to.

The saga of Bad Rats has taught us that even the worst game can find success in how hilariously bad it can be. It's a tough balance to find, where the game has to be terrible in a darkly funny or endearing way while also being mechanically sound enough to get through. Our new friend Nicolas Eymerich has the makings of such cultish appeal, but sadly never quite reaches that far into hilarity or awfulness to make the cut. Aside from the obvious bits he isn't even that bad at first, but once the puzzles start cropping up his adventure screeches to a very unwelcome stop.
The title tells you everything you need to know up front, really. Nicolas Eymerich is an inquisitor serving the Catholic church in France sometime in what feels like the Dark Ages. Trouble is brewing in a small town called Calcares, and our friend is tasked by the local abbot with uncovering the cause. Before he departs on his quest though, there is a wealth of information and secrets to gather in the abbey. I'm not sure it's enough to fill an entire game, but that's all the ground that this title, Book 1, is going to cover here.
You may notice when you start the game that the title screen depicts Nicolas glaring at you from behind burning menu buttons as DOOM-style programmer metal plays in the background. This is what you're getting with this title, not a faithful depiction of the 14th century clergy but an impossible badass battling heretics and the supernatural forces of evil with naught but his acerbic wit and withering disapproval. Nicolas is like a badass elemental, completely incapable of speaking above a menacing whisper unless he is shouting, glaring at literally everything in existence, and assuming that all people, creatures, and inanimate objects are in some way sinning against God Himself.
Amazingly this never really gets old, and in fact makes the game pretty funny as you start rolling through the ridiculous puzzles. Despite being confined to the dozen or so scenes that comprise the abbey, there are pagan talismans to make, secret libraries to reveal, and foul heretics to drive out before you even start your quest to Calcares. Nicolas reacts with acute distaste to nearly everyone in the abbey, and is given some pretty colorful ways to insult people's heritage or threaten them with damnation. And to be fair most of the locals ARE degenerates, like the abbot who couldn't be more Palpatine if he tried and the cursed fellow who can't stop thinking about ladies' bottoms.
Since this is a point-and-click adventure you're going to find plenty of items to use, most of which you won't know what for when you first find them. This one also has the unfortunate habit of not letting you take some things you'll need later until you know what you need them for, but obviously does not do this consistently. Items can also be hard to pick out from the game's weird mix of decent 3D and incredibly low-res 2D. There's a particular puzzle in the library about collecting scraps that's nigh impossible without looking up where the last piece is. Honestly, most of the puzzles are going to trip you up due to either vague instructions or finicky interfaces.
That's one big knock against The Inquisitor, that a walkthrough (or liberal use of the built-in hint system) is going to be necessary despite the postage-stamp-sized scope of the game. Your journal is almost worse than having none at all due to some very, VERY rough English. And then when you find what you need to do, Nicolas is going to give VERY unhelpful feedback unless you're already clicking the thing you need to click. That's not real likely either when you need to take a specific paving stone out of many or highlight some text you can't even read. You're going to face plenty of frustrations trying to puzzle through this one yourself, especially with how slow Nicolas is getting around and how he can get hung up on walls and stairs.
Ultimately it's just not a very polished game, and despite the hilariously over-wrought dialogue and interesting glimpses of plot the shortcomings pull it down too far. The puzzles are more irritation that challenge from start to finish, in part because of the muddy graphics that are going to get on your nerves eventually. The interface is awkward and ugly, and just getting around the abbey is a pain even with fast travel between rooms. And if you can somehow overlook all this it's only Book 1 of a two-book tale, with very little to inspire carrying on to the meat of the plot in a second game. I wish I could recommend this one for its so-bad-it's-good elements, but there are too many just-plain-bad elements heaped on top of them.

This is a very basic and plain roguelite game (yes, I'm inventing words).
Basically you just wander around some kind of dungeon with more or less useless character:
- knight - has a special attack that deals 3 HP damage to enemies adherent. This attack reloads very slowly after killing enemies
- rogue - has a chance to disarm traps - seems useful enough
- mage - probably has some special ability, but I couldn't unlock it
You have like five items in this game:
- potion - restores all of character's HP
- key - allows descent into next level
- teleport - allows one time teleport to any square in the minimap region
- flare - provides some light and turns enemies into turnips (?) that you can eat for 1 HP each
- fireball - shoots some damage dealing line that can turn into corridors and leaves some light behing
- some coins and treasure chests that add coins which do nothing
You can encounter astonishing tiles along your journey such as:
- crumbling ones that deal 2 HP damage when you fall into them!
- healing tiles that heal all of your HP!
- spike tiles that deal 1 HP damage, terrific!
- normal tiles that you just walk on untill finishing this game!
- beacon - well, this one is pretty useful as it provides light to quite large area thus turning enemies into turnips
So on, so forth...
Combat is very simple - you stand against some enemy that won't even chase you if you back up (except ghosts and probably skeleton mages) and you deal 1 damage to each other. Player character has some chance to deal critical 2 damage to enemy. That's all. Using an item does not count as an action, thus if you have 1 HP you can use your potion and continue fight. Believe me, it get's pretty boring pretty fast. You better play Desktop Dungeons, at least there are some unlockables.
Overall this is a pretty shallow game. Pixelart graphics are nice, true, but this won't fend off long agains boredom that stabs you in the back like some rogue in Dungeons & Dragons after 15 minutes into the game.
But still, this one is free, go and check it out for yourself.
EDIT:
Okay, after some thoughts this game is not that bad. It's ok if you like to play some light games that doesn't require much time to dig into. I just can't recommend this one in comparison to other games that are out there, but still if I would give a dollar for this one I wouldn't regret that.
Surprisingly, playing a rogue in a roguelike game is... interesting.
EDIT 2:
This is indeed a fun little game. Just playing knight and mage makes it is so dull. Try a rogue instead.
Really, when you play as a Knight it takes like about forever to charge your smite attack and you need to actually beat many monsters to gain levels. Usually you also trigger many traps and lose many hp. Playing as a mage you have one useless ability that seems to transform teleport orbs into fireball item only when you find one particular Transmute Tile where you can transmute those items. Also, mage levels up really slowly and gets into like every traps on the way. This game is somewhat not balanced at all. If you want to have a nice time just pick up rogue, he'll level very fast and has ability to disarm traps which gets really useful pretty fast. Alternatively, you can also try playing as a knight but this may be a bit tedious. Mage imo is unplayable at all.
This game is also a bit buggy, if you want some proof then take a look at discussions page.

Snake pass is a really well-polished and charming game that puts you in the shoes... uh well you know what I mean, of a snake.
The controls are quite intuitive, and I picked the game up really quickly. Although you might struggle at times, it's part of the game's challenge and you'll be able to retry every obstacle again until you get it right.
The controls are simple. You have the option to play with a keyboard, but I chose a controller as I found it easier.
One of your buttons moves your character forward, while another lifts his head upwards. This allows you to scale small obstacles in front of you. Finally, you have a grip button, which will tighten your body around whatever you are wrapped onto.
With these basic abilities, you can scale everything in the game. The fun comes in when you need to go up tall scaffoldings. The tricky part is not falling, so you need to make sure you wrap around poles on your way up to fight against gravity. The game really feels unique through its mechanics.
You have the ability to ask your little hummingbird friend to grab and lift your tail. This is quite situational and can help sometimes to counter the weight of your tail if you feel you're about to fall off a ledge, but I found it can get in the way if you want as much "snake body" as possible to wrap around stuff.
Levels are quite large, and are littered with different kinds of collectibles, which incentivises exploration. Although it is all optional, and you can simply go for the main 3 gems needed to complete the level.
The music is really great, and made me feel super happy. It goes very well with the charming aesthetic of the game. The colours are vibrant, and the animations look cute. It's nice to see a game with these kind of graphics again.
However, I have two gripes with the game. The first is the slight lack of checkpoints.
Sometimes you die and might lose 5 minutes of progress, and it's frustrating to have to recollect the stuff you already did. I get not letting you keep the stuff you collected if you die, because it takes away the challenge of some of the collectibles. You could simply slither over a precarious beam, grab the coin, fall to your demise and then respawn, easy. Part of the challenge is coming back alive after collecting it. But it would be nice if the game could somehow checkpoint you as soon as you get to solid and safe ground, or perhaps just have a checkpoint waiting near deadly drops so you dont have to go aaaaall the way back after failing.
My 2nd problem with the game is you need to move in a sort of zigzag motion to actually gain speed and move forward. It can be quite tiring if you are going long distances. I get that it makes sense, and snakes do that, but I would have honestly prefered just holding forward and moving like that. It's not a huge problem, as it's quite rare to do it so frequently, but it's still an annoyance.
Overall though, I'm having a lot of fun with the game. It's a really charming world ot be in, and the gameplay feels very rewarding! Recommended

Other reviewers have touched on the negatives. Some of the backtracking can get pretty annoying because actions become available that weren't possible in earlier trips through a given area. But that isn't too unusual for this kind of game. Even if you end up having to use a walkthrough, it is still worth it just to get through to more story and atmosphere. But overall the puzzles are not too hard to figure out.
Make sure you play it in Latin! I think it really makes for a totally different experience. The main character is pretty much a reprehensible, predatorial guy from the start, so don't approach the game looking for a warm and fuzzy time. You may not sympathize with him, but you will probably want to keep going to find out what he will do next.
If you have any interest in medieval times, religious history, or just dark, atmospheric, intriguing adventure games, I really don't think you can go too wrong with this one. After playing this I'm definitely looking forward to the rest of the series.

ORIGINAL REVIEW FROM THE GAMES DEBUT ON STEAM: This game is great! I follow Trek on facebook and was skeptical of this game.  Trek never gives up though, and despite a failed kickstarter, David Prassel decided to give all the backers a copy of the game anyway.  I was blown away when I started playing, I haven't enjoyed a twin stick shooter like this in years.  It's done very well, even at it's earliest release.  Not a whole lot to do, but the potential is crystal clear.  This game takes what was great about Orion Prelude and gives it a cool isometric angle and a big graphics upgrade.  I can't wait to multi with my friends and conquer this universe, good job Trek. You guys rule.  Trek is not the developer we deserve.....but the one we need most.
ANGRY UPDATE: as of 4/10/2017 there have been a lot of additions.  Ships, missions, online, and....microtransactions?  Gotta say, wtf Trek? This game shows ZERO polish and you want people to pay for cosmetic things? How about give the game better playability before adding that cash grab crap.  As far as depth, it's about and inch deep and a mile wide.  I am pretty dissapointed that Trek has shown so little effort in actually polishing this up.  Most of the gameplay that exists here, has been in place since this released.   So much is annoying, like the rough speed of the ready up bar filling, the horrendous beep that the harvester makes when it's in need of repair, the clunky/sticky way the "jetpack" feels (can you call it that if the boosters are in the characters feet?) the animations in the top down and 3rd person are pretty bad, and the first person interaction of getting jumped or executing feels crappy and all over the place like StarForge.  The ships are dissapointing too, the pathetic pewpew they make leaves me feeling like it's a 3d version of asteroids for atari. Do a mission and a NPC straight up says "Thanks! Here's a free ship!" sooo much breaks the immersion of the universe they are trying to create. The dinos show little improvement over what I've seen in the initial release, still have rough textures, the flyers still flap while they are dead on the ground.  I couldn't even get through the tutorial without doing it 5x because I kept finding bugs that would break the instructions and prevent me from proceeding.  I thought at this point the product would show polish on the existing features, but it seem that they would rather increase the scope and leave things broken and rough.  I hate to say it, but at the stage the game is at right now it's like StarForge + Dinos, robots and microtransactions.  It feels like a cash grab.  What once showed so much initial promise has become a mess that I am not sure can even be fixed.  I bought my buddy a copy for a dollar, now I regret it.

If you were looking for the spiritual successor to the X-Com franchise, Xenonauts feels like the game you’ve been waiting for. Even though The Buraeu: X-Com Declassified and Enemy Unknown/Within were great games in their own right, they just didn’t quite capture the same feeling that the classic games had. While some things need to evolve and change, there’s something to be said about making a recipe with most of the same ingredients to enjoy the meal you remember. (That’s especially true if they are going to say that it tastes similar.) I covered a lot of the basics of this game in the X-Com: Enemy Unknown VS. Xenonauts review so I’m not going to cover everything since Goldhawk Interactive finished up everything that needed fixing to transition from Early Access to Launch status pretty smoothly.
Let’s start with difficulty shall we? That was a trademark aspect of the originals. (I still can’t complete TFTD.) I started Xenonauts on the Regular difficulty and had both starter interceptor planes shot down in one-on-one dogfights. (At which point I had nothing to shoot down enemy aircraft.) The enemy craft ended up landing after downing my two aircraft giving me my first mission… out of pity. During the pity mission (which happened to be a night mission of course) I had lost two soldiers before I got ten spaces from my Chinook from enemies I couldn’t see. Needless to say I started over and changed the difficulty to easy. I usually don’t like playing games on easy, but this game just kicked me in the nuts and laughed in my face.
Thinking that the game was going to be too easy after the difficulty was changed was a bad assumption on my part. That little dead alien in the corner reminded me that I shouldn’t let my guard down. This little bugger skirted around the edge of the map taking pot shots at my guys almost killing two of them. I was throwing out flares left and right to try to find him to no avail. I eventually found him by sending one soldier randomly to the side of the map and just happened to spot him. Needless to say, when he became visible, the bullets went flying.
Moving on, research has been overhauled to be more convenient for the player. Let’s just say that you go out on your first mission and you clean house very well. When you get back to base you have only a few options to research, general concepts like alien electronics or alien interrogations if you managed to capture an alien alive. What about the dissections and the alien craft that you left behind? Well, it’s being taken cared of. That’s being done behind the scenes and you’ll get that info in good time and the other related research options therein. You still have plenty of things to research so don’t feel robbed here; Xenonauts makes research feel streamlined.
Another interesting note is that wounded soldiers heal more realistically. This is a neat update while at the same time pretty frustrating. I liked it when people just took a few days off and then poof they were combat ready and good-as-new. In Xenonauts they take time to become combat ready with reduced stats and even more time to fully recover. When the number of days are up for your soldier to enter the field again, they are given a percentage of how much they’ve recovered. You’ll have less health to run around with and lose when you get shot. As time goes on, they do get better, but that’s with time.
There are plenty of different looking locals between deserts, desert bases, towns, farms and enemy bases. They have different maps for the same type as well so you’ll never really feel that “you’ve been here before”. That is a very nice feature, because few things feel as cheap than reused levels. Some may call the graphic choice dated, but not only does it look nice aesthetically, the devs do a great job setting a creepy atmosphere with it. I really like the presentation of Xenonauts.
One last note, the NPCs in Xenonauts are freaking amazing. Some are just helpless civilians and do stupid civilian things, but the guys with guns (soldiers and farmers) actually use thier guns to defend themselves. I’ve had some levels be finished by some random farmer killing an alien before my guys got to the part of the map. Well played Goldhawk Interactive, well played.
Score: Tasty!
There is a lot to love here for fans of tactical games. Nothing feels rushed and sometimes that’s a concern people have when games come out of Early Access. It’s all smooth running and gunning here. With the varied locals and very nice looking isometric scenery, there is some really good “retro” (if you want to call it that) eye-candy to be had. Goldenhawk Interactive doesn’t go out of their way to revamp the series with light blooms and next-gen graphics. They pull from what made the originals so great and modernize it. I have nothing bad to say about Xenonauts (especially since they allow me to lower the difficulty setting). I will try a harder difficulty later, but as of now I appreciate having my ego padded a little more.
