Even though I've only played 12 and half hours of this game, I would recommend the hell out of this game. It's super relaxing, you can listen to foreign radio stations, and you can make that sweet, virtual cash.

First off, I wonder if I am one of the few, or only, actual HGV1 (40 tonne) licenced trucker (who spent many years on the road hauling various loads across the UK and Europe) who actually bought and plays this game! Although I gave up driving for a living, I still get the occasional itch to jump in a cab which was one of the reasons I gave this game a go. So far I must admit that it's better than I expected and has soothed the itch and I don't have to worry about tachographs, not getting home when expected, the police or Ministry of Transport stops or the boss rattling my cage for another job to get done by yesterday. I can drive and relax, stop when I want and have a life :P
Graphically the trucks are amazing and driving the DAF XF brings back many memories. The vehicles and trailor handling is also pretty close to reality which adds a nice touch to virtaul driving. One massive bonus was being able to listen and connect to 'Trucker FM' live radio within the game which I really didn't expect. There are many other radio stations you could tune into including the BBC stations (yawn) and many European ones too. The choice is yours plus it makes for a boring drive along a motorway, less tedious. Just keep an eye on your onboard satnav and you won't go wrong.
The ability to customise you unit (as you level up) is a nice touch although they are somewhat limited so far but enough to satisfy the custom build. These range from paint jobs and some of them are trully awesome, bull bars, air horns and spot lights, transmission, cab interior fittings (fridge box, laptop, sun glasses, etc) and many other improvements. We have all seen some amazing tucks on the road where drivers have added their own touch to their unit, you can do the same here without the expense it would generally cost.
In the game you can build up your company, hire drivers etc and push towards having a more CEO management role but then that defeats the pure thill of being behind the wheel running from point a to point b, c, d, etc.
Now, onto the scenery graphics. They may not be mind blowingly great but they suffice. If you are spending too much time observing your surroundings then you ain't paying attention to the road ;) You will spot well known land marks and they do look pretty good. In all, it's the driving experience which should keep you hooked. If you like pretty pictures and scenery then do the tourist thing and trawl your photo albums.
You can further expand the game with add-on packs (DLC) consisting of routes, paint jobs, trailors, etc., although they offer more, they're not that necessary. Some can be fairly cheap, others cost nearly as much as the game itself. The content in them will vary in what you get for the price. Some will seem ok for value, others will be a let down. In a way I can see the cost helping with further patched and game development but I also feel that some companies seem to exploit their addicted gamers.
To sum up. For those of you that have always wanted to know what driving trucks are like, you should give this game a go even if just for a short time. You will learn more than you realise and may adjust your own driving habits while on actual roads in your cars, being more considerate to truckers themselves and what they go through on a daily basis.

This is possibly the greatest zombie game I've played in a very long time. It's on par with Left 4 Dead 1&2, Resident Evil and any other great zombie games that you can think of. Why's it so great? Because it's a realistic survival scenario. You and a group of up to seven other players (I think that's about right) must make it to the end of the level completing a number of tasks to get there. Think Zombie Panic Source and Codename CURE but a lot more sophisticated.
Ammo is extremely sparce, so you'll be relying on your melee weapons and teamwork to make it to the end of each level. If you're in luck and do find a plethora of ammo and a gun that takes that type of ammo, you might find it a little useless in some cases, such as a small room, or people standing in front of you.
One cool thing I picked up on rather quickly is that you can actually kill infected survivors so that they don't come back and try to eat your brains like it's an all you can eat buffet. A couple bullets to the head or a whack with a fire extinguisher will send them straight on their way to the pearly gates of Valhalla. And there's an achievement tied to doing this so I was offing people left and right like it was a Walking Dead convention.
There's a nice variety of weapons in the game, from your most useful ones (Fire axe, Fubar and Sledgehammer) to your not so useful ones (Everything else). I found I only use those three weapons I listed because they're just so damned effective. Hold down M1 and release it for an insta-kill that will most likely hit the zombies head clean off. While other weapons such as the baseball bat and fire extinguisher are available, they aren't nearly as effective as the other weapons in the game.
Zombie wise, you've got your normal, everyday zombies. They sound a bit, y'know "uuuuuuugh", and so on, you know the type. Shambling, walk slowly. However the sheer number of them in this game makes them dangerous as hell, you'll need to be thinking constantly if you want to survive for a minute in this game. Along with these shambling fools, you've got fast zombies. You know the ones, like in Left 4 Dead 2, running around everywhere, probably after you. Along with these runners, you have children zombies. May I just say, these child zombies are the most annoying ♥♥♥♥ers in the entire game. They're so small and fast. Keep your eye out for them.
There's two gamemodes in this game, Survival and Missions. Survival is basically, you guessed it, survival, with FEMA coming in to rescue you after some point. I think? I dunno, I never made it far in survival, where I strive is in missions. Well, missions doesn't seem like the right term for them but they pretty much are.
I'd like to make special mention of the community of this game. You guys are great! Truly, you do a great job of making newer players be welcomed and this game is definitely one of those games where you can just drop in and function like a team.

A short platformer that centers itself around using what it calls “eversion,” which changes the state of the world.
30-60 minutes
Platformer
5/10

is a fairly simple platformer, you walk left and right, jump across platforms, jump on enemies heads to dispose of them, and collect gems; pretty typical platformer fair. The gimmick for this game is the ability to “evert,” which can only be done at certain points of a level. Everting is activated simply by clicking the key assigned to do so at an evert point. When you evert you change the world around you to an alternate reality. There are 7 different realities in use (plus an 8th hidden one), though most levels only use a small number.
You need to find eversion points to change the world so that you can progress though out the stage, as it will change small things about the world that let you progress. It’s not rocket science figuring out how to use eversion to advance, as it’s all pretty straight forward.
When you begin the game the world starts out very happy and cheery, bright colours and all that. As you descend into the later stages of eversion, the world gradually shifts darker and darker.
The gameplay itself isn’t really anything fancy. In the early levels you’ll notice it draws influence from the original
This is most notable in the first stage, as it bears a striking resemblance in how the beginning of the level looks.
The gems scattered throughout the game for you to collect don’t serve any purpose, except to unlock a secret level at the end of the game. I didn’t take the time to unlock the secret level, and after pulling it up on youtube to have a look at it, I don’t plan to either, as it doesn’t look like it’s worth the time.
So is it worth buying? Eh, only if you want a short little platformer to kill an hour (if that). There’s a free version available on the developer’s (Zaratustra Productions), though the Steam version features some minor graphical and audio updates. It’s normally $5, though it’s really not worth that price, so I’d wait for it to go on sale. I wish I could give this game a neutral rating, as it’s not good enough to really recommend, nor is it bad enough to advise against purchasing. Take your pick based on if it looks interesting to you or not.

EDIT NOTE: This review was written when the game was just launched on Steam in Early Access. According to comments, a lot has changed. Treat this review more as a standard on what the game was like when it was launched.
So I bought this game mostly because its built with Unreal Engine 4, particularly because I've been playing around with UE4 also.
First of all, this game has a lot of stuff missing, and thus a lot of improvement to be had. (Hey it's an Early Access, it's to be expected) I have only played half an hour of the game(note: Steam was down for maintenance when I was playing, hence the lower gametime on my profile). So read the review with a grain of salt, especially when it's about missing things. As I haven't explored much of the available gameplay. Which may explain why I don't recommend this game yet.
(I'm guilty of writing a review with only so little playtime, but since the game just released, and the only complaints have been it shouldn't be a third person shooter, I figured I'll write some issues I'm seeing that are more legitmate)
-Gameplay-
I've only spent half an hour playing it so far. Solo, with keyboard and mouse, default difficulties and map. It has been a bit boring, but I can see potential in it. I may make some comparsions to Magicka, Helldivers, both games by Arrowhead Studio or with Diablo 3 since it can also be considered a top-down action game.
Guardians of Orion has infinite ammo, with a reloading system. The switching time for the weapons between primary to pistol, vs pistol to primary seems almost the same, making gameplay rather dull. In fact, it seems as if switching to secondary pistol once the primary needed to be reloaded, then switching back renders the primary fulled loaded again.(Not sure if bug)
There is no aiming distance for the grenade, only a direction, making it nearly impossible to land a proper grenade, especially when the grenade travels at a fixed distance.
Compared to say Helldivers, there is no particular weakness spots when hitting an enemy, Making aiming a very simple task. There is no turn speed involved either, unlike say Helldivers where your turn speed is reduced based on certain situations. (Such as when you're firing, or if you're in a mech)
I used the Assault class, which has the abiilty to use the jetpack. It's more of an evade for a set period of time button, while still able to shoot enemies, as there is no disadvantages from being above ground. Thus there is no turning off the jetpack.
Because movement speed is the same even when you're shooting, there isn't any decision involved in whether or not you should run or shoot.
There is a dodge roll button, but in the 30 minutes I've played, there has been no reason to dodge roll, especially if you have a jetpack, and a blink ability.
The blink ability loses its control in the target location, if you use a keyboard, since the location is depended on where you're moving, I imagine it to feel more good when playing on a controller with an analog stick.
Sprinting's only downside is that you can't shoot while sprinting, and the fact that the camera zooms in a bit. You can infinitely sprint.
I'm not sure if there's friendly fire, but I couldn't shoot the objective I was defending, so I would assume it to be a no. (Will check multiplayer later)
There are power up drops occasionally when killing enemies, but those don't really alter the gameplay decisions, other than basic attributes, like movement speed, fire rate, health regen, etc.
Overall, there isn't much decision making when playing the game. Especially when it's all cooldown involved, and there is no concept of a scarce resource, such as limited ammo. The idea of dodging and avoiding enemies, seem bland. More crowd control abilities may also bring more gameplay decisions in.
There are skill points you can invest in, which I hope brings in more decision making into the game. However at least for me, the first 30 minutes playing solo has been really boring to play.
-User Interface-
It's an early access game, so it's not a surprise that the UI is rough looking. For any Unreal Engine 4 devs, it's obvious to tell a lot of the progress bars are using the standard UI provided by UE4. There isn't much of an indication of what each bars are, but it can be quite obvious after 5 minutes of playing. Top bar being health, then shield, ability power, and exp.
There were two different objectives during my games. Defending the Harvester, basically a wave mode, and Eliminate these enemies. The fact that the latter was called a Side Objective, but yet refusing to do it, basically stops the progression of the round/game, seems to beg the question if it really is a "Side" Objective.
The mini map is very basic, with a simple map image, and circles to represent the player and the enemies.
As expected, the UI would probably be polished later on. But for now, it serves its purpose at the moment.
-Audio-
I'm really not picky about audio, there is some voiced dialog such as "under attack". The gun sounds fine as far as I'm concerned. So nothing much I have to say about it.
-Overall Conclusion-
Game has a lot of potentials, do not expect anything like Magicka, or Helldivers sort of gameplay. There is a lack of decision making involved at least for solo.
I will be updating this review as I spend some more time playing this game, especially the multiplayer side of things. At the current state, the only reason to buy it is for the reduced price, and for the sake of testing, and supporting the developer. If you're buying it to have a solo time, I do not recommend.

welp this is my first shot at an actual review so here it goes.
the good:
-isometric view is a pretty interesting take on the horde survival genre(with some side missions)
-unlike the previous game(orion:prelude, which gives you a discount on this game, and is in itself a pretty good horde survival game), there seem to be many more classes coming, with each class having its unique abillity and weapons(assault can take the high ground with the jetpack, for instance, allowing alternate routes)
-the game seems to take a more casual approach(atleast for now), with the lack of resource management and running back and forth to shops. this does mean that if you drop-in to a lobby in advanced points of the game you wouldnt hinder your team or become a charity case
-much more fast paced movement with the added blink abillity, and new interactions by enemies in the form of fatalities and grapples(which would remind you of dogs from call of duty, except less dramatic because of the isometric)
-the skill tree is not too confusing and simple, albeit a little lacking at this point
the bad:
-atm the game is a little jittery and stutterish. its not at the level where itll ruin your game, but if youre a FPS(frames per second) junkie, or a bit more sensitive to jittery pictures, it may annoy you. nothing you cant ignore if you choose to enjoy the game
-the isometric view does take some getting used to, and somewhat takes away from the difficulty of this genre
-the lack of resource management and shops takes away from the normally hectic purchasing and gear-upgrading that add spice and take away from the redundency of this genre
things that arent good nor bad(atleast in my back)
-there isnt a huge variation of maps at the moment, however its not a big problem as they can still be enjoyed if the game is played casually rather than hardcore grinding
-there is only one game mode at this point(given the game has only just gone up with early access that is to be expected), but it is pretty well made and given this game's *ancestor*'s variety of modes and how well they were made, im very much looking forward to the things to come.
TL;DR : interesting game, if you dont mind the isometric view it can be very enjoyable despite the slightly jittery graphics, although kind of lacking in depth at the moment. i recommend it at this point as im both enjoying my time and expecting something even better to come.

This game is not fair.
Let's get that out of the way right off the bat. If you're looking for something you can play well and have no chance of failing horribly, this is not it. One bad mission, one stroke of bad luck, can send you spinning down the path to destruction.
However, there are a great many selling points that keep me coming back to this game; while it isn't fair, if you accept that you will have a good time. This game forces you to think. There will be many times when you will think, "oh, there's probably no aliens there; I can afford to rush or leave it unguarded". Well, if you think that, stop yourself. Mistakes are not dealt with lightly in this game, and rushing is not a luxury you can often take.  Likewise, always have a contingency plan for when you miss. No - scratch that- have three. Because if you leave your team in the hands of someone with a shotgun, and that Andron manages to survive those shots, you just lost a valuable team member, if not two. Leave enough time for your rifleman to pop around the corner and finish him off, or else you will cry. Remember - 70% chance to hit is just an optimistic way to say 30% chance to miss. This game does not like impatience.
But it's just so *satisfying*! Blowing your first corvette out of the sky, capturing that first xeno, and clearing out every last alien crash site feels great. And you get the satisfaction of knowing you did it right. Plus this game has all of the options you can possibly want in terms of ground battles. It all works just as you'd expect, and the customization in loadouts along with the options you have in ground battles in terms of strategy makes the game very compelling, and keeps me coming back every time I get frustrated. In the end, no, it's not fair, but there's always something you can do to even the odds, and it all depends on just how much time you're willing to take.

I don't know what to say about this game besides it's amazing, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).

Famaze is a casual dungeon crawling RPG. You move up, down, left, and right to navigate a map in the upper screen. In the lower screen you will be given a representation of the characters and the environment. You can attack enemies by walking into them. There are a small variety of items to find in the mazes. You can hold two items at a time, but they will respawn upon use or loss so you'll never be out of supplies. There are traps that make the mazes hard to navigate safely, as well as monsters to fight. You can gain XP through that or lighting large torches. Shedding light on most enemies will turn them into items for bonus points. Gold is also around for points. Some enemies, however, will be awakened when you shine light upon them. There are lots of litle ins and outs of the game depending on the situation you get into with the randomness, but it's overall incredibly simple. Your main goal is simply to find keys and use them to open up the next level.
Honestly, I only played a bit of this one and it got boring and repetitive pretty fast. It's a time waster. It's easy, casual, simple, and fun in short bursts. However, in the sea of games on Steam, it doesn't have enough to stand out, nor is it more worthy of your time than many other games. The only reason I can recommend it is that it's free. It's not a bad game, but much too simplistic and repetitive for my taste. The visual style is neat, the concept is okay, and the music is cool, but it's just not enough to keep me coming back for more. Famaze gets a 3 out of 10 for being a neat little free game that can kill some time, but ultimately isn't worth wasting your time on unless you truly have that much time to waste. But hey, it's free so try it for yourself.

Sweet baby Jesus, where do I begin with this mess? Well, I suppose the beginning...
When Ferrum's Secrets: Where Is Grandpa? first starts, it actually looks quite promising. The graphic style is a little different than most of the HOGs out there, which struck me as a nice change of pace, but then things immediately started to go downhill...
...I should've begun to brace myself when I saw the "Unity Personal Edition" logo upon startup. That is, almost unilaterially, a sign that the developer has not invested in their tools or platform, and is more likely a hobbiest releasing their first game. Sometimes those things turn out well, but usually not. And in this case, Unity was a poor choice. It's what defined the interesting graphics style, because a lot of the environment is comprised of solid, 3D objects, but it also means that the game runs terribly. And by that I mean you will, upon seeing the mouse pointer move, literally, seconds behind where you are trying to point, scream "holy crap, the LAG!"  Seriously, I was running this game on a Lenovo X1 Carbon which, while not a hardcore gaming machine, is a pretty nice laptop. Perhaps its super-high resolution was to blame, but the entire game just ran like a dog. I would expect this if I were trying to play Far Cry 4 on this laptop, but the performance is completely inexcusable for a casual game. If playtesting had taken place on enough variety of systems, then this problem would surely have been unconvered and (hopefully) resolved. It was bad enough that I almost bailed out at the beginning...but I'm stubborn and a completionist, so I hung in there until the end.
The next significant issue is the localization. OMG, THE ENGRISH! Seriously, the translation is consistently, laughably bad. Now, in the authors' defense, their English is still better than my Polish (a conclusion of original language I reached by looking at the domain for the support email), but if you're going to publish a game for money where the biggest market is English-speaking...well, it needs to be better than this. I don't ask for perfection, but this wasn't even close.
Even if the above things weren't a problem, the plot was so loosely constructed that I was constantly reacting to the (barely understandable) dialog with thoughts like, "why in the world would he do that?" and "that makes absolutely no sense at all...there's no motivation there, financial or otherwise." The characters' actions often seem pretty random, and the solutions to situations are all-too-often completely obtuse, when there is an obvious and simpler way that something should have been solved, especially given the environment and items in inventory.
There are a couple of interesting puzzles, sometimes with weird mechanics, but interesting nonetheless. But a lot of them feel janky, and many are just mail-it-in HOG 101 throwaways like picture sliding puzzles (which, note to HOG develoepers: nobody likes those...please just stop adding them to your games).
A couple of the cut scenes were neat, and that's where the nicest graphics are seen...but they usually only last for a few seconds, and all of those pretty pictures are mostly wasted as a virtual blip on the radar for the game.
So no, I can't remotely recommend this game. I will say to the developers, though, that you have some good ideas and are obviously motivated. I recommend that you spend more time investing in an engine that works well for this genre of game and will run smoothly on more platforms, and also invest in things like proper translation, playtesting, etc., if you want to be a professional shop. You have potential, but you need to up your game a LOT if you truly want to publish good software that will receive good reviews. I think that you can do it, but you'll need to put in the work.
[side note: if you get this in a bundle, just idle it for the cards...getting 100% achievements means at least 3 full play-throughs for each difficulty level, and it's just not worth your time.]

is a hidden object and puzzle game. Your grandfather, an inventor, has disappeared and it is up to you to piece together the clues and find out what happened to him.
: The game is very easy to pick off, even for people with no experience of the genre. You have a couple of areas to explore, offering a few puzzles of different types: hidden objects, tile flipping, object assembly to name a few. The story is told through scattered notes you find and a few interaction with other people you encounter. There are different collectibles to find within each difficulty level, requiring multiple playthroughs to get them all.
: The text has serious syntax flaws, part of which is incomprehensible, and has in all appearances been translated to English through a poor man's Google Translator. The story seems to have been thought up by a child. I mean,
sounds like the plot of an 80s Saturday morning cartoon episode. Graphics and 3D object models are easily put to shame by games such as the 1993 version of
, while music is recycled from other games (assuming there is any sound at all in the area you're in). In addition to lacking variety, the puzzles are extremely easy or simply make no sense (use a wrench on a push-button to fix electrical wires. Wait, what?). The game is short and un-engaging, achievement hunters are likely to be the only ones caring about a second and third playthrough.
: ★☆☆☆☆ - May it rot in your backlog
I said this game was easy for newcomers to hidden objects games, but I wouldn't recommend it even to them as it's a poor example of what can be expected in the genre and might even scare some away. This is an amateur project, unworthy of people spending any money on it. Don't buy, just...don't.

XENONAUTS FANBOIS BEWARE : THE FOLLOWING WILL BE A HARSH COMPARISON TO THE CLASSIC XCOM (1994 - 1995), DO NOT READ THIS REVIEW IF YOUR WELLBEING DEPENDS ON CONSTANT GLORIFICATION OF THIS GAME OR IF YOU GET UPSET EASILY :
(scroll down if you want to read about reality, please)
1) in parts buggy
2) bad, miniscule research
3) interesting aircraft-recovery, losing a craft costs nothing but WILL cost time (usually 72 hours)
4) difficulty-progression is worse / more steep than in XCOM (yes, the real, classic ones) - basically you have 2 years  ... which is far from good and isnt any fun --- unlike XCOM in which the player has at least a decent amount of time before♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan
5) available money seems adequate at first - but if you dont want to lose after 2 years you will need to invest EVERYTHING and fear every loss because that can (and will) end the game. Thats XCOM on high difficulty, in this game its medium. Thats sad.
(i dont remember the exact difficulty-names, sorry)
6) research doesnt make much sense - the results are well explained but its senseless to gain knowledge about ARMOR during PLASMA RIFLE reseach, for example - that should've been available after "alien alloys" .... and its only a small example
7) air combat is a bit more fun than in XCOM - but its also a bit harder
8) air-retreat has a big bug : the match ends only once the UFO (!) has left the screen, even if your fighter has already left
9) ground combat is ... not bad, it basically looks like XCOM with high resolution but in that case i prefer a lower resolution - either polish the classic combat in ways which make it better or keep it like it is .... there is no in-between, everything else looks pretty cheap to be honest and thats exactly what this game is -- even the dying-animations (if one could call em that) are cheap and consist of .... one (?) single step - in XCOM it was at least 2-3 per alien.
10) Music is good but the soundeffects are pretty bad - most sounds are missing or replaced by very bad ones
11) It has no XCOM-like feeling, the ground combat does not instill fear, there is zero tense anywhere and  it looks like ... something boring.
12) ground combat-view is not rotatable. Yes. One of the most important features in tactical, turn-based games is missing. XCOM had it. Because its necessary.
13) the world map looks bad - even XCOM had a (much) better one, even in 3D
conclusion : its worse than the classics in some ways. The few additives make it worthwile for a few hours but thats it ... if you want a new (and ACTUAL) XCOM-follower this is not your game, its basically a bad version of what should've been released from the original XCOM-developers a few years after the last of the (original) series ... not bad but also not really good.

Awesome Turn Based Strategy(TBS) game.
I have only clocked a few hours into this game, but what I have done has been very enjoyable.
Not being big on games with a lot of text etc I have oddly found myself quite interested in the new entries that popup as you progress through the game, these detail new technologies you find, autopsy reports and other general info.
The game puts you in charge of administering and controlling a organisation designed to intercept and stop and alien threat via advancing human technologies to and expanding your organisation deployment globally to defend against said alien threat.
You do this by initially building a base, which gives you two interceptor jets, a helicopter transport and a crack team of individuals to neutralize any alien threats.
Your base is equipped with a radar that covers a set range and when UFO contacts are detected you can launch your interceptors to shoot the target down.
This is done in Real-Time and basically has you controlling the weapons and direction your plane(s) fly.
Once you down the UFO you can deploy your transport of troops and land at the crash site to secure it in TBS combat FOR SCIENCE!
I will not get too deep into it,
The game is straight forward, easy to understand and follow the dev has done some great work in the lore and story and  it is simply enjoyable to play.
Well worth the price if you are into TBS games and or the XCOM series.

I like indie games and I like HOGs, and I feel sad I'm giving this a thumbs down. The game is made with the unity engine, which creates a different play experience than most Hogs. Scenes can be manipulated to give different angles of view, which is unique. The game is obviously a labour of love for a very small development team, in which a lot of care was given to the puzzles and interactivity.
The reason I can't give it a thumbs up is the fact that it feels unfinished, the art assets are incredibly bad, especially in the HO scenes, the english translations of the original language seem to have been done in Google Translate, the UI is horrible and covers both clues and text in some scenes, and the music is the same royalty free music score that has been used on multiple games before.
All that is before we even get to the completely incoherent story line. The object of the game as the title suggests, is to find your grandfather. The game begins in usual HOG tradition be exploring his home, looking for clues as to his whereabouts. Then all of a sudden, you are transported and working with a witch to find him, and then you are a detective trying to piece together evidence against a master criminal, and then you are James Bond, taking out robotic henchmen and disabling a giant airship. It just makes little to no sense and the poor english (if you are playing in english) doesn't help the story in any way.
If you like indie games and want to support the developer, buy it. I've seen much worse first games, but this one needed more time in the oven before release. Oh, and it has kittens, lots and lots of kittens.

The Game Itself (fact):
This game was developed by an all star cast of great composer Disasterpeace, successful pixel sprite artist/programmer Oryx, and the electric rennaissance man Reckahdam (programmer, musician, and much more).  Content-wise, this game has about 15 levels in linear order.  Not worlds- levels, and this number includes the five or six bonus levels that have about 20 aquares in them.  There are only three characters all available from the start.  It does not fit a computer screen properly.  Each real level will take, at most, ten minutes to complete, and can each be completed in under a minute.  The game has branching paths to choose between that the player must go down in separate playthroughs to collect pieces of a magis stone, which is close to artificial lengthening.
This game has a few bugs, including that when the spacebar has multiple functions it decides what it wants to do, like activating a trap that will harm the player instead of going through a door, or going through a door instead of using a special attack.  A bigger bug makes the character disappear when they collect the last magic gem shard, making it impossible to see the true ending.  In hard mode the game may become literally impossible to beat, which will force you to resart the game (although it won't take long to get back to where you were or get stuck again).  The music has been hailed all around, as it is made by the critically acclaimed artist Disasterpeace and it is available to purchase for the exact price of $4.99.
The Game Itself (oppinion):
The presentation could have been entirely redone for full screen by putting the maze-screen and action screen on the left and right and making them bigger, and it seems lazy to only allow you to see what monsters and items are when they are two squares away from you, when the screen also lets you see three sqaures.  The developers for sure knew about these and probably other bugs I haven't discovered, and were even told about them, but left them in when they could "break the game".  That the game is so short is a problem, especially since these levels seem so simple to design.  The gameplay is also very simple (explore until you find a key, then find an exit while hitting monsters to subtract on hit point from each of your health bars, and use items+plus your characters special ability to stay ahead of the game), even though the variation of monsters and items is perfect for this very short experience and the three characters are each interesting and well-balanced, the general strategy will always be the same (only use items when necessary, save health for traps, and locate the way out quickly but try to last long and gain points/xp).  Some will like the small variations (like myself), while others will be totally bored.  The soundtrack is truly wonderful, I have not seen a professional review that does not complement it, and I bought it separately, but this game is only on par with a very good flash game or a good phone game, and does not include the soundtrack for a download, so it should cost less than the music.  Also, the music does not repeat in most cases, which is a wonderful artistic choice, but then you are left in silence until the key is found or you decide to go to the next level, which could have at least been filled with some simple beats from the other incredibly skilled musician on the team, Roger Reckahdam Hicks.  The sound effects could at least have more variety, each character makes the same noise when the hit a monster and move.
Overall, this game is very fun and a great concept, but short, incomplete, bugged and flawed.  Because an all star cast, a dream team, put it together it is horrrible and unexpected that it ended up like this.  I voted for it on greenlight thinking that if success on Steam was in the developers vision they would go back to work and make this game great, but as soon as they got in they released this title before even putting steam acheivements in it, then raised its price by 4.99 and deleted the free version!  This is just plain old exploitation of Greenlight and the people of steam, along with a dishonorable rejection of making art as opposed to making a profit, however small- this is an offront to the romance of independant development.
The History:
Those three indie titans got together to make this game way back in the 200Xs.  They were going to make it for phones, hence the strange shape of the game and arrangement of screens.  They carried on for quite a while, but the game was generating less and less interest from the public, no income, and the developers had many other projects looking more hopeful (the Famaze soundtrack was created  at the same time when Disasterpeace made the Fez soundtrack).  It was put into Greenlight, but wasn't being voted for, so it was put into stasis.  Eventually (2013) the game was released in flash for free on Oryx's website, where I found it and loved it, and Disasterpeace put the soundtrack out for sale.  That would have been a very sad end to Famaze, that it would die with a wimper on Oryx's page, but then Steam started Greenlighting 100 and 50 titles at a time!  Was this it, was Famaze going to find some fans in the Steam Userbase?  Would the developers sit down together and expand it to something wonderful like it easily could become?  Absolutely not!  It was made downloadable, the price was raised, and it was dropped into the Steam marketplace with all the pomp of dropping a banana peel into the trash!  The developers cast aside all of their honor and integrity as artists when they put this unfinished product here, and insulted every one of their fans by expecting them to put money into it when it is just a flash game- they insulted you!  Even if the game itself sounds great, when used like this it is soiled and turned entirely into garbage.
F2P Update:  All of the developers were confronted at the time this was written, but none commented back or replied.  I do believe that I might have been slighty harsh in my delivery, and even made an apolagy, but until we can hear how it ended up how it was from the mouth(s) of whoever published this, it is right for us to be upset about what happened.  It was pointed out to me that this game was put into a bundle a few days after it was released on steam, and was recently in a bundle just before becoming free (which means some were cheated out of their cash, again, but it is a step in the right direction).
As said in my apolagy, all people go back on their honor, so the publishers should only be treated as if they made a mistake.
No matter what has happened in the past, even recently bundling right before going F2P, the game is free now, as it should be.  This controversy should be over.  On the other hand, I have not heard from any of the big three, so we have no idea if this was not thought through entirely, or a cold hearted bussiness plan.
Lastly, because there has been no dialogue, we cannot know if the publishers have learned from this, or would do it again.  We need to have a public statement to clear all of this up.  A youtube video could be made, and the comments turned off, if you do not want to see hundreds of people insult you (as is the case with the internet).  I truly hope that I have been fair.

Short, fun game. Finished it in one sitting, tempted to go back and get all completionist on it. It's a cute game with a very effective atmosphere. As others have said it's one of those better played than explained situations.
I am recommending this game but I'm reluctant to because of some things that I feel should have been fixable.
<CRITICISM>
First criticism: As far as I could find there was no native controller support. Sure I could Joy2Key it or something and if I were to go back to 100% it I most certainly would do that but if you're going to charge money for a platformer in this day and age you should support at least the bare minimum of controllers.
Second criticism: If you AREN'T going to support controllers (or even if you do really) either make sure your mechanics are really smooth and satisfying or don't rely on cheap tricks like long jumps you have to make with a block above you while enemies loom ready to intercept you. That's just one example and in the greater scheme I'm saying either get creative with how you create challenge or tone it down a bit. This game was surprisingly unforgiving and frustrating and it really took away from the atmosphere after a while.
In a way it felt like it couldn't decide whether it wanted to be a Mario/Super Meat Boy style experience or whether it wanted to be a Braid style experience. I feel like it would have been a better game if it had chosen Puzzles and Atmosphere or Unforgiving Platformer and spent more time polishing whichever one they chose.
</CRITICISM>
With all that said, the game wasn't long enough to get extremely mad at and was cheap enough that that didn't bother me. The atmosphere and scenery made up for the lackluster mechanics and overall it was a great way to spend a bit of time. I do recommend you pick this title up, especially if you catch it on a sale. Happy gaming and stell'bsna n'gha...

This strategy-horror hybrid is a retro-themed series of lengthy levels (four of them), each one of which parodies horror films from the 70s and 80s. Between a level on Friday the 13th, The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Halloween. and Alien, the game offers unique objectives/design that test a player's intuition and reaction time. It most certainly doesn't hold your hand, and completing a level by surviving is greatly rewarding. In one, you have to kill three serial killers; in another you have to avoid a cultist family while collecting gas, and so on. There's a lot of variation and the game most certainly never grows stale.
In some ways, I really enjoyed this game and I want to give it a thumbs up. However, the boss fights are absolutely unforgiving. So much so, that a very tiny mistake can force you to restart the entire game. This is atrocious game design, particularly for a game in which mistakes are easy to make (due to time or otherwise). Because of this, I can't fully recommend this game. The point of gaming is fun, and fun doesn't describe my entire experience with this title.

Lets start shall we...
Aftermath is the game the developers behind Warz/Infected Suvivor Stories wanted having a bit more control over the development. However it feels like nothing has really changed (even though there has been some noticeable difference). To break it down
==============
The Good
==============
1. Larger focus on crafting, character customization (even though only one character you can change pants, shirts and hats)
2. Character animations looks pretty decent.
==============
The Bad
==============
1. Feels like nothing has changed - when you first enter the world it feels like your thrown back into Warz/Infected. Your first greated with a very basic character system and faced with all these options regarding crates and credits. There isn't a proper tutorial to help you understand the basics.
2. Crafting - Feels extremely boring and confusing. You have many survival games entering the whole break down any item you see and use those items to figure out if they can be used to craft something, if you find the right stuff you unlock a blue print...Aftermath could of focus on a more improved system like that however they went back to the basics where only certain items can be brought down (found 10 backpacks and couldn't break them down for materials), the requirements aren't shown on what you require to build some items and you have blue prints all over the place for you to collect instead of you trying to mix and match. It felt very boring to me
3. World - It's a new location then Warz/Infected however it doesn't feel exciting or wanting me to explore. I spawned next to a large city and found most buildings were locked up or very plain/empty without much detail and just didn't feel like I was really in the world like many other survival games try (large forests, cities burning or completely wrecked with details and blood showing something bad has happened.)
4. A.I - I found the current zombie A.I very weak and almost the same as before. They got stuck a lot even though I just walked in a cycle they sometimes just lose sight of me and stand there screaming. A few times I was able to pass a large horde of zombies running and jumping without even having them seem at least somewhat interested in eating me, they just stood there even when I got close they just stood looking at nothing...however when I started to crouch/sneak they started to go wild...okay. They just didn't feel like a threat.
The large issue I have with Aftermath isn't the game itself but how the developers made it while having a huge chance of making a great game. From having a bumpy Warz/Infected I was hoping they would grab the knowledge and break the game down back to basic levels and rebuild a better game even if it was starting with a small town and then opening it bigger (kind of like how the Forest or H1Z1 handled their open world aspect keeping a lot of focus in one area and then start opening the next after it felt ready).
Again I played Warz/Infected before (don't have the steam version) and enjoyed the closed testing and bit after the whole launch issue, even though it ticked me off how they did that when a lot were saying it wasn't ready on the forums. But either way it was still somewhat enjoyable to play with but with Aftermath I felt bored even though helping a bunch of randoms try and clear the city but we all felt a bit bored and ended up leaving. I really hope they add more to this and maybe scale things back abit and focus on completing one thing at a time...
I will look forward to trying it again down the road but for now don't waste your time, if you have H1Z1 or even Warz/Infected I think you would be enjoying it more then Aftermath at it's current state. It just doesn't feel ready or interesting at the moment.

Okay. Lakeview is nothin' but bare-bones pixel graphics. However, if you have even an iota of imagination to fill in the grisly details that the game often mercifully omits, guess what?
This is easily one of the single most hinder-clenchingly, sick, twisted, and terrifying games ever made.

And the minimalistic visuals only help the horror, inviting your mind fill in all the gorey details. The well-placed musical stings perfectly accent the aural ambience that gives every part of this collection of micro-terror titles a constant sense of dread and suspense.
My only gripe is that the original flash game, which inspired this anthology, is not available in this set.
It's freely available on any number of sites, but its absence is still something of a bummer.

This game has the same feel as the original X-Com, much more so than the Firaxis remake. While the remake has a small team, they tend to feel more like some sort of action movie super team. In Xenonauts, your team dies. And dies. And dies some more. When you reveal the map, you only increase the tension for those places still hidden, the awareness growing that as you eliminate hiding places you are only closing the range and make it easier for the unknown enemies to perforate your squad with vastly superior firepower. The fire superiority enjoyed by your foes makes no difference to the mission generator, often outnumbering your soldiers as well. You deliberately harden your heart to avoid becoming too attached to that one officer who can move a quarter way across the map and still have time units and accuracy to put a shot through an alien's eye because you know it's just a matter of time until...BANG! And your favorite is a crumpled corpse on the ground, not even identified by name.
Then you finish the mission (if it's not a total wipe), go back to base, and hire some more, ready to do it again.

This game is excellent, not just for an early access game, but overall. While it clearly needs polishing, bug fixing, and needs more features and content to keep me coming back, what is there so far is brilliant.
You play as an Astronaut who lands on a procedurally generated planet with nearly nothing. You have your spacesuit, which can store some oxygen and power. It slowly generates power, can store 8 items, and has a mini 3D printer to make useful gadgets out of raw materials. The power is only good, at first, for using your terrain modifier tool. This is how you harvest materials, among other things.
You also have the habitat lander you arrived in. It provides limitless oxygen, so long as you stay within a few metres. You can extend this range by placing tethers, made in your mini printer, or by expanding your base using resin harvested from the planet.
The game (so far) has no end goal. You have a planet to explore at your whim, and later you'll be able to explore the rest of the solar system. You have plenty of control over how you do so, too. Nearly everything you can build can be attached to other things, in various ways. Things fit together intuitively.
I won't give this game a numerical rating while it's still in development. Though it may well be the best early access game I've ever played. It also ranks decently high among finished games.

This is something of a milestone here at the HOGuru's Haunt. That name is not going to catch on, I'm guessing. The milestone, though, is something else - this is the first all-3D HOG I've even encountered. It may be the only all-3D HOG there is, although I'll have to do some research into that. I'm used to the occasional 3D backdrop, and I've seen plenty of 3D animated cutscenes, but Ferrum Secrets is the first time I've seen someone build an entire world out of polygons and then dump a bunch of items in one place and expect me to sift through them. Based on this audacity alone Ferrum deserved a look, and I was certainly surprised by what I found.
Criteria 1: To what degree do the puzzle screens look like a thrift store vomited on my monitor?
Almost not at all. This is the first thing I noticed about Ferrum Secrets - objects seem less random and arbitrary in 3D. I'm sure this is partially a factor of the novelty, but the internal consistency of having the various clickable items all made of the same basic lines and textures as its surroundings massively simplified the struggle of getting artwork to match that so bedevils 2D HOGs. This could easily sound like damning with faint praise - 'everything looks terrible, so the objects fit right in!' - but that's not my take on it at all. While the environments may be primitive, harkening back to the days of Myst or D, the locations they depict - a trashed house, a run-down factory - are the kinds of places one would expect to have scattered piles of refuse, so setting HOSs there seems natural.
Criteria 2: Are the searches justified by the premise/story?
Not entirely - the hidden object screens are largely of 12:1 construction, other than one diversion to find plants for a potion. The game's developers at least recognize that this is an issue, so they cover up the problem with a figleaf explanation, having their heroine announce that she should 'clean up' the various areas if she's ever going to find the item she needs. The screens aren't then constructed so that a variety of items actually have to be removed in order to find the important one, but at least some effort is being put in.
Criteria 3: How well do the various puzzles and object searches meld together to form a coherent whole?
The game is all over the map here. While I applaud the interesting choice of engine and art style, it's impossible to overlook how shoddy and random much of the construction is. The HOSs are well-designed, and there are some fairly clever puzzles - especially one that takes advantage of the 3D camera to let players move around a series of pipes that they need to turn on and off. The story around them is just odd, almost as if it was cobbled together around the assets that they developers had on hand, rather than starting with the plot and constructing from there.
The story concerns an evil fog that has fallen over a city, and the disappearing scientists who are somehow involved in its creation. Nothing wrong with that, other than the fact that there's no fog to be seen in the vast majority of the game. The most puzzling thing, however, is a strange interlude in which a witch helps the player brew a potion to cure an arbitrary illness they gained in the previous chapter. If it seems like the witch in question looks like she's ready to his something with a magic staff, that's because she's obviously a pre-made model that the developers simply dropped into the game, irrespective of how it fit into the setting. It's incredibly jarring to be playing a game about stopping a steampunk zeppelin from using chemical weapons on a metropolis and then suddenly have a sidequest send me into a magical dungeon to find reagent. The whole sequence obviously exists only to pad out the game's extremely short running time, so I was understanding - but it still derails attempts at narrative pretty badly.
Despite its extremely short running time and fairly basic puzzles/HOSs (I neglected to mention, but 3D hidden objects are much easier to find than 2D ones), I was fascinated by Ferrum Secrets. Yes, that's entirely due to the fresh concept, but if nothing else, this game should encourage other developers to take risks with the genre. This isn't a great game, but as a proof of concept that HOGs can work in far more broad environments than had previously been believed, it might just be an important one.

Ferrum’s Secrets is amateurish, but in a charming way. It is not a good hidden object game by any means, but somehow can entice the player to stay on board until the story’s end.
Ferrum’s Secrets: where is grandpa is the kind of indie title that, by all accounts, should be considered terrible. Yet there is something in its crude stumbling of a design that makes it interesting; intriguing, even.
It is difficult to tell where that mysterious charm lies. Visually, it is nothing special: a typical Unity engine game, where even the hidden object parts are 3D scenes of hard-to-recognise low-polygon blocks. (On the other hand, the environments are full of attention to little details.)
The rest feels like some half-finished adventure game with a strange difficulty curve. It is mostly straightforward, like any decent HOG, except for chapter 3. There, get ready for endless backtracking and a maze where it is more difficult to find the entrance than the exit.
The story is, well, a mess. Awkward dialogues, hard-to-follow plot about some kidnapped grandfather who is one of the key people in some steampunk conspiracy orchestrated by an evil factory owner, and an entire chapter that I swear was pasted from some other, unfinished game. It is not hopelessly terrible, but I wouldn’t blame anyone who gives up trying to follow this plot.

Ferrum's Secrets does a few intersting things, but ultimately is too tedious to keep me gripped.
Firstly, the absence of much sound and music makes the game feel a bit empty.
The 3D models and textures are okay, nothing special or horrible.
That stuff is what matters least though, as the important aspect is always gameplay.
The problem with Ferrum's Secrets is I found the gameplay very frustrating. Many times, it's not obvious what you can and can't click on, and the fact that objects you can interact with are so close to scene change borders. There were quite a few times where I tried to grab something, but found myself going to the next area by accident.
I also felt like not all of the puzzles were very intuitive. There were a decent amount of times where I just used the hint button because I lost my patience with trying to understand what to do.
The game does a decent job at trying to keep the gameplay fresh. There are times where you walk around interacting with objects and placing them around as you'd expect. Other times, the game will have you play a mini object-finding section, where you have a list of random items to find in a scene. These were all pretty easy and didn't add much to the game in my opinion, but it was a nice change from the regular gameplay.
You'll also occasionally have small puzzles to solve that have their own made up rules for that section. Figuring the right order of switches, or turning off the correct pipes. Again, it's a welcome change of pace, but they weren't incredibly fun.
Overall, it's a decent game, but it doesn't offer anything special enough to make it worth getting through some of the frustrations the game comes with. If you're a great enthusiast when it comes to this genre, perhaps you can still find a bit of fun in this one for a cheap enough price.

If you haven't bought the game after that announcement, you probably never will, because frankly kittens are its only selling point. The writing is terrible, the sounds are cheap, the 3D modeling is very cheap, the puzzles are awful, movement is clunky, but there's a kitten in almost every scene.
How awful are these puzzles? Let me give you an example: your task is to pick up all golden animals that are stored in some wooden cabinet, but you can't just take them, you can only take those in the list, and as you take them new animals get listed that you may then take, until --surprise-- you have taken them all. Note also that words don't stay in place on the list, but they move around. Another task is to assemble a light bulb (a science wtf in itself without a way to fill it with an inert gas). There's a handy wall poster with the parts labeled 1 through 4, but that won't help you any because you need to start with a cable that is not on the poster or it won't work. Of course once you take the bulb the useless cable is left behind. A third example? You need to get to a switch panel with a simple light-flipping puzzle in it, but it is padlocked; you found a key, but it fell to the floor, and rather than pick it up yourself (with a stick or something), the kitten has to do it, so now you need to throw some cat food item next to the key, and then a spider appears and scares the kitten, so you have to open a toolbox with spider poison to somehow make the spider vanish so the kitten can fetch the key for you. Trust me, it does not get better, and I haven't even mentioned the spinning hidden objects puzzle yet, which is an idea that nobody else has done before for a good reason.
Whoever played this and said they enjoyed it is lying. Or they like kittens a lot. I don't.

Ever heard of early access survival games made purely of Unity assets? Welcome to the hidden objective version of it.
I bought this game because it was one sale and I was curious how a 3D HO game would look like. Unfortunately it turned out it was not worth it. It's just a really, really bad game.
The options are basically non existant. There are windowed mode on/off (which doesn't work anyway) and audio on/off.
There's no intro or any introduction whatsoever, so you don't really know what's going on, what universe are you in etc. Shortly after the beginning you learn that you are some girl who's looking for her missing grandfather.
The first chapter is rather pleasant and consistent, however the rest of the game looks like an unfinished school project (this would certainly be a fail at my university).
The story is very poor, inconsistent, full of plotholes and generally makes no sense. We jump between modern times to medieval ages (I guess, we're in some hut with an alchemist casting spells), back to modern times and at the end we even encounter some "robots".
There are some basic sound effects, but there's only few of them and you hear them only occasionally. The music is quite pleasant, perfect for this kind of games. There's only one theme but it's not annoying.
The game is made of Unity assets and you can see how the developers got lazier and lazier the longer they were working on it. The "robots" in the last chapter are just soldiers painted black, stuck in a shooting animations without a weapon. The novelty of the 3D HO game wore off really quickly and became just annoying. I've never seen a "loading" screen in a HO game before.
Hidden object scenes are not randomized so there's no replayability value (who would want to play it twice anyway). Puzzles are very easy and offer absolutely no challenge. Some of them (e.g. the safe) are very counterintuitive and if you leave a puzzle and come back to it, there's a high change of it getting bugged (it starts from the beginning, but the graphics are just as you left it).
The GUI is horrible. Especially maps seem like they were made in MS Paint.
At the end of chapter one there's a very bizzare spinning hidden object scene which made me feel rather sick. Lucikly there was only one, because it wasn't pleasant at all.
I can't recommend this game, even if it's in a bundle for $1.

Oh boy... here we go again. I'm going to review this game as neutral as I possibly can, but I will be touching on some very strong opinions because of my past with this dev team. "Romero's Aftermath" is developed and self published by a spin off group named Free Reign Entertainment. I say spin off because the majority of the dev team came from War Z/Infestation Survivor Stories. Some of them were existing devs from the start, some joined further into the War Z project, and now, some are obviously new. The "lead" or head of all of this is none other than Sergey Titov. You will remember his stellar leadership paving the way for War Z which is arguably the single most controversial title to EVER hit PC Gaming.
That said... this is an open world, survival horror game. There is rumor that George Romero has approved of the use of his name in the title... but I wouldn't count on that lasting after he learns about this game and the dev team. Most people turn and run as fast as they can when getting involved in this group. That all said, I will try and be as neutral as I can be for the sake of the review.
I reference graphics early on because a significant portion of gamers wont touch a game unless it's top tier standard in the graphics department. Well then look no further. If you're one of those types, don't bother downloading this game. The textures are extremely sub-par. I'm not entirely sure if this engine is to blame or the lack of dev experience... but they are exactly the same as War Z was which is a 3 year old game. Nothing has changed. I don't understand why the devs can't improve on something which was poor the first time around. Anyway, don't expect to be blown away by anything here.
Now most survival games have almost no storyline. But plenty of open world games do. So while this game is both, it has no story at all. Don't expect anything in terms of questing, bits of story (like newspapers), NPC's, or anything else that would add weight to the game. It is kill, or be killed. You can do a bit of base building, but ultimately you need to go out there and gather supplies to survive.
There is a sort of side quest system in place that allows you to complete "objectives" in a town like getting a generator fixed, that will give you a reward. But, don't expect to profit much from this, and certainly don't expect much in the way of depth to the "side quests".
The meat and potatoes of this game is the combat. The majority of what you'll be dealing with, is combat. Whether that be killing AI zombies, or other players if you choose the PvP server... you will need to fight at some point. The store page talks about being a trader and such... but that would be near impossible without a little bit of fighting first.
The mechanics of combat is pretty terrible and clunky. The animations make it hard to really fight well. It's pull sniper duty, or spray. You can try some low level tactics with other players... flanking and the like. But the engine and how the game plays leaves little room to really enjoy the combat. It's mindless killing.
The Zombie AI in the game is horrendous and makes combat with them impossible. You just swing or shoot and at some point the AI dies. Coupled with the terrible performance (see below)... don't expect much in the way of ENJOYABLE combat.
Weapons can be "upgraded" (attachments) and you can get skins for them. A LOT of skins in fact. If this is something that interests you (like Counterstrike players) then you might actually like that aspect of the game. The player too can be "upgraded" with various skins (all sorts of clothing items from hats to masks to shirts to pants). So if having a slightly unique appearance (not a long of ways to change your face and body)... then you'll have fun grinding for cash or paying for the in-game "premium" currency (GD)  to get the items.
I run a PC with the following specs:
AMD FX-8370 (8 core CPU) @ 4.01ghz
G.Skill RAM 16GB @ 1600mhz
Asus GTX 960 2GB
Windows 10
The MOST frames I pulled with the game nearly maxed out... 15. The average frames I pulled looking out to nothing was around 10 or so. Which even for a beta, is absolute trash. I was so frustrated with this latest version of the game when attacking a zombie at 8 fps, that I had to stop playing. I would have at least given it another 30 minutes or so... just couldn't do it.
There's also a LOT of pop in with graphics. Especially player gardens that seem to pop up within 50m or so. It was surprising and annoying. I was not at ALL impressed with how this game ran.
I talked about clunky animations and due to the shart performance, the AI was laggy, clunky, and impossible to combat. I had to struggle at 8fps to run circles around the AI just hoping that between slideshows, that I was hitting something.
The history of this dev team is going to weigh down on how their game is received and probably the future of it. Don't expect this game to set standards and raise any bars at all. With it's ridiculous fps problems (which is sub-par for most dev teams), poor animations and lacking combat... this isn't a game most people will enjoy.
There are some interesting features (skins and such) that some people might like. But it doesn't balance out the issues the game has. Even if it is in a beta state, this game is severely struggling and will continue to struggle.
The only thing going for it, is it's free. But there are some pay to win features that ruin that for most people. While you can't buy guns and ammo with real life cash like in War Z, you can buy blueprints. That's a HUGE advantage vs a player who spends nothing. Which plays heavily on multiplayer.
In the end... do I think this is a game you should get? No. If you want to play something for free with absolutely no intentions on committing to it... try it. But it's not worth it if you ask me.

If you go into Aftermath, don't go in with the old War Z marketing fails in mind to sour your opinion before you give it a chance. There's actually a lot of content here to enjoy and it works quite well.

I got this bundled with a video card purchase.  I'd barely heard of it (I don't keep up with new releases really), and I let it sit for a couple of years before I got around to playing it.  Was that ever a mistake!  This is simply one of the most fun games I've ever played.  I was never really into RPGs until Mass Effect introduced me to the shooter/RPG hybrid.  This one knocks it out of the park, providing the best of both worlds.  Skills, abilities, and JUST the right amount of addicting grinding and looting so that it scratches that Pavlovian itch but doesn't become tedious.  It's an actual benefit and feature of the game, not cheap tricks by the developer to addict the player/pad the play time.  And it's a nearly flawless  FPS with plenty of variety of weapons to suit anyone's desired play style.  The great gameplay is then wrapped up in fantastic writing centered around clever and just plain hysterical dialogue and ridiculous characters, and dropped into a mind-numbingly huge and intricate world.  Attention to detail just oozes out of the game everywhere.
I want to go back and replay for a variety of reasons, but I just can't do it right now because the game's too huge and too awesome to devote that much time to for a replay.  I wish I could comment on the multiplayer, but for one, multiplayer in general isn't usually my thing, and I was late to the party.

Let me break this down for you.
The game advertises customizing your guns to fit your playstyle. Unfortunately, to do that, you will need to grind. A lot. First you have to grind contacts to unlock that gun, then you have to grind kills to get upgrades for that gun (that may not even be the upgrade type you want).
And the grinding will NOT be fun. The playerbase is all but gone, which means matchmaking (not that it was EVER good) is horrible. Expect to be stomped on constantly by the folks who have spent plenty of cash for the much more effective ARMAS weapons. Also expect to be matched up against gold players as a bronze or silver a lot. They hang out in the bronze districts because there's nobody to be found in silver or gold.
So if you like being forced to open the ARMAS store every time you open the game (unless you turn off Steam in-game), having UPGRADE NOW flash at you every time you finish a mission, and having to get your♥♥♥♥♥stomped on for hours upon hours because there's literally nobody else to play against, this game is for you.
If you don't like lessons in masochism, do not play this game. I tried. I really tried to enjoy the game, but I just couldn't... and I fear you might not either.
Unless you drop a couple hundred dollars and start mowing people down. Then you might like it.
EDIT: Lest I forget there IS a way to get the cash shop guns by grinding tons of in-game cash and daily limited Joker tickets. So if you're a masochist, this game is for you.

Famaze is a unique, casual sort of dungeon crawler that borders on being strategy and planning. There are two halves of the game, the top and bottom. The lower half shows a 2D side view of you and everything around you. The top shows the mini map. This map is what you'll really be paying attention to. You move north, south, east and west by moving up, down, left and right. This is why I say you'll be paying attention tot he map, because the bottom of the screen is a 2D side view of the action. Right and left on the side view isn't always east and west on the map. So if you're pushing left looking at the bottom of the screen and you can't head west on the map, you won't go anywhere. The object of the game is to find the key and get to the locked door. There are a certain amount of randomly generated mazes to get through, where you then see your statistics and get an ending. Its not about the finish though, its about the journey. With the randomly generated mazes, every play through is different. Every death means a new dungeon to explore.
The map is a maze of hallways, with no rooms. On the map you see the halls, walls, your location, enemies in red, items in dark blue, rutabagas in sky blue, treasures in yellow and sleeping enemies are dark red. You can see these things a certain distance away from you so you can plan to avoid things accordingly. Some enemies will move, but treasures, rutabagas and items will not. Your map starts out dark, but the more you explore, the more of the map gets uncovered.
These enemies are easy, you don't fight them so much as bump into them with you both dealing damage to one another. To fight, just walk in their direction on the map. Its that easy. You can stand in front of a foe without them attacking. There are a variety of enemies with different habits. Purple slimes will blot out some of your explored map. Skeletons will rise up after you walk by them. Ghosts will steal your items. Wizards will chase after you. Cycloptic floating heads are asleep in the dark until you light up an area near them, then they'll wake. There are of course standard attackers like paroling spiders, goblins and the more difficult fat red trolls. You can run from most enemies without them following you.
When you start the game, you select from three classes. The knight starts with a health potion and can use a charge attack. The thief can see and disarm traps, and has a teleport potion to almost completely avoid combat. The wizard can transmute an item and has a powerful fireball. This fireball plows through enemies on your map. Even enemies that you're not fighting, the fireball travels straight down the hallway destroying lesser foes in its path. Its effective, to make up for the wizard's low attack power. The only problem is that the fireball counts as an item and can only get used once before its gone.
You can get XP from defeating enemies and lighting torches in order to level up and make combat easier. The torches lit are worth far more XP than enemies you defeat. After the first level, its difficult to increase XP, so it becomes worthless in my opinion.
There are no weapons or armor. You have what you have from start to finish, so this isn't a traditional dungeon crawler. Less micro management makes it easier for casual players. Instead, it is the items that mix up the game. You can hold two items at a time, to use them, hit the number keys. Potions refill your health. Flares light up a small part of the map while killing nearby enemies and turning distant ones into rutabagas. Even if an enemy walks into the light, they will transform. A teleport potion will let you transport yourself to anywhere on the mini map in the upper half of the screen, but not the full map. The key counts as an item, so it takes up a slot in your inventory to make things more interesting. There are several items and objects littered through a maze. Dare I say almost an item for every enemy depending on the map.
Along the way through each maze, you'll find all these items, but you'll also find torches, lights or lanterns. Whatever they are, when you light them up, the map around the area brightens up. Much like a flare, but a larger size. So active enemies turn into rutabagas, cycloptic heads wake up and traps now show up on your map. That's right, Famaze has traps, so if you spend your time completely avoiding enemies and running from them, eventually, you'll find hidden traps. These traps only damage you and without the light from a stationary torch or a flare, you won't see them.
The entire story revolves around the rutabagas, the mad king has turned them all into monsters, and you need to turn them back. So the real object is to hit lights, that turn the enemies into rutabagas and then collect them. These rutabegas give you health for touching them, so it leads me to believe, you're actually eating them. Eating the things you're trying to save. It is probably a lot easier to transport them in your stomach than to carry them in a sack. It doesn't matter though, it all goes to statistics at the end of each level and the end of each game.
As for the treasures, they are nothing more than a score at the end of each level and I'm sure add up to more at the end of each play through. You'll find standard treasures and treasure chests. Sometimes the chests contain more gold for your score, other times its spikes. Risk and reward. There are even health floor tiles that refill your energy just once and teleportation tiles that send you to a different part of the map. These all blend together to make the game more interesting and engaging beyond what I find in deeper less casual dungeon crawlers.
Also in the maze are seven collectable artifacts. I'm not sure if all seven are in each play through, but I was able to find the first two on my first play through. Then I found the rest in following play throughs. I think it is a way to extend the life of what is an hour long game. On top of that, you unlock a harder difficulty after completing the default quest.
Between each level you'll see a random charming scene over your treasure and rutabaga score. Its a nice addition to what could have just been a score screen.
The lower half has a great 8-bit art style. Charming sprites without much animation. As the game progresses and you go maze to maze, the backgrounds and music both change. New enemies get thrown in, so I feel like there's a good sense of progression. The music itself is good and fits into a dark chip tune feel of wandering through a dungeon. Yet, the music doesn't loop it just stops until you find the key. Maybe less is more, but I wish the music would loop or something.
Now for the downsides. The game is vertical since it has a top and bottom half. I feel like its meant for a smart phone and not a computer screen. Double clicking the game will make it full screen windowed, but it does nothing for the resolution. Its just a black screen with the game in the center. The game has no mouse or native controller support. I'd much rather play the game with a controller especially with how simple it is.
With everything said, I can recommend it. Maybe its not for hardcore dungeon crawler fans since it feels more like a strategy, but people that want an easy little pick up and play game that strays from the norm. While its a charming, easy to play game, I don't think there's enough fun here to keep me in it for that long. It would be the perfect game for a phone.
