Oh man. I wanted to like this one, God knows I love HOG games, but just, no.
In Ferrum’s Secrets you play the role of some girl who goes look for her grandpa (an inventor) who was apparently abducted by an unknown person for unknown reasons. Okay, to be fair the reasons are kinda sorta disclosed in broken English at some point, I had kind of stopped paying attention by then.
The story itself could be a decent typical HOG one, and the game could be an average one as it had a good general idea, but the execution was just awful.
From the start the game was annoying: The windowed mode provides no resolution options, leaving you with a window the same size as your screen, making the mode pointless. There is only one option for sound/music - muted or not. If you mute it, you miss out the in game sounds which aren’t too bad, but if you don’t mute it you’re driven insane by the ill-fitting music on the menu. There’s no voice acting, thankfully. The menu itself is unpleasant to look at.
The graphics are so-so. They’re done with Unity and are 3D, people look pretty decent, but everything else looks pretty bland and blends in. The 3D adds the annoyance of making the game slow and laggy.
The UI/GUI is awful looking, huge, clunky, and obscures clicking areas in some cases. The clicking areas of items is rather specific too, and sometimes you found yourself trying to click an item placed at the end of the screen only to end up in another location because they kind of overlapped.
The tutorial is short, in the way, and not overly helpful.
You’re thrown into the game with no explanation of what you’re doing there, no intro, no background, no nothing. And while I love the cats, I had started to wonder just how many friggin’ cats did this grandpa had before the girl decided to make me note at last that it was just the same cat (hers) following her around.
Most of the story is told through notes or through written dialogue that just goes by too slow in some occasions, and way too fast in others. This would have been easily solvable by allowing the user to click to get past the dialogues.
It also needs some major editing because the English in it is terribly broken.
Also, it can’t seem to make up its mind if it’s about inventors, magic, or both, as we’re all in a steampunk-like kind of setting at the start and then suddenly there’s this druid/witch like person. Ok?
The Hidden Object scenes are boring, either too easy to solve or have words that are a bit weird that made me search for the object for way too long because it wasn’t quite the right word.
The minigames have no explanations; granted, most don’t need them as they’re fairly simple, but then there’s a couple where you’re not really sure what you’re supposed to do. At all. And get no help, because… The Hint system is inconsistent. You never know when it will or won’t work. Sometimes it gets stuck in a loop or forces you to an unnecessary step (ie. carrying a light) when there’s no need to, in order to have you progress.
Oh, and finally, the spinning hidden object area was horrible. I was lucky it didn’t last long enough to make me dizzy, but it had some small items to try and click on which moved way too fast as the things spun, which only made the torture longer as I couldn’t click the exact pixel I needed.
On the upside, it’s kind of cute that you can interact with a couple objects (bump them aside or tip them over), and you can choose the game difficulty, but it hardly makes up for the hassles.

Ferrum's Secrets: Where Is Grandpa? is a HOG game from an indie dev, it's main feature is its 3D.
The pros:
You can choose the difficulty as in most of the HOGs: casual, advanced and expert mode.
3D environment, when you click on a place to investigate it the camera pans and zoom on it
Music/ambiance is nice and soothing
Story is really interesting and intriguing
Dev is obviously a cat lover, like me :)
The cons:
No sound options but there's almost no sounds anyway, only music; it's very odd. The story is badly told: no intro whatsoever and all the bits of story are hidden in the journal (which isn't even pointed at by the tutorial!) or in hidden notes scattered in the game. That's definetly not a good way to tell a story -.-
Plus the very rare story texts stay on screen for a too short time, they should wait for an input instead. Throughout the game a lot of centered texts pop up could have been added to explain the player progression, instead of a small 1 line text displayed on top of the screen for 2 seconds exactly. The 3D enviromenment makes everything like a maze so a few holding hands texts would help. Funnily enough, clicking around aimlessly makes a big window of text appear and nags you for looong seconds. And you'll see it often since you cannot see your way or because you're trying to find what you're supposed to do to advance.
The mini games are awful: obscure, with no explanation. The 3D view made the first one annoying and confusing, the second one had buttons and lamps that were too tiny. Luckily they can be skipped. Mini games should be totally scrapped and redone.
The HOG screen are too dark and uninspired and the lack of sound while picking objects make it very odd. The objects to pick are ugly, texture-less and sometimes tiny. The first HOG screen was nice, but the rest quickly went downhill.
Most of the screens are too dark (really!!) and it's hard to see the useful items in there. Tools are all amost black, and the hidden collectibles are almost white. the whole house being almost pitch black is funny since the missing grandpa was an electrician, he obviously wasn't very skilled haha... So maybe an angry customer got his revenge! ^^
Navigating in the rooms is not obvious at all, you'll often miss other room entrances unless you
pointed your mouse on the correct exact pixel. Navigations arrows would help.
I cannot help but think that the number one sale argument of the game - it being in 3D - quickly
becomes its cons as it makes The navigation too confusing. Add to that the screens being too dark, the lack of sound and the lack of dialogues and story. The game would benefit from a bit of patching and updating - it feels unfinished as it is. The base is really good, but it definetly doesn't feel finished.
It was a bit hard to decide whether to upvote or downvote. I don't want to punish the game with a No as it doesn't deserve it, but I wish there was a Meh vote instead. As for me I didn't even finish the game, couldn't stand the never ending dark room after dark room after dark room with not a slight idea of what I'm doing or going. I gave up in "Living Room II". It's just not fun. I love HOGs games but this one is more a tech demo. As a glance at the screenshots will tell you, the graphics are awful.  Rather than use hand drawn sprites, this game instead uses crude models for objects.  Not only does this obscure the identities of many items in hidden object scenes, it also combines with the bad lighting effects to create frequent pixel hunts in the rest of the game.
This is made even worse by the narrow areas in which to click and use several objects.  One of the crowning moments of fail was when I used lubricant on a rusty gauntlet.  It didn't work, so I tried the hint button, and I was right all along!  Except, oh wait, I was supposed to put the mouth of the bottle on the gauntlet, not the middle.  Silly me!
Dialogue from NPCs only stays up for a couple of seconds at a time, much of it can't be repeated, and very few objectives get logged in your notebook.  Combined with the attrocious English translation, this led to several cases where I didn't know what I was even supposed to be doing.  Top that with the aforementioned pixel hunts, and I don't think I would have made it through without the hint button.
The hidden object scenes do that thing where only part of the list appears at a time and you can't click items that aren't listed.  It's not even justified like in Artifex Mundi's crafting puzzles.  It's just a pointless annoyance.
The only case in which I would recommend
is to an aspiring game developer who wishes to see a prime example of how not to make a hidden object game.  To everyone else, stay away!

Rust is a sandbox survival game which is certainly not for the faint hearted. This is a game which has really come along in terms of design since it's conception with Rust Legacy. Firstly, being able to have large server populations with ~500 players is something the gaming world has desired for a long time, and Rust fulfills that. The UI is well thought out and nice to interact with compared to most other games. The crafting system is extensive and there is a progression element as any item blueprints you learn are permanently added to your characters crafting options, meaning they reamain with you even if you die. Combat is patchy, as lag and general jankiness are sometimes an issue (compared to most FPS titles). You can play this game alone or with groups of various sizes. The in-game VOIP is pretty decent. The map is huge. Be prepared to die a lot and learn the hard way. I can see this game sticking around and being continually updated for a while - even once it gets out of early access.

Sonic Adventure...I have very fond memories of playing this game as a child. However, this may be one of the better Sonic games, but looking at it now...it's nowhere near as good as I remember it.
But something to remember about this game is that it's the first 3D Sonic game! It was a risky move on Sega's part since the jump to 3D could have either turned out very good or horribly wrong, but Sonic translates very well in 3D, with him acting the same as in the 2D games. This game even introduced a move that would later on become a series staple, the homing attack, where Sonic will automatically lock onto and attack any enemy near him. And it was a much-needed addition to the 3D game, as it allows him to, well...home in on enemies in order to attack them easier and reach higher places.
The game is split into six different campaigns, each with their own character that (actually) plays differently: Sonic, Tails, AND KNUCKLES, Amy, newcomer Gamma, and newcomer Big the Cat.
One of the game's biggest strengths is actually the story. It of course involves Eggman trying to take over the world, as always, with a large ship known as the Egg Carrier.
However, what he also does is reawaken an ancient, evil water-monster known as Chaos, who changes form and becomes stronger each time he absorbs the Chaos Emeralds. The lore behind Chaos and how he came to be is very interesting, and is also surprisingly pretty dark and tragic, which's rare to see in a Sonic game.
Well...in a way that's actually done right, that is. *shivers at the memory of Sonic '06, Shadow the Hedgehog and Sonic and the Black Knight. But that's a talk for another day.*
As for Tikal, the surviving member of an extinct tribe of Echnidas, she basically serves the same role as Naminé: explain exposition and backstory, and nothing more. What at least makes her a bit more interesting is that she was the only one who saw the good in Chaos in the past, when everyone else viewed him as nothing but a destructive monster that should be killed.
And Big is the biggest and dumbest doofus in the world, but in a way that is strangely endearing.
Gamma's story is the strongest and most heartbreaking out of them all. Sure, he follows the trope of a robot originally built to kill learning to care about living things (*cough cough* Android 16, The Iron Giant, Bastion), but because of this he has to fight and destroy every one of his other robot brothers that Dr. Eggman created as well. And that ending...oh my lords...
Sadly, the game hasn't aged that well due to the terrible camera, horrific voice acting where the characters talk over eachother and the music is too loud to even hear them, and dialogue that's delivered awkwardly and has little to no regard for lip-syncing.
As for the graphics...I mean, they're fine for what they were at that time. Save for the humans, who look like box people.
There's also these huge hubworlds to move around and explore in between levels, like in a Sandbox game. While there isn't as much stuff to do as in said sanbox game, you can talk to NPCs, find upgrades for your character and do special missions within levels. And best out of all, find Chao Gardens. Which I'll go more into later.
As for said levels, Sonic's are of course the best, being that you can dash through them at adrenaline-filled speeds. And you have Tails at your side almost all the time, like in Sonic the Hedgehog 2, who can be controlled with a second controller. Which's as close to multiplayer as you'll get in this game.
Tails's campaign involves races against Sonic, which gives you an incentive to move through the levels as fast as possible, and you also have his unique ability to fly, which allows you to reach shortcuts in order to best Sonic.
Knuckles's campaign includes finding the shattered pieces of the Master Emerald, three of which are hidden in certain areas within each level as a radar at the bottom of your screen will blink faster whenever you're close to them. I liked these levels because they're a unique game of hide-and-seek, and require you to be very wary and meticulous of your surroundings. They make good use of his abilities as well, which are a wide array that includes punching things, climbing walls, gliding, and later on digging.
But after these three campaigns is when this game begins to lose its luster.
Amy and Gamma's campaigns are simply okay. Amy's is very slow and has you be pursued by a robot all throughout it. While you can't destroy the robot, you can stun him by hitting him with your hammer, along with smashing the enemies and obstacles within your path.
While Gamma's levels are simple and straightforward due to just blasting through them with a lock-on lazer beam, and the addition of a time limit makes them unforgivably stressful.
Yet those two are amazing compared to Big's campaign. Like...I sincerely hope that whoever thought putting FISHING in a Sonic game was quickly fired later on.
There's nothing mechanically wrong with these stages, being that you simply fish in the water until you end up catching Big's friend, Froggy. But they're just so boring and unremarkable that I almost couldn't get through them as a kid. Not because they were difficult, but no part of me actually WANTED to complete them. At least the other campaigns have you actively DOING something, but here, you just sit around on your butt doing basically nothing but waiting. In a game meant for you to ACTIVELY BE DOING THINGS.
Clearing them all unlocks the final boss, where Chaos absorbs all the Chaos Emeralds and basically becomes Godzilla.
But what trumps everything else is the Chao Garden. Oh my lords in heaven, the Chao Garden...
While it's very simple, the Chao Garden are areas that you access in the overworld that brings you to a, well...Chao Garden. Here you can raise your own Chaos, give them items and animals (which you get from the destroying enemies) in order to make them stronger, and have them compete in various minigames. It's incredibly addictive, and I remember spending more time with this feature than the actual game.
The soundtrack is pretty nifty as well, even if the character themes getting annoying after a while due to them playing EVERY time a character appears.
There was also a rerelease of this game titled Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut, which includes 60 additional missions, a way to unlock and play all the classic Sonic games, and if all emblems are collected, then you will be able to play as Metal Sonic in the Sonic stages.
Excuse me while I go emblem hunting.
In the end, while Sonic Adventure may not be as fantastic as I remember it and has aged very poorly, it's still a solid Sonic game. Even if Amy and Gamma's campaigns are generic and Big's is mediocre, and the voice acting and camera are horrendous, the fast-paced and exciting Sonic and Tails campaigns, ingenious Knuckles campaign, the open-world exploration and mesmerizing Chao Garden cause it to be an overall worthwhile experience. I recommend it to any Sonic fan or anyone who wants to get into the Sonic series.

Eversion starts off as a jolly happy platformer where you control Zeetee, a walking flower with adorable eyes. It plays and looks very much like Mario; you bounce around collecting things whilst killing monsters by landing on their heads. Get to the end of the game and rescue the princess. It’s all very basic stuff – or so one would think.
What makes this game unique is that the main character has the ability to manipulate the world around him. When that happens, certain objects in the game change. Clouds solidify, making them safe to walk on. Trees become withered, allowing you to walk through them. Monsters stop moving, plants turn hazardous, rocks turn into rock monsters, and so on and so forth. There are seven different stages of world alteration, and not only does it change the graphics and objects, but also the music soundtrack as well.
As you traverse each level (there are eight in total), you experience… well… let’s just say you experience. Sorry to cut this review rather short, but saying anything else might result in unintentional spoilers.
I’ll round it off by saying this; Eversion is no Spelunky. It’s no Shovel Knight, and it’s certainly no game that will last you several weeks or months. That’s Eversion’s one big drawback; it doesn’t last very long. I’ve played it for two hours, and virtually uncovered everything the game had to offer.
Having said that, I recommend Eversion to anyone mature, who want to discover something a little out of the ordinary.

Game is clearly inspired by the old friday the 13th movies. If you enjoy those films or simply find them hilarious. This is most likely game for you.
You are not told what to do but that is simply the charm of the game. You control four characters and attempt to stop, avoid and/or escape what ever disaster is eventually hapenning in the "chapter".
Game has four "chapters" with each lot of interactions that eventually you learn and exploit to reach your desired ending.
Completing a chapter with "Good Ending" unlocks special mode for that chapter.
Chapter One: Four summer campers and dog get attacked by very resiliant killer on a small island. Bonus Mode - Zombies!
Chapter Two: Four people are stuck on a property with very sadistic family that have created obstacle course of death. Bonus mode - Treasure Hunt
Chapter Three: Four youngsters are attacked by ghost like serial killer. (This one is really cryptic but forgiving as you can die and continue your progress. Returning from death is big part of the puzzle)
Chapter Four: Inspired by dead space. This one is key hunt in very limited time. I don't want to spoil this chapter because it was quite satisfying to figure out how to beat it.
Epilogue: After you beat all four chapters you can find sort of prequel. There is no much player choise in it, just visual storytelling.
Secret Level: It's not much of a secret level. It's the "Chapter selection" level. It doesn't seem to tie into the story. just fun easter egg that is hinted at in first minute of the game when you are thaught the controls.

After over 100 hours and unlocking almost every single achievment, I can say that this is the best game ever made.
It's super easy to understand, but nearly impossible to master. It has a large (and balanced) difficulty curve, a lot of stuff that wants to kill you and many functional objects as well.
This game isn't hard in a way that you get killed by random falling apples or the piece of floor you touched was bad. Every time you die, it's only your fault. It really motivates you to keep you going forward and at the same time makes the game fresh, fun, and frustrating at times.
Also for those who want more of a challenge, there's also a dark world version for each level. They have exact same layout or concept, except far harder. There are even achievements for completing an entire chapter without dying once.
Get this game if:
-you love platformers
-you like difficult games
-you want a serious challenge
-you hate yourself
-you want to hate yourself more than you do already
-you want to smash your keyboard/controller/desk/wall/house/dog/mom/wife/Edmund
DON'T get this game if:
-you don't like difficult games
-it's on sale
Protip: don't buy this game as a gift to your friends. Like, really. Don't.

It plays like X-COM without being a direct copy of X-COM.  Xenonauts offers you a lot more in the way of tactical planning and decision making, while still leaving room for you to fall into your own pattern and strategy for successful missions.  The variety of weapons is a huge upgrade from X-COM's typical Pistol/Rifle/Heavy weapon, and the balance between the weapons is pretty spot-on; you can use whatever you like, provided you plan accordingly, a strike team of pure pistol-wielding xenonauts is totally viable.
The research text is flavorful and a nice addition, immersing you more in the world and the reality of the invasion while still offering some form of believability.  The geoscape is far more lively, with alien activity being broadcasted as "casualty reports" around the globe when left unchecked, and rather than a single UFO or a few on the same mission appearing, you get swarms of UFOs appearing all over the globe simultaneously, each operating on its own agenda.  This makes having a competent airforce not a luxury but a necessity.
While the game is far from perfect, it still gave me literal days of playtime fun, along with a few agonizing losses and times of near rage-quitting.  Definitely a must play if you enjoyed any of the X-COM games, including the newer reboot.
Just remember to close the door before you end your turn and keep your eyes peeled for reapers.

The strategic aspect of this game is spot on.  Building facilities and managing your budget are key aspects to this game.  And the most enjoyable.
That being said, the tactical part of this game sucks.  It is ENTIRELY based on a poorly designed random number generator (RNG.)  The RNG determines if shots will hit or not.  Your shots frequently miss (and your soilders are ex- SPECOPs by the way,)  while shots from the aliens will pass through several solid objects, including shields and other soilders (without injuring them) and fatally strike a soilder you were retreating.  Shots will frequently miss even at point blank ranges with all weapons, especially with shotguns and sniper rifles (I mean, really, shove the gun down the xeno's throat and pull the f---ing trigger.)  Your troops seem to have failed basic training (read: boot camp.)  They will FREQUENTLY panic without even being shot at.  They will throw down their weapons and run (I once had a soilder run INTO a UFO.  (What the f--- made you think of that idea dumba$$?)  You can not sling a soilder's weapon, throw a grenade, and unsling the weapon (so its back in your soilder's hands) during the same turn.  Needless to say, this make a panic smoke grenade impossible.  It seems that some doors are incapable of being closed (really, you're in the military and you can't close certain doors?)  It seems your soilders are incapable of melee combat without a certain weapon (a stun batton.)  (So, let me get this straight, you DON't know how to slam the butt of your rifle into a xeno's face?)  I've also had issues with soilders throwing grenades at thier feet.  (I'm not even going to say anything about that.)  Finnaly, the alien's psionic abilities are completly imbalanced.  Theroretically, they are capable of mind controling a soilder they can't even see while he is still on the dropship (and possibly dropping a C4 charge with zero turns on the timer.)  Not good at all when a core mechanic of the game is permadeath.
(My English teacher would be saying to start a new paragraph here, so...)
Then there are bugs.  Aliens seem to be capable of seeing through walls (then running up to your assult trooper holding a shot gun and blow his (your soilder's) brains out.  Meanwhile, your three other soilders covering that door don't do a damn thing.  I've had issues with blank screens and freezing as well (and this is a very resource unintensive game runing on a gaming PC.)  I've had soilders get shot, survive, and then drop dead as soon as my turn begins.  Finnaly, in the year 2014, this game uses a launcher.  A launcher that will not launch itself with certain background programs running (i.e. firewall and anti-virus.)

At some point I think I bought the entire Apogee / 3D Realms collection and this is one of the games in there. It’s a fairly standard platformer for the era and DosBox diligently emulates the tremendous amounts of strain these games used to put in CPUs back in the day. Meaning that the game plays at below 20 FPS at all times, making it rather unplayable by modern standards. Enemies can hit you as soon as you can see them and often times it’s not really all that clear what actually hit you.
As is typical for old PC platformers from back in the day, the color palette was nowhere near as refined as on consoles. Backgrounds harshly clash with foreground elements and make the levels a pain to navigate. There are no objectives beyond going right and reaching the end of a level, yet the game is littered with different collectibles that add to a score I’m not certain actually does anything.
If you’re really craving for the dark ages of old-school PC platformers because your parents never bought you an NES, SNES or a Mega Drive, get this. Otherwise, it’s time for the PC gaming master race to accept that there was once a time when consoles really were better.

Let's see, how to explain the awesome that is this this xcom knock off (Yes, it's a knock off, but a GOOD one!). If you liked Enemy Unknown and never played an XCOM game in the past, this might not be for you. If you DID play the old XCOMs and liked them, this is for you. Comparing this to Enemy Uknown, it takes away the watered down feel and brings back all the management complicity that made the older XCOM titles awesome. Don't get me wrong I loved Enemy Unknown, but whereas EU is more focused on action and less on micromanagement of your orginization, Xenonauts basically brings back the full spectrum management feel. Right down to the base building, research, combat, interceptions, etc. It just feels more robust than EU and more like the old XCOMs I loved. Thats my take on it anyway. IMO worth the buy and a good SP time killing machine.

Okay, First. Let me preface this - I'm a LONG time WarZ Vet as well as a long time supporter of Aftermath. I have to this date, somewhere between 400-500 hours clocked inbewteen the Closed Alpha and Open Beta. So, take from this review what you will.
+ PROS:
- Looks nice
(Had a big grahpics downgrade since Alpha, but that should help those with less powerful computers.)
- Big map
Plenty of camps and towns to visit.
- In-depth crafting
(Items require blureprints to craft, which can be found in the world along with items that can be broken down into core materials to use for crafting.)
- PVP.
Its not EXACTLY the same is it was in WarZ. The PVP is slower, but is a good mix of risk vs reward. A skilled palyer can easily take out sever opponents at once.
At the time of writing this, Items drop on death, including guns and ammo. Guns take a durability hit of 50% and ammo that was in the person's backpack is reduced by 50% for the victor (an anti-KoS measure). Annoying as it is, it works well in the envornment,
- Liberations.
Generators - Gas cans - Wrenches, and a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of zombies. Liberate a town, and get rewarded with factory-grade weapons and ammunition and powerful meele weapons.
- Base building.
While not FULLY implemented yet, you can build bases and place storage containers in them to store gear. Very time consuming but a good, rewarding experience for players to take the time to build them, think of it as you "home away from home". (JUST DO NOT BUILD ON NOVICE. YOU WILL BE LOCKED OUT OF THE SERVERS AFTER 15 HOURS OF PLAYTIME!)
- SKINS!
This excites me. Im already a sucker for skins ($1,600 spent on CS:GO. RIP). Having the chance to spaltter the brains of my enemies with a Hello-Kitty Sniper? ♥♥♥♥ YES!
The skins arent lazily done either, they're really well made, high-res skins. Just do be aware CRATES COST MONEY TO OPEN! You can, however, find keys rarely in the world itself, either on the ground or off zombies.
Now, onto the Cons, which of course the game has.
-CONS
-Geared SLIGHTLY towards a P2W model. Its not quite there, but there is evidence of it in the resource packs, more specifially the "Assault" pack, which allows you access to armour, guns and Ammunition Blueprints, combined with a materials Resource pack, its a recipe for P2W disater if not carefully managed.
- Poor/Inadequate Optimisation
The game has recently been downgraded graphically, due to the poor framerates, it is apparent if you look at the transition between closed Alpha and the Beta.
It is worth noting here that the game runs exceptionally pootly on Laptop GPU's and Some AMD cards (R7/R9 respectively).
-Same zombie models
This is more of a personal gripe. Seening the Zombie models from ISS isn't a breath of fresh air, but they'll hopefully get an update soon.
- Cheaters
Yes, this ol' topic again. There are cheaters, not gonig to deny that. But if you can get through the inital 15 hours gamepaly and onto Prime servers, they shouldn't bee too much of an issue. The devs have reassured me that working on the Anti-Hack is their main priority.
-Not a huge selection of guns
There are:
- 4 Assault rifles
- 1 Sub-Machine Gun
- 2 Shotguns
- 4 Hanguns
- 1 sniper
Other than that, not much really to complain about. Personal things, really, Most people tend to stay on thje north of the map, so if you're new starting out, I highly recommend the South or the West side of the map.
Good luck, and I'll see you ingame, Survivors!

This is another title I sincerely wish had a "So-so" or "Neutral" option for reviews. Having said that, here we go:
Aftermath is a Zombie survival game wherein players take on the role of humans scavening and attempting to survive in a zombie apocalypse. On paper the whole idea sounds BRILLIANT. However this games got a long road ahead of it for a few reasons whilst a good deal of things working for it too:
Allow me to address the elephant in the room. Yes, this game WAS made by some of/much of the staff/assets behind "War Z". I will be the first to state that I pre-ordered and was burnt by the developers well enough that I wouldn't be above accepting an aluminum bat and time alone with those whom pushed to release War Z in the state it arrived to it's audience.
I have seen nothing to suggest the items in this game are EXCLUSIVELY available to paying players. I found multiple mods/items that are available on the market entirely by scavenging in towns. On top of that, travelling to "Safezones" allows the players to sell various items they find in exchange for currency to buy those very same items premium customers can. Granted at a notably higher rate, but this game is ENTIRELY capable of being played for free.
The addition of PVE to the game is something I (and many others, I imagine) were hoping to see as an option in War Z. That being said, from what i've seen and been told, its only available for a certain period of time, a point that leaves a sour taste in my mouth. I personally prefer PVE in many survival games, and nowadays all one can really find in terms of Sandbox Survival games is "Hardcore PVP" games. I get wanting to press players into joining the PVP side of things, but I feel there are other ways to encourage PVP without alienating another potential audience.
This ties back into #1, This is a new game, a free one. Aside from food and VERY basic supplies, there is far less available in this game on the Micro-transaction market than there was in War Z. On top of that everything available via MTs is also available by saving up cash from selling random items you find in the world. I'm willing to give the developers a chance merely because this title is free and theres enough new content to suggest they're TRYING to dig the bullets out of their foot they so quick to put there in the first place.
TL;DR New game from developer that dashed any respect much of it's fanbase had, trying to make a comeback, enough new content to consider giving them a chance.
Update: With the removal of PVE restrictions, I am willing to give this game a recommendation. While I personally wouldn't drop money into this game, I have seen enough to believe there is potential here.

I've played this game since childhood, but I've never managed to beat it until recently. With that being said and done, I can give it a proper review. First of all, I recommend this game. It's very quirky, odd, funny at times (usually because of how stupid everyone involved is) and the levels are well-made, with the exception of some camera bugs and odd glitches.
The story is terrible. But, it's terribly funny too. There  are some great moments, you'll probably laugh at the infamous jazz hands and .... extremely odd mouth movements. Some moments are genuinely sad and stand out a lot, but most of the time you're getting laughably bad cutscenes, etc.
The game looks dated, but not that bad actually. It has a unique, enjoyable style that a lot of early 2000s/late 90s games have. IF you're an HD, everything must be perfectly modeled guy, you'll probably cringe.
The music is awesome.
Gameplay wise, it's Sonics er... proper jump to 3D. The levels are always fun IMO besides the Big stages, and even those can be completed in less than 10 minutes. Some stages overstay their welcome, particularly the 2nd to last ones are usually the culprit.
If you've never played this game before, you'll have fun exploring and finding things out. If you have a brain, you can find almost everything with time. There is a bunch of extra content in the form of replaying missions, looking for hidden medals throughout the world, unlockable Sonic titles, and the ever amazing Chao which you can sink thousands of hours into (if that's your kind of thing.)
Over all, I'd give this game a solid 8 out of 10.

This is one of those games that makes me wish Steam had a "Meh" option.
Yes, I've only played it for 45 minutes, but that was enough time for me to get the "regular" ending, along with taking a ten minute bathroom break during play time.  Don't read too much into that.
It's a (mostly) solid platformer, comparable (sort of) to the first Super Mario Bros., except the jumping gets a bit awkward at times.  My level of irritation at some of the level design, though, often ended up outweighing my level of intrigue, which is unfortunate, because it doesn't propel me to find all the collectables.  So, in that respect, as a platformer, it's pretty "meh," maybe on the "no" side of the review spectrum.  Same with sound.  It irritated me.
It's the rest of the game, however, that pushes me to suggest this game with a "yes" review.
Every review of this game that you've probably read that says it's scarier than it looks is (mostly) right.  It's definitely an offputting, nervous game, and, as the developer states, not for those of "nervous disposition" or something.  And he's right.  This game'll make you think twice about playing it at night.  But, all told, I didn't find it THAT bad.  While it did catch me off guard multiple times, I don't think it's the kind of game that's going to give you nightmares.  Unless you're a prepubescent, then it very well might.
So, it's a short, okay platformer with a twist that's worth seeing (though maybe only on sale, or the free version online, of which I hear there is one).
Oh, and some final notes: the graphics, while being pixelated, are pretty tight and often unsettling, as the game promises, but the gameplay is standard platformer with interspersed segments of dimension shifting, which may have been original in 2010, but is no longer terribly novel.
Let's sum it up: Buy it on sale.  It's worth your time, but maybe not worth a whole five bucks.

FAMAZE is the simplest rogue-like i know. Originally made for phones and the browser FAMAZE was a really fun little rogue-like that was perfect if you only had 5  minutes or so. The goal of FAMAZE is to find a key and to get to the end of the dungeon. In most rogue-likes, when you move, the monsters move too but in FAMAZE most monsters are stationary. They just block your way. Attacking monsters causes you and your foe to lose 1hitpoint. In order to stay alive you need potions that refill your life. The catch however is that you only have 2 inventory slots. This mechanic leads to alot of strategic thinking. FAMAZE also has a rather interesting lightning mechanic. If the light touches an enemy it turns into an healing item. This is an easy way of defeating your foes. So FAMAZE is a fun little rogue-like that is perfect to play while downloading a huge game or so ;D. If you want a strategic rogue-like that is really complex look somewhere else(ToME is perfect if you're looking for that;D) Simple but fun!

TLDR: Great little RPGMaker title that suffers from translation typos but has a solid core and decent story. Free soundtrack included that is not listed on store page which is AWESOME.
Aside from some minor translation errors (improper use of words and spelling mistakes) that are common with most RPGMaker games, this is actually a solid, well-built title.
The amount of scripts in the game seems daunting, and the more you add to an RPGMaker game the more it tends to mess things up, but things gel and work cohesively very well. I've encountered only some slow-down issues (the game suddenly drops to 5-10FPS) with the Dev has stated they are working on fixing it.
As for the story, it's actually intriguing. The aformentioned typos are a little off-putting, but it is well crafted and has kept my attention so far. The Puzzles are standard, with only a switch one giving me serious pause until I figured out the trick. Then, it was actually rather ingenious in how simply it actually was.
Is it worth the price? I got it on sale for around 5 bucks CAD. Right now, for me, it is 7.79CAD. I would say it's well worth that price, and a must-buy on sale if you're a fan of games of this type. For an RPGMaker game it has a suprising amount of polish.
Also, of note, is the Launcher they included with the game and the extras: I LOVE IT. It's something I think ALL RPGMaker games could benefit from, as it lets you decide if you want to start the game in fullscreen or windowed, and what ratio to make the game screen. It also offers direct links (no digging around Local Files) to the Artbooks AND it comes with a full soundtrack which was not mentioned on the Store's Page. Bonus!

Great story, suprisingly imaginative use of RPG maker, and just the right amount of creepiness to make the puzzles enjoyable whilst keeping the atmosphere intense, but not over the top. I'm really emjoying it!
BTY - I got a framerate slowdown issue - This is resolvable by pressing the Alt and Enter keys together.

The best bit about xenonauts is that it is an awesome port of a classic game with updated graphics and a few cool new ideas and changes.
The worst bit about xenonauts is that it is an awesome port of a classic game that was not implemented fully. So much of this game is half way done and not fleshed out fully.
Let me explain.
It's prettier than original x-com... if by prettier you mean higher resolution. There is no way to rotate the map, no way to zoom the map in or out (well... you can change the resolution i guess), no minimap, fences and doors obscure everything behind them unless there is a npc or player model on that square... the list goes on.
The geoscape is a mess. It's a flat projection of the world that takes as long to travel around the pole as it does at the equator and radar ranges are perfect circles. This would not be a problem except someone decided to be clever and program in a realistic day/night transition that even moves up and down with the seasons. It's not game breaking, gameplay is balanced around the flat map and perfect circles...
Yet I can not get over the realistic day night line. If you're going to do one bit right, you have to do all the bits right, not half of it.
You can set things on fire! But there is no incendiary ammo, and things you would expect to burn (hay bales, wooden buildings) don't. Once again, it's a lovely mechanic ripped form original x-com that is implemented half way.
This basically applies to every single item in the game. Research, manufacturing, base development, combat, tooltips, in game information, etc.
I'm enjoying playing this game... in short stints. If I play too long the flaws grate too much and I get frustrated with the game instead of enjoying it.
If you can overlook/don't notice the flaws xenonauts is a solid x-com remake and is be a lot of fun.

Xenonauts. It's greatest strength is that it's X-com. It's greatest weakness is that it's X-com.
If you're an older gamer, played the original X-coms, and just wanted them to get a graphics update and maybe some mods on being able to better organise your units and maybe a few updates, look no further. You've found it.
If you don't know what this "X-com" business is about, both X-com and Xenonauts are tactical and strategic games where you defend earth from an alien invasion through a specialised organisation and squad who deals with the aliens.
You'll respond to the aliens by shooting down the UFOs using regular human fighter aircraft, and then landing a squad of soldiers with just plain old human guns near them to clear out the survivors. After that, you'll begin to research better technology. Laser rifles, faster aircraft to take down the UFOs, armour that protects from the alien weaponry, and so on.
You will meet several different kinds of aliens, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, and figure out why they're invading. But most importantly, you're going to stop them. You're going to take all their technology and make it your own, and you will end up with several bases across the world to find, and destroy any intruders who push into your atmosphere.
As for the changes between this and X-com, they are mostly good. You have an airstrike option on alien crash sites so that you don't need to do everything or have them expire when you've been too busy dealing with other sites, though it will provide you with far less rewards than if you send in a squad of soldiers. There are new pieces of equipment, such as the shield. You'll no longer need to micromanage every last clip or laser battery in your arsenal and order the construction of small things like two laser batteries - Just keep track of the ones you bring into combat so you don't run out. There are now more involved air battles, along with air terror sites. And cover, along with range, now actually provides a bonus or penalty to your shots. You don't have to worry about this turning into a chest high wall simulator though, it works out well and you don't have to stay in cover. It's just a suggestion that increases your soldiers' lifespan. There are some others but they are mostly positive. One I'd say is slightly negative is that you can not land on a UFO and blast a hole in the ceiling to enter it as you could in the original X-com, though if you never played that game(And even if you did), you might not even notice that option isn't there.
Mechanics wise, it works out very similar to X-com, with an isometric view and tile based map. I've found some maps had too little vertical space sometimes but often this wasn't a big problem, the controls are pretty good, mainly just using your mouse to command your units.  It's turn based, with a world map to place your bases on and do your air battles, and a base overview where you can build out your base by modular rooms.
Interestingly, I've found that the difficulty settings actually changes AI behavior, rather than the lazy way of just giving the AI more armour or damage. I'm not sure if it also gives the aliens more stats or makes it more difficult to get money for the player, but the fact difficulty settings actually improve the AI is something that many AAA games completely fail at.
In the end, it's X-com. It has most of the strengths of X-com, but it also has the flaws of X-com. You may need to restart several times if you're new and you might get discouraged. A random lucky shot could kill off your best soldier and send the nearby rocket launcher guy into a berserk panic state right into your own squad. If you're not used to it, you'll wonder just how long the campaign keeps going and it may turn into a game of 'whack-a-UFO' for you with slow or barely noticable progress. Or you may simply not have a clue what's going on until the aliens are already in a better position than you.
Even then, it's a very good game. I would say it's worth grabbing it at some point if you want to see what the fuss is about, or because you want some more of the X-com from long ago (Without looking at Interceptor or Enforcer for now)

This game is a masterpiece. Even though it might not appear tobe much on the outside, after all, it is a Half-Life 2 mod, it is surprisingly fun, and never really gets boring. You have a wide array of guns at your disposal, along with unique melee weapons, from kitchen knives to chainsaws. There are two gamemodes, objective and survival.
Objective has you and a group of other survivors get from Point A to Point B, while completing objectives along the way to get rescue. Survival has you and other survivors defending zones from waves of zombies, with scripted supply drops.
One of the best aspects of this game is it's focus on teamwork. While objective is possible to solo, it is still hard, and survival is practically impossible without a team. Where it really becomes noticable is in certain objectivd missions, though.
For examples, Cabin has you hooking a car battery up to a generator to call for rexcue, except the generator is surrounded by zombies, requiring one of the survivors to grab the battery, and the others protect him.

Another aspect is that this game is actually quite difficult. Ammunition tends to be scarce, requring you to only take shots that you really need to take, instead of just mowing down hordes with a run-n-gun strategy. Every time a zombie bits you, you have a chance of bleeding or infection. Bleeding does damage to you over time, and can only be stopped by bandages, while infection is permanent, and can only be put off for three minutes by taking pills.
One of the best loadouts is the SKS, Beretta M9, and Baseball Bat.

I'm not sure how to review eversion. It's an interesting short game with an inspired premise and fantastic soundtrack, but it's been available free for about five years now, and the Steam version doesn't do enough to warrant a purchase over just playing the free version. It does have achievements and trading cards, both of which are pluses, but the game itself is still just a short novelty, albeit an interesting one. Full 360 controller support is missing, something that really isn't acceptable in a commercial platformer, and while the game has a level editor, it doesn't come packed in with the Steam version for no explicable reason. The only real reason to pick this up is if you played the free version and want to support the developer, which is admittedly why I bought it when a coupon came my way.
I like eversion's style, it appeals to me a lot, and I loved it when I first played it, but I wish that the Steam release had at least gotten some basic additions like another set of levels to play through, full controller support, and having the level editor included, or even better having Steam Workshop support for custom levels. If you're paying for the game, you're going to be disappointed, and if you're paying to support the dev then why are you reading reviews. I like this one too much to thumbs down it, but the paid version does way too little to warrant any enthusiasm.
Also fair warning it's pretty damn hard, especially if you collect all the gems, though given the short length that's kind of a plus in my book.

Xenonauts. It's greatest strength is that it's X-com. It's greatest weakness is that it's X-com.
If you're an older gamer, played the original X-coms, and just wanted them to get a graphics update and maybe some mods on being able to better organise your units and maybe a few updates, look no further. You've found it.
If you don't know what this "X-com" business is about, both X-com and Xenonauts are tactical and strategic games where you defend earth from an alien invasion through a specialised organisation and squad who deals with the aliens.
You'll respond to the aliens by shooting down the UFOs using regular human fighter aircraft, and then landing a squad of soldiers with just plain old human guns near them to clear out the survivors. After that, you'll begin to research better technology. Laser rifles, faster aircraft to take down the UFOs, armour that protects from the alien weaponry, and so on.
You will meet several different kinds of aliens, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, and figure out why they're invading. But most importantly, you're going to stop them. You're going to take all their technology and make it your own, and you will end up with several bases across the world to find, and destroy any intruders who push into your atmosphere.
As for the changes between this and X-com, they are mostly good. You have an airstrike option on alien crash sites so that you don't need to do everything or have them expire when you've been too busy dealing with other sites, though it will provide you with far less rewards than if you send in a squad of soldiers. There are new pieces of equipment, such as the shield. You'll no longer need to micromanage every last clip or laser battery in your arsenal and order the construction of small things like two laser batteries - Just keep track of the ones you bring into combat so you don't run out. There are now more involved air battles, along with air terror sites. And cover, along with range, now actually provides a bonus or penalty to your shots. You don't have to worry about this turning into a chest high wall simulator though, it works out well and you don't have to stay in cover. It's just a suggestion that increases your soldiers' lifespan. There are some others but they are mostly positive. One I'd say is slightly negative is that you can not land on a UFO and blast a hole in the ceiling to enter it as you could in the original X-com, though if you never played that game(And even if you did), you might not even notice that option isn't there.
Mechanics wise, it works out very similar to X-com, with an isometric view and tile based map. I've found some maps had too little vertical space sometimes but often this wasn't a big problem, the controls are pretty good, mainly just using your mouse to command your units.  It's turn based, with a world map to place your bases on and do your air battles, and a base overview where you can build out your base by modular rooms.
Interestingly, I've found that the difficulty settings actually changes AI behavior, rather than the lazy way of just giving the AI more armour or damage. I'm not sure if it also gives the aliens more stats or makes it more difficult to get money for the player, but the fact difficulty settings actually improve the AI is something that many AAA games completely fail at.
In the end, it's X-com. It has most of the strengths of X-com, but it also has the flaws of X-com. You may need to restart several times if you're new and you might get discouraged. A random lucky shot could kill off your best soldier and send the nearby rocket launcher guy into a berserk panic state right into your own squad. If you're not used to it, you'll wonder just how long the campaign keeps going and it may turn into a game of 'whack-a-UFO' for you with slow or barely noticable progress. Or you may simply not have a clue what's going on until the aliens are already in a better position than you.
Even then, it's a very good game. I would say it's worth grabbing it at some point if you want to see what the fuss is about, or because you want some more of the X-com from long ago (Without looking at Interceptor or Enforcer for now)

Something about the screenshots of Xenonauts always put me off playing the game in the past, I couldn't put my finger on it; although I think the game itself looks great, the screenshots didn't do it justice. But as a big fan of the early X-com games as well as the 2012 reboot I was lured towards Xenonauts, it was one of those games that got under my skin, I kept looking at it on steam, on the fence as to whether it was worth the full asking price; I'd have to say after completing the campaign that it most definately is.
Where as the 2012 Firaxis X-com reboot was more of a reimaging, Xenonauts is an up tp date version of the older X-com games, bringing back time units and a whole list of other unit statistics giving the game a certain retro charm.
The main story arc of Xenonauts was brilliant, although it's another version of what has gone before, in my opinion it's a story which is more believable than those that have gone before it. The pseudoscience that backs it up is second to none and the tech tree that backs the game up brings some fantastic ideas with it, bulking up what we're used to in this type of game, again all of the research topics are given great entries, made to sound believable, as if all of the technology could potentially exist.
The new additions over the original 90's X-com are great:
- Realtime air to air combat between your fleets of interceptors and UFO's
- A variety of weapons for ground combat, shotguns, assault rifles, LMG's etc
- Suppression effects for human and alien units
- The ablilty to see a soldiers stats before you hire them
- Flashbang grenades for assaulting enemy units
- Cover that offers units protection and can be effectively flanked
In addidtion to the above the alien units are all unique and all have unique combat tactics/ablilites which maintains a real "alien" feel to the first encounters you have with them, more than once I struggled to comprehend what I was faced with on the battlefield resulting in a last minuite change of my tried and tested tactics.
All in all, a must for fans of the 90's X-com games; as well as those who enjoyed the Firaxis reboot and don't mind learning the new interface.

APB:R is a mechanically solid game with amazing customization options -including an option to upload your own music and play it with an in-game radio, but it's seriously marred by punishing hardware demands and one of the worst communities not actually directly affiliated with an organized Hate Group.
APB:R's got a mean learning curve, too, and not just in terms of gun fighting. High skill players also know the city and it's many alleys, highways, ramps, and neighborhoods quite well, and being travel time efficient is one of the greatest advantages for completing missions. You'll need to know the weapons as well and that's also not a trivial task.
The setting's quite detailed as well and fairly intriguing. There's a lot going on in this tale of a city committing suicide to save it's life and it's told from many different perspectives by a few dozen well composed NPC's. Shame it's also not an ongoing story.
A word on microtransactions: there are quite a few of them, and more coming all the time. Much of it is exclusive, but usually cosmetically. If you don't care what your OCA or NTEC looks like, you can unlock -permanently- weapons that'll perform just about as well as anything that costs real money. In terms of what's "necessary" Premium time nearly doubles your income and contact progression rate, and that'll really start to tell once you get deep into the game and start seeing max level 15 contacts.
And much as APB:R's servers look like a dumping ground for unwanted (and tragically unaborted) children get this straight: it's a business, not a public park. Servers cost money, money means selling stuff. Get over it, or uninstall.
APB:R has a real and an active hacker problem. The worst offenders are the Americans, so keep off the game during American holidays and afternoon hours. Fair Fight helps, but it's bad to the point of hacker cadres bragging about how they stay in APB:R just to ♥♥♥♥ with the devs, and who can point you at all their favorite forums and programs.
In Global Chat -just ask.

Sure his K/A/D is 17-3-0, but he's "just that good."
Especially with one of the worst weapons in the game*.
So _pro_.
That he's also driving a completely stock version of the basic free car also means nothing -he just decided to reroll.

And who apparently can track you through walls?
Can make jumping max-range hits on targets behind 90% cover with a sniper rifle?
I sound salty; I am.

Eversion is a game that takes a fairly simple idea and turns it into a great puzzle game that's both frightening and lighthearted at the same time.
A lot of people consider Eversion to be a "short" game, but that's not true. Eversion is the perfect length for a game like this- it doesn't drag itself on with needless repetition; it doesn't bog you down with a bunch of throwaway mechanics you only use once; it doesn't try to make itself overly complicated.
What Eversion DOES do is use it's game mechanics flawlessly- you'll use every resource on the level to get the full completion, and then you can move to the next level. The level design is great, the art really makes you feel like you're a part of this decaying façade of a world, and the music sets the tone of each "world" perfectly.
This is a perfect game for someone who enjoys horror games, but is tired of the same old jumpscares that startled them last year.

By its impact and overall features complexity, the greatest Grand Theft Auto title ever made. Yeah, even after the GTA V PC release. How's that, you may ask? Since when some junk based on the engine dated like 15 years away, is better than all the licked clean and glossy Euphoria engine stuff?
Well, Euphoria is a good engine, sure, but not perfect. It's great with some physical effects, and all... But some things it can't do, while its competitors - can. Like when you need to exit the car and the doors are blocked, Euphoria still just respawns you outside the car. And Wei Shen from Sleeping Dogs will exit the car like he should - by smashing the front window with a kick and climbing out on the hood! And that's only one example! If you look around, you'll find many cool options that Rockstar haven't implied in their games, and that's really sad!
But not when we're talking about San Andreas. For its main selling point at the moment is obviously not the visuals or engine complexity. No, people, it's all about the spirit, the mood that the game is providing. San Andreas - it's a raging youth, a bit crazy but overmighty and unstoppable. GTA 4 and GTA 5 - are quite different, and much more grim and unattractive by the same basis - the mood game's providing. Yeah, Luiz from the "ballad of Gay Tony " and Franklin from GTA V are slightly more cheerful guys you'll might even roll with someday... But Niko Bellic, Johnny Klebitz, Michael and Trevor - especially Trevor - they're all so horrid guys that I wouldn't like to walk the same road with. And it's the same thing as with the character from Mafia 1 in comparison with characters from Mafia 2 & 3! I just don't like those guys, I don't feel compassion for them - so I don't like to help them with sorting out their troubles, and so on.
So there is the thing why San Andreas is better than GTA V. Compassion. Sympathy. Carl Johnson, being just the same mass murdering criminal as the whole other bunch of Rockstar characters, is still a better person to hang out with.
And, talking about the technical side, San Andreas even by the year of 2004 is tremendously big game. I've played it in 2005, in 2008, in 2011 and only the 4th time through I've found the triathlon event there. Stunning feeling.
So, my mark is obvious 10/10, and not of some nostalgia, but just as the feeling after I've made it through GTA V, which I'll mark lower. Peace, people.

Xenonauts: Xenonauts is a turn-based combat, alien defense simulator. You play the role as the commander of a special military force designated Xenonauts, who are tasked with the defense of earth from extra-terrestrial invaders. You’ll manage multiple bases you place on the globe, build ground and air forces to combat the alien threat, and defend humanity. Research technology gathered from shot down UFOs, and craft advance weapons, armor, vehicles and aircraft to keep toe to toe with the aliens as the get progressively tougher. Xenonauts is a fantastic spiritual sequel to X-COM UFO Defense, with the entire game playing out almost exactly the same. With that come some very odd choices.

You can’t rotate the map and there are many situations where targeting becomes an issue, and a great irritation. Aliens also like to use the open and close door tactic; during the alien’s turn, they can open doors which close for them after their turn ends, this means they will stay glued to the other side of a door, come out the on their turn, take shots at your soldiers and retreat back to safety, however, when attempting this tactic yourself, the door stays open the entire round, meaning the aliens are free to shoot back during their turn. Aliens even seem to know this tactics as many times they are often waiting right behind doors, making it very annoying to advance through bases or UFOs without a guarantee of losing at least one soldier along the way, the only real remedy I found was blowing the doors to high heaven.

The other unfortunate, and boring part of the game is the aircraft combat. The aircraft combat is a top-down view where you set waypoints for your ships to travel, it isn’t easy to change the flight path on the fly and the whole experience feels very slow and unbalanced, I almost always resorted to the auto-resolve, which has its own problems. When auto-resolve is at 100% it’s a guarantee victory, however, if you engage in the real time combat you can actually lose all of your fighters. On the flip side, there have been battles with an auto-resolve 0% rating but, when I engaged in the combat I was able to win. Also, alien space ships seem to have unlimited ammo while you have a very limited amount for your own fighters. The whole thing felt messy and unrewarding, you don’t get to see your ships engage in the combat other than green radar blips you see all the time, so auto-resolve seemed the best and most convenient way to deal with the aliens, this is a pretty big part of the game aside from ground combat and it’s a shame it isn’t more exciting or balanced, there’s also no way to take down aircraft without damaging it.
The other major complaint I have is the lack of mission variety, crash sites are won either by eliminating all aliens or capturing and holding their ships for 5 turns, alien bases are won by either destroying the power core or eliminating all aliens. Those are the only two varieties and couple that with small map variety and the game can start feeling very tedious. Some other things felt missing like a graph for finance and approval ratings from the various countries and just some minor graphical bugs I’ve experienced.
I’ve enjoyed my time with Xenonauts, and would like to see it expanded upon, with more maps, missions, added tools and utilities, and better combat and varied environments. I could go into more detail, honestly, I’m seriously happy with Xenonauts despite my gripes with the combat aspect, I want more and always have and will and the game here is very well crafted with great visuals, music and atmosphere. Thankfully there is a great modding community who may add all that I could think of in a Xenonauts game, but, in the future, I wish for the game to be successful and for more to be added on by the creators.
TL/DL; Xenonauts is a great spiritual sequel of the X-Com series. If you like those games remotely, you’ll love this one. It’s heavy with atmosphere, mostly great combat, the thrill of progress and the feeling you get when you nail a tough mission with flying colors.
-Thumbs up from Royial

============================================
XENONAUGHTS
============================================
Overview:
On the face of it Xenonaughts is a high quality 2D planetary defense game with stratergy and minigame elements with a little story telling all thrown in and mixed with a heavy influence from the Xcom Series and perhaps a bit of a steep price tag for an indie game attatched.
What the store doesnt tell is that the actual gameplay is a fantastic weave of impeccible timing, forced strategic and tactical improvisation and improvement, and delightful frustation when your elite squad wipes out for no apparent reason other than "better guns" which will often cause you to swear vengence upon the alien scu- "liberators" the developers have done a fantastic job with this number which i shall go into further detail below, fair warning though.
!!!!WALLS OF TEXT!!!!
You have been warned
============================================
The Guts:
Simply a fantastic game, I have been gaming for a little over 10 years now and I almost exclusively play stratergy and/or survival games, and of all the stratergy games I have played this has to be the most perfectly timed and tailored one fo them all at no point are you ever truely able to outgun the enemy your often outnumbered and if you turtle up one grenade or well placed lizard thing and your squads dead forcing you to rethink and restratergise without overwhelming you add the fact that if you dont plan and execute your stratergy and tactics right or do something stupid you cna lose your entire squad (and the alien victory conditions) adds an element of survival which automatically triggers the "KEEP EVERYONE ALIVE!" switch in me keeps me coming back after a rage quit form losing my entire squad (and not saving :P hey i refuse to accept a wipeout!).
the Pacing is also fantastic at no point are you ever really given too much to handle if you know what your doing (excluding the terror missions I failed everyone because of those *Censored tangent* reapers, the fact that both you and the aliens can build and attack bases also just putrs the cherry on the cake for me simply amazing the thrill i get when i discover an alien base, the first time i did i literally shouted out YEA I GOT YOU NOW YOU ALIEN MOTHER *censored* ... course it was 1 am and i got told off but still xD
to be fair there are a couple issues, 1 would be the graphics BUT it IS an indie game but if your into the more modern games it may not be summin you can get around, personally? i loved it, simple but detailed enough to let you know whats what and tell the differance between an alien lizard and a rock and perfectly fits the top down stratergy feel for me, the second is bugs there are a couple which are frequent such as aliens shooting through walls or the psionics unnerving your men from start to finish regardless of location and distance BUT both of those and much much more are covered in the community edition which i have started playing and that just adds that extra little something to really finish off the game.
============================================
The Meat of the matter:
the game itself is split into 3 distinct parts, the first is the tactical display, a screen with a selection of tabs ranging from geoscape (live view of the planet) to base planning, research military assests such as squads vehicles hangers etc all the way to a alien encyclopedia (did i spell that right?)
the 2nd part is minigames which in itself is a novel but entertaining little piece fo frustration that i have never been able to pull of yet (but that may have something to do with the single fighter in use at any given time) where you cna either auto resolve or play yourself,
the third is the meat of the game for me, ground combat a classic top down view of the map where you can use the terrain to your advantage and i reccomend you do some fo the enemies only think 2 dimensionally which is fantastic for the sniper up on the third floor but terrible for the heavy round the corner from him about to be eaten alive
============================================
Conclusion:
I cannot praise this game enough the developers have done a simply fantastic job that i havent seen anyone else do so far and the fact that they are putting some community mods into the next patch as official parts of the game just instills so much confidence in them i am really excited to see what they do next.
my advice to anyone who loves stratergy, alien invasion, or base defense there WILL be something for you here, if your a fan of indie games or high quality design this is DEFINATELY something for you.

*** Euro Truck Simulator 2 ***
I have a license to drive heavy trucks with heavy trailers, and I have experience with most of Scania, Volvo and Mercedes trucks. However, I have never driven semi-trailers though. And that's what you do in this game. So far, I have not been able to drive a truck with a "normal" trailer. Maybe this game is all about semis?
What impresses with this game is the details. The details of the trucks, the details of how the truck behave and the details of the environments you drive in. Just wow. This is not a game for those of you that want a fast blasting action experiance. This game wants you to take your time with it. Follow traffic rules, respect the forces heavy trucks and so on. This is no GTA! You WILL be penalized for every crash, excessive speeding and general road rage you commit.
Pros...
- Licensed trucks
- Real roads under (somewhat) real conditions
- The graphics are good
- The sounds are good
- The credibility from a driver's point of view is in focus, with the angles ( you lean out through the window etc)
- You have the option to listen to the most common radiostations from each country while driving
Cons...
- I guess the graphics could be a tad better?
- There is no option to slow down the free look movement mouse speed from inside the cabin (from what I have found out)
- Lots and lots of DLC if you want the complete package
Final verdict...
This might change when I got more gametime, but so far I give it a 8/10. It's great! Recommended for all of you that want to experiance how it is to haul heavy cargo over great distances

This game does exactly what it says, You drive a realistically simulated truck/trailer combination through Europe, mix in some RPG elements and managing options and voila: Euro Truck Simulator 2.
Simulators are gameplay heavy, and this one's no different. So its important that it lives up to its name. And it delivers.. without being overly complex. You might have trouble driving a big vehicle on the narrow european roads at first, especially if you dont have any driving experience on public roads, but after a while you understand that this game is meant to be played at a slow pace. Gracefully "forces" you to play slow.
And this is where it starts to shine. rewarding your patience with a great feeling of achievement when you finally understand the trick to reversing your trailer into position, or passing the border between Belgium and France after a long playthrough and seeing the road architecture; signs, roads, police cars, the nature change. It starts to draw you in and before you know it, you're able to buy and upgrade your own truck drive anywhere you want. Upgrade your character with new cargo options and driving longer distances. switching on the light when the day turns to night and the small details like seeing the small, barely noticable light switch changing direction on the dashboard. Illuminating the dash computer and important switches. SCS has grasped the magic of making an accesible believable simulator while still giving experienced truckers that extra edge, putting on the differential lock when struggling in the mud, or lifting the middle axle to save on fuel and tyre wear. The damage model is however poorly simulated. Due to licensing reasons the trucks have no visual damage at all and is being shown in percentages. Once a high % has been reached the engine will start to stall occasionally. It would have been nice to have a more detailed damaging model where you gradually loose coolant for example or running a flat tyre.
It looks like the developers made the right balance between performance and eye candy. This game is not meant to be played for the graphics obviously but the game looks pretty with sunrays pouring through the dense trees south of Germany with the mountainous backdrop off Austria in the distance. The trucks ofcourse are the diamond of this game. Shiny and detailed with loads of external and internal customization going on with the steam workshop allowing for even more customization. Of course the trucks also sound the part like you expect. small details in engine and blinker sound reveal what truck you are driving. However it would be nice to actually hear the difference when putting different exhausts on your truck.
This game will definitely appeal to alot of people, even for people remotely interested in truck driving. It gives me the content that i have dreamt for for years. The game makes one feel at ease when driving long hauls. The debut of this great concept of a game is generating idea's for the future like being able to visually inspect your truck/engine bay for damage. Right now SCS has the succesfull recipe for the best trucking game to date and safely secures the future of trucking simulators.

I going to state this honestly. Sonic Adventure is an awesome game, and I spent many hours on it as a kid on the Dreamcast. This version, however, and dx in general, I feel is a very flawed port. The graphics just look off, and a lot of the collision just isn't good. Also, I have major issues with the control, which also just feels wrong to me, the homing attack won't always target enemies in front of you, and will on occasion, target something off in the distance. Another issue is the chao garden, though this is specific to the steam version of this game, and I do understand that there isn't much they could do for this (other than, ya know, put in a minigame system or something). In all the console versions, there was a function to make your chao grow through minigames (the Dreamcast having an rpg that could be played on the vmu, and the gamecube port giving you an option to play minigames on the gba). This version lacks that in it's entirety, forcing you to use only animals to grow your chao. Luckily, some of these issues have been fixed by the betterSADX mod, fixing the collision and graphics, and restores it close to the version that I know and love. I can recommend this game only with the BetterSADX mod, however, be aware that chao isn't quite as fun as it was in earlier versions.

Hot on the heels of the hot mess that was No Man's Sky - Astroneer aims to be in part what NMS claimed it would be. The difference between these two games is that Astroneer states what it plans to be as a game, and then promptly meets those goals.
A rather delightful little game, Astroneer invokes the serene and peaceful atmosphere of Minecraft through excellent musical pieces, while boasting its own adorable isometric art style that is capable of a quite surprising beauty. Only close to five hours in, I've spent most of these hours on one singular save file and played both solo and with a friend. Both experiences were enjoyable, and the game in its current state is a very promising sign for the future its heading in.
It should be noted, in my experience anyway, that the game isn't particularly challenging by any means. Arguably the most challenging thing about Astroneer so far is inventory management, because the backpack has very few slots to begin with and if you equip a battery and an oxygen tank the way I did, for extra exploring freedom in small doses, you have even less space to play with. The game also doesn't appear to offer a great deal of diversity presently, or perhaps I was just generated a terrible planet with one singular dust storm that likes to blow by every now and then - sometimes throwing a rock in my face in the process.
Environmental hazards trip you up once and then never do so again unless you simply fail to notice them. Being able to shape terrain at your whim is an incredibly fun mechanic, but it does lend itself to leaving you a lot of power over the environment and thus nullifying any threats of the environment as you learn how to avoid them. (Which normally involves just digging the whatever-it-is up and stealing its Research nodule.)
Astroneer is a fun game. It's full of a good potential and carries an endearing charm even in its current state, and I was able to happily spend two to three hours in one session alone with my partner just seeing what we could build, where we could go and what we could break. (Tethers are your best friend if you want to move heavy and large objects. Trust.) I would hesitate against recommending it for its current price tag because it is a little repetitive and as much fun as I have with it, I don't feel like the game has enough features to boast about for it to warrant being so expensive. That, and it's also early access, and regardless of how much I like a title, I would always hesitate to recommend purchasing an early access game these days.
But is Astroneer a bad game? No. No, not at all. It's a lovely little game full of promise and charm, and once it has just a bit more content to help bulk out the experience, it will come with my full recommendations completely.
