Did you ever want to drink beer, play with fire, shoot your friends into the face, run away from the horror in the sewers, fight off an alien infection and throw the dead bodies of your former friends towards Rednecks to defend yourself? Then this may be a game you should take a closer look.
is a collection of four plus one short games (plus another very short drug induced fever dream game) centering around well known horror movies. You start the game in front of the cinema which is at the same time the main hub to choose which episode from Lakeview Cabin III to VI you want to watch/play and also a mini-level itself. All movies have in common that there is absolutely no hand-holding. It is a sandbox experience where you have to figure out everything yourself compirsing with what an object does, where you can/have to use it and actually starting with what object you are holding since it is not always clear (due to the simplified graphic). This is often fun and interesting, mostly refreshing and sometimes really, really frustrating. Also in common is the fact that in every episode you can switch between four playable characters. But let's look at each episode separately.
Lakeview Cabin III is the "first" movie you can choose and also the simplest one. You and your friends are counselors in a camp and everything is fun until something murderous will start hunting you. The goal here is simply surviving and killing what is hunting you. Every item is always in the same place so you can slowly refine your strategy. Find the shotgun, try to chop it down with the axe or just burn it with fire. Or feel the despair losing one character after another.
Lakeview Cabin IV is the second movie. You and your friends ran out of fuel in front of a mansion somewhere in nowhere. You have to explore the surroundings and find four canisters and bring them back to the car. In contrast to the previous episode there is some randomization including the order of rooms and where what items/enemies are placed. Sounds easy, right? Did I mention the bloodthirsty Rednecks? Well, still easy. Did I mention the rat mutants?
Lakeview Cabin V is both fascinating and frustrating. Like episode III everything is always in the same place. Goal is to put an undieable killer to its final rest with the help of some demons. In contrast to all other episodes you can't really die here. It is more of a puzzle episode. But here the sandboxing gets really frustrating because the puzzles are really hard to figure out. Episode V appeared some time after the initial release. As such there was a community waiting for it and figuring everything out themselves. Brilliant idea on the paper but frustrating in reality since you have nearly no chance to get everything alone.
Lakeview Cabin VI is more action orientated again. It is more difficult in the puzzle aspect then episode III and IV but a lot easier than V. Problem is that you may be burnt out after episode V and not paying much attention to the obvious hints. In this episode you play a group of janitors, cleaning the space station after a party. Places are always same but item placement is randomized. This would be an easy job but someone might not have read the memo about not getting infected by alien parasites. And if you don't find it fast enough hell might break loose on the station in no time. And even if you find it ...... there is still good chance to die.
All in all there is much diversity in the episodes but you need to have a small experimentor gene in you (because using guides from the beginning would be boring as .....). In every episode there is also a small mini-game which can occupy you for some minutes. You can unlock those by completing the episode the first time.
The complete package is in total very enjoyable but you may find yourself burnt out slightly by episode V. Also do not be fooled by the cute graphics. The game can be - at times - surprisingly suspenseful and violent.
PS: If you have any question just write in the comments and I will try to get back to them as fast as possible.

Slime Rancher is original and aesthetically pleasing, but I find myself asking "where's the game"?
Traditional sandbox games, such as Terraria, SimCity, and Factorio, are fun because you can build a base and optimize it. Slime Rancher offers little in these respects
The player builds corrals to contain slimes and gardens to grow crops. These structures are prefab and can only be built in certain locations. Structure placement doesn't matter as there's no synergies between buildings. Structures may be upgraded with 4 or 5 upgrades to improve their performance.
Outside of upgrades, there's nothing the player can do to influence the growth of crops and slimes. There's no risk of crop failure. Slimes aren't in danger of dying. Essentially the player runs around, throws food into corrals, collects the plorts, and earns gold. There's no challenge to this game.

According to the roadmap more slimes and zones will be added, but I don't see anything that would add interesting challenges. I have haven't written off Slime Rancher, but for now I must give it a thumbs down. $20 is too much for a 5 hour game.

To put it simply, Xenonauts is an oldschool remake of the classic X-COM. And that means it retains the brutality of the original while still being incredibly fun to play.
The graphics, while somewhat cartoony in places (notably cars) serve the art style well and convey the message of grimness throughout the game.
Sound is fine, but some noises I found hurt my ears with headphones. Other than that not much of note aside from the good soundtrack.
UI is somewhat complicated but easy to learn, while providing most of the vital information to keep your guys from not dying a horrible, awful, painful, and plasma-y death.
Gameplay, the big G.
It feels like X-COM. Not in a shoddy knock off way, but in a "The devs knew what they were doing when they made this glorious game graced by the almighty Gaben himself" way, complete with Time Units, Panics, and a boatload of potential ways for your poor plasma sh-err great soldiers to die. This includes fully playable air battles (which I recommend autoresolving for the most part), terror missions, abductions, and my love/hate favorite, the classic base defense.
Have I mentioned how hard the game is? It is pretty difficult, but if you have played X-COM style games before, you will know what you're doing, but still get completely and utterly pimp slapped if you act like your soldiers are Rambos and Rambas.
All in all, get it, or get plasma-ed.

I have about 200 hours into this game -with Mr. Torgue's Campaign of Carnage, Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep, the Psycho and Mechromancer packs, both Ultimate Vault Hunter packs, and many skins packs- and I can easily say that this game is super fun, with or without friends. The guns are all super satisfying just to shoot, from the simple Poor quality guns to the Legendaries. Progression actually feels like PROGRESSION, from the levels to the story advancement to even skin-gets. The "Badass" rank system may not feel like its doing much when you first start playing, but if you plan on playing for longer (which you probably will), it really adds up to your benefit. The story is actually pretty damn good, with quite a hefty amount of backstory to each individual character that you can discover throughout the game (particularly Handsome Jack, hes legitimately amazing and terrifying at the same time when you look into him). The best part is, once you've geared and played every possible way, you can bring in your friends and watch them struggle as you once did to comprehend how the game works. That is, if they're new to FPS's or RPG's. If they're veterans of either category, they'll be fine. Nonetheless, the game is fantastic. However, my only problem with Borderlands 2 is the copious amount of DLC offered, with the story-adding packs coming in at $9.99 a piece, the content-adding Headhunter Packs at $2.99, the level-cap-boosting Ultimate Vault Hunter Packs at $4.99, and each individual skin pack at $0.99. However, you could easily just sell trading cards or steal your parents credit card to get these things.
TL;DR - Game is good, but quite a few DLC, but still really content-filled: 8/10

I have actually played this about an hour total besides the Steam-time.
This is a sprite-based sandbox homage to 80s horror and creature films - films I love a lot.  You play as multiple young people trying to survive against various baddies or monsters.  There is no apparent goal other than to survive, hence the sandbox.  You can pickup and use various things around the area.  Little is explained, not even the controls - they're meant to be contextual, as there is a button prompt when you are near interactable items.
However, I found the simplistic nature of all this combined with the cryptic nature to be a major turnoff.  I was basically walking around bored waiting for the bad guys to show up (takes a long time on the first area), then when they do I did not find myself engaged enough to even really desire to fight them - not helped by very short reach attacks.
I pretty quickly realized there are ways to spring traps on the bad guys, and that's probably the real way to survive, but the very difficulty in even understanding what does what, coupled with how quickly you can kill yourself (throw a lantern by accident in a room, you're dead).  I just lost interest really fast, as I realized it'd take a ton of retries and trial and error.  This reminded me a bit of a rogue-lite, in a sense, only without the scaling skill set you usually have to acquire in those games.  Of course, I have mixed experiences with rogue-lites personally - if you like them a lot, your mileage may vary.
I get there's clearly meant to be some humor involved as well, and that just didn't quite work for me either.  Watching somebody else play would probably have been funnier actually, and I may give that a try one day.
If you really enjoy tinkering around in sandboxes, you may get more out of it though.   For me, it just doesn't work.

TO CLARIFY BEFORE I BEGIN WRITING THIS REVIEW I HAVE NOT FINISHED ALL OF THE CHAPTERS HOWEVER I HAVE PLAYED ENOUGH TO WRITE THIS REVIEW.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
To sum this game up as a slasher parody would probably be sufficent enough however I feel that it is a little bit more difficult to accuratly describe this game. For starters this game is based off horror movie cliches and popular slasher flicks while at the same time presenting a unique approach at the horror genre. For a 2D pixelated game this one actually proved to be nerve racking at times. I can not describe how absolutly terrifyed I was the first time the killer showed up in LVC3. Moving onward the games soundtrack compliments the 80's/90's vibe the game gives off. The use of keyboard synths and dark ambient instrumentals proves to make the experiance all the more chilling. The game also has elements of dark and often crude humor such as going to the bathroom in order to drop a item from the ceiling or commiting incest in order to summon a monster.
To break down each episode and how it makes itself stand out from the others:
LVC3 puts in the place of a group of camp conselours as they are stalked by a murderous duo on the island.
LVC4 has you play as a band whose tour bus has broken down at a mansion inhabitated by cultists and a slaughterhouse where the Leatherface-esque "Pigman" lurks awaiting its next victim. This installment introduces a sanity effect in which as you kill people the screen reddens and various hallucinations occur.
LVC5 has you playing as the standard 80's teenagers as they try to fend off a mysterious killer. This chapter has a unique "underworld" effect in which dead charecters can be "resurrected" which plays a key role in the episode. This chapter also had multiple endings one of which requires beating LVC3 without any charecters dying at any point.
LV6 takes place persumably in the future on a space station where a virius has broken out infecting members of the crew and presenting you with the mission of gathering survivors off the ship and into escape pods while fighting against the alien virius. This finale to the series has a item transportation system eliminating the need to travel everywhere to get one particular item.
There are however a few things that I would like to see changed or atleast fixed. For starters the gamepad reccomended sequence at the start of the game seems unnessacary as I made large progress in the game using a standard QWERTY keyboard. Therefore I feel that this sequence is not important and should be removed. My second problem is that in LVC5 the killer seems to have a very odd spawn rate as at the start of the chapter the killer will spawn constantly often interfering with trying to preform the deathmarks ritual while later on near the end of the chapter he will almost cease to spawn causing long waiting periods in order to finish the chapter.
Before rating this game I should also point out that this game is equal parts skill and luck as you must have good reflexes and thorough understanding of the controls while at the same time it is possible to breeze through some areas purely off of random events or lucky item spawns. This all being said I would highly reccomend this game to any slasher horror fan or someone just looking for something fun and original. Personally I would rate this game at a 9/10. I hope my review sways your opinion of this amazing game and convinces you to buy it.

Hot on the heels of the hot mess that was No Man's Sky - Astroneer aims to be in part what NMS claimed it would be. The difference between these two games is that Astroneer states what it plans to be as a game, and then promptly meets those goals.
A rather delightful little game, Astroneer invokes the serene and peaceful atmosphere of Minecraft through excellent musical pieces, while boasting its own adorable isometric art style that is capable of a quite surprising beauty. Only close to five hours in, I've spent most of these hours on one singular save file and played both solo and with a friend. Both experiences were enjoyable, and the game in its current state is a very promising sign for the future its heading in.
It should be noted, in my experience anyway, that the game isn't particularly challenging by any means. Arguably the most challenging thing about Astroneer so far is inventory management, because the backpack has very few slots to begin with and if you equip a battery and an oxygen tank the way I did, for extra exploring freedom in small doses, you have even less space to play with. The game also doesn't appear to offer a great deal of diversity presently, or perhaps I was just generated a terrible planet with one singular dust storm that likes to blow by every now and then - sometimes throwing a rock in my face in the process.
Environmental hazards trip you up once and then never do so again unless you simply fail to notice them. Being able to shape terrain at your whim is an incredibly fun mechanic, but it does lend itself to leaving you a lot of power over the environment and thus nullifying any threats of the environment as you learn how to avoid them. (Which normally involves just digging the whatever-it-is up and stealing its Research nodule.)
Astroneer is a fun game. It's full of a good potential and carries an endearing charm even in its current state, and I was able to happily spend two to three hours in one session alone with my partner just seeing what we could build, where we could go and what we could break. (Tethers are your best friend if you want to move heavy and large objects. Trust.) I would hesitate against recommending it for its current price tag because it is a little repetitive and as much fun as I have with it, I don't feel like the game has enough features to boast about for it to warrant being so expensive. That, and it's also early access, and regardless of how much I like a title, I would always hesitate to recommend purchasing an early access game these days.
But is Astroneer a bad game? No. No, not at all. It's a lovely little game full of promise and charm, and once it has just a bit more content to help bulk out the experience, it will come with my full recommendations completely.

Eversion is a short and atmospheric platformer, which can be both cute and horrifying. Depending on how skilled you are with platformers, this game should take 1-2 hours to finish. There are 3 achievable endings, from which 1 of them is tricky to get.
The concept of the game is that you are moving between different layers while you are collectiong gems and finish the stages. The higher the layer count, the more the scenery and the atmosphere decays. Without telling too much beforehand I can ensure you, the cute scenery you see in layer 1, will soon be turned upside down.
The switch between the layers occurs at different points in the stages where you can evert to the next or the previous layer by pressing the eversion key. Every layer gives you a special advantage which you need to collect certain gems or finish the stage. The game can be a bit tricky sometimes, but overall it is neither too easy nor too hard. If you are a platformer maniac, this will probably be really boring for you, though.
The BGM of the game is really nice and is different for each layer. Don't forget to increase the volume, because sound will play an important role with your gameplay experience!
The game comes with a total of 14 achievements and 5 trading cards. I personally think the achievement count is pretty low and there could be more achievements added. It was rather easy to get 13 out of the 14 achievements. The thing which really bothered me was the last achievement. Because I am kind of an impatient person I looked it up and damn, this is something noone would think of.
But overall, I can say that this game is really fun even though it is short. Im not sure if it is worth the full price, so if you are not that much into platformers but still want to give this a shot, I would wait until it is on sale.

Platforming-wise, this game is not very difficult, but there are some not-too-easy puzzles involved. The atmosphere it provides is great (partly due to the good music), as is the "story" and the ending. All in all it takes roughly 2-3 hours to complete, and way faster if you just want to do the main story.
I can recommend this game, but I'd buy it when it's on sale, just because the playtime needed to 100% it isn't that high.

Generally a good remake of original UFO: Enemy unknown in year 1994. Would want to give the game "recommend". However, the unrealistic setting in regarding to the financing, world political, world economy setting (by comparing to another xcom title - x -com : Enemy unknown) and the excessive punishment setting which prevent me to enjoy the game.
1. The organisation is poorly financed by the world and expectation is unreasonably high. Easily get financial punishment without a proper reason. Unable to expand due to financial problem.
2. Reward setting is poor. Success in high risk mission do not end up with equivalent high reward. (Destorying an alien base do not get apprasal from the local government)
3. Financing setting is poor. Limited option to get additional financing. Reselling price of advance equipment is unreasonably low just like the alien technology is commonly available to the world
4. With such high end technology and elite soliders on hand, the organisation can simply choose to walk away and get financial from other source (selling alien technology, equipment in black market, team with the most rich in the world) and deal with the alien threat on its own (just like some other sci-fi fiction). Therefore, the excessive punishment setting in the game is not enjoyable. Beside, if the government choose to kill itself, who care. The end of the government does not mean the end of the world, so long the organisation continue to exist. Sadlessly our real world actually telling you this in these recent years.
Anyway, the main point is, as a simulator, it would not be harmful if the game include the original rule set, improved rule setting and custom rule set for player to suit their style.

I'll get the obvious out of the way; if you liked XCom Enemy Unknown, you will probably like this.
If you liked XCom Enemy Unknown, but at times wondered:
- Why can I only send one strike team at a time? Why only one base of operations? Why only one interceptor at a time?
- Why do my troops seem to have seemingly unlimited sources of conventional ammunition?
- Why are the aliens so reactive to my scouting that I'm rewarded for crawling forward at a snails pace to 'discover' groups one at a time, rather than actively scouting things out?
- Why don't the aliens ever try a direct attack against XCom (if you have enemy within, why didn't they try for a conventional attack a second time?)
then get Xenonauts; which does an amazing job of both bringing up the level of depth and realism that I've come to love from XCom (don't get me wrong, I think XCom is one of the best games out there and I love its character and offerings), and delivering something thats still unique and distinctive.
If you're looking for a game that does an excellent job tracking what a campaign against a hostile alien invasion might be like; Xenonauts is amazing. Buy it; buy it now!

Sonic Adventure was the most advertised launch game for the Sega Dreamcast in 1999. Being Sonic the Hedgehog's true jump to 3D, years after many platformer mascots had their 3D debut, it was an important step for SEGA and Sonic Team to redefine what Sonic truly meant in the polygon era. Their solution was a 'cooler' redesign of many characters, many varied playstyles, a complex soundtrack filled with many differing genres of music, and a storyline filled with many connecting plotpoints. In other words, this ain't a 'retro' platformer.
Unfortunately, this port seems to be plagued with resolution and lag issues. The notion that this Steam version is actually a port from multiple consoles and PCs over the past 20 years is astounding. I hope SEGA can patch this game in the future. In the meantime, you can use the mod 'BetterSADX' to achieve the correct graphics and set the resoultion to your heart's desires.

Sonic Adventure is rather old. You can definitely SEE that by any screenshot or video of the game. However, it’s widely seen as a classic among Sonic fans and, like most classics, it still holds up if you can get past the visuals. Sonic Adventure is rather true to its name. It feels like an adventure, which is my favorite part about it. There are multiple campaigns that show different perspectives of the same story unfolding. While there is quite a bit of overlap in stories, each offer their own unique playstyle and takes on stages that makes this game feel like a bunch of shorter games.
Sonic – Sonic has classic 2D platforming stages and, as the face of the game, has the most levels (which is good because many put his story up there as the most fun). The only flaw is the casino level where you’re forced to play pinball.
Tails – Tails has a bunch of really short levels that are oriented like a race. His flying power’s pretty fun, so it makes me sad how short and…oddly specific this story is.
Knuckles – Knuckles is put in the middle non-linear, open levels with the goal of finding three pieces of an emerald. It’s a “hot-cold” kind of game, as little radars blink faster and faster as you get closer to each. They don’t tend to be as frustrating as one might expect.
Amy – Amy has 3D “platforming” levels where she needs to reach the end while being chased by a robot throughout. “Platforming” is in quotation marks because Amy is very slow with limited movement options. Thankfully, the campain’s short, so it’s over before it starts to actually slog.
E-102 – E-102’s levels are more “run and gun” where you have to make it to a boss at the end of a stage before time runs out…while blasting your way through it with your arm cannon. This is one of the better campaigns, aided by its surprisingly good story of this robot struggling to understand others.
Big – Big’s stages are fishing. Yes. You need to explore an open stage with multiple pools of water until you find your frog in one of them, then manage to get him to bite your lure to fish him out. This is easily the worst part of the game and where I got stopped. However, it’s best to just look up a guide and push through it, as completing every campaign unlocks the final boss.
Overall, the stage gameplay is consistently fun. However, every character has overworld sections where they need to go to specific places and do specific things in order to get to the next stage of, well, the actual game. I get that it helps the game feel more like an adventure than just a series of levels, but at the same time I still find myself struggling to remember where to go or what to do in these parts and it slows the game down even more than it does even if I knew everything. Thankfully, a little fairy is usually around each area to point you in the right direction, but there are some parts where that simply doesn’t count.
As far as other elements go, the story’s alright. Nothing award-winning, but cohesive across all the campaigns. The music is great, definitely no complaints there. The cutscenes are…something. They’re bad, but in a funny way with the super weird facial expressions and voice deliveries that I quote frequently. The game’s old, so you might run into a few glitches, but I think the glitchiness of this game is way oversold and it’s really not that badon normal playthroughs. There are Chao in this game that you can raise, but if you want a Chao Experience then you should definitely look at the sequel, Sonic Adventure 2, instead.
Overall, the direction this game took with multiple campaigns with unique playstyles is really fun and makes the game seem like something unique. If you aren’t put off by its age, I’d give this classic a shot!

APB Reloaded is basically a F2P GTA with shoulder switching and always MMO.... what this does Better than GTA is the customization, where you yourself can make your own symbols to put on your clothing, cars and even your own death tunes (songs that play to an enemy when you kill them)
Now first off APB is infuriating when you start and you'll either want to quit quickly or bash your head against the wall untill it breaks. This is a game of skill which you only get through playing it, the social can help you to unwind when you get frustrated by giving you a quick chill place and you can spend some time customizing your character to what you want....
The gun play is fairly standard 3rd person shooter style, but allows you to swap which shoulder you fire your weapon, alowing you to expose as little of yourself as possible, something i wish more TPS did.
Thats what the games about out of the way.... now for the elephant in the room.... Pay-2-win. Funny enough, it's not really that prominant, people will say "oh this or that is so OP" And some weapons are questionable for sure.... but this takes the weapons roles into consideration... youre not going to use a SMG to do a snipers job... and your not going to take a bolt action rifle into a cqc environment.... Some players do do this and for what it's worth, it's take alot of skill to pull off what they do, successfully. But for the most part, weapon modification is what seperates the pay-2-win guns from the standards, which people can do once they have their roles up enough to unlock both weapons and their mod counterparts, alternativly you can get the weapon you want, but buy the mod from the in-game marketplace from other players... and usually not for that much money, about 20K more than the retail price at 60K for the marketplace mods....
All in all, APB in my opinion is a good,well rounded, if a little frustrating game, with most hackers being weeded out, daily, the gameplay is fun if has a steep learning curve and the cuastomization is what really sets this game apart from any other in it's class.

Lakeview Cabin Collection features a romp of 80s style horror parody platformer-puzzle hybrids in which the goal is for your group of friends to survive the onslaught of a mysterious and cliché killer. The 4 chapters start at 3 for some reason and each has their own team and theme. In Lakeview Chapter 3, it’s a bunch of spring break types vacationing at a cabin haunted by a murderous duo.  Chapter 4 seems like a page pulled right out of The Hills Have Eyes with a little Texas Chainsaw massacre mixed in. Chapter 5 is a Jason-Freddy combination and Chapter 6 practically screams Alien. The content is all episodic and can be entered in any order you choose from the movie theater hub level.
Stages in LCC can be a bit cryptic as you start each one in somewhat peaceful conditions and it may seem as if there is nothing to do except wander around. This is an easy mistake to make as just about every stage has some sort of timer before various events are thrown into motion, potentially sealing your doom if you are not prepared enough. Each stage has a variety of weapons for you to fight back against the killers with, and careful use of combined forces is absolutely necessary if you want to be able to take them down.
If you plan on playing this game without a guide, expect to spend a lot of time doing trial and error before you finally figure things out. Some chapters are pretty obscure so don’t feel bad if you have to pull up a guide for help as there are plenty in the steam community. Either way, I managed to put in around 13 hours in Lakeview Cabin Collection which is a great deal for the price. Worth picking up if you’re into cheesy 80s horror movies and enjoy a good puzzle-mystery.

** One-sentence review:  Unique, Difficult but Fun Old School Game **
The Lakeview Cabin Colleciton began with a flash game on Newgrounds and since has evolved into a game with mechanics of the early days of the PC gaming industry but with some modern twists.  This will either make or break the game for you because you're given nearly nothing in terms of instructions and the puzzles and planning quickly ramp up to extreme difficulty.
Yet this is part of the game's charm; nothing is really explained and the best learning is through experimentation.  There's little you can rely on from other games to help you -- there will be no prompts, the clues will be subtle and the combination of pixelated graphics and a complete lack of any examination functionality means you have to learn by playing and trying different, sometimes ridiculous things.
While this might seem like a negative -- and for some players it really will be -- there's the other factor that experimentation is a lot of fun, especially in the first episode.  Your failures and successes have the potential to be spectacular.  You're free to make the characters do anything you want, and a great deal of the hazards that apply to you also apply to most everyone else.  There's a great amount of darkly humourous value to be had in managing to kill someone with popcorn or exploding something with more force than what was expected.  You're free to smash your own allies with anything you can lay your hands on (including whole/parts of bodies) or engage in various kinds of lewd behaviour.
Each episode has its own drastically different style and game play all while using the same engine.  Episode 1 (LCIII) allows for a lot of juvenile humour and is the most open ended.  Episode II (LCIV) is suddenly a lot more serious, which is surprisingly effective as it still retains some of the goofier elements like very make-shift weapons (candles, flares, bodies).  Episode III (LCV) is suddenly a full-on hardcore puzzle game (including retaining the modern design of being unable to actually lose).  Episode IV (LCVI) suddenly throws things in an entirely new-yet-old direction, and this doesn't even cover the Hub world with its hidden surprises.
Including solving a puzzle using vomit in the Underworld.  It wasn't meant to be solved that way, but it worked.
The Lakeview Cabin Collection is a rare comedy-horror combination in the gaming world -- it's very darkly funny, and yet also manages to rank up the tension, suspense and horror (it's not scary, but it is unsettling and purposely becomes moreso if you analyze it).
Plus every time someone gets a rake in the face it makes me laugh.  Moreso when it's a menacing killer.  Who's on fire.  While psycho strings are playing.
PROS:
- Extremely imaginative and creative engine.  Almost everything has multiple uses.  Many things have hidden uses or amusing mis-uses.
- Well done pixel graphics; starts out simple and then gets surprising.  The pixel graphics also match the budget-restricted feel of old horror movies.
- The game FEELS like a series of horror cult classics with appropriate musical stings and over-the-top, pixelated gore.
- Ridiculous combat.
- Extremely clever puzzles.
CONS:
- Hit detection and consistency is off; it was designed so certain enemies really do need to be hit from the back but in a game where characters react to just about anything the no-sell comes off more like poor hit detection rather than being ineffective.  Thrown item hit detection is also a bit wonk, and some items can only be used once for no reason and with a lack of universal consistency it feels more 'off' than it should.
- The complete lack of real guidance may turn off some players.
- Some mechanics take a leap in logic; to fuel a minibus for example one must hurl the can towards the 'right spot' on the bus as opposed to putting in an object use button or automatically using it (like shells are automatically placed in the shotgun).  This stands out more when most objects are fairly intuitive.
Overall, if you are a fan of horror, a fan of ludicrous game mechanics that lets you do things just because you wanted to, and enjoy some truly old-school game play from a time before established practices, this is probably the game for you.
If you prefer games that plainly explain things -- including mechanics and story -- you might find the Lakeview Cabin Collection more frustrating than fun.

This one's good, but with caveats.
The basic concept is innovative - commercial games generally don't tweak their players this way. Not surprising though considering this was originally freeware.
The main mechanic is both interesting (even if it's not entirely original) and executed well, with the level design making good use of it, and fun twists every so often. The aesthetics follow through on the premise as much as is feasible given the style and budget.
That's the good stuff, and it's good enough for the game to deserve a look, especially considering it's cheap and short.
There are however two problems, and they can be pretty big ones depending on how you approach the game - first, the platforming physics are... less than perfect, with unintuitive hitboxes, relatively low jump precision and limited air control. The issue is exacerbated by the level design, which requires high jump precision in tricky hitbox situations in several places, and the second problem, which is bad checkpointing. The player gets unlimited lives and resumes at checkpoints, which is a good decision, but the checkpoints are relatively sparse, and worse - they are usually placed at the beginnings and middles of levels, not after most difficult parts, which means that you can fail a difficult section due to poor mechanics (at least that's what it feels like) and then have to go back and redo the better part of the level, which is always frustrating.
It's worth noting that this only becomes a real problem if you're trying for the secret endings, all gems, or 100% completion, etc. - a regular playthrough should be fun, moderately challenging and mostly frustration-free for most players, so if you're playing for the experience the game will accommodate you and you'll get plenty out of it.
Definitely worth a look!

Xenonauts is easily the best Turn Based Tactics/Strategy game I've played in long time. I did not play the original XCOM or even the other spinoffs, so this review won't help you if you're looking at it from that perspective.
We'll start with the core of the game, combat. Send your elite commandos all over the world to accomplish many different objectives. The combat is turned based, so you have plenty of time to think about your strategy, which is really important because around every corner, you're soldiers could meet their death. The better armed and usually physically stronger alien invaders have a clear advantage. If you're careless, you're dead. Customize your soldiers with gear/weapons to suite the role you want them to play and to suite your tactical preference, but watch out....when they're dead their dead for good along with all the expensive gear you may have equipped them with.
You'll face many different types of enemies, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. You'll need to adjust you tactics nearly every mission, depending on what you're facing and what area of the world you're in Urban/Rural/Desert/Arctic. The maps can get a little repetitive, apparently there are not that many, but there are plenty of map mods available or you can make your own.
The second part of the game is managing your military, as a whole.  You begin the game facing an enemy who has a clear technological advantage, but thorugh research you can implement Alien technology for your own purposes, but it's expensive and time consuming, so chose wisly. Playing the game on normal, you'll always feel one step behind the aliens as they ramp up their invasion. You'l need to build bases to protect the nations of the world, who are funding you! Let too many aliens thorugh, an you'll lose the nation, loose too many nations game over man.
I have about 40 hours in so far and I can highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys thinking tactically or strategically. It's a fun game you can play for 30 minutes at a time or settle in for a good 6 hour marathon. The combat can get a little repretive in the beginning, but as the game progresses I actually started to notice it less. I also downloaded some map mods too.
I would give it 4 out of 5 and a must have for lovers of strategy.

The only weak points I see are that the tactical locations are all very similar - they're using prebuilt tile maps and not randomly generating locations - it breaks the immersion a little bit when you  realize you've played the same map on a previous play. The dog-fighting mini game isn't very fun and you don't seem to gain anything by not using Auto Resolve. The Civilian AI could be a better too, as they seem to just run around in random patterns without any real objective or tactics. Keeping yourself in the black seems a little bit too difficult as well - but they provide full modding ability if you want to tweak any of the games parameters to tune the difficulty.
Those points aside, I really love this game. I enjoy approaching it like a roleplaying game - naming all my soldiers and coming up with Cold-War-Esque code names for my bases, dropships, and vehicles.
Highly reccomended for fans of deep strategy or tactical games.

It provides you with no direction whatsoever as you're plopped into a horror movie scenario (Friday the 13th, Halloween, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, and Aliens) and forced to find your own way of survival. It's definitely worth experiencing, but I recommend buying it on sale due to a few major omissions from the developer that damage the overall experience. Lakeview Cabin would be a perfect fit for local multiplayer, it would be seamless, but instead you're forced to play single player and awkwardly cycle through four playable characters at a time. The other omission is allowing the player to distinguish between throwing, dropping, and "using" items. This game is 99% interacting with items and it gets frustrating when you can't do something as simple as throwing them on command.

In terms of my thoughts on the game itself, I can agree as a long time Sonic fan that much like pretty much every Sonic game made after the Genesis/Mega Drive era, this game is definitely not for everyone. It does a lot of things right that other 3D Sonic Games severely missed the mark on, but in other ways it's age definitely shows. (I mean it was originally released as a launch title for the Dreamcast way back in 1999 after all.) Even so, it still manages to have a lot of charm and for those that grew up with it, various aspects of it still hold up pretty well today.
As for this particular port on it's own, this is just about the worst port of Sonic Adventure 1 imaginable. Not only does it lack proper support for widescreen resolutiuons, but it is very poorly opitimized. But with BetterSADX and the Dreamcast conversion mod installed, it actually becomes the true difinitive way to play the game! Better than both the GameCube version and the original Dreamcast version combined!
There really is only so much I can say about how much this mod improves the Steam version of the game. I suggest you watch BlazeHedgehog's video about it for more info:

This game introduced a lot a of decent new elements into the Sonic lore and franchise at large, including what is actually a perhaps an underrated story (perhaps not always told in the best of ways however). Unfortunately, it also introduced some more controversial things too (e.g. Big the Cat, a restriction on the use of Super Sonic, shooting mechanics in future games etc). The music is also extremely memorable and fits well with the game.
I give this positive review, however in my opinion this game is slightly above a neutral or mid score rating. There are some great ideas in this game, but unfortunately they are not executed very well. The game is riddled with bugs (though not as bad as Sonic 06), the camera sucks, and Sonic Generations really shows just how outdated and inferior the game has become. The game could really benefit from a remake, at least to fix some of the shortcomings of the dated and flawed gameplay.
A further criticism is that this version does not have widescreen out of the box. Instead, I strongly encourage the use of mods to rectify this, as well as other improvements and bug fixes being on offer. Overall however, there are far worse Sonic games, and while it's a shame that this is ultimately a flawed product, it does some charm that warrant a playthrough for any Sonic fan. Perhap not so much for non-Sonic fans however.

TL;DR - Admissable 3D Platforming on the PC, there are games that have been ported to Steam that don't work, this isn't one of them. Broken camera, but players can easily adjust.
As far as ports onto Steam go, Sonic Adventure Director’s Cut is done well. Although many argue that the Steam version, derived from several other ports, does a poor job of preserving certain qualities of the original SEGA Dreamcast release of Sonic Adventure, the game is still easily playable and is an enjoyable platformer. There are many mods that can be easily found and installed to solve lighting and texture issues, and the gameplay holds together far better than many a failed port that can be found on Steam. Sonic Adventure Director’s Cut does have many technical issues and rough edges. However, if you are looking for a casual, inexpensive 3D platformer, this game will probably get the job done.
Geared mainly towards younger audiences, the subject matter of the game is hardly sophisticated. For those who have never played Sonic Adventure or any of its ports before, keep this in mind, as the writing and story are often cringeworthy, and one of the least redeeming qualities of the game. Older members of the audience can still find enjoyment, however, in many of the gameplay mechanics, whether they are returning to this game for nostalgic purposes, or if they’re newcomers entirely.
Completion of the game can be much more lackadaisical than internet reviews of Sonic Adventure might suggest. If you’re simply looking to complete the Story Mode, you will most likely avoid all technical problems often associated with the game. For newcomers, the assortment of supporting characters allow for a change of pace from the main game. Sonic’s levels are the greatest in quantity and, some would argue, polish, but the other characters offer different challenges that, while far from perfect, are able to break up repetitive gameplay. The younger target audience might find these characters more appealing for their role in the story, while older audiences will be able to appreciate the variety of gameplay introduced in levels that require fishing, racing, or scoring points for destroying a certain number of enemies. The soundtrack, another childish and quirky aspect of the game, is fitting and in many places well written to fit different levels. Graphically, the Steam version is a port of a console game from the early 2000’s, so keep that in mind when you see the many awkward poses and ridiculous facial animations. Side game mechanics like the Chao Garden and the additional emblems for replaying levels with more stringent requirements can be avoided entirely if one simply wants to play casually through the game.
As someone who purchased the game for both nostalgia and a love of 3D platformers, I can honestly say that Sonic Adventure has very many flaws. It took me approximately 40 hours to complete every achievement that the Steam port has to offer. Having simply done a casual playthrough of the game as a child, I knew the general layout of the whole game, and had explored most of the side mechanics. I include this here to explain that the 40 hours it took me to complete this game entirely was with prior knowledge of the game, needing to do very little exploration. That said, it would probably take someone unfamiliar with the game upwards of 50 hours, depending on how quickly they adjust to many of the quirks you might come across going through the game.
In regards to the most popular complaint with Sonic Adventure (which I’d like to also complain about), the game’s camera can at times be extremely poor. A casual playthrough will probably experience few to no camera issues. However, in order to complete the game’s achievements, each level is required to be repeated for each and every character, and so the player must experience these levels numerous times. In my 40 or so hours, the most glaring issues came from places such as Sonic’s Icecap
, Lost World
, Sky Deck
, and Final Egg
, Knuckles’ Lost World when flying too quickly, and Big’s Icecap when trying to leave any underwater area, to name a few. In general, despite being a Sonic the Hedgehog game, moving and turning at extremely quick speeds can cause serious issues where the camera gets left quite far behind, and obstacles that are coming up very soon cannot be seen whatsoever. Many segments where a character bounces off a spring also do not adjust the camera properly, causing players to fall to their death that they are unable to prevent in any way at all.
These might seem like gamebreaking issues to some. However, those with even the smallest amount of patience can quickly adjust – they are byproducts of a time when 3D platformers by third party developers were becoming popular and therefore were encouraged to be produced. Quite infrequently will you find yourself going through a level and becoming frustrated with this game; if you’re not meeting the goal in time or can’t find the objective, there’s most certainly a trick or method you’re missing that can easily be looked up. There are a number of reasons that many people return to Sonic Adventure other than degeneracy, so taken with a grain of salt, Sonic Adventure is a relatively enjoyable and affordable 3D platforming experience.

This is the X-Com reimagining we've all been waiting for.
Xenonauts was clearly made with enormous respect and admiration for the original, but this affection never stopped Goldhawk from reaching deep into the game mechanics and touching up everything that needed fixing, and many things that I never thought could have been improved. The result is not a mere 1:1 copy, and much more than just X-Com with a better interface. It's a refinement of the original, keeping the brilliant and still enormously engaging core loop intact and polishing it to perfection.
If you never played the original X-Com games, don't even try. They are hard to get into, and thanks to Goldhawk, there is simply no need to wrestle with them anymore. Xenonauts delivers the same experience that made the original a legend, except better in every possible way. A fantastic achievement.

Once upon the time there was a fruggo named "Froggy G." who loved pizza more than anything. More than he loved pushing bot lane. More than he loved vulturing kills off of Vinnies who are trying SO DAMN HARD despite the nerfs. He loved it so much he wanted to make a historical video game about the earliest known records of pizza delivery 1577 years before his time. He learned to code, which was a challenge as he reflexively attempted to swallow his monitor whole each time it displayed the italian flavor discs he so worshipped, but the froge persisted. Days into nights into weeks into months into years. His life committed to his endeavors so thoroughly it began to find ways to find a way to negatively impact the health of a football-shaped alien frog. His employers desperately nerfing the competition to even the fields of the atrophied froge, his heart no longer in the intergalactic battles as every splash dash free autoparry was nearly interrupted by his musings on how to properly integrate a currency system, teleporting back to base at inappropriate times so he could take down a note on more upgrades for the leveling system.
The entire war was forced to shift awkwardly into a tangled mess, a shadow of itself, just as the frog it tried to accommodate did, but bit by bit, through perseverance, persistence and pizza the frogola learned and pushed forward. But of course, there was trouble, the higher ups dissatisfied with having to constantly tolerate and bend over backwards to cope with the side effects of Froggy's project attempted to stop him. They should have known better to attempt to come between a hurtful racial stereotype space frog and his love of pizza. When the legion of Zurian interns came to confiscate his dear laptop with no cloud storage the G knew his time as a game developer was up, but if he thought fast, the time for pizza was only beginning. With a resounding "Yoman" he took hold of the portable computer in his clammy, awkward, clumsy hands, clinging it to his chest as he realized what he had to do. He splash dashed, like he never had before. Every shred of effort he'd denied his employers was paid back all at once with interest, the helpless, clueless interns bowled over and decimated by what could only be described as the unholy offspring of a cannonball and a tsunami. So intense and speedy were the frug's sweet moves that in his wake he found he'd not only torn apart his pizza-hating employer's goons but torn a new one in the time-space continuum. Closing his eyes he gave a silent prayer to the gods of all that was cheesy to give safe passage to his labor of love, flinging his laptop into the vortex of uncertainty just as it had begun to close.
They say now, if you play the game's intro theme backwards you can still hear the voice of that Frog with dreams (for pizza) almost as big as his stomach (for pizza) as he mournfully says "I see ya, but I really wanna pizza."
I don't own a Pizza place but if I did I'd put this game out front arcade cabinet style and watch the customers roll in.

Being the CEO of an up-and-coming intergalactic pizza joint is no easy business, especially when you're up against the likes of conglomerate pizza pioneers like Big Pizza. Pizzarian is the story of one small pizza business and its rise into the glamorous yet dangerous life of intergalactic delivery service. You'll be faced with managing your pizza stock and ship upgrades, with the perils of the planetary orbit and the traffic of space highways that flow with them, and with making every piping hot order of cheese-y goodness arrive to their destination in an orderly fashion.
The high-speed deliveries you make are broken up into two separate arcade-inspired sections of dodge and shootem'up action, with management of your ships and upgrades inbetween deliveries. Using hard earned money on new ships is crucial to extending your future trips and making sure you hit each delivery target with utmost precisions, and ships themselves come with a variety of badass retro references ranging from ships likened to the Vic Viper from Gradius to weapons humorously taking after the Nintendo Zapper remembered so fondly.
With such rapid forays into bite-sized arcade stages Pizzarian is the kind of game you can pick up for a few minutes at a time, but thanks to the progressive nature of growing your ship and business is also easy to zone out on for much longer.
The claustrophobic and nerve-wracking traffic in Pizzarian is, as you'll soon find out, not much different from the real world. The rage inducing flow of slow moving trucks and various jerks cutting you off shows no end, and the only way to survive is to be a jerk back. Cutting off all four corners of another driver is, while a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, the surest way to prove your space superiority and earns you the highest boost to your "Cool" meter. The road rage runs high as you rush to swerve and cut off any unsuspecting opponents of the road while the warm buzzing of nostalgic chiptunes drives your high-octane car dodging.
Once you've survived the quick and heinous traffic section you stop off at your first selected planet in a very Xevious-like top-down vertically scrolling shoot'emup section, where instead of shooting enemies with bullets you try to accurately fire steamy hot pizzas into the homes of your loyal and waiting cosmic customers. The deeper into the galaxy you go to visit these hungry planets the more planets you discover, appearing on your map for future runs to extend your trip and allow for even crazier pay to save up for those super sweet ship upgrades.
The game super charming, and too addictive for how simple it is. The fact that the pizzas you deliver cost you your hard earned money that you could be using on upgrades makes every shot at every customer that much more crucial, and the stunts you pull off for increasing your "Cool" meter and in turn gaining more cash for upgrades so much more rewarding.
tldr;
With a great retro style featuring multiple color schemes, some seriously groovy 8-bit music (I've had the map system music stuck in my head for a week), and a great sense of humor Pizzarian is a game with tons of variety packed into one nostalgic arcade trip. And even if you aren't a super retro enthusiast, it offers some of the quickest blasts of condensed fun for a ridiculously modest price making it the absolute perfect coffee break (or pizza break!) game.

Let me start this review off by saying that this game is the spiritual successor to X-COM all of us fans of the original have been waiting for. Now, before all the Firaxis fans come out of the woodwork to make angry remarks, I have nothing against XCOM - from what I've heard it's a very good game in its own right; however from what I've seen (yes, I haven't yet had a chance to play it myself - yet - although the opinions I've heard/read and videos I've watched all seem to agree on this), the Firaxis remake changed the formula that made the original great into a more streamlined experience, that had been tailored to appeal to a larger audience - thus removing some of what made X-COM so enjoyable for some of us.
However, Xenonauts has very much kept the formula the same. The basic gameplay mechanics are spot-on compared to what the original X-COM was like, except with some much needed touch-ups. First and foremost is the game resolution and interface - no longer will you need to suffer with an 800x600 resolution window and a clunky UI where the buttons don't reveal much ("What does this do? Oh I just placed some primed C4 at my soldier's feet"), and the interface taking up a third of the screen! Xenonauts has really improved these aspects and honestly, I really think that this alone makes Xenonauts worth considering, due to the sheer increase in playability that has resulted by actually having a nice, clean interface that didn't come straight out of the 1990s.
Secondly, there are the combat improvements. They've really changed up the air combat in this game from what was in the original, and although I acknowledge that it's not to everyone's taste, it's certainly a lot closer to it than what X-COM's air combat was like, to be quite honest! All you really need to take into account are the manoeuvres (roll left/right and afterburner, primarily) for each plane and once you've gotten the hang of timing them and avoiding enemy fire, you'll be dropping those UFOs like flies in no time! (Although, don't mistake this for a lack of difficulty - some of the UFOs that get sent down to earth can be quite punishing!)
As for the ground combat, not all that much is different from the original X-COM: soldiers are nothing more than fodder (don't grow attached and restart the game if you lose some; they're all expendable and you should always have a couple of Chinooks' worth rotating in and out of active duty, so you've always got some skilled backup soldiers in case a mission goes bad) who can all be killed by a single well-placed round by an alien if they're unlucky (it's always a "lucky shot" if the aliens happen to get you - ALWAYS ;) ), so using cover and smoke is very important. On a similar note, one of the things that Goldhawk have added to ground combat is a suppression system, where if your rounds miss the aliens (or vice versa) but either hit their cover or whizz by near them, they will become suppressed; meaning that they will drop to a crouch, will be unable to perform reaction fire in your turn and will have reduced TUs (Time Units) in their following turn.
As for cons, I must say there aren't many. I'd say the only real cons are are there's not a HUGE variety of the randomly-assigned nationalities - although there's still quite a lot - and former units that help add some background to your soldiers, as well as the variety of generated maps being rather more limited than what was in the original X-COM. Although again, this isn't a great issue unless you replay the game a lot (but then again, who wouldn't?). However, due to the fact that modding this game has been made to be quite easy, there are community-made mods out there that remedy both of these cons.
In summary, quite frankly I'm no longer able to recommend the original X-COM to people, simply because THIS exists, and that it's regular X-COM, but with some really nice improvements. If you've been hanging out for X-COM but want something a touch less dated, then definitely pick this up! I'm honestly very happy I Kickstarted this game a while back and I consider the extra money I sink into the game by buying gift copies for friends to be money well spent.

Spiffing! As everyone knows, unlike the reimaged XCom that came out recently, this Xenonauts is an update of the original Xcom. And it's very well done.
You have the base management. Placing bases for their radar coverage, with hangars to send ships out to intercept alien craft. Then send in your landing vehicle for your troops and maybe a buggy to go round gunning down the survivors of the crashed alien craft.
Could also be going in to a Terror Mission. To fight off the aliens and save what locals you can and maintain relations with the nation so terrorised.
Might be the alliens attack your base and gun batteries you've chosen to build may or may not be enough, and then have to clear your base of aliens the hard way.
Could be you discover a base the aliens have set up. Going in to clear it room by room.
The base management leaves a lot of room for playstyles and mistakes. Setting up labs and workrooms for scientists to research alien tech and engineers to make new toys. So many toys. Found it best to keep the enhanced workshop action at the base your soldiers come home to, other bases wouldn't have access to the alien materials unless you start sending parcels of items back and forth.
Extra radar arrays widen the coverage of each base, and extra bases spaced around the planets are essential in ensuring few alien craft get to run amok without you sending in your ships.
When you do that, you can choose to send 1-3 ships all together. So that requires you building hangers at various bases around the world too.
When  your ships catch an alien craft it gives you a % of success for an automated dogfight, but you can elect to go in to manually direct the aero-action.
When an alien craft is downed you can send in your foot troops, or, just have an airstrike deal alien stragglers. Youll get a bt of money that way but no chance of acquiring fancy alien tech to play with.
The land battle is as ever a turn based game.  Your mooks have a number of points they can spend on moving, kneeling, turning, shooting, luzzing grenades, equipping the med pack from your backpack to use on a wounded ally, or battering an alien over the head with a stun rod.
With shooting there's a few choices in how accurate you're prepared to be, more accuracy costs more points. Cover reduces the ahcne of success while kneeling raises it.
You could leave your mook with points unspent in which case they're stood there prepared to fire at any alien bugger that hoves into view. Their reflexes stat comes into play then, whether they get a shot off before the alien does.
Stats like those and strength (covers how much you can carry without movement penalties) and bravery are automatically improved when they're used. So it really hurts if someone dies.
If a xenonaut is hit and hurt they'll spend some time in the med-bay you built. Dead ones, there's a slim chance they recover, less so the more they're hurt.
It seems rather well designed. The learning curve is about right. The arms race between you and the aliens is in your favour if you get on top of R&D early on and keep it flowing.
One of your more beloved xenonauts taking a powerful hit and dying can really sting though. You could be brave and suck it up, or go back to a previous save point.
It quite a moddable game in regards "numbers", so you could adjust such things as the amount of money here or there if you want. It wouldn't affect the current game, just the next one started.

Eversion is a simple, basic 2D side scrolling platformer. The only twist being that you have the ability to shift environments (eversions). You can shift from six different eversions: deception, erosion, desolation, apprehension, confusion and commotion. Every shift will change colors and backgrounds. The shifts will also turn bushes from leafy, to dead so you can pass through them and into deadly thorn bushes. Some enemies into stone and brick platforms into crumbling blocks. You cannot just shift on a whim, you need to find the invisible area you're supposed to stand in and then shift eversions. When you press the eversion button, if you're close enough to the correct invisible spot, you'll see a ring around it for a brief time. If you're stuck, that usually means you need to backtrack and find the invisible spot.
The gameplay is simple. Like Mario you can destroy bricks by jumping into them and make a gem appear out of blocks by jumping into special ones. Eventually, you will get to see this magical kingdom for what it is. Horrifying, dark and grim. At some point, enemies will spurt bright red blood partially obscuring the screen. Although some might boast this as a horror game, there's nothing really horrific. I was too busy laughing at the giant hands that comically shoot up from death pits. Its too bright and simple of an art style to really be horrific.
There are no power ups. Every hit is instant death, but that's okay because there are no lives. You just respawn at the start of the level or the last checkpoint. The game boasts 8 worlds, but really these worlds are just 8 levels. A world to me feels like it should be more than a level. I was able to breeze through the game in half an hour and that's even looking for invisible eversion points. At the end of each level you hop on a ground flag. There are no bosses, in fact there really only seems to be three enemy types in the game. Monkey claw, goomba and some sort of stone beetle.
Upon completing the game, it just crashed back to the desktop. The only replay value is going back to collect all 240 gems to get better endings that reference better properties. Once you get a gem, it the game considers collected, even if you die on the same run, that gem will not be there. Not having any consequence of death makes things way too easy. This is a quick diversion without any challenge. The forum is full of people giving away 66% off coupons and others talking about how the game is free.

A very fun game with a hard edge of challenge. Not for those into glass track runner zombie games. (Left 4 Dead, CoD Zombies, etc.) These zombies shamble, and take more hits than the average. Each different one having unique features of difficulty against them. The runners will be your worst nightmare after wave 5. Guranteed.
I like how the game pins the fight against the zombies in the eyes of regular people, instead of just built mercaneries who crush the heads of zombies with their massive pectorals. The fight is in your hands; it all boils down to skill and luck in the end of it all.
For those not interested in survival, there are the optional objective-based maps where you need to escape. Perhaps a better alternative to get used to the game with those modes, then to go to survival if you feel confident.
I do like some things the game did. Proved to be worth the download in the end.
The realism factor is taken into play very seriously. This is basically your most realistic game in a semi-realistic setting. They get shot in the head, they die. You lose stamina very quickly. Barricades don't last. Pills that don't fix the infection forever. You can't tank weapons on your back. Scare weapons all-together.  It wouldn't be that way in other games, where you can find a bunch of shotguns or deagles in the lobby of a hospital.
The zombies are hard to kill. Power weapon or not, they are survivors. They can take quite a bunch of body-shots from a pistol, let alone a rifle. Runners are even harder because their heads bob much more faster than your crosshair can keep up with. You'd usually kill them when it's too late. And the children; while easier to shoot in the head, not as easy to spot. They blend into crowds very well and are pretty nasty ambushers if not spotted right away.
"GWAFIX, GWAFIX, GWAFIX!!!1!!" For a source engine mod, this is pretty spectacular in the graphics department. Certainly not half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥work here: textures look like they belong, sprites in the correct looking places and style, special effects and other minor details add to the immersion of this shambling dystopian city at war facing an army of infected; just magnificent.
Lots of weapons. There are plenty of choices between weapons to find in this game. Either choose a rifle, shotgun, pistol, or a melee if you're skilled. But start small, and work your way up. Because rolling in with a M4A1 with zero experience, wasting a whole clip on a single zombie is frowned upon by many.
It's Free-to-Play. It's most likely one of the few 'good' free-to-play games out there. By 'good' I mean you really don't have to pay a cent. It's all you see, all for free.
However, there are a few things I don't like what the game did, and should be improved.
There are still some bugs that need a-fixin'. Holding a chainsaw with one hand or mysteriously changing clothing after getting infected. Because being bitten makes your clothes tattered and ruined. Nothing you haven't seen in another source mod, but some various ones still remain.
The grace period for getting infected is rather short. Mind you this game is all about realism, but I don't think you get infected holding a zombie for a milisecond. Isn't it by blood transfer through the eyes or being bitten that makes it happen? (Eh, just a minor complaint though.)
The themes lack difference. I know this contradicts my statement about the graphics a tad, but it's true. There haven't been many 'sunny' levels that aren't mods. It's usually dawn, dusk, or night. I can image the zombies could survive sunlight. At least I hope.
Unsupportive players. This isn't the game's fault, but more towards the people who play it. I've had multiple instences where there are random deathmatches happening on round one. Others include: players horading weapons / areas of the map, cheating (rare), random kicking, teamkilling, and refusing a player pleading death while infected, (also rare.) More instances lie in this game, but it's to be expected with any game that has friendly fire, or exploitable tactics.
All in all, I love this game, even with it's flaws. I had high hopes for this game being released, and it's perfect in timing and execution. I don't throw around this alot, but this game can certainly make game of the year if it's still updated with the things we want and need. Like it was when it was being developed. It could easily be snuffed if they just release bugfixes and nothing more.
Give this game a shot. I bet you will stick around, still trying to get good with the pistol. After a few months of play, you'll walk out with your favorite weapon kicking♥♥♥♥♥ And you'll enjoy every second of the time you played between the start and end of things. Yet it doesn't have to end. The fun never ends.

Greetings Again!  Next on the list is part three of the Rain Slick Precipice of Darkness series by Penny Arcade.    It is no secret that I am a huge fan of RPGs and especially those of the classic JRPG style and this game definitely matches the theme, but is it something I’d recommend you buy?
Wall of Text:  The story resumes where it left off but with a very different feel (and a new development team from what I understand), gone are the voice over acting and everything has been brought back to a time when 16 bit was all we could do.  This includes the graphics, the audio, everything; even the menus are done in this style.  The game even has a small segment where you go 8 bit for a while.  The story does follow along the previous two but I found myself losing some of the content due to long periods of text boxes.  To be honest, I really should have just taken a bit of a break at those points.
Punch-A-Thon:  Mechanically the game plays very similar to any old school RPG that you’ve seen before with a few small twists.  You don’t use mana in the same was you normally would, instead of having a mana pool that you deplete you start at zero and gain one every turn.  This moves into the second design choice, where you regain all items, health and clear all status effects at the end of the battle.  This is nice but it leads to one of the few problems I have with the game, ie battles can feel like a chore at times, leading to effectively what may feel like a never ending boss battle and have the rewards of normal encounters.  Don’t get me wrong however, if you take a 15 minute break from the game you get refreshed and are ready to jump back in.
Another one bites the dust:  Complaints, well I would have liked to see random encounters (still limited by static enemy locations) but at least there is a place you can ‘grind’ a bit here and there.  Many of the classes feel less useful than the others and there seems to be a great deal of useless abilities.  Maybe that is just my play style.  The game did feel overly simplistic but so did the previous ones, this game is less of a innovation than a tribute to what came before.  Still, I regret nothing and am happy that I played to the conclusion (though I still cannot beat the Dark Clones in the secret dungeon).  I do both enjoy and am annoyed with the power escalation mechanic (enemies get stronger each turn) but it is a good way to prevent turtling, which happens to be my go to for bosses, so yeah…).
If you’ve played the previous games of this series you really don’t need incentive to buy this, in fact I feel it would be silly not to, why would you leave the story unfinished?  For those of you who haven’t and am looking this as a standalone game, I’d say the game itself is worth the purchase if you can stand the fact that you are starting midway through the story, I’d really recommend buying the whole lot but to each their own, enjoy!

This is the third instalment of the Penny Arcade games involving Gabe and Tycho at "Startling Developments Detective Agency." It takes you on another wacky adventure involving strange enemies, subtle hints, pop-culture references, and awkward humor.
Story: It does continue after the events of the first two games and DOES reference them multiple times. I would recommend you play the first two just for the sake of knowing the characters and themes, but ultimately the references are short-lived and not too specific. This is pretty typical storytelling involving otherworldly plots, strange creatures, and unknown villians. The story is very streamlined (in a good way) and provides a good reason to keep going. It's rare that the plot drags along or forces itself too fast. However, it definitely falls short in certain aspects. There are specific moments towards the end of the game where the tone and direction of the villiany takes a very strange turn. A certain character performs an act of random evil and other characters react harshly, but only for a few lines of dialogue. Everything continues normally after that. The ending feels less fleshed out, but still pleases.
Humor: This definitely has to be its own category for these games. The first game didn't necessarily connect with me every time, but this one did. Almost every joke landed for me and the subtle references to either, one of the first two games or some pop-culture reference made me laugh or go "Hey! I know where that's from!" There are two major sources of humor: the dialogue and the flavor text. The enemies have hilarious flavor text (most of the time) and should always be read when you have time. The dialogue was easily the best in the series up to this game. The character interactions were always on point and the personality flaws of each of them are represented incredibly well. Almost every situation brings out the best of their wackiness.
Gameplay: This is a completely turn-based combat system involving one action bar at the top that each character and enemy moves along at its own pace. You have a threshold where you determine an action and then a waiting period before it's performed. This allows you to use a mechanic called "interrupts" where you push the action of the enemy back towards the beginning of the bar. It's not incredibly necessary to learn the mechanic of interrupts since enemies get stronger regardless of whether they act or not, but it can definitely help you through tougher battles. The biggest flaw with the action bar is that you never know how much your speed will affect the character's movement through the bar. Your portrait might be slightly ahead of the enemy, but it might act much faster than you, even with a short distance to the action threshold. I did play this on veteran (I think that's what it's called) and it was a nice challenge, but not incredibly hard. The game gets a bit overwhelming towards the end with the number of class abilities, but it pleasantly stops itself short by not dragging the ending of the game out.
There's only a specific number of battles in the game, not unlike the other games, but you'll be more than happy with growth of characters. Class combinations are tricky but you can change them on the fly with no problem. It's a good mechanic. It plays a lot like a typical Final Fantasy game with some interesting mechanics taken from other games of the genre.
Replayability: There is not a ton of replayability, but certainly enough if you're looking to challenge yourself. There is a coliseum for infinite battles and an optional (free) dlc dungeon for another class, but the humor won't add as much the next couple times through. I got about 15 hours of solid gameplay from the title by taking my time and enjoying the story. I recommend you do the same.
Overall I find this game to be the best in the series (not including the 4th) up to this point in terms of dialogue/humor and gameplay, but it falls short on the story. It lasts just long enough, not overstaying its welcome, but really has shaky parts that don't connect well and a problematic overarching plot. It certainly has problems, but the sum of the parts definitely evens out the whole.

I've been a fan of Zeboyd Games' works since Breath of Death VII: The Beginning hit Xbox Live Indie Games way back when (seriously, it's been like 6 years or something?). Both that title and Cthulhu Saves the World took Dragon Quest style RPGs and added an element of Douglas Adams style humor to them. But, great as they were I always wanted to see what the pair could do with a more Final Fantasy style aesthetic.
PA3 answers that for better and worse.
The combat is great, as Zeboyd has made a cool system that combines FFV's (or III, or your favorite FF that has jobs here) job system with a turn system inspired by Grandia.
It's fantastic. It's super fun, and each battle feels tightly designed and intentional.
But that's the biggest flaw, as well. This game approaches RPG design in a weirdly similar way to Final Fantasy XIII - it's heavily guided. While this allows for great detail and care to be given to each battle, you don't get the enjoyment of exploring, regardless of if that freedom is an illusory veil or not. I don't mind the use of a Mario 3 style map system, but I did wish the actual areas you explored had more freedom and chance to shine. Some cool areas felt like they had more stories to tell.
Which is the final part of the puzzle. I enjoyed the story as someone who didn't really play the first two games in this series. I knew going in I was playing a third game that heavily changed the format AND took away Penny Arcade's penchant for foul humor and language. It doesn't really feel like a Penny Arcade story, and that's both a plus and a minus, depending on who is playing.
The tl;dr is I enjoyed this game and wrote this review because I'm not sure why it's tagged as an 'RPGMaker game' considering it was developed in the now extinct XNA for Xbox Live Indie Games and Steam. But hey, doesn't really matter.

However, the fact that the developer and overall style of Episode Three and Four changed makes me want to caution new players from diving into this world. I could not bring myself to finish Three, as the enjoyment died off entirely. The latter half of the series looks like it was made in RPG maker, which by itself isn't a drawback, but is pretty stock combat/features with no flair. The storytelling/humor seems to have left the series entirely but that point.
One and Two are definitely still worth playing, even if you don't plan to play the rest, but it seems pretty hit or miss as to whether people enjoy the latter two. You've been warned.
