In case you were just wondering how to make a lemon cake, it's your lucky day, because here's how you make a lemon cake:
Ingredients:
1/2 pound (2 sticks) unsalted butter, at room temperature
2 1/2 cups granulated sugar, divided
4 extra-large eggs, at room temperature
1/3 cup grated lemon zest (6 to 8 large lemons)
3 cups flour
1/2 teaspoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon kosher salt
3/4 cup freshly squeezed lemon juice, divided
3/4 cup buttermilk, at room temperature
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
For the glaze:
2 cups confectioners' sugar, sifted
3 1/2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lemon juice
Instructions:
Step 1: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease and flour 2 (8 1/2 by 4 1/4 by 2 1/2-inch) loaf pans. You may also line the bottom with parchment paper, if desired.
Step 2: Cream the butter and 2 cups granulated sugar in the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, until light and fluffy, about 5 minutes. With the mixer on medium speed, add the eggs, 1 at a time, and the lemon zest.
Step 3: Sift together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt in a bowl. In another bowl, combine 1/4 cup lemon juice, the buttermilk, and vanilla. Add the flour and buttermilk mixtures alternately to the batter, beginning and ending with the flour. Divide the batter evenly between the pans, smooth the tops, and bake for 45 minutes to 1 hour, until a cake tester comes out clean.
Step 4: Combine 1/2 cup granulated sugar with 1/2 cup lemon juice in a small saucepan and cook over low heat until the sugar dissolves. When the cakes are done, allow to cool for 10 minutes. Remove the cakes from the pans and set them on a rack set over a tray or sheet pan; spoon the lemon syrup over them. Allow the cakes to cool completely.
Step 5:For the glaze, combine the confectioners' sugar and the lemon juice in a bowl, mixing with a wire whisk until smooth. Pour over the tops of the cakes and allow the glaze to drizzle down the sides.

I had Sonic Adventure DX on the GameCube and loved it when I was younger. Sonic Adventure 2 was my favorite, but I really liked this one too.
Unfortunately, Sonic Adventure 2 doesn't hold up to my standards nowadays.
Sonic Adventure 1 on the other hand? Despite a lot of people feeling it hasn't aged well, I actually think this game is still a ton of fun to play!
Sonic Adventure 1 starts a trend in the series of splitting the gameplay up into different styles. Whether it adds enjoyable variety or ruins the game is up to you. I'll give my thoughts on all of the play types.
Sonic has speed stages. These are simple - run from point A to B. This is the style Sonic is known for and it works pretty well in a 3d environment. The controls are pretty solid and the camera isn't too bad. The level design is good, but fairly linear. All the branching paths in the classics don't really show up here. That doesn't change the fact that its still fun playing through all the levels.
Tails has speed stages as well, but with a race element. The levels are edited a bit to have new routes Tails can fly through and you have to be a computer opponent to the goal. While his stages are pretty short, its still fun to take advantage of his flying mechanic and explore new level paths. Pretty fun and very Sonic styled.
Knuckles has treasure hunting stages like the ones in SA2. These are all about finding parts of the master emerald scattered around in a level using hints and a radar. Knuckles controls great, but finding gem shards isn't ideal. With that said, its still a decent amount of fun to play through and explore the levels in a new way with his gliding and wall climbing abilities.
Amy's levels are somewhat speed-based and involve running away from a large robot until reaching the goal ring. Most people don't like her levels much, but I actually thought they were pretty damn fun. Amy can reach a decent speed when running forward and jumping around with her hammer ability is a ton of fun. There's some neat platforming sections and even puzzles for her to solve.
E-102 has shooting stages like the ones in SA2, but they're WAY better here. E-102 controls so much better than the bulky mechs and can actually reach a good top speed. His levels are very short, and I would probably only rate the gameplay as decent but its certainly not the chore it is in SA2.
Big The Cat..... he has the infamous fishing stages. Its boring. He has no interesting controls and is very slow. I've played games with cool fishing minigames. This isn't one of them. Its a complete drag. Some of his levels can be finished really fast, but this is the only gameplay style that is truly terrible.
Apart from that, there's some optional driving minigames. Not necessary, but fun enough. Only one stage requires driving and its actually fun there. There's a couple flying stages as well. They're not all that great, but tolerable.
Then there's the Chao garden. Its just as good here as in SA2 really. I actually prefer the gardens and layouts in this game. I found myself spending a little time raising them this time around. If you're into virtual pets, then you'll get some fun out of it.
Sonic Adventure's gameplay isn't strictly speed Sonic levels, but unlike in SA2, I actually think its a good blend. The only levels I really dislike are Big's, but Sonic, Tails, and Amy's stages are a great time to be had while Knuckles and E102's are a decent way to mix it up.
Unlike SA2, this game is much more than "1/3rd" fun.
On top of the gameplay styles, there's also some hub-world missions you can do.. and there's a ton of them. Lots of extra gameplay to be had. You can also unlock every Sonic Gamegear game which is a great bonus. I think the Steam version requires a mod to put that feature back in, but I'll talk about that later.
Sonic Adventure has an amazing soundtrack. I can't say much more than that. Its just fantastic. Awesome guitar instrumentals, upbeat themes, and the variety is great. Seriously, this game is worth playing for the music alone.
The visuals are okay for an early Dreamcast game. They don't look great today, but its really not something I'd call a nightmare.
The story is fairly cheesy and a bit scattered between the characters. Not really a game you'll want to play for the story, but I will say it ends in a fairly nice way.
This port is.. okay I guess. Its had a lot of work. It used to be HORRIBLE, but Sega came through and patched it so that it supports proper resolutions and controllers. Performance wise, its fine.
I didn't find this game very buggy at all, unlike SA2. It was a pretty smooth experience.
On PC we get mods and I have to recommend "BetterSADX." It really fixes up the game, adds proper support to just about everything, and brings back missing features. Seriously, even if you don't care about mods you really are going to want to get this! And if you are interested in mods, there's all kinds of stuff out there to check out as well.
Sonic Adventure was a great game when it came out.. and maybe I have an unpopular opinion, but I think it still holds up. Its a fun game with a solid variety and a kickass soundtrack.
While I don't really recommend its sequel SA2, I think its worth playing this game if you're a big Sonic fan, played it in the past, or are interested in early 3d platforming.
Very fun. Also, Sonic Heroes is a lot of fun too. It was much better than I remembered. All it takes is a simple patch for widescreen and some button mapping and you're set. Mentioning it here because it never made it to Steam, which is a shame. But if you're interested in this early 3d style, check it out as well.

Labyrinthine Dreams is an adventure puzzle game (maze, funnily enough) in which you follow and guide Beth, a young woman on death's door, through the distorted maze of (parts of) her life. The game can be frustrating to say the least.  It actually is comprised of some RPG elements in that you save up money to get upgrades which in turn get you more money.  There is some levelling with XP that allow you to choose from 3 upgrade categories.  There is also a pool of "coolness" points that, in the short time I've played, haven't made much sense to me.  You apparantly are supposed to scrape other vehicles without causing damage, and doing so is supposed to increase your coolness level.  However, after having scraped hundreds of vehicles it didn't seem like my coolness points were going up.  At some point, and seemingly at random, some text popped up next to a vehicle I had just scraped, exclaiming "Cool!" and I saw my points go up.  Unfortunately I have no idea what was different about that situation vs. all the other times I scraped a vehicle.  Obviously there is a bit of a learning curve with this game.
The game itself is actually comprised of two mini-games.  The first is to get the pizzas to their destination moon without wrecking your ship by swerving through lanes of traffic.  If you wreck, you lose the pizzas and the money you spent making them.  I actually found this part of the game to be rather tedious.  I understood that I needed to survive the traffic, but the whole coolness system and what one is supposed to do in traffic still doesn't make a lot of sense to me.  Unfortunately the tutorial didn't spend a lot of time on this aspect. The second part is delivering the pizzas to their destinations.  This took me a few rounds to get right as the tutorial didn't actually explain that the way you deliver the pizza is to "shoot" it at the house.  Originally I had been trying to drop off the pizza by hitting the button just as I was over top of the house; sufficed to say I couldn't figure out why my delivery numbers were so low.
Overall, it's a well made game, albeit confusing when first starting out.  The tutorial can really use some polishing; in particular, it should give a better explanation of the coolness system and more precise instructions on how to raise your coolness points in traffic.  One last note: the music.  I can definitely see the background music being devisive amoung players, as there only seems to be one (or did I hear a second) song the whole game, and though it is somewhat catchy and reminiscent of bygone games of old, many will definitely feel the need to turn it down or completely off.
All said, I give it a 7/10.

I bought it even though I never played the original XCOM games, but I still liked it very much.
A good third of the game you spend watching a world map and sending air fighters to fend off alien UFOs. You can autoresolve the air fights and a calculation will tell you whether you won and how much damage your planes took, but it is much more fun to run the 2D eagle view simulation to navigate the fight yourself.
Each time an enemied UFO crashes, it creates a crashsite that can either be airstriked to deal with the alien survivors, or approached with your soldiers in ground battle to recover alien technology to either sell it your advance your own weaponry, whcih becomes an essential part of the mid to late game. The ground batlle for me is the most interesting part of Xenonauts. It is very strategic and thrilling and you really develop feelings for your experienced soldiers and mourn for their unexpected deaths. But still there are sometimes so many Crashsites to deal with (each one can last up to an hour, if you are a careful player) that it can get a bit tedious in the long run.
Although the ground battle is the essential part of the game, the real strategy lies in distributing your very expensive bases, airplanes and soldiers over the globe efficiently without losing your relations to a contintent that provides your funding in return. I personally considered the game very challenging even in Normal difficulty, since everytime you feel you can somehow cope with your enemy, the UFOs and ground units get even stronger and higher in number. Some elements can also be quite frustrating (for example your armour and good cover are worth nothing when a "reaper" approaches over vast distances out of the fog of war and one-hits your soldier making him an armored zombie enemy, too). The AI is not super-intelligent (especially not the civilians always blocking your way), but challenging.
I enjoyed the game very much, but it could be considered a bit repetetive in its basic principle (manage upgrades -> UFO atttack -> shoot down planes -> intercept crash sites -> manage upgrades). The writing and the "science" elements in the well-written codex full of some beautiful artworks as well as the soundtrack set you right into that alien mood. Atmosphere, emotion and suspense 10/10, gameplay 7/10, since it feels quite repetitive in the end.

Have you ever played games on a NES, Genesis or SNES? You know how there's a whole bunch of classic platformers there which have extremely simple controls? Well Super Meat Boy is exactly the same formula but better. The controls are extremely simple: Move, jump and hold down a button to run. That's it, do you need anything else besides that to make compelling gameplay? Apparently not, as this game manages to become an indie classic with nothing more than those inputs. However, the magic is in the responsiveness of those controls, and Meat Boy handles extremely well, responding to every little nudge you give your control stick in a very natural manner.
The game is extremely hard and punishing for mistakes, but it's far from unforgiving. As soon as you die you get to try again, and again, and again until you either beat the level or put it down because it just got too hard (until you unavoidably try again, since the gameplay is so compelling). The level variety is great, several mechanics get recycled but not in a bad way, they get reused in new ways each time to test your ability to understand how they function and overcome the hazards they present. You'll definitely remember your struggles vividly even after you turn off the game.
As for the narrative and characters this game is not pushing any boundaries (Rescue the girl, defeat the villain, same old thing as Mario) but that doesn't mean it's not endearing: You'll come to love Meat Boy because of his cheery nature and his innocence as well as his will to keep trying, you'll remember some of the bosses fondly, and you'll either hate the main villain with a passion or want to give him a hug. The bottom line is that you will most likely remember the characters despite them never uttering a single word through the entirety of the game, and that's compelling storytelling if you ask me.
The visual aspect is very solid: clean enough to tell what's going on at all times, stylistic enough to be memorable, varied enough to stay fresh and avoid visual boredom. All around just really good visual design.
The music is on another level, definitely one of my favorite videogame soundtracks ever, Danny B. Never fails to make the game ambiance that much better when he composes for a game (Also see Crypt of the Necrodancer for another solid game with music by him).
This game is an indie masterpiece and a complete classic, whatever flaw you may find in it is simply overshadowed by how competent it is at doing everything it sets out to accomplish. Definite recommendation and a must have for anyone seeking good platformers, a challenge, or pointers on how good game design can make a game an instant classic.
Vaas Montenegro once said: "Insanity is... Doing the exact same ♥♥♥♥ing thing, over and over again, expecting♥♥♥♥♥♥to change". If you disagree, play Super Meat Boy.

Let me start out with this statement: THIS IS A TOTAL PAY-TO-WIN GAME
In order to have anything remotely considered as good or efficient, you need to spend at least $20. Believe me when I say that, my cousin spent $20 on a half-decent drift car. Don't worry though, the pay-to-win premise isn't exclusive to cars. If you're in a mission against someone who's spent $50 on weapons, you're probably going to get maybe one kill on that person the whole time.
Let me finish with this statement: THE THEME OF THE GAME IS NOT BAD
The idea of cops and robbers battling for control of a metropolis is a very interesting one. On one side, there's a gang of ruthless, punk-like criminals that would do anything for a quick buck. On the other side, there's a group of sideburn wielding "police officers." The reason I put police officers in quotation marks is because the city's government is so desperate to contain the criminals that they passed a law that legalizes vigilantism. Essentially speaking, all the police officers in the city are the same as the criminals, but they have a badge.

Even with this interesting theme, this game manages to fall short (very short) due to insanely unbalanced gameplay. Without $50 invested in this game, you cannot do well in missions. All in all, save your money. This game is not good enough to be worth that much of your paycheck.

Alright guys, I’m going to lay it all out there. As the spook-time approaches us, it’s times like these where it is a golden opportunity to get comfy, and enjoy the season for all it’s worth. This game is prime for that. Done in the style of the retro days this game pays homage to the horror greats, in only what can be described as a horror-comedy-puzzle game. On the surface it’s 4 levels. But it is so much deeper than that, with 2 secret levels, an epilogue and a plethora of references, possibilities and combinations, this game is not dull for a moment. Surprisingly enough it keeps you on your toes despite the pixel-ness. It’s great fun to have everything fall to pieces in the blink of an eye. No matter how prepared you are, one wrong move, mistake, innocent oversight causes everything to come tumbling down and you, your dog and your friends are dead. It’s a golden game with great atmosphere, fun times and enjoyability to be had. Regardless of the scenarios you find yourselves in, this game is suitable for both fans and newcomers to the genre alike. If you’re interested in everything going haywire, confusion, spooks, and a fair amount of laughs, this game is for you.  Enjoy.

I was kind of surprised to find this game, along with a lot of other games from the Dreamcast Collection, available on Steam. This is a childhood game of mine, and I thought: I wanna relive those fond memories. My original disc for the GameCube was broken by a big scratch on it, and the game on here was only 8 bucks, so I thought: why not?
I'm now pretty much finished with this game again, and I have to say: it was a really fun run, once again. Although the controls, especially when playing with a WASD or arrow-keys-alignment on a keyboard, are hard to get used to in the beginning, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. The game also isn't without its glitches, but the continuous feeling I got, which went like: 'Hey, the game went like this in the past!', makes up for that. It's priceless.
A very big part of the game was very easy, but 100%-ing this game is absolutely off the table for me. All six storymodes except for Big's were very fun, Gamma's and Sonic's were my favorite. I dislike the whole fishing mechanism with Big; catching the bigger fish is ridiculously hard. That's one of the reasons why I can't 100% the game. Sky Chase, of the Sub Games, is also hard to get a topscore on. I've finished all missions except for mission 44, the one where you have to catch the biggest metal fish as Big. I've collected 124/130 emblems so far, so I haven't unlocked Metal Sonic's story, I can't give my opinion about that. The final boss battle as Super Sonic was a bit of a letdown in the sense that it wasn't atmospheric enough and was highly frustrating, although the difficulty was just about right for me. Chao raising and racing is very satisfying and fun, definitely glad they also implemented these cute little creatures in Sonic Adventure 2: Battle, the other game I bought out of the Dreamcast Collection.

I remember getting this and Crazy Taxi for Christmas for my Dreamcast, and literally playing both throughout the entire night. I loved that game to death.
As for the other ports though, I'm kind of iffy. The GameCube/PC 2004 ports aren't very good. They added new content, but at the cost of more bugs and glitches and worse lighting, making the characters look like plastic.
And then, we have the Steam/PS3/X360 version, and oh man, this has to be the worst. To give you an idea, you can't set it to fill up the screen, and it's stuck at a 4:3 aspect ratio inside a square. To make matters worse, this version was carried over from the PC port, bringing along a whole other slew of problems, and adding more by removing some of the content that the PC port added. It just sucks.
So, if it sucks so much, why am I recommending it? Well, here's the answer: BetterSADX. It's a free program you can download and install that patches this port to make it the best it can be. I'm talking full native resolution, widescreen, and even an incredible job at restoring the original Dreamcast version, bringing back the lighting, removed or replaced rings, and even the original textures of the characters and objects. All in glorious HD (or 4K).
Because of BetterSADX, I'm recommending this game to fans of Sonic and classic gaming in general. Kids' standards for game graphics nowadays have been increased dramatically, so you guys won't see much in it. But I see a pretty good game, a wonderful restoration, and a major part of Sega history.

You enjoyed the previous Rain-Slick episodes and also enjoy old-school turn-based RPG's like Final Fantasy or Pokémon - ones with simple graphics but a lot of variety and depth in combat.
At first glance, this can look like a disappointing step backwards... a cheap knock-off in order to finish the story. But this isn't quite the case... In practice it's more a trade-off: The reduction in graphics and interactive combat system has been substituted with a greater array of foes and a very extensive combat-class system which delivers new moves and abilities frequently.
It's not necessarily better / worse... just
.
So whilst you can no longer block attacks... you can now choose whether Gabe goes the way of the gardener or just turns into a dinosaur and calls it a day. Or both! Because who doesn't like a green-fingered velociraptor that's conscientious about the local bee population?
There's ultimately greater strategic depth this time around, particularly where you can disrupt turn orders, schedule repeating moves and think about elemental damage too. The classes are brilliantly varied and very creative, more so than any other RPG I've come across. Plenty to mix-and-match and experiment with. The combat is also clever in that enemies get stronger the longer the battle goes on... creating a clever race against time and breaking possible stalemates. Like before, there are no random encounters, but considerably more battles this time around - some that even come with fun rules / conditions, which always livens things up!
The dark humour from before is also still there - charming and daft as ever. If anything, the free reign to go a bit more abstract this time around has blown open the doors to brilliant off-beat humour. The dialogue is great and the enemy designs are also brilliant - particularly where each one has a comical tag-line. Always a joy to read, especially where there are a lot of cultural references, parodies and awful puns to be had.
It's not without its downsides, however. Firstly, the story feels a bit shoe-horned into the plot: A lot of battles and fun chit-chat and then suddenly a major plot element squeezed into a brief dialogue. The sound effects are also a little basic and repetitive - a thudding 'tak', a sweeping 'fwschi' and a 'bwoop' for magic effects (of course)... So not the sharpest in effects. But solid gameplay indeed (except fighting your way through a haunted house
- which sucked) augmented with additional free DLC / dungeons has made this a very strong follow-up to the Precipice of Darkness series. Despite being quite the jump from the previous style, the quality still feels very much there.

This quickly became one of my favorite RPG's as well as my personal favorite game in the PAA series, and with good reason. There's quite a lot I'd like to say, so let's get to it.
The game takes place 2 weeks after the events of Episode 2, but what's neat is that you don't need to have played it to understand the story going into Episode 3, as they immediately give you a summary of prior events upon talking to one of the statues in the Detective Agency. That alone makes Episode 3 easy to pick up and play, and the gameplay will keep you around for the long haul.
While not a terribly long game, around 10-12 hours or so if you go for the true ending as well as completing all of the free DLC and Coliseum, Zeboyd and PA pack a ton of charm and wit throughout the adventure with Zeboyd's 16 but art style and PA's keen sense of humor. There's quite a bit of text to read, mind you, but it's so well written that you'll thoroughly enjoy reading every bit of dialogue. The characters are true to their PA roots, with Tycho and Gabe taking center stage throughout the game. They work well together and have many a hilarious moment of banter with one another as well.
Regarding the gameplay itself, Zeboyd melds classic turn based battles with a unique spin on battles themselves. Characters gain 1 MP per turn to use various abilities with a differing degree of cost. You can play this to your advantage by taking a turn or two to Defend, which not only lets your next turn come by more quickly, but also let's you stockpile your MP for more powerful attacks. A cool little convenience feature is that your HP is fully restored after every battle, making party upkeep that much simpler. Zeboyd also showcases a wide variety of classes, called Class Pins, to choose from. Each character has their default class and are able to equip two additional Pins to add to the variety, offering a wide array of abilities and passive effects for that character. One nice thing about this system in general is that every Pin will still gain EXP even if they're not being used, though at a slower rate. Every Pin has their uses as well, making one of them feel like a waste and encouraging player customization and experimentation.

Eversion is difficult to review without spoiling it, but I'll try.
Eversion is, at it's core, an indie platformer/puzzle game. You play as Zee-Tee the Astrik (*), who is on a quest to save Princess Nehema, who has been captured by things that look a lot like Goombas. Along the way, Zee-Tee can evert to different "layers" of the world by pressing SPACE in certain areas, Things are quite different in each eversion layer, so everting is often required to progress.
Along the way, Zee-Tee can challenge himself by trying to collect all 240 gems, which will often require backtracking at certain eversion layers. Thankfully, your gems save even if you quit the level or die within, which is great for some of the harder levels.
The only real complaint I have about this game is how short it is. The game can easily be 100%ed in an hour, but if it is your first time playing, it'll probably take 2 hours or so to collect all of the gems and rescue the Princess.
All in all, Eversion is a very interesting platformer that is worth taking a look at. If you want to try the game out before you spend 5 dollars on it, the creator has a freeware version on his website. It doesn't have achievements and it's missing a handful of time attack levels, but it should get you used to the game.

Currently the cheapest way to get this title is to buy Serious Sam Classics - Revolution, which in itself would come with the two original encounters, plus the actively maintained version by Alligator Pit. Given how old the original titles are, the main question is, does the price reflect the value of what you’re getting? The answer is, "very much so".
First of all, the game play is straight forward and simple, you shoot and kill everything you see moving. Should the said things shoot back, jump and dodge at best you can against the hoard. This brand of action worked well back then and it works well today. You can boot the game right out the box from Steam and it would just work on pretty much every operating system Windows had for the last twenty years.
Multiplayer from Steamworks is supported on Revolution, but if you are as stubborn as I am and strive for the authentic LAN experience, Game Ranger works with this title perfectly. I have completed this in two sittings with a friend and the game only crashed once during the whole seven hours, with the crash due to my buggy router and crappy internet.
Graphics wise it held up fairly fine, I can always tell which creature is which from a distance, and the game supports wide screen along with a range of resolutions. Though if you are the type to complain about graphics, HD version is just around the corner on Steam and that’s perfectly fine also. Not to mention the hotness that is VR version, which is actively developed upon by Croteam.
Gunplay is good and all weapons serve a purpose, just because you picked up a shiny shotgun doesn’t mean you can ditch your pistols. Though I wish the mechanics were a bit more complex. If I recall correctly, only the initial pistols require reloading and the arsenal lacked any sort of recoil. So you just aim and shoot, over and over again.
Now, if I were to nitpick and complain, the music and sound effects would be it, since they were just a little mundane to my liking. Serious "Stone" Sam does have some voice lines, but they are far and few in between. There are more than a few different music tracks, but none of them are memorable. Also, if you happen to play on the high difficulties, the last two stages can seem a drag. The computer would just throw wave after wave at you, pinning you on the same scene for tens of minutes.
With all things considered and judging this without my nostalgia goggles, I will still recommend this title to all FPS fans. With frequent discounts during sales, this is practically a staple for most libraries on Steam.

Let me start out with this statement: THIS IS A TOTAL PAY-TO-WIN GAME
In order to have anything remotely considered as good or efficient, you need to spend at least $20. Believe me when I say that, my cousin spent $20 on a half-decent drift car. Don't worry though, the pay-to-win premise isn't exclusive to cars. If you're in a mission against someone who's spent $50 on weapons, you're probably going to get maybe one kill on that person the whole time.
Let me finish with this statement: THE THEME OF THE GAME IS NOT BAD
The idea of cops and robbers battling for control of a metropolis is a very interesting one. On one side, there's a gang of ruthless, punk-like criminals that would do anything for a quick buck. On the other side, there's a group of sideburn wielding "police officers." The reason I put police officers in quotation marks is because the city's government is so desperate to contain the criminals that they passed a law that legalizes vigilantism. Essentially speaking, all the police officers in the city are the same as the criminals, but they have a badge.

Even with this interesting theme, this game manages to fall short (very short) due to insanely unbalanced gameplay. Without $50 invested in this game, you cannot do well in missions. All in all, save your money. This game is not good enough to be worth that much of your paycheck.

If Borderlands 1 had that many guns, Borderlands 2 can't have more that what it boast right? WRONG! This game have about 87 million guns, far more than Borderlands 1. It's practically able to make gun lovers climax from hearing the gun counts. Anyway, its an FPS game with RPG-esque elements, with an emphasis on FPS actions.
In this game, you get to choose 4 characters by default, an additional 2 if you bought the character DLCs. Each characters have their own action skills and skill trees. Depending on what you decide to invest on, you can get either a medic build, glass cannon build, melee build etc. They also poses no restriction in terms of what weapons you can use, so fire away, Vault Hunter!
As mentioned earlier, guns. Lots of guns in this game. Lots of guns to shoot mobs at. Lots of guns to burn mobs at! Lots of guns to dissolve mobs with! Ahem, basically there are lots of guns. In addition to guns, you have other miscellaneous items that help to boost your characters, similar to RPG trinkets. There are many bonuses that they can provide such as increased health regeneration, boost to skills, more ammo per magazine, higher fire rate etc.
The story of a game is basically about you, a Vault Hunter, trying to fight against a tyrannical corperation, more specifically, one dude. Who is handsome. I think. Along the way, you will get side quests, in addition to your main quests for the storyline, like RPGs. At the end of the story, you may proceed to the next difficulty, or if you are already at the highest difficulty, farm bosses for the best loot possible. Many characters from the first Borderlands return as NPCs or supporting characters as well.
One of the main thing I really liked about this game is the respecable skill trees. You don't need to create a new character, just find the nearest characterization station, and reset your skills! Easy way if your skill build is not working, or if you want to try another build without creating another character. Drop rate, oh boy drop rates. About half of my playtime here is just farming bosses for the loots that I want. The drop rate is not that bad to be honest, at least better than other RPGs I played, such as Diablo 2, since each bosses and a slightly higher chance to drop a specific item. If you wanna get, for example a Lyuda, farm Gettle. That's it. No need to farm other bosses just to find that Lyuda.
Character dialogues are really cheesy, and fun! For example, an enemy Psycho started quoting Hamlet while chasing me. He talked for 2 whole minutes, reciting the entire line for that act in Hamlet. I had to aggro him just to hear him out completely. Or Krieg the Psycho (DLC character), which keep talking about nipple salads and having the shiniest meat bicycle. It's completely incomprehensible, yet funny to hear all the time. And Gaige the Mechromancer 9the other DLC character) will keep talking how n00b they are, or rambling about anarchy and smashing the system.
As mentioned, this game is similar to an RPG, so eventually the mobs get stronger and stronger. Normal headshot won't kill instantly, depending on the gun damage and the mob health (unless you are overlevelled or you have a really good gun with a good stats). So in the end, it goes from ripping and tearing mobs apart to fighting meat sponges. Their damages ramp up as well, but beware, some mobs can 1 shot you into a dying state. During dying state, you need to kill someone to revive, or get someone to revive you if its coop. Otherwise, it's back to the respawn stations. Some mobs are fine, like animals, but the humans? "I'ma hide behind this cover, and I'm not gonna take pot shots." Good luck from killing that coward though. Death does not make you lose experience though, only money, so it's not so bad. As mentioned, due to the meat sponges tendency of the mobs, basically this game is screaming at you to play it in coop. It's more fun that way as well.
Overall, I would highly recommend it. Fan of the first Borderlands will really like it, FPS players may enjoy it, though some RPG elements may or may not be to their liking. Drop rate are reasonably fine. Soloing the game is possible, but it's way better to play it in coop. Also get the GOTY edition. The DLCs are really worth it (though I have yet to get them, eventually I will).

Okay, let's get serious. This game is amazing for it's price. It's a complex puzzle box from the depths of hell! It's filled with all kinds of secrets, changing gameplay, gratuitous violence, sex, human sacrafice and amazing atmosphere for something that just uses the pixel graphics!
The game consists of four levels based on horror movies: Lakeview Cabin III, Lakeview Cabin IV, Lakeview Cabin V, and "Cabin 6." I'm torn between whether I like V or IV more.
III is quite simple: Kill the killers before they murder each and every one of you in your drunk, naked sleep. There's a lot of ways, the zipline, burning them to a crisp, getting really ballsy and going toe to toe with them with a weapon (hasn't worked for me yet) or ramming a highly explosive motor scooter into them, and more!

The only thing I lament about it is that the series is finished and that we will not get anymore lakeview cabin. But all good things must come to an end.

It's a puzzle game that contains an old subject, but educational nonetheless. I think it tries to convey the message of not losing hope even in the darkest of time through the story of this young girl, who struggles with both life and a chronic and rather fatal disease.
The puzzle types seem to reflect the themes of the girl's life. First is the only-turn-right puzzle, which is about the "right" choice that society seems to press on us, and on her father and her in the story. Frustrating, but the "rule" dictates that it's the only way they can advance.
The second puzzle, which actually spans throughout the game, is the battle with her disease, and the rule is very unfair for her.
The third puzzle is turning the car in the direction of the arrows. This relates to her father, who died in a car accident. But, through her father and mother's words, things are not quite so.
The fourth puzzle is step on all tiles. I think it reflects her dream, to dream high up in the sky and conquer all.
The fifth puzzle is when she's free of her body, drifting away in space, finding the way to her "ship".
The game tries to convey the optimistic message that even all goes wrong, there is still hope, and you can get through it no matter what. A little too optimistic and simple to be honest, but I can't say it's wrong. People are different and complicated, one solution is right for this person may not work on the other, but I value its effort. However, I agrees with one point is that we should try to cherish what's truly important to us, may it be family or dream or whatever, instead of chasing after society's expectation.
I'll recommend this game for people who enjoy a good casual story and puzzle game.

Labyrinthine Dreams is truly a game that is well deserving of its “Very Positive”, as of this writing, review rating.  The game has a story that a lot of people could relate to in one way or another, with a lot of depth.  Don’t believe those saying the game and the story are disconnected, as they’re actually really tightly connected on a very deep level.  I can’t get into it more than that without giving too much away, but if you wander around and use (Z Key) the random objects in the very first area it’ll start to paint a picture for you that’s fairly easy to follow.
This game is mostly a puzzle game where you have to plan your movements carefully in order to complete each area.  Sometimes you have to outthink the moves of other NPCs.  Sometimes you are limited in the directions you can turn.  Sometimes the ground even vanishes as you use it, leaving you having to carefully plan your route to the end.  Sadly I do have a couple gripes with the game and I’ll go through them one at a time;
First, I found the limitation on video resolutions to be a bit of a letdown.  The game is set to a strict resolution (640x480) and that’s the only video mode there is.  You can go to a full-screen mode in which the area around the window is just black, or you can stretch it to full-screen which has the effect of seriously degrading the video quality.  For those with wide-screens, even the full-screen stretch leaves you with black letterboxing on the left and right.  I would have liked to have seen at least a high-resolution mode added for those (like myself) who have resolutions set over 1600x900.
Secondly, I found there were several bugs that heavily affected game play to the point where exiting and reloading the game was the only option.  The most notorious bug was the “Additional Keys Disabled” bug which hit me within the first 3 maps.  The map was designed so I could only do left-hand turns and walk forward but suddenly (after a map reset) I found myself ONLY able to walk forward.  The game had accidentally disabled the left-hand turns in addition to the right-hand turns.  I was unable to correct the problem without exiting the game.  I also found the “bad guy” would sometimes get stuck and the AI couldn’t figure out how to chase me, which made some maps too easy.
All in all the bugs aren’t really enough for me to not recommend this game.  The cost of a few bucks is a fair price and if you can see the link between the story and the puzzles you’ll really enjoy it.

Ultimately, my biggest issues with this game come from two sources.
First, the gameplay is just so clunky and slow. There was multiple times while playing that I needed to move in a straight line for a long time and ended up zoning out, since it takes about 1 second to move a single tile, and overshot where I needed to go and needed to reset the map. This led to me just getting more bored with the game and encountering this issue more often. I don't believe this is a limitation to the RPG Maker engine, but was instead a design choice by the programmers. If the game changed the speed, or was even just mouse controlled instead of controlled with the arrows, I would say the that puzzles were better.
The overall quality of the puzzles though, well, it all goes downhill after the first batch. The forest puzzles where you need to go in each direction was really neat and I'd never seen something like that before, the car puzzles were just boring with no way to fail and could be solved just by mashing directions, the demon puzzles weren't too bad but they felt inconsistent, the sky puzzles were a step up in quality from the car and demon ones, and then the game ended on sliding puzzles which no one likes.
Now my second criticism of the game is the story. I didn't like the story, but that's not what I'm going to complain about. The game has you solve these completely unrelated dream puzzles and then it feeds you a bit of story. Meaning the story and gameplay are completely disconnected. Unlike something like Professor Layton, where you solve various puzzles for people to get information to progress the game's plot, or even to solve something blocking your progress, this game has you solve completely random puzzles.
The game said in the credits that this game's story is based off of a story written by the creators of the game, personally I'd say just go read that.

No More Room is a survival horror FPS zombie game. Weapons are limited, so survivors have to make the best of them. Also, there are two types of gamemodes. In the survival gamemode, there are zones to maintain. The zones can be defended if the imposing zombies are killed, however if the zones fall, the survivors lose. In the objective gamemode, survivors complete a series of tasks, so that they can be safely extracted. If the survivors die or take too long to reach the point of extraction, they lose. A player can run a LAN server that any other local player can join, but assuming there aren't any local players in the area, it could be played as a singleplayer server. If a player wants to play with other specific players, they could run a multiplayer server. A multiplayer server would show up on the Internet, so any other player could join, but servers can be protected by passwords. If a player runs their own server, their latency will be pretty low, but the latency of players connecting to their server will be significantly higher. Running a LAN server is ideal for achievements, many of which can be obtained by getting a certain number of kills with the different weapons in the game. No More Room in Hell is free and players can even create their own maps. Good game, 9/10.

This is a really good game, and in many regards, this is indeed XCOM's true successor.
- The tactical game feels a lot like the original, with the same dilemmas and cold sweats, but with a nice gameplay refresh integrating modern concepts such as cover. It is a real success; the general way you play the game is very faithful to the original game, but it is significantly deeper and more interesting.
- The same can be said for the strategic game. The general feeling is the same as in the original game, but it is much, much more complex and the game has little forgiveness for people who make wrong choices.
- The interception minigame is really nice. There are a few problems that should be solved (some dogfights which have good success chances on autoresolve are actually unwinnable if you try to play them) but it adds something that had not been attempted or done right by any of the previous XCOM-inspired games.
- The general cold war atmosphere is nice and the flavour text (research reports, news ticker, etc.) fleshes out the universe nicely. All the text-based universe description is a real success.
- The music is good, and the sound effects are good too.
Now a few criticisms:
- The graphics. Seriously. The geoscape and base layout screens are OK. The background art (research/engineering screens, etc.) is decent, even though it lacks something. Everything else is horrible. The aliens, the equipment, most of the armours and almost everything in the tactical game is ugly, bland and unremarkable. I would go as far as saying that I prefer the visuals from the 1994 game in their VGA splendor. They are pixelated and often cheesy in a 90s SF way, but they have a character that is completely absent here. Even the recent X-COM: Enemy Unknown, which is much more bland and soulless than Xenonauts in many ways, easily wins this match.
- The UFO missions eventually become repetitive. True, you can airstrike crash sites, but it is often not an economically viable option, and the combination of low resources, quite slow research and high enemy activity leads to phases of the game where you have nothing else to do than wait for your research/engineering projects to eventually complete while playing non-stop difficult missions which look a lot like one another, have each the potential to wipe your team, and do not bring you any reward except some cash and the chance to live another day. This is somehow realistic, but not so funny.
- This is not a true Linux game: the developers juste made special efforts to make the game run correctly with Wine. This is not nothing, and I don't blame the developers, but Wine compliance is not the same at all as a native GNU/Linux version, and I find it misleading and disappoingint to see it listed as a "Linux game" on Steam. (And even more so since
) This is one of the reasons why I so readily bought this game, and although it is a fine game, on that point I feel cheated.

Also has a very active modding community which will give this game some staying power.

On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness 3... what a title. In fact, the writing in this game was probably my favorite part. Constantly making clever jokes, the dialouge never got old. As a turn based fighting game, I enjoyed the skill variety and the mixture of class options. I hadn't expected any kind of depth from a title like this but they surprised me.
The item system was lacking in my opinion since the best gear was handed to you as a part of the story anyways. My only other complaint would be that the story line was a bit hard to follow. Now, perhaps that's my fault since I didn't want to invest a whole lot of plot-thought but I am also concerned that the original two titles would have been a prerequisite.
While I can reccommend this game, I do so with some reservations. I don't feel particularly excited about playing the next game in the series and that seems like a bad sign. However, on a rainy day if you like a little dry humor this is a great way to burn time and snag a few chuckles.

Here is a game that largely matches expectations without exceeding them. If you're looking for solid, retro-RPG combat and witty writing then you'll find it here at a very reasonable price. However, the story behind all the sarcasm and jokes, while entertaining enough, lacks tension and impact. It sets up the following game for a more interesting setting and conclusion, but that's not enough to elevate
game's narrative above "mostly forgettable".
Precipice of Darkness 3 does a great job of bringing complexity and flexibility into its turn based combat. Each party member has one permanent base class that matches their personality. In time you'll unlock two additional class slots for each character that can be swapped at will between battles. You choose from a pool of bizarre classes that allow you to easily experiment until you find a winning combination. I really like that unused classes still gain experience and level up, just at a slightly slower pace than the in use classes. This negates the chance of any class becoming under leveled to the point of discouraging you from trying it.
In battle the game uses a combat bar to queue actions that is much like the old Grandia series and, more recently, Child of Light. It is one of my favorite turn based systems that allows for characters and attacks of varying speeds as well as strategic interrupts of enemy actions. To be victorious I needed to make proper use of buffs, interrupts and adjust my strategy to account for enemy weaknesses and resistances. I played on the Veteran difficulty and found it to be on point except for in one area called The Bank of Money that had a frustrating and unusual spike in difficulty.

The city map that you use to navigate from area to area is very plain with linear paths that don't allow for any deviation or hidden surprises. The exploration areas are genre standard mazes of corridors, barriers and rooms. Their layout is pleasing, including treasure chests, non-random enemy encounters and silly descriptions when you examine some objects. Visuals are definitely not this game's strong suit. They get the job done without being outright ugly, but the best compliment I can give them is that there are some creatively comedic enemy designs.
Having not played the previous two games nor read much of the Penny Arcade comics I'm coming at this game without a preexisting attachment to the characters. While I did enjoy their distinct and quirky personalities, they only grew on me a little over time. There are some decent attempts at character development, however the priority is clearly on humor over substance. As for the comedy, for me it was consistently amusing without ever being a truly laugh-out-loud level of funny. It's worth noting that I did not feel like I was missing anything from not having played parts 1 and 2.

My total playtime clocked in at 15 hours for all the content this game has to offer. It is a modestly successful entry in the relatively sparse field of games that place a heavy emphasis on comedy. I am comfortable recommending this game to any old school RPG fans out there or Penny Arcade aficionados.

Eversion Review
I'll try and fairly state what I can without spoiling too much, although if you simply watch the trailer you already know what's going on here.  Eversion is at its core a puzzle platformer, and a clever one too.  You control the flower-faced hero named Zee Tee and rescue the princess, so if you've played any NES game before you already know what to do.
Gameplay is basically platforming but with a dimension-warping mechanic where you jump through alternate worlds.  You may have to change something in one world in order to affect the other world and then you can get to where you couldn't before.  It sounds hard at first but with a bit of practice you will eventually understand what to do.  There are collectables throughout the stages to give some replay value, though I wasn't too interested.  Things do get shaken up later with different enemies and slightly different ways to play the stage, though generally things remains the same throughout.  Of course, the other dimensions might just maybe chinge things up a bit.  I will warn you, it will get stressful.
All I can say is don't watch videos of it or look up other reviews because the main thing here which I didn't discuss will be totally spoiled.  Simply play Eversion and experience it for yourself.

I HIGHLY recommend this lovingly-constructed tribute to the '80s' most iconic horror films.  It has the puzzle-solving feel of old Sierra On-Line adventure games (e.g. King's Quest and Quest for Glory), in that there are several well-defined obstacles, which can be overcome in a variety of ways, limited mostly--but not entirely--by the player's creativity.
The "collection" features four full games, each one a tribute to a set of horror films from the '80s.  Respectively, the games pay tribute to the Friday the 13th series; The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and The Hills Have Eyes; Halloween and A Nightmare on Elm Street; and finally Alien and The Thing.  The game's own lore recapitulates some major themes from these films as well, besides that of masked, blade-wielding serial killers: there are twisted family relations, backwoods satanic cults, revenge from beyond the grave, haunted video games, plus references to an in-game "true story" on which the Lakeview Cabin "movies" are based.  It's tempting to say more, but I don't want to spoil anything!
In each game, you control four protagonists--usually teenagers, the likes of which get butchered by slasher-movie antagonists.  In each game, you have a limited amount of time, and a specific set of resources--some hidden, some out in the open--to prepare for a confrontation with at least one serial killer.  It's your job to switch back and forth between your protagonists in real time, find whatever you can use as a weapon, set traps, and manipulate your tiny environment to your advantage, so that your whole team can survive a horror movie.  The creator obviously loves '80s slasher films, and the multitudinous references, alongside a compelling lore, will captivate anyone who's hosted a marathon of scary movies during Halloween.
It's best played with a controller.  I have a Mac, so I just grabbed a generic PS-type controller with a USB port from Best Buy, and it works like a charm.  The controls are incredibly responsive, and the interface is reminiscent of old NES games like Super Mario Bros 2, or Chip and Dale Rescue Rangers, where you can pick things up from your environment and throw them.  (The game's creater--just one dude--mentioned the latter NES game as inspiration, and it shows.)  Additionally, the game bears an inescapable similarity to Maniac Mansion--i.e. shifting control between characters to deal with antagonists, who move in a real-time environment.
The score, appropriately, is reminiscent of John Carpenter.  Most of it is triggered by events: stacatto strings punctuate every stab wound; plodding, low-register, single-note piano hits accompany the killers' approach; it's scored like the horror films to which it pays tribute.  As such, it's nothing you'll want to play in your car on the way to work--no more than any other horror soundtrack.  But it fits the game wonderfully.  You'll jump in your seat more than once, when masked antagonists suddenly appear from the shadows.
The detail in the game's environment is incredible; the author obviously thought of hundreds of things the player might try to do, with just as many hilarious ways to die as there are ingenious ways to win.  At times, the gameplay can be frustrating--BE PREPARED TO DIE A LOT, A WHOLE LOT.  DYING A LOT IS REQUIRED TO FIGURE OUT YOUR ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS IMPORTANT NOT TO GET FRUSTRATED WITH THAT FACT ABOUT THE GAME.  (In part V, it becomes a downright game mechanic!)
When you get to part V, you may feel tempted to use a walkthrough, although I would suggest looking up as little as possible.  Just look up the Bible reference and the morse code parts (it was a♥♥♥♥♥♥move to include puzzles, which required such solutions... I say this, even though I think this is one of the best and most creative puzzle games I've played in decades).
The art and graphics are pixelated, reminiscent of VGA Sierra games, like King's Quest I-IV.  There are a varety of sprites to accompany the variety of things you might try as a player; in all, the characters' interactions are hilarious, which compliments the horrific setting.
Seriously, you get four interesting, creative, independently-made games for just ten bucks.  I would advise getting them, and NOT USING A WALKTHROUGH.  Trust me: when you figure out how to survive the killers, all on your own, in any one of these games, you cannot help but leap up and cheer.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The little brother of Gearbox Software's "Borderlands", Borderlands 2 is the second major entry in the series. It mostly improves on the first game's already unique features, but there are some changes that could have been left out.
One of the first things you might notice if you're a Borderlands veteran is the characters. First of all, you can not play as any of the original four Vault Hunters. Instead, you have Zero (the Assassin), Maya (the Siren), Salvador (the Gunzerker), and Axton (the Commando). Some of these characters are fairly similar in terms of skill sets to the original four, but Borderlands 2 brought a lot more to the table. Zero has a cloaking ability, where he deploys a decoy of himself and turns invisible, allowing hassle-free movement around the battlefield. Maya can use phaselock, which will hold an enemy helpless in the air to be pelted with bullets or rockets. Salvador, the Gunzerker, can use his ability to dual-wield weapons of any kind. Yeah, even two rocket launchers if you want. Axton can deploy his Sabre turret, which is similar to the previous installment's Scorpio turret, but leveling up a certain skill tree can allow Axton to deploy multiple turrets with rocket launchers and the ability to stick to walls.
On top of having new characters, players can now change the characters' appearances moreso than in classic Borderlands. You can unlock color schemes to choose from, as well as head customizations. Some other options are available in the form of DLC, but you'll soon be emptying your wallet to acquire all of them along with the major DLCs.
Vehicles have changed a bit. The game still boasts the agile Runner in its two variations, but mid-game missions bring the heavy and more powerful Bandit Technical, also known simply as the Technical. It has some weird, unconventional weapons, but they pack some serious punch.
Another huge improvement is the HUD (Heads-Up Display). The original Borderlands opened a little screen that covered everything up to allow you access to missions and inventory management. Borderlands 2 instead zooms out to show your character looking at a holographic projection in front of them, that you can then use from there. It's a lot cooler than the old one, for sure.
Once again, Gearbox delivered some excellent DLC, including some that extend your level cap to 72 and then allow "Overpowered" or "OP" levels on top of that. The main DLC packs add some enjoyable campaigns and new vehicles as well.

I saw the news post on Labyrinthine Dreams' price reduction from whatever it was before (I think $4.99?) to encourage people to not abuse Steam's refund policy, but I would have paid that and then some just for the music, the mazes/gameplay, or the story alone (even better, Steam Trading Cards for Badges!). I played Precipice of Darkness 1 and hated it, the shallow real-time combat system with mini-games that had you clicking like crazy on imprecise targets ruined it for me. I skipped 2, not wanting more of the same.
This is very different and a great improvement. First, it captures much better the spirit of the JRPGs of old it's emulating. The combat system isn't incredibly complex but has some depth to it, and with each character eventually combining two classes of your choice with his basic one, experimenting is fun.
Now like previous Zeboyd Games titles, this game is kind of lacking in terms of interface. There's no way to examine your character stats during battle, to see how much some effect buffed or debuffed you. You can't examine a class without equipping it, either, which makes for tedious shuffling when you're trying to determine which class combo is the best. And for some reason you can see the stats your character would have when buying weapons, but the same isn't true for equipment.
All in all this game feels stuck in an alternate timeline where the last console that came out was the SNES. Sure, it improved on classic JRPGs, but modern turn-based JRPGs like Shin Megami Tensei have refined the formula a lot and feel much slicker to play, as well as faster even on higher difficulties. In POD 3, raising the difficulty to Veteran mostly made the enemies feel like bullet sponges, with fights dragging on quite a bit - this automatically gives the advantage to the enemy since they grow in power every turn, a system I'm not too fond of.
The story is sometimes funny but not gripping, I was a bit bored in some dungeons since I wasn't looking forward to the next narrative bit. But overall there were some good moments and the combat mechanics kept me interested just enough to keep going.
Verdict: Worth playing, and it's won't eat a ridiculous amount of your time.

A remake of the original TBS classic X-Com:UFO Defence from the 90s.
If you played any of the original Microprose X-Coms and were disappointed with the Firaxis reboot's lack of depth, then Xenonauts will not disappoint.
It plays very similar to the original X-COM with some extra polish as you'd expect 20 years later.
My favourite aspect is that the game has been opened up to the modding community, and there are some great mods out there that vastly expand the tech trees, maps, equipment etc etc.
If you aren't familiar with the original, the game is split into a strategy layer, where you intercept UFOs, build up your bases, equip your troops and aircraft, do research etc, and a turn-based squad combat layer where you investigate crashed and landed UFOs, alien bases, terror sites etc.
You never have enough money to do everything you want, and the difficulty ramps up as the invasion progresses.
The graphics may seem a bit antiquated, but it's all about the gameplay, and rolling out your strategy for defeating the alien invasion.
The ambient music is excellent, and the hours fly by as you get immersed in the game.
In my opinion, a must-buy for any fans of the original series, and recommended for any TBS fans.

Why go throught all the trouble of making such a realistic remake if it is to break all the realism by making the earth flat ?
The original XCOM had it all right, the earth was a sphere.  And I'm not just speaking about the type of map projection used, I'm talking about the way aircrafts are travelling, the way radar ranges are depicted and things like that.
I don't feel like I'm defending a planet, I feel like I'm defending a flat table with a distorted map drawn on it, or more accurately a cylinder since the map connects on the sides.
In this game, on the ''flat map'' globe, the radar ranges are circular, no matter where you are on the globe, well they should'nt, the range of the radar should be factored for the fact that it's a flat map, it should widen towards the poles, otherwise the map is all wrong.  Every aircraft travel in a straight line, just like if the earth was flat, well they should'nt.  The map is distorted, and so are the trajectories and distances.  Now what would be the advantage of putting a base on the north pole, since the distances are so wrong when you consider the earth as a cylinder with very wide poles.  For example, in real life, the shortest route from the southern tip of Chile to Australia doesn't involve going all the way on a due east trajetory, it should be trought the south pole.  ( Where is the south pole anyway in this game ? )  By using such an unrealistic approach to the ''globe'' aspect of the game, it really breaks a big aspect for anybody who liked managing strategically the globe part in XCOM.  Once again, the original game from 20 years ago had it all correct, why change that ?
Don't get me wrong, I'm going to recommend this game to any XCOM fan.  XCOM was one of the greatest game of all times and any attempts at bringing back some memories of it should be funded and encouraged.  This remake is an excellent game, with one unnecessary big flaw in my opinion.

It's XCOM+
Superior to UFO Extraterrestrials, equal of UFO Alien Invasion, not quite the departure in story and quality that UFO Aftershock was. It does what it promises to do, deliver classic XCOM gameplay without the bugs/DOS limits.
True-to-original gameplay with benefits of tech advances and without limitations of 1994 hardware. Artwork isn't pixellated or low-res, but remains 2D. The maps are 2D as well, with some tile/LOS issues, but that is just the flavor of this game. There is no need to specifically select a grenade, move it into the soldier's hand after removing the rifle, then use the nade in combat. Select it from a quick-menu and throw at the enemy. The proper TU cost will be calculated based on where the grenade was in the inventory so it costs the same, just makes gameplay easier. Inventory/equipment can be arranged and saved for future use making it possible to edit existing classes or create your own. Building Missile defences no longer requires you to dismantle outdated facilities to replace with new tech versions. They upgrade automatically when new tech is researched. Saving time and making sense. Xenonauts has many similar improvements over the original XCOM while keeping the gameplay essentially the same.
EDIT
There are greater departures from the original gameplay. Developers removed the ability for the player to construct manufacturing complexes and use them to create wealth by trading new technology and devices. This was exploited in the original to make funding meaningless. In Xenonauts, your budget is the direct result of your actions in defending funding governments. Let them down enough and your budget will constrict to the point of utter failure. There are no "points" you and the aliens score, only collateral damage caused by them and bonuses paid for UFOs shot down. You will sell small amounts of alien item, but it's a pittance compared to the gravy train you could ride in XCOM: UFO Defense. Budgetary restrictions are so severe at higher difficulty levels, that even most grizzled veterans will find it difficult to manage, and will probably lose more than once. Great news if you found all your squad-level tactical games too easy and forgiving.
Tactical combat is also extremly dangerous at the highest difficulty level, to the point of it seriously not being worth it just for the sake of leveling soldiers. You will have to fight to collect researchable items or to prevent alien terror, but outside this you will not want to engage in too many battles, certainly not without decent equipment.
Air combat is expanded. It takes place in a simplified RTS setting, though it is possible to autoresolve all encounters. You risk taking damage either way. Unlike the classic, aircraft shot down are not lost. In a rare moment of forgiveness, Xenonauts will recover downed aircraft, although it can take 72h to drag the remains back to base.
In addition to bringing back classic XCOM gameplay, Xenonauts manages to recreate the addictivness of the original. Your mileage may vary of course, but i personally managed to clock 23h during the first three play sessions. And i found myself thinking about different tactics or wondering how the hell i'm supposed to beat the game at all.

This is a collection of pixelated sandbox horror excursions. Each episode thematically riffs off classic slasher films like Friday the 13th and House of 1,000 Corpses. These episodes are fairly short and meant to be played multiple times. The episodes are connected by a hub world in the form of a movie theatre.

You have four characters that you can switch between, but only one of them has to survive to win. Occassionally, you'll need two or more survivors to solve puzzles such as opening doors, triggering traps, or procuring items- but these are usually optional tasks. There are various items and interactable objects scattered throughout the levels, some of which are merely "toys" to mess around with, and some which have a practical application. Each chapter is completely open to the player to do as they please, save for a few locked doors and hidden items that require a brief task first. You will have time to explore a little before the killer spawns, but sometimes you can speed this process up by "summoning" it via common horror movie tropes such as having premarital sex. While the game is completely open, there is usually a series of steps that need to be taken to get the good endings.
As a gamer from the SNES generation, I absolutely loved this game for its Pick-Up-And-Play attitude. If you like retro indie games, there's no reason not to check the game out.

Some of this game can be very hard, especially when playing the first time-and although it can be frustrating, figuring it out is always very rewarding! Even after I had all the achievements, it still hadn't bored me!

++ Battle system is like Grandia. (It has an Initiaive Bar for when each character's action will occur).

+ Reasonable length. I got ~35 hours out of it. You could also spend less or more time.
+ 16-bit style is well-executed.
Cons
- I recall the menus being tedious to maneuver through.
- The class system is unique, but messier than it needs to be.

I have never played the old 1990s X-Com this was based on, nor was I a really big supporter of the Indie game scene. My attention was directed towards Xenonauts, after a chance splurge had me acquire the new Firaxis X-Com, and while I found that game fun, I wanted something more challenging. Something mixing the depth of Jagged Alliance 2, with the concepts found in X-Com. And I found that in Xenonauts.
After setting down my cash for this game after it's release, I have found myself hooked on it. The game has a great challenge to it. and I find the setting choice (Early 80s Cold War) to be very unique given most games of this type focus on the near future (201X) Earth. If X-Com: Enemy Unknown is a fun, console-ish romp, Xenonauts is the thinking man's version. You are facing a constantly mounting war against aliens, where you feel the underdog. You have to manage very limited finances, as well as maintain success in both ground and air engagements. You have to plan your base deployment, and do it very sparingly. You will quickly find yourself running out of money in this game if you aren't careful. You can also find your best men slaughtered by bad choices in ground tactics or your entire aerial squadron grounded for three days of repairs if you make a bad call while aliens ransack the world.
This game is not brutal, but it doesn't pull it's punches. It reminds me of the old days of gaming, when PC graphics power had a "ceiling", so games had to focus on depth and gameplay. Xenonauts doesn't have the prettiest of graphics, but graphics is not it's selling point nor should the game be judged on such.
My only complaint regarding the game, is that you can't use any successful profit-making skills in it, and while this has been addressed by Mods, my attitude towards Mods is skeptical, at best.
I highly recommend Xenonauts, as it is a very amazing game given the limited resources the developer had. I'm now looking towards Indie Games, cause of what I saw Goldhawk Interactive do with it's Kickstarter campaign.
I hope Xenonauts gets an expansion or some new additions, and that it's future is *NOT* left in the hands of User-Made Mods.

As far as X-Com "clones" go, this one is tops.  I have played them all (UFO: After-X series, UFO: Extraterrestrials, XCOM, etc).
It takes the factors from the original and makes a few modifications, giving old players of the original (and TFTD!) a new challenge as well as making the same addictive gameplay accessible to a new generation (both with graphical and UI improvements).
+UFOpaedia is in-depth and has good art. Adds immersion and a bit of humour (but never feels out of place).
+BASE BUILDING DONE RIGHT!  None of that watered-down XCOM stuff here!
+TIME UNITS (or their rough equivalent)!  None of this move/shoot boardgame-y junk! (Though I love boardgames, it was over-simplified).
+Destructable terrain and an AI that knows when to heft a grenade (evil reminiscences of TFTD here).
+A sensible economy.  The player can't abuse his workshop and is forced to yield results on the tactical side (though you can carpet-bomb UFO crashes and get 1/2 the value from the scrap if you're tapped out for ambulatory soldiers!).
+Improved interception mechanics, with the option for manual control of the X-Y manuevering and engagement style, or simply an estimate and quick resolve mechanic, should you so choose.
+Remarkably stable!  The original crashed on me just about as much, so no complaints here.  Also, there are auto-saves should this occur.  A real sanity-saver (even for the non-save scummer!).
+A good random number generator that does not feel cheap or arbitrary.  Some serious consideration was put into it, as the same shot sequence (yeah, I scummed it to test) does not yield the same result or "seed".  Not a knock at XCOM, as even the Holy Jagged Alliance 2 has that.  This game just generates it fresh and, resultantly, keeps things fresh!
+A good tech tree that makes sense and has a good variety. Even outmoded gear still has a situational reason for retention, making you carefully consider your composition.
In short, all the delicious fat and none of the calories.  The ONLY thing I would add would be Coop campaign multiplayer, but realize this to be a pipe dream.  However, examples of merging Strategic and Tactical in multi can be found in Sword of the Stars and Dominions 4...  Wink, wink, nudge, nudge?  I'll say no more.
Buy it!!

The original X-COM series (Enemy Unknown, Terror from the Deep, and even Apocalypse) were among the most-immersive, deeply-strategic, and thematically-beautiful games of the 1990s. 2012's reboot was fun, but it failed to capture the sophistication and complexity of the original: it lacked the ability to perform micro-customisation upon your soldiers (Want a strong guy whose job is just to carry ammo for everybody else? That's fine!), bases ("Science" base at a secret location, surrounded by interceptor bases? No problem!), or mission strategy (Plan to fight a retreat back to the dropship, dragging the bodies of the stunned aliens with you for later research, losing the battle but advancing the war? Go on then!). And it suffered, for it.
Xenonauts, however, takes the genre back where it belongs: gritty, strategic, and with every game completely unique. More-impressively, it does so in a world that's subtly-different from that of the original series: starting deep in the Cold War, and with aliens whose motivation and strategy is innovative and new, even to fans of the original series.
It's not perfect: you'll read science reports that make reference to weapons you haven't yet invented, because you're doing things in the "wrong" order... but at least the game
you do things in the order that makes most-sense to you! I'd have enjoyed being able to use alien psionics against them, as you can in the original series (and even in the reboot), but (unless I simply missed out on the appropriate research opportunities), that's sadly absent. And there are a few bugs, although I didn't come across any game-breaking ones.
But what Xenonauts
is one of the best strategy games I've seen in recent years. Whether you loved the original X-COM series, or the reboot, or didn't play either... it's got something for you to enjoy. Go play it, Commander.

Absolutely Amazing!
Faithful to the original X-com, xenonauts keeps the core gameplay mechanics and tense atmosphere that made the original so awesome. Personally, i see xenonauts to be superior over the new X-Com: ennemy unknown, because the gameplay is alot more tense, visceral and complex. But not only does it come true to the original, it even expands on some concepts, adds alot of new mechanics and gadgets such as the deeper air combat missions and increased arsenal of your soldiers.
Time units are back, and so comes the class-less soldier promotion system. it is up to you to choose the exact equipment and role of the soldier, and you can come up with very individual loadout choiches perfectly fit for the individual stats of the soldiers, adding alot more depth to equipment. Like in the original xcom, there is a fog of war and aliens shoot out of the dark. if you are careless with a soldier and run around a corner without looking to your side, you will soon run into trouble.
And the thing that makes a real xcom game: Absolutely hilarious/dramatic soldier deaths, situations that escalate quickly, missions that end up in absolute disasters and horror. The best moments were when a plan just did not work out, one soldier after another dies, and suddenly it becomes all about saving the remaining soldiers from their certain death.
The music adds to the atmosphere, and so does the fantastic art direction. I absolutely love the minimalistic, but effective graphical design, and the grim soldier portraits really add alot to the entire scenario.
Occasionally there were some minor bugs which i hope will get fixed someday, and the only thing that annoyed me was the fact that there was no option to change the camera angle, as it would have made navigating trough corridors and detecting the location of grenades on the floor alot easier. Additionally the vertical view of the soldiers seems to be a bit weird, because walls do not seem to obscure the vision of soldiers on upper floors very effectively.
All in all a very well rounded, challenging and absolutely awesome experience, and for anyone interested in an xcom game, i can safely declare xenonauts as the new gold standard for this genre.
