Yet another entry on the plethora of cutesy retro styled indie platformers, at least, that’ll be your first impression. Eversion was made for an H.P. Lovecraft-themed game competition and it becomes very apparent after a level or two, in which the inane becomes unnerving, and the unnerving becomes insane. This is achieved by having the player character shift through different parallel dimensions in each level, changing the scenery, enemies and making objects in the environment warp into walkable platforms or deadly hazards.
All these elements collide and you’re left scrambling around each level, slowly plunging into the deeper layers, trying to keep your cool while you solve the puzzles so you can collect every last gem and unlock the final level.
The game is of a rather short length, since its gimmick is just that, a gimmick. After travelling through the different layers and seeing how the world transforms you’ve seen all the game has to offer. Fortunately, Eversion is aware of this and will not overstay its welcome, unless you feel like editing levels or playing the time attack mode.
If you’re on the fence, I strongly recommend checking out the free version from the author’s website. The graphics are simpler and the resolution is halved, allowing the player to fill in the gaps with his imagination, making the experience more intense. And if you enjoy it and feel like doubling on the graphics quality, support the author and getting slightly more content, purchase the Steam edition.

Starting with the cons:
Managing items on your backpack needs to be tweaked, I've had to fight far too many times to get organic stacks attached to my backpack generator when its attached to the right side. A classic 2Dish inventory setup would work wonders, rather than trying to manage moving items in a 3D space using only 2D movement. Either that or lower the backpack when you press Q.
Tech tree needs to be freed from the bloody maw of RNG, I should not have to wander around some space rock looking for pods/space junk to input into the research station in the hope that this one will have the plans for a truck. Especially since I know how to make a rover by default. Speaking of already knowing things, you'd think a space faring species would already know how to make trucks and other technological items. So why do I need to research how to make a truck from an alien blob? Perhaps instead of recipes from research pods, maybe make it so that you learn new sources of building materials? It would be cool to learn those the mushroom trees I dug up by the hundreds to learn how to make a truck could also be used to make resin or compound.
Generators need to sense when there is draw on the power grid or not, having coal or organic stacks get wasted because the generator uses everything up even if all batteries and crafting stations have full internal batteries is rubbish. Power stacks are consumed as needed, so why don't generators follow the same rule?
If you want to experiment with another Minecraft in space style game, give it a shot. It's fun to explore and out racing dust storms in a rover is a thrill. However, I would recommend waiting until release or at least until this thing gets out of pre-alpha if you're the kind of person wary of early access.

Xenonauts has captured all the fun, excitement, and intrigue of the original X-COM games, and only intensified them in this amazing revival. With over 100 hours of play time logged on this gem, I can safely say that it is one of the most immersive and fun games I have played in a long time.
I have played Firaxis' X-COM and while I loved it, it still failed to quite capture the true spirit of the the original series. Not a problem with Xenonauts. Playing it feels like it was made by the exact same developers that made the original x-com, but with the approach and complexity that decades of gaming refinement have brought to the table.
I've heard some friends express a disenterest based on the graphics, but I can assure you that the elements of the game itself more then make up for this, and seeing how some 3D modeling can end up looking rather...cartoony or kind of silly (Planetary Annhiliation, Showrun Returns), I find it pretty refreshing.
I can't say enough about the content of this game. From the well written and detailed UFOpedia, that keeps a detailed description of every relevent item/creature you will come across and/or research, the rich histories of your team members; their prior combat experience, assignments, countries of origin, etc; to the HUGE tech tree to be plotted and explored.
The game takes place in 3 seperate environments...the "Geoscape", where you lay out your bases, set up manufacturing and research, hire and equip your soldiers/engineers/scientists, and watch for alien activity. Once an alien ship is spotted, you must dispatch interceptors to shoot down the enemy. Once your interceptor has engaged the ship, the second environment is entered
In the second phase, the "Tactical Air Battle" phase, you control up to several interceptors in a top down arial battle against the enemy ships. I have seen this tactical phase balance and transform as it was developed, and can say they have done a fantastic job with this and the balance as you research and develope more powerful crafts.
The 3rd and final phase is the "Tactical Ground Combat" phase, in which you control your customized team of soldiers (and various Heavy Weapon Platforms) in turn based combat against the alien invades after you have shot them down. You may also enter this phase without shooting down an alien ship if you get your lander to an already grounded UFO, a terrorist site in which the aliens are already grounded and engaged in terrorizing a major city you must defend, or an alien base they have established on Earth's surface.
There is a fantastic variety of terrain, maps, aliens, weapons, armor, etc throught the game, so it always seems fresh, even 40 to 50 hours in. even after my 120+ hours of gameplay (have played offline at times, who knows how many hours there) I still see new maps and have to come up with new strategies/approaches depending on situations.
All in all I would recommend Xenonauts to any gamer that won't be caught up on a lack of graphical complexity, and especially for anyone who likes management, strategy, simulation, or turn based games. At $25, this game is a great buy. I think the only thing keeping them from charging more is the lack of advanced graphics. The content is certainly up there with any Blockbuster game, in my opinion. Thank you to the fine developers at Goldhawk Ineractive for a wonderful product.

I've played thousands of hours of old X-COM (UFO Defense, Terror From The Deep, Apocalypse), and over 500 hours of Enemy Unknown/Within.  I'm enjoying Xenonauts tremendously.  Details follow, but if you're a fan of the old-school X-COM games, I'm already telling you that you should check this game out.
Xenonauts describes itself as a "spiritual successor" to X-COM.  It's important to note that they were very probably not talking about Enemy Unknown/Within; the differences in polish will disappoint you if you're expecting that level of visual quality.  However, as a successor to -old- X-COM (UFO Defense, Terror From The Deep, Apocalypse) it succeeds pretty brilliantly.
The look and feel of the Geoscape is very UFOD/TFTD (only much prettier), while the tactical aesthetics are much more like Apocalypse turn-based mode.  Bases have radar ranges determined by the number and quality of detection facilities present, but the range limits are far more visible than in previous games.  This makes it far easier to understand the coverage consequences of base placement.
Ship Combat:
X-COM ship fights (even in EU/EW) are like sumo wrestling.  The ships' locations on the field are completely abstracted away, and there are hit percentages simulating mobility, so you see two craft holding relatively still and slugging at each other.  Misses look more like bad aiming than evasive action.
In Xenonauts, the ship combat display is a 2D grid wherein momentum and turning radius count.  Weapons have ranges and firing arcs, ammo and fuel count, afterburners are a thing (but see: fuel counts) and missiles have their own maneuverability values.  Defensive maneuvers exist for evasive actions, and a dogfight isn't always 1:1 -- in fact, encounters can get up to 3 vs. 3 in some cases; as UFO's begin to appear with escorts, and fighter squadrons roam in packs daring your interceptors to come out and play, you respond by sending attack groups instead of lone planes.  There are light and heavy interceptor classes, with maneuverability, range and armament consequences.
You can't form an attack group out of craft from more than one base, unfortunately.  I'd have loved to see a rendezvous point system wherein disparate fleets could join up, but ship combat is a fun, complex mini-game in and of itself and a strategy guide could be (and probably has been) written just for that facet of gameplay.
NOTE:  There are -way- more UFO's in the early part of the game than in any iteration of X-COM.  This becomes important during...
Ship Combat Aftermath:
You can send troops to fight at a crash site, but that's not always an option.  You probably don't have enough strike teams to cover every site where you've shot something down, especially early on when a single Condor is still a match for anything the aliens field.  Rather than letting the sites rot and taking a PR penalty with the nation where they crashed, Xenonauts provides the option to call an airstrike and saturate that area, then send a non-combatant cleanup team to salvage what it can.  This results in a static amount of cash based on the class of crashed craft, and a few recoverable items, but no soldier experience or personnel equipment captures.
Soldier Management:
Enemy Unknown/Within introduced the concept of soldier classes; a Rookie, upon promotion to Squaddie, was assigned one of four classes.  That class distinction determined what stats increased when the soldier was promoted, what weapons the soldier was allowed to carry, and what special abilities became available to that soldier as rank increased.  It's a novel concept, but there are downsides.  Class assignment is for life, for one thing, and there's little room for creative misuse of inventory -- you can't load down an Assault trooper with grenades, for instance.  Nonlethal weapons were considered Items rather than weapons in EU/EW, as well, which meant that you had to choose between that and grenades, or extra armor, or whatever else.  It added importance to the range of choices, but only by limiting them.
Xenonauts doesn't have classes, but it does allow you to assign a soldier a role.  The main differences are that any role can technically carry any equipment; there are customizable default equipment templates for each role; you can change a soldier's role in the barracks anytime the soldier is on base; and you can create new roles.  Weapon disparity is a little wider, and there is in fact a "laser shotgun" and other mechanics-only nonsense, but in general the strategic and tactical choices you can make in Xenonauts is far wider and more granular than in its ancestors.
Tactical Combat:
Oh, man.  Where to start.  Quick list of things that don't require explanation:
- Stun rockets are a thing.  You get them as soon as you get stun grenades.
- You don't have to wait half the game to get stun grenades.
- Nonlethal melee weapons exist, and they're weapons -- not some other item class.
- All soldiers carry an infinite number of flares!  (But vehicles don't.)
- Vision arcs are back.  An unarmored human has a 90-degree effective vision arc.  (Heavy armor can reduce this.)
- Cover is not a light switch like in EU/EW, but rather a stack of calculated obstruction percentages like in older X-COM titles.
Stuff that might require some more description:
- Range matters a lot.  Different weapons are optimized either for long-range armor-piercing fire, or massive trauma at point-blank range.  You have to make sure you send the right soldier for the right tactical situation, all the time; the aliens are as merciless as they ever were in TFTD, and a soldier caught at a disadvantage is very probably toast.
- Area denial is a real thing.  Enough shell-shock (automatic weapons fire, explosives, etc.) in the immediate vicinity of a soldier (human or enemy) can cause them to become Suppressed, which takes away their TU's (no reaction fire from that soldier), and reduces the TU's they get next turn by 50% (no burst fire, probably no grenades, just movement adjustments OR one decent shot).  Heavy weapons and vehicle weapons are wonderful for this, but remember ammo is being counted.
- Reaction fire is not solely a function of the reacting soldiers' statistics -- reaction initiative is calculated using (get this) modifiers determined by the weapons and equipment worn by both the active and reactive soldiers, Reaction stats, and *TU's the reacting player has left*.  That doesn't just mean that low TU's result in snap shots; it means that high TU's can result in normal or snap shots, and low TU's can lead to the reactive soldier being unable to respond fast enough even though he technically has enough TU's to take a shot.  In addition, assault weapons actually inflict a reaction penalty on anyone calculating reaction fire against them; carrying a shotgun actually makes it much more likely that you'll get the first shot in a point-blank, room-to-room encounter.
Summary:
The mechanics of Xenonauts are closer to what I've always wanted X-COM to be.  I'm not in love with the tactical display's graphical quality, but if there's a sequel, I'll look for that to improve.  Meanwhile, the game is a beautiful example of this game type, and the creation and maintenance of it is behavior we enthusiasts should reward by burying the developers in enough money that they decide it would be crazy not to make another one.

I just bought this game yesterday, so I don't know all the in's and out's of it, but I'm going to write my preliminary reactions.
Xenonauts wins on the feeling alone.  I haven't played the X-Com games, new or old, but I have to say that something about the "look" of the new one turns me off, a bit.  While the AAA style of that game left a bad taste in my mouth, the old fashioned presentation of Xenonauts is quite refreshing.  The excellent paintings and graphics evoke a definite "X-files" atmosphere, and the soundtrack has an excellent atmospheric dread to it.  It is quite fun to send your squads through the map, clearing buildings and establishing perimiters, hunting down that lone bug-eyed freak who you just know is going to pop out and blast your guys with a burst of plasma fire.
The amount of detail and depth in the simulation is quite good, especially for fans of strategy games which are more complex.  Woefully, many games these days have a "press x to win" mentality, but this game doesn't.  You have to carefully manage your funds and figure out your own strategies.  Should you build a second base early on, to keep the Russians convinced that your organization can do it's job?  Or do you spend your disposable income on tricking out your North American base so that you can more efficiently capture alien tech?
To sum it up, it's a little bit of SWAT 2 and a lot of X-files, all rolled up into a wonderful old-school experience.

Add on top of that how badly Sonic Adventure aged, and you have yourself a fun game lying beneath with a horrible camera and some questionable level design leading to some unfortunate deaths.
I do think Adventure is a better game than Adventure 2, definitely not technically, but it's a less stressful game with better treasure hunting stages and imo better mech levels. I also prefer Adventure's music, though this is all opinionated.
If you haven't played Adventure and want to, don't get this version if you have a console- preferably buy the Dreamcast version, though the GameCube version is also an okay choice.
It is worth noting that there is a conversion mod to make this game play like the original Dreamcast release, which works great, but none of the issues present in the original release have been fixed. If you *really* have to play the PC release, this is the best way of doing so, but I would still suggest playing a newer, better aged sonic game.

Super Meat Boy is an extremely challenging platformer game.  It features a simple, but humorous story, but the gameplay is what really shines here.  You can run and jump your way through several uniquely themed worlds consisting of many individual levels, each more challenging than the last, with new types of obstacles regularly being introduced along the way.  With many different characters to unlock, secret stages, the even more difficult dark worlds, and leaderboards to compare your performance with the world's best, the game has great longevity.  I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the platformer genre, so long as you enjoy a challenge.  Just try not to throw your controller too much.

I bought this game very, very cheaply. Half off its already low price. Steam coupon. Cheaply enough that I figured if it turned out to be a waste of my time, I wouldn't be out a lot of money.
You'll notice that my time played on the game is quite short. How about that.
I like puzzles. I play a lot of games with ACTUAL puzzles. But mazes aren't puzzles as far as I'm concerned; there is no brain involved. Here, they've tried to add a little brain by making each set of mazes have a different rule which they don't tell you. Or maybe they try to tell you. I THINK the game was trying to tell me the "rule" of the forest maze, but did so in such bad English that it took me three screens to realize the actual rule: In the forest, you can't turn left or back up. That's it.
So then I went and looked at some walkthroughs and realized the rest of the game was just more mazes, with a rule change every four maps or so, plus a story which, frankly, seems pretty obvious just from the first few panels of dialogue and the unsubtle clues in the maps (really, IV stands scattered all over the woods, that's the best you can do?). Yeah, yeah, dying, hallucinating, in the hospital, replaying life, trying to figure out whether to go on, monsters from the brain - I've seen that before, seen it done better.
Oh, well. That's why I buy 'em cheap.
If you're really dying to see how this story comes out (ha, ha) go watch a walkthrough. Even at the tiny price this isn't worth it.

June 4, 2015
I had been working through my backlog, and feeling better in my twitch skills, so I decided to work on beating Eversion completely. I have learned a bit more about the game, and will requalify my review.
Honestly, I was wrong to think this game was hard. It's actually not challenging, just inconsistent in executing jumps at least on keyboard. Disabling the Steam Overlay helps to reduce input lag, but the game is still not tight like Super Meat Boy. Movement is fast and slippery, which makes precision more cumbersome, but it can be done. The gameplay is really basic, simple platforming with minor dimensional differences.
I feel the big problem is that the game does little unique. In truth, you are paying for a minor graphical update, since the game is free online at lower graphical fidelity. For the price, this graphics package is quite underwhelming. There are several palette swaps, but the animations are only a few frames. Music is repetitive, and starts over every time you die. It all feels cheaply put together, more rusty than retro.
The game is short, dimension shifting is more for the brooding plot than for gameplay, and the ending could be reached in a few minutes. As for the plot, despite "inspiration" from Lovecraft and any kind of written material, the plot is laughable. I understand platformers are not known for story, but Braid and VVVVVV did a heck of a lot more in story along with gameplay. For a game that sells itself on "the twist", that twist just made me think that someone needs to stop playing in MS Paint. It feels antiquated, and reminds me of the shoddy romhack creepypasta stuff of Mario online. Those elements probably had a larger influence on this game than Lovecraft ever did.
So the story, gameplay, and graphics are all mediocre, doing little new. VVVVVV just seems to do everything better. Saira is a great puzzle-platformer option with probably 3 times the content, better graphics and music, and is fully free forever on Steam right now. Eversion fails to impress anymore, and feels more like a joke. The developer never bothered to capitalize letters in the few announcements made for the game, so maybe the whole thing really is a joke. Still, not worth the price, as the game never goes on sale anymore.

I have no idea how describe Eversion. Lets just start with the basics shall we? Its art style is overly colorful to say the least. Its music is throbbingly annoying and will be engrained in your mind forever (think the music of pokemon), especially the song that plays on the first level. The gameplay is frustrating to say the least and is not "fluid" or "tight" as some might say. Honestly, the only person who can say that the platforming is good should be the people who have never played a platformer before (the original super mario bros. was programed more tightly), and even then thats a STRETCH.
Despite all of this I can say without a doubt, I have never been this afraid of a game before. Not whats in the game, the game itself. The unknown entity haunting the game. If you have ever heard the creepy pasta "BEN is dead"
, playing this game gives you the same tingling down your spine as the game begins to try to get in your head.
If you enjoy a good psychological scare that makes you want to shut off your computer, play this at night in the dark... your welcome.

It took a long time for me to try this game. I'd played the original Tomb Raider when I was a kid and didn't really get the hang of it. Having bought the complete Tomb Raider bundle a few years ago I tried to play from the first releases again for nostalgia more than anything, but still couldn't get on with it. So this time I decided to skip the earlier games and restart my Tomb Raider experience from this one, having read reviews of the previous games and deciding this one was a good place to start if I wanted to get into the Tomb Raider games. As I completed this game and I'm looking forward to the next one I think that was a good decision.
This game does show its age a bit, especially if you have to switch off next generation graphics to get past a crash, but overall the story line is enjoyable and the game play not too bad.
The puzzles add a nice touch of challenge to the game which doesn't just involve killing stuff. I couldn't be bothered trying to collect all the hidden artifacts though. For me it just distracted from the games story and I don't feel it added much to this games experience, especially if you're not interested in unlocking the extras.
If you've not played Tomb Raider games before then it can take a bit of getting used to only being able to look at Lara. It can also be a tad annoying when you can't get the camera to look at where you need to go and so you have to make a blind leap of faith hoping Lara will grab hold of whatever you're aiming for... which thankfully she does. It's also feels unnatural at first that Lara moves in relation to where the camera is looking instead of the direction she is facing given the third person view you have of Lara, but stuck with it and it doesn't take long to get the hang of it.
One thing I did find very annoying was the camera angle drastically changing automatically at certain points like at the end of a sequence of cliff face jumps. So I'd be merrily jumping along a cliff (which is failing away so I can't hang about) and I see what I need to do at the end and as I do my final jump in the right direction the camera swings around and I jump off the sodding cliff instead of where I wanted to go. :( Ah well. Thankfully the check point saving in this game is pretty good and dying never puts you too far back in the game.
All in all a good enjoyable game. Now onto the next one...

This game is... Something.
Basically, the premise is that you play through rip offs of classic horror movies. LVC 3 apes Friday the 13th, LVC4 apes Texas Chainsaw Massacre, LVC 5 apes Halloween, and the 6th is a combination of Alien and The Thing.
Each level is an open ended adventure puzzle game, essentially, with each one having distinct objectives. For instance, in 3 you are simply trying to ward off the killers without all four of your teenagers (that you control one at a time) dying. In 4, you are searching a truly demented mansion and slaughterhouse for gas so the band you play as can make their next gig. In 5, you try to avoid a Michael Meyers esque killer while summoning monsters that can bring him down.
There's a lot to like with this game. For one, each level is very distinct from the others. The first is probably the most open ended and trial and error one, because it's a very small, confined setting. It's the one that is quite tough to figure out, but once you do, it's pretty rewarding. Plus, there are lots of things you can do in the environment, so it's fun to experiment. While 3 is relatively tame despite the gore, 4 and 5 ramp up the creep factor. Yes, believe it or not, this game actually manages to be pretty disturbing and creepy thanks to its sound design and creative use of visuals. Both 4 and 5 have an extremely macabre and dark feeling to them that 3 simply does not, and it's pretty welcome.
I will say that certain elements stand out as flawed. For one, the layout of the buildings in 4 is entirely RNG, and it can glitch so that, without giving too much away, you can't continue. This is really annoying, as I've died more than once in that level simply because of the rng. Additionally, 5 is one I simply needed a guide for. Tomb Raider Legend may have been the first Tomb Raider game I spent any amount of time with, back in the day. It was less than a dollar a week or so ago, so I decided to pick it up for my Steam collection, and give it a whirl.
On Windows 10 (or possibly Steam), saving doesn't seem to work. I most likely need to run it as Administrator, but I'll get around to that later. It supports Widescreen, and it supports Full HD, but some of the scenes look strange because of those settings.
Tomb Raider Legend was a soft reboot of the Tomb Raider series. I think that the previous storyline had written itself into a corner, or perhaps the gameplay was terrible. I do remember that when I played TRL for the first time, I was impressed with the platforming and the combat. Having come back to it after the 2013 reboot, I'm less impressed. It's not that it's bad, but the camera has managed to make me fall off of a number of platforms. It's not as intuitive as the newer game.
I think that the Angelina Jolie movie came out at about the same time, and you can see the influence of both, in how much of an indifferent psychopath Lara is, or how she has a computer expert and a nerd to feed information to her out in the field. She is confident, is Lara, and she does get around, and dress up. It's a world-spanning adventure, and it's fun, I must confess.
Overall, that's what I do like about TRL, is that it is fun. Lara is having fun, and we're right there having fun with her. The QTEs are awful, and some of the sections are rather painful, but I did enjoy TRL when it came out, and it's an okay distraction now. I just need to fix up the savefile issue, and it should be good to go.

Wow!  There have been a ton of games that have tried to do what X-COM: UFO Defense (or UFO: Enemy Unknown) succeeded so well with back in '94.  A scope that seems global, and you have soldiers that may well only make it through one mission alive.  Casualties are expected, and you feel like you are engaged in a true war with the aliens.
2012's XCOM by Firaxis is fantastic--it plays well, it's easy to pick up, and it's fun.  Still, to me that game felt more like an action movie.  I had six soldiers that survived more often than not (then again, I don't play the super high difficulties, so that might change things a bit).
Xenonauts puts you into a larger scale war, with dozens of troops at your command that you will need.  And some will die.  Heck, many will.  But this game has that skin-of-your-teeth feel to it that the original X-COM had.  The graphics are similar, and almost and updated version of the mid-nineties hit.  Yet there are numerous improvements that help troop and base management, the interceptor game became more strategic (with wingmen!), and there are more options overall that let you take the war to the aliens.
I'm re-learning the strategies to win all over again, like it was twenty years ago.  And I'm having a blast doing it!

Also, I would suggest saving often (f6), because you never know when you'll die by some B.S thing like a random red giant scorpion man. If auto-save is a feature, turn it on!
I would suggest buying Serious Sam Bundle for £8.50. It is Seriously worth it, for those who love a good shooter.

This is a completely new review. My last one only told of my experience and nothing about the game mechanics. First off, you control 1 of 4 teenagers at any given time that can be cycled through at will. There are different ones in the 4 episodes that come with Lakeview Cabin Collection, although Cabin 6 is in beta currently, you can still play it. Each "movie" is set in a different setting with (obviously) different characters and maniacal serial killers. Some of them even have multiple killers... I'm looking at you Cabin 4...
The game really builds a sense of dread as you take down the killer with one blast and you approach him to see if he's dead he'll inevitably pop up, bash you, take your weapon and murder you. From that, you'll be so shook up, while you may have 3 more characters to formulate a plan, they will likely all perish in a rather gory fashion until you wise up and search for more supplies hidden and use them to your advantage with your surroundings.
The game does not shy away from dark and gory subject matter either as a lot of my screenshots can attest. All in all, it keeps the surprises coming. It consistently will make you jump. You know the little pixellated killer may pop out or is just on the other side of the door, your heart rate won't care, it will climb. You will get panicked. Then you'll die and try again. It's a very fun game that has basic puzzles you uncover through exploration and using the tools at hand rather logically.
Sound also plays a major role. You may find certain items by listening when you throw something... is that a sock that sounds metallic when thrown? Must be something inside... Is the music ratcheting up when nearing a door? That psychopath may be ready to pounce out... just maybe...
It's impressive what a one-man team was able to produce on this. The level of detail for pixel graphics and the sound is impressive. Wind chimes blow in the breeze. There's a day/night cycle with some light weather effects. I couldn't recommend it more.

Borderlands 2 is the sequel to Borderlands 1, which is basically a gun lover's wet dream, due to the insane amount of guns in that game. If Borderlands 1 had that many guns, Borderlands 2 can't have more that what it boast right? WRONG! This game have about 87 million guns, far more than Borderlands 1. It's practically able to make gun lovers climax from hearing the gun counts. Anyway, its an FPS game with RPG-esque elements, with an emphasis on FPS actions.
In this game, you get to choose 4 characters by default, an additional 2 if you bought the character DLCs. Each characters have their own action skills and skill trees. Depending on what you decide to invest on, you can get either a medic build, glass cannon build, melee build etc. They also poses no restriction in terms of what weapons you can use, so fire away, Vault Hunter!
As mentioned earlier, guns. Lots of guns in this game. Lots of guns to shoot mobs at. Lots of guns to burn mobs at! Lots of guns to dissolve mobs with! Ahem, basically there are lots of guns. In addition to guns, you have other miscellaneous items that help to boost your characters, similar to RPG trinkets. There are many bonuses that they can provide such as increased health regeneration, boost to skills, more ammo per magazine, higher fire rate etc.
The story of a game is basically about you, a Vault Hunter, trying to fight against a tyrannical corperation, more specifically, one dude. Who is handsome. I think. Along the way, you will get side quests, in addition to your main quests for the storyline, like RPGs. At the end of the story, you may proceed to the next difficulty, or if you are already at the highest difficulty, farm bosses for the best loot possible. Many characters from the first Borderlands return as NPCs or supporting characters as well.
One of the main thing I really liked about this game is the respecable skill trees. You don't need to create a new character, just find the nearest characterization station, and reset your skills! Easy way if your skill build is not working, or if you want to try another build without creating another character. Drop rate, oh boy drop rates. About half of my playtime here is just farming bosses for the loots that I want. The drop rate is not that bad to be honest, at least better than other RPGs I played, such as Diablo 2, since each bosses and a slightly higher chance to drop a specific item. If you wanna get, for example a Lyuda, farm Gettle. That's it. No need to farm other bosses just to find that Lyuda.
Character dialogues are really cheesy, and fun! For example, an enemy Psycho started quoting Hamlet while chasing me. He talked for 2 whole minutes, reciting the entire line for that act in Hamlet. I had to aggro him just to hear him out completely. Or Krieg the Psycho (DLC character), which keep talking about nipple salads and having the shiniest meat bicycle. It's completely incomprehensible, yet funny to hear all the time. And Gaige the Mechromancer 9the other DLC character) will keep talking how n00b they are, or rambling about anarchy and smashing the system.
As mentioned, this game is similar to an RPG, so eventually the mobs get stronger and stronger. Normal headshot won't kill instantly, depending on the gun damage and the mob health (unless you are overlevelled or you have a really good gun with a good stats). So in the end, it goes from ripping and tearing mobs apart to fighting meat sponges. Their damages ramp up as well, but beware, some mobs can 1 shot you into a dying state. During dying state, you need to kill someone to revive, or get someone to revive you if its coop. Otherwise, it's back to the respawn stations. Some mobs are fine, like animals, but the humans? "I'ma hide behind this cover, and I'm not gonna take pot shots." Good luck from killing that coward though. Death does not make you lose experience though, only money, so it's not so bad. As mentioned, due to the meat sponges tendency of the mobs, basically this game is screaming at you to play it in coop. It's more fun that way as well.
Overall, I would highly recommend it. Fan of the first Borderlands will really like it, FPS players may enjoy it, though some RPG elements may or may not be to their liking. Drop rate are reasonably fine. Soloing the game is possible, but it's way better to play it in coop. Also get the GOTY edition. The DLCs are really worth it (though I have yet to get them, eventually I will).

There are different rules for each and every game mode, but for every game mode there are two different teams; Counter-Terrorists and Terrorists. The terrorists’ objective in most game modes is to plant the bomb at one of two bombsites (A or B), wiping out any Counter-Terrorists they can. The bomb takes 40 seconds to explode and during this time, the remaining Counter-Terrorists must attempt to defuse this bomb. It can be considerably difficult for the Counter-Terrorists to defuse, or it could be a walk in the park; it all depends on teamwork.
Teamwork is an absolutely HUGE portion of this game; it is absolutely necessary to get along with your teammates and devise a plan to win effectively. In the “Competitive” game mode, the first team to win 16 rounds is victorious. To achieve this goal, you must be willing as a player to communicate verbally with your teammates, know all the different portions of the map you plan to play and how to navigate the map with ease. If you really get into this game, it is undeniable that you will experience some stress from time to time, but it is vital you know how to control that stress; if you let the game get the best of you, chances are you’re not going to be in the proper attitude to win.

But the story is engaging and fun, the soundtrack is fantastic, even the graphics are good, especially with the BetterSADX mod improving them. I wish there were more Sonic games like this.

Made by Zeboyd instead of Hothead, this is just a much more fun game than its predecessors.
You swap the 3D for 2D sprite graphics which may upset some people who don't care for the aesthetic, but it was not a bother for me.  Music is more catchy.  You lose the descriptors on every minor object in the world, but those held no meaningful value so not really a loss.  Environments are just placeholders for progression... but that was still true in the previous game too.  At least there's no backtracking.  Game takes a more serious tone here so if the comedy that overlaid everything in the first two games was a detriment to you like it was to me, then you will appreciate this change.
Game mechanics become more traditional of RPGs, so no un-fun QTEs every fight this time around.  There's a meaningful amount of customization and planning, compared to the first game where every upgrade was limited and linear.  Its just more fun all around.
Its just more fun.  Definitely enjoyed myself this time around.

This is, perhaps, the best GTA game in the history of the franchise. I think that pretty much anybody who's ever played GTA knows about this game, and I'd dare to say that, in most cases, this is the one people remember the most. While the other games from the 3D era were pretty good as well (I'll always have a soft spot for Vice City, which was my first GTA ever), this one takes the cake. Rather than being limited to a single city, like previous games (or a bunch of cities divided in levels, like the original GTA), this one's set in an entire state, with three large cities (Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas), a bunch of small towns, and lots of countryside to explore.
The game feels HUGE. And it's not just a big map that's pretty much empty unless it's a plot-essential area. You can easily go around exploring and find places with great detail (for the time) that are completely irrelevant to the plot; in fact, there's large areas of the map that you'll never go to if you only focus on the story, and this includes some small towns. Still, they're there, to make the world feel alive. When it comes to the main cities, they're pretty good, and, again, there's lots of details here and there to make them feel like scaled-down versions of the real cities they're based in.
The gameplay is what you'd expect from GTA. There's shooting, there's carjacking, all the good ol' GTA stuff. However, this game was the first in the series to introduce some light-RPG elements. Not only could you customize the way CJ looked by changing his clothes and haircut, but you could also make him fat, or have him train at the gym making him stronger and learning new combat moves. And his skill with vehicles and weapons could improve as well the more you used them. There's also tons of side missions and activities besides the main plot, including the classic odd jobs like Vigilante on Paramedic, and a few new ones as well.
The storyline of the game is great. It begins with CJ returning to the hood after 5 years, and, like many GTA games, it's a story of working your way up from the bottom. However, what makes this one stand out in my opinion is that it isn't only about the rise of a powerful criminal, but it's also about family and friendship. Pretty well written, with some serious moments, along with some great humour. Not to mention a lot of references and callbacks to previous games from the 3D era.
The "soundtrack", or rather the in-game radio stations are pretty good; there's a wide variety of genres, and the actual soundtrack played during cutscenes and such is good as well. Not to mention that you can add your own music for the radio stations, so you can always listen to something you like while playing.
Well, I think that's pretty much everything I've got to say about GTA:SA. I really recommend it, as it is one of my favourite GTA games, and the one I played the most (both on the PS2 and on PC).

In a way I wish I could have the ability to share the incredible experiences that I had while playing this game with this review.
I sadly don't think i'm that aware of myself, nor am I familiar with my ability to express myself purely, and completely, honestly.
I can only say that Grand Theft Auto San Andreas is in a lot of ways the "epithome" of not only the Grand Theft Auto series, but in my opinion, of open world games.
This is the formula that Rockstar created, refined and polished to perfection, and while the game might have technically some issues that range from minor, to abysmal, I don't think anyone can deny that this game, at the very least, has had a significant impact in their lifes, in one way or the other.
This is a game that is beloved by people that played it way back when it originally released, up until newcomers to the series that are simply curious about the legacy of this game.
The story it's excellent, the characters, the missions, the complete an utter range of jokes, ideas, concepts, and experiences that are packed with detail in your journey are merely the fragments of what this game holds. In it's attention for developing an enjoyable experience, and a heartfelt one at that, Rockstar turned the flaws of their games in benefits and values, that are shared perfectly with this example of a game.
Even when everything in the game feels dated, old, and mechanically flawed, objectively flawed (whatever that means) the game somehow manages to revert difficult and often hateful missions into pieces that conform something bigger, something memorable.
Even after years from the game's release you can see that people still share their memories trying to beat missions like "Wrong Side of the Tracks" a mission that is not only difficult thanks to the "tight" controls over your vehicle, but also because of the dependency of the game's a.i.
Altho as much as I can praise the game's story, the game's incidental experiences that you can get sometimes by simply driving around listening to the incredible selection of songs that are available in the game's radio.
There's a significant problem with the game's pc version.
For starters, the game is missing a lot of content from the consoles versions of the game, cars, effects, enviroments, textures, etc... There's a lot here that conforms an incredible atmosphere and enhances what is already an excellent game, that's simply missing, with the only ability of instaurating this "features" with the use of mods, thanks to the incredible, and still active community that still keeps itself passionate even after 12 years from the games release.
As I said, a true testament of the legacy of this incredible game.
However if it wasn't only the missing content there are other issues, the game has problems running at framerates higher than 60 framerates per second, while there are other people that debate the game also has problems while even surpassing 30 framerates per second, either way it's something that I haven't personally experience in my time with the game, that as you may see from the Steam's recorded time, it's not much.
This is simply because I have had to "downgrade" my game's version from 3.0 to 1.0, the first, and most compatible version with the modifications created by the community now a days.
It's been the only wat that i've found myself actually enjoying the game, (as much as I resent the phrase) that the developers intended for me to play.
If that wasn't enough, new versions also eliminate certain songs from the different fictitious radio stations in-game. Something that as I said I haven't experienced thanks to the ability to downgrade and mantain the original first game's released version intact by also having to, sadly, move the game away from Steam's game directory.
At it's core, I love this game, I have incredible memories with it, and I think it's a game that you owe yourself to play, if you love games, and certainly, if you love Gta, this is a game that in my opinion deserves all the praise and remembrance that it gets even now a days, it's a game that can have frustating missions, repetitive ones at that, other times it can be sad, but for the most part I don't think anyone can't deny the game it's a fun and entretaining time to experience through and through.
This in a lot of ways is also the last Grand Theft Auto game released for the Sixth generation of consoles, and similarly to how in a way Grand Theft Auto 5 was that for the Playstation 3, and the Xbox 360, even while they re-release that game for newer platforms, including pc, this is a firm, a departure and a letter of love from Rockstar games towards its fans.
The gameplay, the characters, the different places and diverse cities that you encounter while exploring the map, the small fragment of time that the leaved since this game up until Grand Theft Auto 4, was enough for people to show there love as well, sharing experiences, creating mods, and even stories that end up becoming part of videogame's culture.
Grand Theft Auto San Andreas it's essentially the definition of what, in my opinion, a great game can be, a great game not only in sales, nor in scores, but in heart, and in memories.
That's the true definition of a successful game for me, a game that 12 years after release people still talk about, still get involved with, both by playing it, as well as in by creating features for the game.
I just wish in a way that "love" had also been shared at it's fullest with the pc version of the game, altho after all this years, I frankly can say that I just don't care...
Mainly with all the mods that are out there.

I'd say I recommend it, but that doesn't mean that Legend doesn't have its flaws.
Biggest flaw is it doesn't particularly play well with modern systems, I ran into the "Fatal flaw" crash a couple times, and had to download a fix .exe file to finish the game, so fair warning on that front.
Other cons:
The tedious, awful motorcycle sections, of which there are two in the game.
The bosses will spam voicelines every ♥♥♥♥ing 2 seconds.  "Bet you wish you could do that, huh?  Bet you wish you could do that, huh?  Bet you wish you could..." stfu Rutland for 2 seconds, damn.
The completely insane default control scheme for kb+m.  The game will teach you combat by telling you to press G to lock on and the shoot with H.  H?  It's auto bound to left mouse by default, why does it instruct you to push H?  Aim you'll have to re-assign to right mouse.  Throw a grenade with K.  In the middle of combat, just take your hand off the mouse, and push K so the grenade goes...somewhere.  Heal with the "home" button.  When was the last time you used that in a game?  In fact, that entire insert-end-home block is in here in some capacity, for some reason.
But once you re-map the controls to something more sane, and as long as you aren't in a vehicle, the game is pretty OK.  Not amazing, but it's OK.  The puzzles aren't too difficult, and the combat mainly revolves around charging straight at the human enemies so you can jump off of their heads to get the airborne damage bonus.
I'd say the platforming was less infuriating in terms of missing ledges than in Anniversary, which is odd considering this game came out a year before TRA.
It's definitely playable, and you can have fun with it, so "recommend".

Tomb Raider: Legend is an excellent game that still holds up in 2017 for a game that was made in 2006. You can definitely notice its age while watching its cutscenes, but that's not something to hold against it.
-The game is not long. The game took me about 6-7 hours to cmplete, and compared to the newer Tomb Raider entries that's jokingly short. Mind you, those 6-7 hours didn not dissapoint (if you're wondering why it says I have nearly 9 hours, that's because I spent a ittle extra time of getting collectables). The story was entertaining and places that the game took place in really interested me, in such places as under a museum in England, snowy fortress in Kazakhstan, and the location of a very overpowered sword in Bolivia. This is not a game to skip out on if you're new to Tomb Raider or got introduced to the series in the new 2013 reboot like I did.
-The camera and controls are wonky. I saw myself dying in a lot of stupid places because either the camera was positioned just so that when I would make Lara jump, she'd jump off to her doom, or Lara had to do a very precise jump that she would miss because I was off by a very little distance. Again, this is to be expected for a 2006 game port on to the PC.
If you enjoy the classic or the modern iterations of Tomb Raider, this and its sequels (which I will review once I get to playing them), this game is a no brainer.

I must start by saying that this is part of a bundle pack with SS2 and SSR and anything I say about this game means nothing since those games are worth the money themselves. Serious Sam was a FPS made in the early 2000's and while it suffered from a limited buget(It was 20$ full price back then) it managed to make a name for itself and spawn a franchise, thanks to it's fast and furious gameplay. The graphics have aged well and has great draw distance. The gameplay is fun and chaotic.The sound track isn't too shabby either.
My biggest problems are as follows. I mentioned the fact that this is a buget game and it does show. While the graphics are great they are also limited. Everything is egypt themed with the enviorment and never really changed. Enemies are limited too. As most of them are the same enemy with either diffrent colors or still act the same way as the other enemies. I would say while there are a lot of designs for the enemies i'd say it really only has four or five. While I love one of the weapons(cannonball) the other ones are also limited. You have a knife, a pistol, two pistols,shotgun,double shotgun, machine gun,faster machine gun,etc. You only really have six weapons max as the other ones are the same but do more damage and use ammo faster.
If your wondering why i'm being critical while I know this is a buget game, then this is my point. While I commend them for this game and it is impressive, the game is so limited that it gets tedious long before the game ends. You end up fighting the same enemies in Level 13 as you did in level 1. And I felt like I seen everything this game had to offer by level 5. Although I did enjoy the final boss. This game simply has not aged as well as other classic shooters. I only recommend it because this is one of three games. And the others are much better in everyway.

Let me get straight to the point first: This is not a terrible game. Maybe not even bad. In my opinion, it is just not worth the money.
Eversion is an Indie platformer which makes me scratch my head when comparing it to the original Super Mario, but only with a flower as protagonist. Of course, this game is a stand alone title, so it has some mechanics on it's own. The most recognizable one is Dimension Shifting. Like it says, you switch between different dimensions which gives the same level a different layout and enemies. With each layer, the level gets more difficult.
Don't get scared though, as this game is hilariously easy. You don't have any lives, so if you were to fall in a bottomless pit or get hit by an enemy, you start at a certain checkpoint. You could compare it to Rayman Origins, but simplified. Besides, it only took me 2 hours to get all achievements, endings and collectables. And I even took my time. But this is of course personal preference as some people prefer short games, which I can clearly understand.
Dimension Shifting itself is a fun mechanic at first, but it gets boring really fast. And that's a shame because it is the main gimmick of the game. If you're interested in puzzles, you might see some light here.
The game only has 8 worlds, which can be completed in a laughably short time. Well, most of them anyways. By doing that you will miss all the collectibles but it still shouldn't be ignored.
The story is ignorable, the music forgetable and the graphics are, while fitting this game, just average. Remember, this is not a bad game but it's just not worth the money. If you are however able to get it on sale or in any other way, give it a go! You might see something in this game I don't.

I took a chance on this game after having seen it on the early access page, and I have to say that, for the most part, I like what I've seen so far. It's a simple, charming game with a solid core mechanic and explains the rules well. In Slime Rancher, your goal is to create a habitat for the colorful slime creatures found on a distant planet, and use them to profit as you explore the environment.
Pro:
-Simple, intuitive mechanics. All the controls you need to know are explained in about a minute at the beginning of the game. The aiming system for the vacuum/cannon is forgiving for players who aren't great at shooters (e.g. myself). There is a guide available in-game that can tell you what you need to do, but I often found myself learning by experience rather than the guide. That is to say, the game teaches well without the strict need for a tutorial, but the tutorial is there and quite useful for those who need it.
-Fast-paced, yet relaxing gameplay. There is very little rush until you encounter some of the more volatile slime creatures later on. The player can move at his or her own pace to gather slime, food, and resources. The day/night cycle allows ample time for time-sensitive tasks to be completed.
-The game provides a very immediate sense of progression and reward. From the beginning the player can set simple, short term goals and use the money earned from the slimes to purchase upgrades either for themselves (the jetpack being an obvious early-game winner) or for the ranch. Exploration is rewarded, as well, as new environments bring new types of slime and food.
Cons:
-The most obvious and serious fault is also one that will likely be addressed as the game is developed: the lack of content. After about 4 hours of play, I felt as though I had accomplished most of what the game has to offer. I have spent several hours since then attempting achievements, gathering money, and showing the game to a friend, but there are only a handful of areas available at the time of writing and much of my ranch sits gathering dust. This is to be expected, as the game is in early access, and several accessible areas indicate that they are in development. Still, at a $20 price tag, I was hoping for a bit more substance.
-A bit of a nitpick, but some of the upgrades for the ranch seem superfluous or do not work as intended. Generally, slimes are contained in corals while on the ranch, and wild slimes seldom come near it. In that sense the Scareslime sees little use. Also, the auto-feeder often dispenses more food than the slimes need, and the plort collector does not seem completely efficient. This can leave the rancher to try and clean up in a coral full of spiky or exploding (or both!) slimes.
Ultimately, the game looks very promising, with simple, intuitive gameplay and a solid system of progression. Those looking for substantial content may want to wait for an update or two, but I would say that I have very much enjoyed the time I put in.

Lakeview Cabin Collection is a parody of classic slasher  movies, obviously directly inspired from Friday the 13th (There is actually a Friday the 13th Easter Egg within the first chapter). Within the first chapter, your protagonists include a group of 4, "racially diverse" friends... and your dogge.
The game mechanics are a bit tricky at first, I wont lie. However, once you get the hang of it, it's like 2nd nature. Trying not to fall and break your characters legs is another challenge if your not so careful, like me.
It is quite difficult to survive the experience with all characters still alive but not impossible.
The ultimate aim of the game is to spend 2 days searching through the area, obtaining items and setting up traps and hiding your dogge to survive against the murderers that attack on your second night. I dont want to give away too much of the rest of the chapters, it really is worth checking out yourself.
Coming out in this episodic fashion, which is great because by the time it takes for them to release a new chapter you should hopefully have gotten through the previous one.
In conclusion its a great game, and definitely woth the cost. (Much better than the actual Friday the 13th Games, hopefully the new game redeems all of that).

A Splendid Horror Homage
Lakeview Cabin makes me jump, but not in the cheap way so many other horror games seem to.  It does it In the proper way, using atmosphere, timing and many of the tricks from the well-thumbed slasher film rulebook. The game uses sound and score superbly in this regard, the sudden cries of the crows seem filled with portent, the creak of a rafter, a door opening somewhere off screen. It all helps build the tension beautifully.  The charm of the chunky sprites and backgrounds lend extra heft to the stabs of panic inducing action, too. The cute pixel characters offset nicely against the horrific situations.
For me, each episode of Lakeview gets better with every attempt. While the challenge of getting one character to the end of an episode without significant blood loss would probably not be enough to keep me playing, it is the detail in the design of each distinct episode and the individual stories that have me returning for more. All the episodes are challenging and amusing in their own macabre ways, each having more emphasis on certain of Lakeview's gameplay elements. If I had to pick a favourite it'd be the puzzle heavy Episode 5. The supernatural elements are clevery used and the suburban setting is perfect, right down to the kid brother's toy laser gun.
My only criticism is one that could possibly be chalked up to my own inferior grey matter. I simply cannot fathom what to do in episode 4. It's great fun to play but invariably I end up with every character reduced to a fine pixel paste within ten minutes and not the foggiest glimmer of a clue about how to progress on the next attempt. As far as I can tell the aim is simply to be suddenly butchered in the most amusing way possible.
As an homage to 70's and 80's horror and slasher films as well as classic adventure/puzzle games they don't come much better than this one.  Looking forward to Episode 6!

I really liked this one speaking as someone who played a lot of old school 8, 16 & 32 bit RPG style games. It's pretty linear, but has some pretty funny points. The class system it pretty good, but at the same time, a little confusing. I recommend getting moves that cause damage over time as quickly as possible.

The third episode in Penny Arcade's series is a much needed detour from the first two games. This is a silly ATB-like RPG based around silly classes. Each of your characters has an innate class and can use one of several secondary classes to complement their abilities.
Although there is an element of strategy, the game isn't terribly hard in the standard difficulty. Every battle is scripted and placed in the map so you can see it coming and, in a few cases, avoid it.
Unfortunately, the story is almost 100% linear. On the plus side, it eliminates the dreaded need of other games for farming. On the other side, this hardly feels as a more traditional RPG in the sense that exploration and discovery is limited to searching every nook and cranny of the dungeons.
It's overall a fun game, but not a great RPG. If you're trying to complete the quad- tetralogy (?) this will feel like a much needed rest from the sometimes sluggish pace of the first two games.

This game has one of the best turnbased battle systems I have evr tried.
It is a nice feature that I start all battles with full HP and max items. It's a very forgiving system as lsing sends you only one tile backwards, and you are able to modify the difficulty on the fly.

You like a nice, freaky, eldritch fantasy story?
You like witty dialogue and references?
You like good old (J)RPGs?
You like the humour of Penny Arcade?
If you could answer any of these questions with 'yes', then you should really consider getting 'On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness' despite its weird, lengthy title.
The story includes the end of the world, wicked dimensions, ghosts, demons, hobos, mimes and all the other darkest parts of all possible realities, spiced with a lot of sarcasm, silliness and fun.
The mechanics are mostly solid classical RPG stuff, with some diversity on class systems and battle mechanics, which can be nice, but can also sometimes feel a bit rocky and may miss some simple options to make the experience smoother. But that barely matters, as the battles are more like little breadcrumbs, or candy on the path through the story and very forgiving, even if you lose one, you immediately pick up again from before the encounter - may vary on other difficulties, haven't tried.
It's not necessary to have played the earlier episodes, it's not required for the story and the style in graphic and mechanics is very different from the previous episodes anyways, but if you'd like to get the whole story from the start, you should start at part 1.
And if you've already played the earlier episodes and even bothered to visit or even search for the rest, why are you still reading reviews and not just started playing already?

Crafting is a lot of fun and feels very different from Minecraft. From my own experience with games, it compares best to Slime Rancher but adds more freedom. You can build...
Batteries, tethers (which supply you with O2 and energy long distance), filters (not sure what they do), solar panels, wind turbines, a generator (which can be fueled with stuff like organic material), cars, and shuttles. So far it has been a delight to play with this system alone and I look foward to more through further updates.
Once you figure out tethers, and subsequently vehicles exploring the planet you start at and other planets is a good deal of fun.
The game looks simple yet beautiful. The aesthetics of the stars or planets in the sky is just superb. The animations and UI are also well made and very pleasing to look at.
1. Performaces improvments: Let's be clear it runs fine overall and I'm sure many of the FPS drops have been noted by other players and the developers. I have a medium to low end PC, probably hitting a bit above the minimum requirements that they currently have set. I've seen forums of people with very good PC's having similar issues so I'm going to assume this has more to do with it being early access. To the developers, I think it would really help to add the ability to change graphical settings. As of now, you can choose resolution, view distance, windowed, and Vsync.
If we make the invetable Minecraft comparison, this is my biggest issue. The graphics "seem" basic enough to make it a game that can run well on most standard PCs. If it could run smooth on near all modern rigs, this game can absolutely be huge.
2. Improvements to the world shaping tool: It is fairly easy to figure out how to mend and shape the world around you. It gets a bit easier as you progress and figure out how to use it. But dammit, sometimes it is very hard to reach stuff high or low. I've recently figured out how to build stuff like a bridge but it still doesn't work as well as I'd like.

I would like to add that I have not by any stretch hit end game and I play alone. So if I mention an idea that is already implemented or in development, I apologize.
- Grappling hook: This would help mend the issue with trying to reach stuff in higher or lower places. Reducing the frequency of falls or difficulty in reaching stuff embedded in the mountains.
- Animal life: I am 100% certain this has been heard of by the developeers and pretty sure they are working on it now.
- Improved base building: Base building already is fun enough, but being able to build big♥♥♥♥♥houses and perhaps space stations gives a lot of incentive to keep on exploring and mining for elements.
- Add entities like a ball and goal post. I was driving around a running into one of those unknown (research objects) and I noticed that you could have a very basic Rocket League kind of deal with this engine. With that alone.
Very good game so far, as long as the developers stick with it, it will be great. Very optimistic. Would recommend for those with that crafting itch.

Tomb Raider Legend is a fun over the top game that literally falls short. I was having so much fun in the boss fight and then it was over :(
It mostly consists of platforming and running around trying to find you're way through ruins and caverns with some combat and puzzle elements. The main goal of it all is to find the pieces of Excalibur. You go to the following places: Bolivia, Peru, England, Nepal, Ghana, and Bolivia...again.
Story: Honestly this is part of a trilogy, so there is a bit of unanswered questions at the end, but it's a solid start. Arthurian myth is intriguing and the connection with her father's archeological career is pretty subtle at first. The characters aren't all very fleshed out to be honest, they have interesting personalities but they're just, kinda there.
Lara is the focus for better or for worse, and she has duality between the pain of her past and the thrill of her present, dangerous life. The most important relationship is probably between Lara and Amanda. Zip and Alister, Lara's personal Geek Squad, banter is light, playful, explanatory. They often react to what Lara is doing and tell her to be careful much to Lara's chagrin. Decide for yourself if you are okay with hearing Lara's two guy friends providing information and opinions while you go about the game.
Platforming: Controls for platforming is a bit clunky at first (for me at least) but key map to your hand's desire and take it slow at first. I promise you, mastering the basics are essential for a smooth playthrough especially since sometimes you wanna get Lara to do something in a specific direction but you do it slightly wrong and then you are like "what's happening?"
Keep in mind these platforming mechanics are camera based which means the direction you want Lara to go will vary by the camera's position. It's a good thing that you can workout in Lara's home, all the basic skills are there for practicing.
Anyway, you can climb, shimmy, jump to ledges behind you, swing on bars, shoot your grappling hook, swing from your grappling hook, pull stuff with your grappling hook, pull with your bare hands and backflip, shimmy up poles, kick stuff, roll, kneel. If you wanna make Lara do something really cool keep on pressing the roll key while Lara jumps. Triple flip!
There will come times when you have to jump on time, or shimmy fast enough to make it without a ledge crumbling under you. In fact this game has QTE sequences where you avoid traps or explosions by pressing a directional button. If you don't follow the prompt in time, Lara hilariously dies.
The combat is honestly not that great. Your only option for evading enemies is taking cover and flipping around.The boss battles are creative enough to be a breath of fresh air. But besides using your environment to slow down enemies and acrobatics there's nothing there to really make it really satisfying.
Speaking of environments, are the levels complex? No. Lmao it's one of the easiest Tomb Raider games in the series in part because it's so linear. It's good practice to survey the areas you're plopped in to see the paths you can take but I just figured it out as I went along. To it's credit unlockables give the whole game a bit more substance and difficulty out of the levels.
In a nutshell, Tomb Raider Legend is a fun little game. Buy it.

Serious Sam is a FPS game with Hordes of Enemies. And I mean sometimes I swear I just fought 100 Enemies.
It has Decent Level design, very fun gameplay and very creative enemy designs.
In the First few levels, it's pretty easy, but then you'll encounter more and more enemies. Just run and gun.
The enemy design is really good. Yes, it's headless and it screams. There's enemies that chuck green fireballs at you, and you just gotta see for yourself the enemies.
The guy who you play as, Serious Sam, will crack a few jokes, like when a bolder drops down, sam will wistle the Indiana Jones theme, although the bolder isn't very dangerous. And after a fight with a ton of enemies, he says "That's right, it's all in the wrist"

I finally completed my first Normal Ironman run in Xenonauts after many rage quits, forced restarts... and forgetting to deactive my C4 explosives only to pink mistify half my squad (way... waayyyy too many times). There were many moments that had me mumbling at my screen in frustration or outright had me getting up from the computer, going to the gym, and lifting things up then putting them down over and over again to get the angst out.
It was incredibly frustrating to have some of my wet-behind-the-ears soldiers survive a few missions and pulverize some Xeno scum, only to watch them get one shot by a well placed shot or devoured by a Reaper I didn't plan for. Cover isn't intuitive (or at least for me it wasn't) and there were multiple times I took position only to watch the alien turn, smirk at me, then plant a plasma bolt square between the eyes of one of my soldiers. Refer back to the rage and lifting portion.
Eventually, after epic (and possibly unhealthy) amounts of nerd rage and QQ'ing over cheating alien scum, how insanely difficult breaching UFOs is (Corvettes! I'm specifically hating on you!), and having to make aggrevating economic decisions... I learned from my mistakes (gasp!), had to learn to accept losses, and got better.
I actually started using squad level tactics like hugging walls, throwing down smoke grenades if I absolutely had to turn a blind corner with no indication of what could be waiting on the other side, NOT sprinting down the middle of the street with my entire squad, then getting upset that I got sniped from a random window, making liberal use of explosives even if it meant I lost some money breaching UFOs, and generally just accepting I'm supposed to be out gunned.
The game is remarkably well paced, freakishly so. Due to the ticker implementation RIGHT when you finally have outfitted your fighter jets or soldiers with the appropriate gear new bigger, badder aliens show up that almost make your hard fought gains obsolete. One step forward, two steps back is a common theme throughout the game that makes you BETTER because you have to actually think about WTF you're doing and why.
I'm a father of three, married, and I have a job that has me at work anywhere from a standard 40 hours a week to almost 60, so it took me a month to get through the game. I guess I could've used the common complaint/logic "I don't have that kind of time" or "I want something I can sit down and beat in a few days" but this was far more rewarding. Yes, there were days where after a 12 hour shift I certainly didn't come home and boot up any games, but the time invested was worth it.
I'm glad I stuck with Xenonauts despite my initial frustrations and will be putting many more hours into it either by tweaking the config file or by downloading mods. I actually tried playing XCOM: EU again and couldn't bring myself to do it.
If you've made it through the wall of text (hurray!) I guess I'd split it into three categories:
The Good:
-Excellently designed game that gives you total freedom, no ♥♥♥♥ty tutorials shall be thrust on you here.
-The pacing is genius! I don't know how long it took them, but the game ups the difficulty at the right moment. (unless you're playing bad, then you'll never catch up)
-Soldiers have no role, you determine what they do based on what equipment you give them. Have a guy with high TU (action points)? Make him your scout! Have a guy with amazing accuracy but maybe his HP is kind of low? Sniper! Found a meat shield with high HP and incredible strength, but he couldn't hit the broad side of a barn at point blank range with a fully automatic weapon? Give him a metal shield and let him be a bullet sponge! Or don't do any of those things, it's up to you.
-Aliens appropriately out tech you through out pretty much the entire game. You genuinely feel an overwhelming sense of dread as you play the game.
-You will take losses, but that doesn't mean you'll lose the game. You can have pretty substantial set backs and still come out on top. (kind of like how life is!)
-Using squad level infantry tactics ACTUALLY works and is necessary.
-Well thought out tech tree and research progression.
-You can mod and edit the crap out of the game to your liking.
-Music is well done and adds to the setting.
The Bad:
-Even on Easy this game will be too much for a lot of people. This will be viewed as an "elitist" comment, but I think that's more indicative of the gaming industry as a whole and not to Xenonaut's detriment. Nintendo games were soul crushingly difficult and only had one mode, now many games I can hand my six year old that he can beat without having to read any of the text.
-Still some glitches/bugs, namely shooting through walls. It doesn't happen too often, but it can make a huge difference to how that one map will play out.
-The game doesn't explain a lot of the mechanics adequately. This can amplify frustration or make it more rewarding as you progress, depends on your perspective.
-Mind control late game is a bit out of whack. I thought it added a great deal of intensity and dread, but it was depressing to watch two of my colonels that had managed to survive +30 missions get possessed and murder each other. I think it's a great (and necessary) part of the game, but still needs tweaking in either lower % success rate (which you can do yourself) or a turn delay the same way Wraiths can't teleport and shoot in the same turn.
The Ugly:
-Graphics. Eventually they grew on me, but it was admittedly jarring at first.

non-serious review:
>punched a zombie in the head
>zombie's brain explodes all over the place
>me and my cousin ROFL like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
>cousin calls me Chuck Norris after that
serious review:
This game is hard as balls, Duke Nukem's to be more specific. In all my experience of playing this game, only like 2 times I won an objective map and once I won a survival map. To expand a little, objective maps place you and your buddies in a series of mostly linear events, whereas survival maps are about holding a certain area off from the zombies which get harder every wave. First few waves you get slow, easy to kill zombies, then you get a tad bit stronger zombies with slight chances for some zombies to have the ability to run, then you get even harder zombies with the chance to infect you and rarely a little zombie kid who hits you and runs away. Oh, and when you get infected, you can either tell your team that you are infected so that they can kill you, find and swallow a pack of pills to stop your transformation into a zombie or just suicide by pointing your weapon, say, a pistol, at your head.
Weapons are pretty rare in this game, like their ammo, but what I found best was using an axe, a sledgehammer or, best of all, a tomahawk and just hold your primary attack button to charge your swing. You can weild with certain weapons a flashlight, and that's where I say that the best weapon in this game is the tomahawk, because it's small, deals a pretty nice amout of damage, and it's also the only melee weapon that you can use your flashlight with (but if you count your fists as melee weapons then it's the second only melee weapon with which you can carry a flashlight). When I said that the tomahawk is small I said that because there is also a pretty nice inventory system, where you can either hold a sledgehammer and an axe and nothing else and move super slow, all your healthpacks, bandages, flashlights and pills with an unlikely chance of having a pistol/tomahawk and a shotgun with ammo aplenty. In this game, you don't have a HUD most of the time, but you do have your ammo bar show up whenever you check how much ammo you have left in your clip by holding down the reload button (and occasionally shouting like an idiot that you have 6 shells left in your shotgun). And you can choose which character you want to play as and what voice to have.
The only downside in the game is that the community can be a little bit bad at some times but if you play with your friends, you will have a ton of fun! And just as I'm writing the review I remembered that you can also have a hammer with which you can nail planks on walls and windows, and that the same hammer is, in my opinion, a direct upgrade of the tomahawk since it does a little bit more damage, has the same inventory space and you can hold a flashlight with it.
TL;DR: This game is fantastic, and above all else, it's FREE!
