Labyrinthine Dreams was an ok game, while it doesn't do anything particularly well it also has no major problems. The story is quite simple and sadly somewhat marred by a narrative that lacks finesse in dealing with its subject matter, you can expect some pretty obvious lines dealing with depression or being stuck in life. The gameplay is decent with mazes you must navigate with limitations on your movement (e.g. can't turn left), other places where you must clear all tiles touching them only once or have to outmaneuver a monster that follows certain movesets.
If you like these kind of puzzles and are ok with its simple story then Labyrinthine Dreams is a decent choice considering it's fairly priced for what it does even when not on sale.

There's not a lot of game to play, but it's well polished and about as high quality as the developers could get, and that's admirable at the very least. It's a short puzzle-adventure game in which you play as a girl struggling with her inner doubts and thoughts, which have manifested into a literal demon that constantly drives her away from her goals and the people she loves. Ludically, this boils down to some traversal puzzles coupled with stages where you outrun a demon in a turn-based maze. Again, not much to it, but it comes together quite well and serves the story.
This is also one of the rare moments where a developer knows the advantages of video games as a medium. At the end (SPOILERS), you are running from the demon down a long hallway, which you can't possibly win (becuase the demon moves twice as fast as you). Then, as Beth comes to terms with her past, you can outrun the demon at last (3 spaces per turn to the demon's 2). You can defeat your demon, but you have to keep moving.
These are the kinds of things, though a little blatantly obvious here, that you can't really convey in any other medium. The game and story aren't seperate, and so you couldn't tell this story any other way. I really hope Solest Games move on from RPGmaker in favor of something that gives a little more freedom, because these guys could actually push the medium forward.

So, this game gets a lot of hate these days, but Sonic Adventure DX is one of my all time favorite games. I know it hasn't aged well, but it has that special Dreamcast charm to it that games like Space Channel 5, Jet Set Radio, and Samba De Amigo all have. The gameplay for Sonic is some of the best in the series. If you keep tapping the Spindash button, he is at one of his fastest speeds in the entire series. Tails gameplay is basically the best of Sonic's. You only go through the fun acts of each stage, but you do have to race Sonic (or Dr. Robotnik), but he's easy to beat (you can beat Windy Valley in one jump). Knuckles' gameplay can be fun. Some people don't like the treasure-hunting gameplay, but it's a bit better in this game than in Sonic Adventure 2, just because Knuckles' "instinct works a lot better in this. Amy's story is a bit like a traditional level. She can be pretty slow, but her levels are made for her. E-102 "Gamma" is a badnik with a gun. His stages are all about getting combos to keep from running out of time. The 6th playable character is someone that almost all fans hate, but I do have a soft spot for him: Big the Cat. His story involves him trying to fish for his "poliwag pal" Froggy. Most people find his story nearly impossible, but if you talk to NPCs, you should figure out his gameplay. Also, there's a sub-plot in his story about a girl who is in love with a guy working at a burger shop. It's a better love story than Twillight.
In short, SADX is a great game that hasn't aged well. If you decide to buy it, make sure to install a mod called BetterSADX. It fixes some bugs, brings back DC textures and lighting, and adds mod support.

Before I start, let me say that measuring a game in dollars/hour of enjoyment is a very silly mechanic. That being said, you can easily spend $20 on dinner out for a couple hours, or you can play this game for countless more.
This game is super solid. Very few bugs I've noticed (like slimes shooting up to the top of the skybox when they eat something in a certain spot) last longer than a situational encounter. The jetpack allowing you to get above the map bounds is obviously an issue for a final game, but this is Early Access, so it's no big deal for now. Maintaining slimes and crops is super easy, storage of supplies is a breeze, and once you figure out the fluctuating income, you can milk the system to it's fullest.
I have noticed that the auto-feeders tend to just dump food out into the pen. I see a pen has an empty auto-feeder, I'm inclined to fill it up. But if I look, there's food littering the pen. Given that un-collected or un-eaten food tends to disappear in the wild, I would assume it'd do so in the pen as well? This theory would leave my hard-earned fruits wasted, which I'm not keen on.
I have also noticed that chickens take AGES to breed. Not really a bug, just noting it.
Excited to see where this game goes, what is added in the future, and exploring all those bits of the game only accessible by jetpack. Will follow this game, for sure!

A bit of modern action, a bit of classic platforming and a hearty serving of badarse Lara makes for a nice, hearty dish! Crystal Dynamics managed to strike a great balance of moden tendencies of gaming (even the ones I don't appreciate, like QTEs, but thankfully, they don't happen very often) and the platforming, acrobatic, risk-of-falling-to-your-death-at-every-moment wholesome goodness. And what I really, really enjoyed? Actual TOMB RAIDING! I really enjoyed and liked all the levels, but King Arthur's tomb ... man, that level was the bee's knees - I loved every minute of it!
So what holds this game from being perfect? Well, apart from the QTEs I already mentioned, I'd point out wobbly, awkward controls which I didn't really like. They're far from being useless and frustrating, but not nearly perfect either. Also, the characters and the story didn't really grab me at all; the story especially seemed a bit half-baked to me, which is a shame - I always loved the stories in Tomb Raider games.
Another negative thing would be very easy puzzles and boss fights. The game is generally pretty easy, but the puzzles and boss fights were just way too easy. I played the game on the normal difficulty, so maybe I'll try it on hard, but seriously, normal difficulty is really way too easy.
As far as characters go, they were very, very unremarkable, including both the goodies and the baddies. Oh well, at least Lara was portrayed well. I really enjoyed her voice actress, too - she has a very nice, agreeable voice that really suits Lara very well. I also loved how angry Lara got at the end of the game, you don't see that very often.
All in all, even in spite of these flaws, this is a fine reboot of a legendary franchise, and a solid, solid game. A few shortcomings, but a whole lot of goodness. I appreciate Crystal Dynamics' success in fusing modern game sensibilities with the classic Tomb Raider attributes we old school TR fans know and love. Legend is definitely a worthy volume in this legendary franchise, and a fine example of how reboots should be made.

I feel like this review needs an old horror movie treatment; Something extra scary with a creaky old voice narrating. "Shrouded in a dense fog with the voices of the despaired dead arising, the tainted blood of B-horror movies oozes out of a computer monitor..."  Yep.  I see the bloody puddles under my chair.  Next to a dirty pair of socks.  Arrgh, my *last* good dirty pair of socks too.  Time to fire up some jump scares and spoopy spoops.
I skinny dipped into the game that night -  a blind playthrough.  Okay,  *truthfully* I would likely leave my underwear on ( modesty be damned ), but you get the idea.  What do you think I discovered?  Why, nothing less than a schizo-spasmic pixelated horror-fest of episodic blood-spattered evil!   And there were pugs too -little ones, running around the screen. Oh, the humanity!
You start outside of a movie theatre in the dead of night, with the disturbing sounds of a dangerous city all around.  Move forward, pick up a few items, search around a bit, and you’ll find the movie theatre dead ahead with three feature films on hand.  These are the episodes you’ll be playing. You can pick any one of them in any order.  I started out with the first door I saw, episode III,  which featured a summer camp terrorized by some rather quick footed serial killers a la "Friday the 13th". Looking at my surroundings I realized I am playing as a group of people, clicking back and forth between them as I would a hand of cards.  So, I can be a teen dude-stud or the cute girl next door.  I searched around and looked inside a building to find a...bedroom.
Right away, I was able to make myself naked on a bed in a cabin having sex with a girl with the sole intention of seeing if I could.  Boom-shocka-locka, it worked!  And that was actually part of the game!  I swear those dudes were digitally man-scaped too.  That's the kind of game Lakeview Cabin Collection is: an ode to teen slasher movies with all the intrinsically nasty bits included.
What is this ode to cinema-du-slash all about?  A survival horror zombie-fest with robo-dinosaurs, perhaps? Pfft.  Puh-lease.  This game is about surviving the nights of murdering crazies and killing them off while unlocking the secrets of the episode.  I think.  In any case: kill or die, that much is apparent.  I began to hunt for clues, take things apart, and solve some puzzles without much idea of what was going on or why.  Oddly, it's a bit like an adventure game in this way with using combinations of items, unlocking hidden things in the background, trying out items on the killers, etc.  And also, there is a significant strategy in attacking the baddies at night.  Yet, it's quite open in design.  Unlike many games, you don't need to perform an action in an *exact* way in order to progress...and for that I am incredibly happy.  Your option list is extremely varied.  A little too varied, even.  Sort of like trying to choose what to eat at a buffet with lots of goodies at the bar.  There are a ton of different ways to approach those killers: motorcycle of death, beer can, gas container, oven fire, lamp oil, hammer, musical instrument, teddy bear, etc.  Granted, some of those items won't do a single thing.  You'll find quite a bit of trial and error in the gameplay.  Which again, may or may not irritate the player into a game rage.  To complete an episode you must kill all the killers. So, best not to goof off *too* much before you end up a pixelated stain on the floor.
What becomes immediately apparent is that you are going to die. Repeatedly.  Over and over and over and over and...well, over.  I can see how that can turn some folks off.  There is only so much you can take of planning a stage, setting up all the right parts, doing all the correct actions, trying your best, and seeing it all fall apart when a slasher is too resilient and kills every last one of your group. For that, I do chalk this game up as - NOT EASY.  Prepare to sink some hours in.
After finishing episode III, I popped into episode IV.  And by that, I mean I died non-stop for a very long time.  This episode is about an all-girl rock band stuck in a compound with a family of serial killers that are simply waiting to be discovered.  Unlike before, you are running to the killers instead of running away as they sneak up.  You're going to be exploring what seems like an endless series of rooms filled to the brim with bloody, twisted murdering nightmare scenes.  It's harrowing to say the least and you get slashed at every few seconds.  But you *do* get to fight back.  One time I ended up soaking my whole screen in red.  Honestly, even after an hour of playing this level I felt like I barely scratched the surface.  It was amazing fun, and a challenge I thoroughly enjoyed, but I was pretty damned horrible at even trying to win this level.  I had to stop and try out episode V.  I knew when I was out of my league.
Now, episode V is much slower.  More along the lines of episode III and I felt like I could tackle it better. Well, at least in the beginning I thought I could.  This episode was hiding more from me than the others.  It's set in - let's say 1987 - you once again are a group of teens and there is a ethereal serial killer involved along with a sort of purgatory of spirits where your soul goes to when you die. You have to figure out what needs to happen when your soul arrives there both before and after you are resurrected - with very cryptic hints.  The puzzles involved are more elusive than in episode III, and the order in which you complete them is slightly more important to finish the episode.  Not that it's linear in that way, I solved several of the puzzles completely out of order, but there is a set of actions that has to be figured out in order to complete the grand puzzle involved.  It's not easy.  Not at all.  And I hate to admit it, but I had to look up a guide just to move on  after getting stuck for hours.   There were secret numbers and codes involved, some hidden in a way that I honestly would NEVER have guessed.  Even looking at someone's guide for hints when I got stuck, I *still* think it was quite hard.  And the cartridge video game...OMG the video game...that took me ages to figure out on my own until I accidentally got it with a naked girl ending. Too bad that wasn't the end!  It was just a small part of a grander series of puzzles to complete.  I'd be spoiling it to tell you any more, but once you attack the killer with all the evil at hand, you will get that euphoric "I BEAT IT!" feeling we all know and love.  Now, I want to go back to episode IV.  And I have.  Still trying as a matter of fact.  The chainsaw dude is just insanely hard to kill for me and I have a feeling there are a lot more people hidden in that house.
Come into this game with an open mind about surviving in a horror movie, *lots* of patience, and knowing full well you will die repeatedly.  Perhaps even killed by stepping on farm tools!  It's not an easy game to complete and you will likely get stumped - maybe a lot.  Be careful you don't get chipped away in a wood chipper when you are not looking!

So, after two Penny Arcade games from Hothead Studios that were strange, weird, and also quite different in many ways, we're now suddenly thrown into an SNES-like sequel made by a single person.
And to be short... this change doesn't really work.
The higher difficulty levels, for example, is no longer about being a test of skill (timing your attacks and defences well), and instead becomes about luck, especially very early in the game. Luck as in who the enemy will randomly target, and with what attack. If they do it in the "wrong" order -which are most of them-, it's game over; but if they attack you in the exact right way, you'll survive. True, after a while you can compensate for this by having your own "level up" area, but that just turns it back into grinding mobs for EXP...
This is particularly annoying considering that the whole point of the first two games' combat system was born out of a desire to make every fight count; non-repeatable, non-random, and the attacking and defending skills being more important than the stats. They'd fixed something that Jerry/Tycho in particular thought of as "broken", and then this game comes and reverts it back to broken again.
The retro graphics doesn't really work either. Much of the charm of the previous two games was that it really captured the aesthetical Penny Arcade essence, especially with the cut-scenes being done in comic book format.
In the end, I played through this game -and the next- mainly because the first two games had presented a really gripping story that I wanted to see done to its finish. And that's pretty much the only reason I can think of to buy episode three and four of this series. Otherwise, steer clear.

Penny Arcade's On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness 3 is a comedic RPG with some parody elements and convenient features. I can't tell you too much about the story, as I don't want to spoil the game. Also, I can't fill you in on the backstory because... I haven't played the first two games. The reason I started on this game, and the fourth, is because they were in a pack and I had played the previous two games the new developers had done before getting asked to do these, which were Breath of Death VII and Cthulhu Saves the World. That's where my perspective is coming from, so keep it in mind. Basically, you're a company that investigates supernatural happenings, and supernatural things happen. So... you investigate them. That's really all I can tell you without getting into potential spoiler territory.
You can explore specific locations on a world map with well defined places to go. Inside these places, you can search for treasure, battles, and main plot points for going there. While there is some interesting story and dialogue, the battles are the meat and potatoes of the game. The battles are nice because they are not random. Instead, they are represented by monsters clearly visible on the map. You battle in a turn based fashion, however there's a meter on the top of the screen. This determines the order the combatants will attack. It will be initially set by speed stats and certain passives, but it can also be changed by using slows, stuns, and interruptions. A combatant can also move up their position on the command line by defending, although this will not allow them to attack on that turn. So why bother? Well, to reduce major damage from a major attack, or possibly to help utilize another interesting mechanic. In this game, you don't have a pool of MP to work with. Instead, you start battles with zero MP and gain 1 MP per turn. So if you want to build it up, you can use items, use certain abilities to boost it, or simply do something that does not require MP. This forces you to manage your health and position on the timeline much more carefully, rather than having magic users spam abilities right from the get go.
So what gives you your abilities? Well, each character starts with their own class. The classes dictate what abilities, passive or active, these characters have. This will affect how you use them. Beyond this, as the game goes on you will receive badges, each with their own additional classes. You get to add one, and eventually two, to each party memeber. This gives them a total of three classes, and many possibilities on how you can build them. However, badges can only be on one person at a time, so you can't use the same class on every character at once. All of the badges and characters level up as you win battles, although the ones you actively use will level up faster. Also, you can further customize your characters with equipment as well.
This game is full of conveniences, such as the aforementioned blanket leveling and visible battles. Whenever you finish a battle, all characters are revived and restored. If you lose a battle, you get to try it again. You can save or change badges at any point. Convenient traveling through an easy world map, with shops in fixed positions and a training area to grind if needed. The game does a lot to try and ease the burdens of RPGs while still being an RPG.
However, I found a few things a bit disappointing. One is that there are too many classes leveling up constantly. It seems that after every battle, at least one if not multiple classes gain levels and often new abilities, which is a lot to look at and manage. You'll be constantly checking your new abilities to see what they do and who they will be good for, depending on how you're trying to build characters. Plus, the fighting system is somewhat complex for newcomers, which detracts from the game's convenience factor a bit. Also, while the game tries to teach you one thing at a time to gradually get you familiar with the gameplay (which I like), it feels like once you finally understand how to fight and manage your badges and equipment and strategize, the game is basically done. It also ends on a cliffhanger story-wise. So, this whole game essentially feels like it is a buildup for the sequel, both in story and basic gameplay ideas. Although the sequel (which I will review once I finish) is rather different in some aspects. I guess I just felt like the game was getting me ready for the real adventure to start, and then it abruptly ended.
Overall, it's still a good game. Fun for people new to RPGs and looking for good value games. The characters and story have enough charm to carry some of the weight. Plus all the conveniences, well paced learning curve, and constant upgrades to manage, make for an entertaining experience throughout. I guess it's good that the game left me wanting more rather than being sick of it, and the extra mode recommended after you finish the main game gives it some more for you to play and satisfy your cravings. However, I'd say that if you're looking at this game, which is only 5 dollars alone, you might as well just pay the 8 bucks and get the two pack because you'll be well prepared to take on the fourth game after this. I got them both on sale for a dollar which was well worth the price. Judging this game on its own, I'd give Penny Arcade's On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness 3 a solid 6 out of 10 for being an engaging RPG experience without the common headaches that befall so many other RPGs.

I took a chance on this game after having seen it on the early access page, and I have to say that, for the most part, I like what I've seen so far. It's a simple, charming game with a solid core mechanic and explains the rules well. In Slime Rancher, your goal is to create a habitat for the colorful slime creatures found on a distant planet, and use them to profit as you explore the environment.
Pro:
-Simple, intuitive mechanics. All the controls you need to know are explained in about a minute at the beginning of the game. The aiming system for the vacuum/cannon is forgiving for players who aren't great at shooters (e.g. myself). There is a guide available in-game that can tell you what you need to do, but I often found myself learning by experience rather than the guide. That is to say, the game teaches well without the strict need for a tutorial, but the tutorial is there and quite useful for those who need it.
-Fast-paced, yet relaxing gameplay. There is very little rush until you encounter some of the more volatile slime creatures later on. The player can move at his or her own pace to gather slime, food, and resources. The day/night cycle allows ample time for time-sensitive tasks to be completed.
-The game provides a very immediate sense of progression and reward. From the beginning the player can set simple, short term goals and use the money earned from the slimes to purchase upgrades either for themselves (the jetpack being an obvious early-game winner) or for the ranch. Exploration is rewarded, as well, as new environments bring new types of slime and food.
Cons:
-The most obvious and serious fault is also one that will likely be addressed as the game is developed: the lack of content. After about 4 hours of play, I felt as though I had accomplished most of what the game has to offer. I have spent several hours since then attempting achievements, gathering money, and showing the game to a friend, but there are only a handful of areas available at the time of writing and much of my ranch sits gathering dust. This is to be expected, as the game is in early access, and several accessible areas indicate that they are in development. Still, at a $20 price tag, I was hoping for a bit more substance.
-A bit of a nitpick, but some of the upgrades for the ranch seem superfluous or do not work as intended. Generally, slimes are contained in corals while on the ranch, and wild slimes seldom come near it. In that sense the Scareslime sees little use. Also, the auto-feeder often dispenses more food than the slimes need, and the plort collector does not seem completely efficient. This can leave the rancher to try and clean up in a coral full of spiky or exploding (or both!) slimes.
Ultimately, the game looks very promising, with simple, intuitive gameplay and a solid system of progression. Those looking for substantial content may want to wait for an update or two, but I would say that I have very much enjoyed the time I put in.

Many people say that Legend forms a trilogy. While it is true that Crystal Dynamics did in fact create three games in the same game engine and release them a year apart, the middle game (or first chronologically speaking) Anniversary, is a remake of the original 1996 game and the story appears to have no impact upon the events told in Legend and Underworld.
Eidos, scum bags that they are, forced developers Core Design to churn out one rushed sequel after the other until virtually no cared about the Tomb Raider franchise anymore due to franchise fatigue and uninspired and rehashed gameplay elements.
Rather than allow Core Design the time they needed to build a truly great next generation game, Eidos gave the franchise to developers Crystal Dynamics.
How did they do?
Well let me get the negatives out of the way first, since there are a lot of them.
First of all the game suffers from a game crashing bug that the developers have neglected to patch. At certain times and on certain levels the game will suddenly crash with the following error box:
A fatal error has occurred while playing Tomb Raider: Legend. Please refer to the ReadMe file for information that might help you solve this problem, or contact Eidos customer support.
Exception at: 24/08/2017 at 11:42:58
Exception code: Access violation (c0000005): (Read of address: 0x0323fa80)
Exception address: 0x005c136b
CPU info:
---------
EAX = 0x0323fa80
EBX = 0x0b3e35c0
ECX = 0x3f800000
EDX = 0x430609ef
ESI = 0x0aacd7dc
EDI = 0x0ab18a70
EIP = 0x005c136b
ESP = 0x0019e810
EBP = 0x0019e8f8
This can thankfully be easily fixed. In the game setup box turn off next generation effects. Once in the game proper, enable it in the settings menu.
I've also encountered some weird texture issues when riding Lara's bike. The road becomes transparent at times and it becomes impossible to read the route ahead.
That's it for the bugs.
Combat is basic and uninspired. A.I is virtually non existent and the gunplay is rudimentary at best. The motorcycle segments (there are two) are frankly
embarrassing and should never have been implemented into the final game. The less said about regurgitated scenery the better...
Every level except the 7th has a lame old gen box fight. Does anyone want that crap anymore?
The game hand-holds the player too much as well. You get button prompts that you can't disable in the main menu, and mini cut scenes that point out the general way in which you should attack the upcoming puzzle.
The game is quite short, and Lara's colleagues get quite annoying with their incessant chatter over her headset. I prefer the solitude of the original games and Anniversary.
Now, what about the good stuff you ask?
Well the story is quite good. It's nice to see a more personal story involving Lara.
The gameplay goes back to what made Tomb Raider great in the first place; Raiding actual tombs and other ancient sites. The absolute best thing about the game is the platforming. The grid based gameplay of the Core games is finally gone now and Lara can move freely and elegantly about her environment.
Graphics are nice, though dated by today's standards.
Overall I would recommend this game to fans of the series, but I would rate Anniversary the better game. Anniversary gives you everything Legend does, but without the bugs or any other the faults I mentioned earlier.
7/10

It's a nice little game. There are only a couple drawbacks that come to mind for this:
First, I think it might be a little too short. You can potentially beat the game with all achievements in about half an hour. Since it's such a straightforward game, there's not a whole lot of replay value. That means leaving it idle to get the card drops. Having the player make choices throughout the game that change how the story plays out could add to replay value and give an opportunity to flesh out the story some.
Second, the game engine is great for 16bit RPGs, but I think this game would have been better suited with something else. A different engine, even something like GameMaker Studio or GDevelop (which is free, open source, and easy to use), would allow more versatillity with the graphics, controls, layout, interface, and also easily port to other platforms, even mobile. This game doesn't use the biggest advantages that RPGMaker has over other engines, which would be inventory, battle system, character stats, etc.
These drawbacks don't mean it's not worth getting though. It's definitely worth a play. The graphics and visuals are rather good for the engine. It has a great story with meaning to it, even though it leaves some stuff to the imagination, which can be good in a case like this. Also, the voice acting is top notch for a game that's telling a story.
The mazes are rather creative. They look really simple, but the machanics of how each one gives it a challenge. It's nice to see mazes that are actually puzzles... or would it be puzzles that are actually mazes?
At any rate, definitely give this game a try if you like story driven puzzle games. It's short, but also cheap.

To give a bit of insight this game has eight levels, you can get every ending and achievement in this game in about two hours, however despite what little there is here, it has charm to it, with the unsettling level and enemy design and tight controls it is fun for how long it lasts, after you complete the game a Time Attack mode opens as well, giving you a bit more replay value.
Note that Eversion is free to download on the creators website, the version you pay for here has more detailed artwork and the aforementioned Time Attack, if you are interested in the game and want to check it out I encourage you to try the free version, but either way this game is well worth paying for, even just to show friends and watch them freak out as the game grows darker.

"The Princess of the Flower Kingdom has vanished! She was taken by the Ghulibas of the north, and it is up to brave Zee Tee to rescue her."
Yet another spin-off of the classic Super Mario Bros., except maybe a more simple, CreepyPasta twist. You play as a little flower character, Zee Tee. You make your way through levels consisting of a set of parallel realities featuring different hazards and soundtracks to match the atmosphere. Eversion is only possible within certain points within each level. Very sharp and simple controls, easy gameplay (difficulty does gradually increase). Not really any story to the game, but you will definitely have a confused look on your face and most likely be on edge of your seat as you discover what each stage of Eversion really is. Although I found myself really enjoying the game (ignoring the fact I had an upset, confused look on my face the entire time), I dont think $4.99 is worth the price; though I was lucky to get a coupon discount for this game. I beat the game in less than 30 minutes with nearly every achievement earned. But after completing the game, there is absolutely no replay value left, as you have literally just made it through the whole game. But let it be noted, there is a secret ending to work for.
+ Deranged illustration change of each stage of Eversion, keeps you interested wanting to adventure further. You dont know what to expect next.
+ Sharp, simple controls
+ Simple achievements and trading cards
- Price not worth what you get
- Very short game featuring only 8 levels, can be beaten in less than 10-15 minutes if rushed
- Absolutely no replay value, other than working for last achievements (if you're interested at that point)
- No story (not exactly a flaw to me, but may be to others)
I definitely do recommend this game, only for the random and unpredictable twists. Entertainment value increases when playing at night. I would love to see reactions from other players when they start getting into the Eversion; but for $4.99, the price is not worth it. Unless you're willing to drop a quick five bucks, I would say to only get the game if you have a discount coupon.

was an enjoyable and quick-paced RPG that was nice to play during my lunch breaks. A lot of the fluff found in longer RPG's was streamlined. I found most of these simplifications to be beneficial to my enjoyment for a quick game to play during my breaks. It was very linear, moving from one location straight on to the next, with only the occasional branch off the main path leading to treasure chests holding better equipment. You can see all monsters on the map, but for the most part you can't avoid them.
Unlike the previous games in the series, this game really tries to be a throwback to classic SNES era RPG's (with a few modern touches to clean it up). I really enjoyed the art style, which is similar to that in
, including the "super-deformed" characters.
In combat, I rarely found myself spamming the "Fight" command, but instead found myself using many useful skills of the various classes. In an interesting twist, you start with zero magic points and gain a single magic point each turn (or from special abilities). It felt a bit like the Default action from
, where I might perform some weaker actions for a few turns to save up magic points for a stronger attack on a future turn. Another twist is that all HP is restored and status effect cured after each battle, which eliminated the wasted time spent healing after each fight. It never really felt like this made the game too easy; in fact, it seemed that each battle was more difficult as a result.
I found a nice combination of classes that I liked to use. This is what I ended up with for most of the game:
Gabe - Brute, Tube Samurai, Masochist
Tycho - Scholar, Crabomancer, Gardenar
Jim - Necromaster, Elemenstor, Dinosorcerer
Moira - Gumshoe, Cordwainer, Apocalypt
While the game occasionally made me chuckle, the overarching story seemed like it was taking things a bit too seriously. It seemed to clash a bit in my mind with the odd sense of humor. Maybe it's because I never played the previous two games in the series. In any case, I always made sure to read the monster descriptions as I found many of them to be hilarious.
After completing the main game, I moved on to the Prelude "DLC". While each character only had one class at a time, I liked that the skills were switched up a bit from the main game. I also found it amusing how your character from the first two games in the series was integrated.
Overall, it was a quick and enjoyable RPG without much extra tacked on. I might give the fourth game a go at some point, but I don't want to jump right into it quite yet.

Tentative THUMBS UP.
Thing to remember is this game is Xenonauts, and NOT X-COM classic with better graphics. If it was sold as X-COM Classic -HD version or something similar.
What that means is that, surprise! there are differences. Bases are now only one level, the world map is 2D rather then the funky globe. Some of the starting weapons and equipment from Classic either require research or are simply not within the game.
Why?
Because it is a different game and let's be honest, if you think classic X-COM was better, then maybe you should go play that instead (hint, I still do - or would if it wasn't so punishingly hard!! :D )
The game is a bit of a mixed bag. Some of the interfaces are very simple, some (research screen I am looking at you) are downright ugly. Combat seems easier (in that it is possible to complete the early ground missions without having half your squad KIA) and the way reports of 'strange' activities pop up on the global map is interesting. You wont spot UFOs outside your radar coverage, but by looking at the reports of corp circles and abductions you can sometimes have a good idea where to send out a patrol.
Ground maps are no longer randomly generated as they were in classic. On the plus side they now look a lot better, on the down side there is no longer the tenseness of simply exploring the map to work out where the drokk you actually are. Hopefully the game will add new maps with upgrades as once you have explored a map for the first time, remembering the danger spots with weird lines of sight is reasonably easy.
Slightly disappointing is that crashed UFOs are no longer massively damaged when you arrive. Player's of classic will remember turning up on a crash site to find half a wall section and some un-lootable piles of smoking scrap and can breach the craft from the gapping holes your air to air missiles made in the hull. This means that every combat seems to back down to going in through the front door. Oh well.
Some of the micromanangement has been removed. Everything you can't use yourself is automatically sold, so you no longer have store rooms full of stuff you are loath to get rid of.
Also slightly disappointing is the study of the corpses you bring back, which are now done automatically. Gone is the choice between removing your limited science teams from the new lazer rifles you want to develop in order to study the latest hunting trophy.
So, I think this is a good game. Maybe not 'great' and maybe not the sort of thing you would be interested in as an XCOM newbie trying to work out what the fuss is about.

Buy it if you can get it on sale & you're bored; get some cheap laughs. It's not a complete waste of money, but you won't get an edge-of-your-seat story though. There's no motivation to play beyond the next cheap laugh. I give it a 4 out of 10.

Remember the old XCOM titles of the late 90’s? They were something truly special, masterpieces of the strategy and sci-fi genre’s, and while we had XCOM: Enemy Unknown in 2012, it’s something I felt didn’t quite live up to the originals due to its simplified nature, such as smaller squads and amount of hand-holding it insisted on. However, if I were to tell you there was now in fact a game that captured the perfection of XCOM in its own way and modernised it properly, would that sound too good to be true? Because that’s exactly what Xenonauts is.
Xenonauts is an absolutely fantastic strategy game heavily influenced by the likes of XCOM and fans of the series will no doubt enjoy it thoroughly as it’s more of an updated throw-back to the older games as opposed to the newer ones. Newcomers to the genre though may be a little lost in its complexity due to the lack of any proper tutorial, however veterans will no doubt feel right at home and find a huge amount of content at their disposal. The amount of in-depth management can make the game feel like it drags on at times, but again, this is partially to do with the audience it is aimed at, so if you are looking for a more fast-paced game you certainly won’t find that, as it’s about being tactical and planning your moves carefully. The graphical style is very pleasant if a little simplistic but the overall cartoon-esque presentation makes it feel dated yet modern at the same time, giving it a very unique vibe. Ground combat was without a doubt one of my favourite parts of the game and is well designed and requires good tactical planning and thinking on the player’s part, even on the lower difficulties.
Summary:
+ Pleasant and clean graphical style.
+ Ground combat is thought provoking and well designed.
+ Good amount of troop customisation.
+ Management is in-depth and enjoyable.
+ Deep and intricate systems for veterans of the genre.
- Ground battles can cause the game to drag on.
- Lack of any proper tutorial.

I was extremely late to the Tomb Raider fan club, having only played my first game in the series last year (this game)...and it blew my mind!
I usually hate shooting games because of the first-person view, so that wasn't an issue here. The exotic and beautiful locations, fun fighting, interesting story, quick-time events that weren't awful, searching to find every relic possible, incredible soundtrack, and overall atmosphere combined with one of the greatest video game characters of all time result in one of the best and most fun playing experiences (if not game) I've ever had!
The thoughtful puzzle-solving also gives some challenging moments (something sorely missing from the reboot series, along with a severe lack of actual tomb raiding) along with having to traverse along dangerous cliffsides and the like. Some of Lara's movements climbing walls, scaling buildings, and swinging from polls and ropes really reminded me of playing a Spider-Man game, which is a huge plus (and to hear Crystal Dynamics is making an Avengers game means they will at least nail his movements). The game also looks superb for it's time.
The only negatives I can think of are the short length of the game and replayability/post-game content. It took me many sittings and at least a dozen hours if not more, but it still felt a little short. I've read others have played through it even much faster. I also love unlocking all of Lara's costumes and bonus content, but after finishing the game it feels a little pointless. The only extra things you can do are playing "speed runs" and completing all of the content in her mansion, which are cool extras, but I would have liked a little bit more to do, especially considering the game already has kind of short. This is a problem most linear-story games have though, so it's not a huge drawback of anything.
All in all, this game might possibly be in my top 5 best video game experiences! As far as a rating, I give it a solid, near perfect: 9.5/10

I say this about a lot of games, but I don't get why this game gets so much flak. The reviews here on Steam are actually mostly positive, and that's good, but most hardcore TR fans I talk to do not care for this one. I'm admittedly biased, however, only really enjoying Chronicles out of the original PSX titles (the least revered one by said hardcore fans) and thinking the reboot games are excellent, so let that say what it will about me for the purpose of making your purchasing decision.
Legend introduces the grappling hook and a modern movement system that the prior titles lacked. Except in a couple situations across 3 platforms (PC, Xbox, and PS2) and I don't even know how many hours, this movement/parkour system was fluid and reliable, creating enjoyable physical puzzles and exploration. The combat is an advanced version of the classic, still locking on to enemies, but introducing reloading and grenades (as well as the revamped movement). On that note, killing rare/exotic/exctinct animals isn't as prevalent here, so you'll mostly be killing relatively generic baddies, but I wasn't really bothered by that. Most games don't really have great rewards for being a completionist (IMO), but TR:L rewards you with new costumes that added great replay value. Let's face it, who doesn't enjoy a good game of Fashion Raider?.. Or seeing Lara Croft in a bikini? Kreygasm
The story is a pretty good one about betrayal and facing the past... And, ya know, raiding tombs lol Other than Natla, I never felt TR games had very good or well defined antagonists, but I enjoyed dealing with Amanda and finding out about how she came to be your foe.
This is my favorite TR, so yeah, I recommend it lol

This is X-Com UFO defense 2.0
If Wasteland 2 is to Fallout, then Xenonaughts is to X-com UFO defense.
You get updated graphics and some minor improvements on the original.  The designer of this game must have logged many hours in Ufo defense and Terror from the Deep because I found the controls to be better than the originals.  I don't recall so many hotkeys being available to speed up the tedium of mouse clicking for 100's of UFO recovery missions, but its in here.
I also like that practically every tactical mission has NPC humans, rather than just terror missions.  There are also NPC combatants that manage to bag a few every now and again.
When I read about the interactive air interdiction I got excited; however, I haven't figured out how to play it.  If I autoresolve I have a 100% chance of downing an aircraft.  If I manually try my ♥♥♥♥ dies on me.  I'm not doggin it; I'm just saying that it bring a new element that challenged me.  For now, however, I'd rather do the autoresolve thing.
How does it compare to Xcom Enemy Unknown?  This is more refined.  We don't have mass appeal stuff thrown in like video cutscenes and cheesy stereotype dialogues (e.g., there is no metro-smexual tension between Dr. Tittsus and P.E. Dr. Bigcuck).  Don't get me wrong; I really enjoyed Xcom Enemy Unknown, but Xenonauts is the true tribute to the original.  It doesn't sell out and try to be fancy.  It is humble, stark, and as forgiving as the orginal.
What else can I say?  I have a feeling that I will be playing this version from now on.  Like I said, this is Xcom 2.0.  Why play 1,0 ever again?
This is the only true spiritual successor in my book.

Originally, my biggest fear for Xenonauts was that it was shaping up to be inspired so heavily by the original X-Com that it was going to be a carbon copy with slightly shinier graphics and a few little adjustments here and there. And I was exactly right. However, now some weeks after release, my biggest fear has somewhat shifted: I’m now very concerned that I can’t drag myself away from the game long enough to finish this review.
Full Review //

8.5/10
Buy at: $10
"Really fun. Great balance. Challenging but not unfairly so. Late 90s graphics. No multiplayer."
PRO:
You can abduct aliens by emptying a character's backpack and stuffing an alien inside. Very well balanced play. A tremendous number of viable strategies. Very good pacing. Challenging, but doesn't take cheap shots. Sometimes your ground units will get their asses handed to them. It's immersive and addictive like a Sid Meier title, and has a great amount of background material (Xenopedia) to give it serious depth. There's a level editor and basic modding tools included. The music and ambient audio work well with the game.
CON:
Air-to-air combat is too easy. The ground combat graphics are bland and somewhat dated. There's no multiplayer mode (!?!?!!?).

I wont be overly critical of the story, as I'm not really a fan of the source material, but I will say that the text drags to the point of being tedious.
What really kills the game for me, though, is how slow the combat is.  There's a good game hiding in there, if you have the patience for it.  I consider the drawn out combat to be a plus, that you have to pay attention and not just mash your way to victory, but when you combine that with slow combat it just makes for a frustrating experience.

This was one of my favorite games to play on the Dreamcast when I was a kid, I loved playing as Sonic, Tails, Knuckles... and that's about it honestly.
Ok, so to be completely honest, this game hasn't aged too well. It has many collision problems, the controls aren't the best, some of the level design is... questionable (I'm looking at you Sky Deck), but it's still a really fun game to play, way better than SA2 in almost every aspect in my opinion (although at least that game doesn't have Big the Cat).
Like I said, I have always enjoyed playing as Sonic, Tails and Knuckles, but there are actually 3 more characters: Amy, Big and E102-Gamma. Each have their own unique way of playing:
-Sonic focuses on classic high speed platforming, all you have to do is reach the end of the level. Standard stuff but extremely fun.
-Tails is similar to Sonic but with a twist: You're now racing against Sonic in most levels and you must reach the end of the level before he does. Tails' levels are shorter than Sonic's but they're still really fun.
-Knuckles' levels are much more 'sandboxey' than Sonic's and Tails'. That's because his gameplay focuses on treasure hunting, specifically, searching for 3 shards of the Master Emerald in every level. I think these levels are really fun too, and they serve as a nice break from all the high speed action of Sonic and Tails, unlike his similar gameplay in SA2 which was modified to be extremely tedious and boring.
-Amy... alright, think Sonic with way less speed, only one (extremely inconsistent) attack, and sometimes being chased by a not really threatening robot. Yeah, Amy's levels aren't that fun to be honest but they could be worse.
-E102-Gamma's gameplay focuses more on shooting... yup, shooting. It's a really strange concept for a Sonic game but it's not as bad as it sounds, at least he doesn't have too many levels. This gameplay was actually given to Tails' in SA2, not only that, but his levels in that game are way more boring than those of E102-Gamma.
-Big... Ok, so what is Sonic known for? His high speed platforming, right? Well, Big is the complete opposite, his levels always come to a complete stop and there's no platforming, instead, you get fishing. Yup, Fishing. In a Sonic game. Seriously, I don't know who thought this was a good idea and who approved this terrible idea but yeah, Big sucks, he's boring and adds nothing to the game. If there is a mod to remove Big from the game, someone please link me to it.
Amy and E102-Gamma aren't that bad, but Sonic, Tails and Knuckles are way more fun and the obvious highlight of the game. It's just Big that I actually consider to be bad and completely boring.
If you're looking for a good story, I don't even know why you're considering Sonic Adventure, or any Sonic game at all, these games have never had good stories. But hey, if there's one thing that has been consistent in most Sonic games (this one is included), it's the great soundtracks. This game's soundtrack is great. I remember sitting back and just listening to the Adventure Menu or Trial Menu themes when I was a kid (and still kinda do today actually).
Anyway, this is still a really fun game nowadays. If you still haven't played it then I highly recommended you buy this, I also highly recommend you get the 'BetterSADX" mod as it adds widescreen and vsync support, which the vanilla version lacks for some reason. Also consider getting the Dreamcast lighting and conversion mod to make the game look even better.

A fun little gem that I seem to keep returning to even though I've pretty much found everything there is to find.  "Eversion" starts out as a bright, cheerful little adventure wherein a little hopping flower guy is seeking to rescue his princess.  But very quickly, things start to go wrong.  Horribly, nightmarishly, wonderfully wrong.  <3
I don't want to spoil too much for anyone who DOESN'T know what they're in for, but this game DOES open with a quote from H. P. Lovecraft for a reason.  You're not going to see Cthulhu and company show up in the world of "Eversion," but you will get that same sense of a normal reality concealing an entire dimension of gibbering madness just beneath the surface, waiting for the unwary person who delves too deeply.  Not bad for a little flower with only two moves (jump and "evert").
Will it scare you?  Maybe.  It didn't scare me, but then not a lot of games do.  It DID appeal to my particular sense of warped aesthetics, though, so if that makes it sound like your cup of tea, then by all means, give it a go.  You could also find the original free version online if you're not sure.  Of course it won't be in HD, the gameplay will be harder, and there won't be any achievements.  And we wouldn't want any of that, right?

Eversion is a game unlike anything I've ever played, it's the kind of game that lures you in with cutsie graphics and sweet music, in other words a Super Mario Bros. clone. But this game is far more than a clone. I also highly advise you take the warning on the title screen seriously.
The story of Eversion starts off very simple with the save-the-princess trope, our little flower hero Zee Tee is tasked with the job of rummaging through the lands to reunite with the Princess. Along the way you'll fight goomba-like enemies that are barely threatening. The main selling point of this game is the Eversion feature, in each level there are points where the background changes along with the music slightly, if you press the evert button in these areas the stage will evert, this changes objects in the stages. For example, if you evert in one stage you can walk on the clouds. This makes way for very creative puzzles that test your platforming skills. But this isn't the main reason the game is infamous, as you evert the stages they start to degenerate, I don't want to ruin the experience but as you start to evert the layers in the later levels you'll realize this game has combined 3 genres. Platforming, puzzle, and horror. As far as music goes, the game has some very delightful chip-tune tracks, which then slowly start to change as you evert. The last track is just a plain heartbeat.
All in all, the game has little over 1 hour of playtime, it's a fun time waster with VERY good plot twists indeed. I'd suggest playing it at night with a friend who has no idea what the game's about.

There’s a part of me – the pessimistic critical part of me always lurking for a new victim to verbosely dismember – which feels compelled to scoff at Labyrinthine Dreams’ optimism and sentimentality. Something in my brain tells me that from a literary standpoint this saccharine monologue told within the dreams of a terminal cancer patient on her death-bed is shallow and driven primarily by the player’s emotions. But what I’ve come to find more and more lately as I’ve begun to take steps to break myself out of depression and hopefully come out the other side a happier person, is…I don’t care what that part of me says anymore.
Labyrinthine Dreams’ may lack nuance and come accompanied by some dreadful artwork (those facial expressions are the stuff of nightmares), but its sincerity and earnestness meant so much more to me than what questionable character designs or clichéd plot points could take away.
Perhaps it’s a tired tale; an expected narrative being directed at people like myself who see themselves so easily in the mundane lives of struggling artists forced to give up on their creative dreams under the weight of a socioeconomic machine. Maybe I’m just looking for reassurance that I’m not throwing my life away by not pursuing a more marketable degree and Labyrinthine Dreams is the relatable, consoling voice I’ve been longing to hear. But then, is that such a bad thing to want? Even if it’s at times trite, does that diminish Labyrinthine Dreams’ message of hope to those in need of it?
This isn’t a review. You’ve likely realized that by now. It’s not a critical interpretation of a work or even a basic bullet-pointed list of pros and cons. It is almost nothing, but in what few words I’ve found to describe my feelings toward Labyrinthine Dreams, I hope it’s clear that it connected to me in a very personal way. It wasn’t deep; I can’t describe it in thousands of words dripping in analogical prose and life stories; I find myself struggling to even write enough to feel as if it could serve as a legitimate recommendation.
All I can say is that Labyrinthine Dreams is honest. Honest about what it is, in its characters, even in its fantasies. It’s solemn and optimistic, that no matter how badly it could go wrong and how much everyone tells you you’re living in a dream, your life is worth more than a paycheck and losing the chance to do what you love. A few years ago I’d have rolled my eyes. Now, this simple positivity has come to mean something deeper to me, and I’m thankful every day that there are people who understand that sometimes all anyone needs is encouragement.

It seems like I've been choosing the games with the feels to play for a while. First
, then
, and now
... This is starting to become a habit. I wouldn't like to seem like a tragedy junkie. I just wished to play an RPG maker game, and look what it has done to me: all teary eyed and big with the decision on Carpe Diem!
In
, our protagonist is Beth; a young woman who is crippled with anxiety, due to the timeless death of her father. In many ways, she is terrified that she may end up just like him. She is trying to deal with judgement, apathy and depression while recounting the events of her life from a dreamlike perspective. She travels within many dream fragments that symbolize both important moments of her life and her hopes, dreams and fears: namely her inner world. Within those dreams, she constantly tries to escapes from a monster, a dark creature that comes after her. For every step that Beth takes, the monster can take two. Is she doomed to end up in the grasp of her inner demon despite whatever she tries?
The gameplay is the marriage of a visual novel and a refreshing selection of movement puzzles. Puzzles are decent, and takes some time to figure all if you were not to use a guide. I'd like to add that, every detail that you come across, alongside with the nature of puzzles you solve, the game world is genuinely symbolic. You shouldn't expect a straight forward story consistency. The story works around the linear concept that you expect from an RPG maker game. For example: for the first puzzle that you come across - The Forest - you are not allowed to make left turns. It gave me the sense that Beth is forced to abide by the expectations of society: one way only. There should be millions of other paths that she could take to finish the labyrinth, but she is forced to use a single one. Beautifully thought!
There isn't much free will, but Beth's tale is so ordinary, so real and everyday; I found no problem on emphasizing myself with the character. The game asks the same question that we ask ourselves everyday: Will I make it? Will it be okay? Am I taking the right decision? Is it foolish to chase a dream? We all are afraid if we do not abide by the rules of the society, and work on a course of 'guaranteed future', we could end up wasting our life after a dream that we shall miss in the end. We all are a 'Beth' when a new day begins.
This is a very short game that you should spare the time to take a look at. At the end, I promise you, you'll feel better about whatever your life may hold for you. I know I feel better, and every Beth is a hero.

Hey guys, after a shítstorm of playtime I decided to give the community some of my toughts.
Obviously, we are talking about a game thats still alive after several years, and it has a reason, but I think this is about to be gone. Back in 2013 I stopped playing this game, and now in 2015 I gave it another go. I was dissappointed, not because it went worse or dead, it isnt. But there is no such new stuff that players were always dreaming of. More than a year gap, and I can say, nothing new, just some OP Armas Marketplace weapons, and a car kit. I was expecting at least a new vehicle, a roadmap, or at least hackers gone (and im not even that courageous to dream about a new district). Anyways, I hope once the server merge is done, devs will give attention to such a stuff like these, so now, I suggesting this game.
The pros:
-Big community, you will always find buddies to play with, or get help.
-Promo codes, I hope devs willing to keep provide them.
-Open worlds with some gamemodes, and different servers for each (to make the matchmaker more fair).
-Random and kinda colorful missions. Every mission is a different story.
-Customization, including: music maker, car sound/kits/paint, Sims like character making+tattoos, and a lots of clothes...And this is the main point of the game, seriously, it has no pair. I would rather describe this game as a F2P art game with shooting possibilities. You can almost literally can customize everything, if you like designing, you will love this game.
-Decent amount of perks/mods for cars/character/weapons, there is no best or worst set, everything depends on your playstyle.
-Marketplace, where you can sell and show your badass stuff. Or buy.
-Events. Make use of them, they are usually nice farming possibilities.
The cons:
-Unbalanced weapons. Some of them that you can buy for real money, are obviously the way more powerful than those you can buy for in-game money, giving a p2w feeling. Still, you can try out some for free.
-Server lags, not an usual problem, altough when it kicks in, you better just log off (I hope server merge will kill this).
-Hackers. They will be always around with tasty aimbot and wallhack. FairFight is not enough to keep them away.
-A lot of annoying no life as$holes, who like to harass others, even if they are on the same side. I just suggest ignore asap.
-Weird car physics. They seem to be too slow and too heavy.
-Designing possibilities are too limited with freemium account.
The two sided:
-If you dont want to play missions, there is a possibility to hang around, race etc...That means of course, if you are on a mission, you still can get rammed and harassed by any other player.
-Epic grinding. It keeps you playing, although without premium account its much harder to get money.
Tips for newbies:
-Do the tutorial missions asap, look for the one that gives you a LIFETIME weapon. You will need it, you really dont want to re-buy your weapon every 10 days.
-Spend some time at Social district and try out every editor. Also, thats the best place you can ask for help.
-If you harassed by anyone "superior" to you, just use "/report *name*" then "/ignore *name*", and if needed change instance.
-Make sure you switched off auto-ready system, so you wont go on mission until you dont want.
-Save money and joker tickets, dont spend them inmedetadly.
-Always go for sure, check your ammo and grenades every time.
-Just a performance tip, when you enter a district, take a trip from its end to the other, so most things will load, and you lower the chance of a performance lag.
I hope some of you can use it. If you have questions just ask. See you on battlefield!

Penny Arcade's On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness 3 is a fantastic RPG and I highly recommend it to any and all RPG fans. It is well made and fixes many problems that I feel other rpgs do. Personally, it is one of the few rpgs that I love solely based on the battles and mechanics alone. It has 3 components that makes this game truly fantastic.
The battles are all constructed so that it is never too hard or too easy. There are no random encounters in this game so you can never be too underpowered to fight an enemy or too overpowered to just easily bypass an enemy. Because of this, every battle forces you to carefully choose your attacks. It's never advisable to just spam the attack button unless you want to die. Also, the lack of random encounters also makes choosing your difficulty actually effect your game. The battle themselves have a sort of timer that determines when a character attacks. the slower the enemy, the longer it takes them to attack. This makes it clear when an enemy is about to attack and when you need to anticipate it.
The game also has a certain mana system that makes fighting enemies a little more strategic. You can choose to spend points to do a special move or do a normal attack to gain more points to do a stronger attack, but that could leave yourself vulnerable.
The class system in the game is well made. Any character can be any class simply by giving them an item. You're never forced to use the same 4 classes every game. The classes them themselves aren't just the generic classes you typically see (like warrior, mage and healer). Each class is very different and creative. Not only that but every class is a viable option. Any combination of classes will be able to beat the game. Just choose what you like best. And because you can easily switch any characters class, you can easily find a class you like.
Another thing that makes the classes unique is that every class has their own special twist. Some focus on defense and protecting other team members. Some focus on battle stances that change attack effects. Some slows the attacks of enemies. They are very different and yet all work very well against enemies. Replaying this game with different classes is pretty rad.

I love Penny Arcade 3 almost solely on it's mechanics and battle system (I do enjoy the story as well). If you love rpgs, seriously, do yourself a favor and buy this game. story - there is a flashback showing Lara as a child with her mother as their plane crashes somwhere in Himalaya, Nepal. they find a cave, where is stone dais with a sword stucked in.Laura touches it, which activates some kind of portal. her mother pulls the sword out and that leads to her vanishing in front of laras eyes.She then sketches the dais and ............well,its not clear how she got out off that mountain, so just lets go with theory that she met british - friendly  yetis nearby and those helped her ascend
in present, Lara is looking for the similiar dais in Bolivia, but it turns out the bad guys were there first, so she takes them down and its revealed, that their leader, james Rutland was led here by Amanda, who used to be Lara s friend but then she became evil because of some ghost thing that saved her life. And you can tell Amanda is evil because she looks like a frontwomen of 90's goth rock band. jokes aside Rutland mentions some fragments, so lara goes looking for them and rest i wont spoil
story (as you would expect) is over the top (in a good way), but also a bit dated (in not so good, but still a good way ) because it kinda resembles mid 2000's action/adventure flick, which is understandable, since this game came out around that time (2006, to be precise).
characters are okay, there is not much to say here - Lara is likeable badass as always and then she has her team that consists of Alistair and Zip and they are fine.The bad guys arent that memorable.Rutland is kinda forgetable and Amanda is more of angry brat, who is furious because she couldnt get to an AFI concert than hatefilled - spirit possesed  villainess
gameplay - its a bit different tomb raider than the one from 1996. Levels are more linear, straight forward and puzzles doesnt involve you searching every inch of the level just to get the key. There are lots collectables that rewards for finding them with new outfit for example.
off course, as a tomb raider game, main focus is a platforming and climbing and its a lot more fluent than it was in the original. Whats also a lot better than in the first game is camera, even though the camera can be sometimes slightly annoying
you have also a grapling hook (which you will use in platforming and mostly to move with objects) and a camera (which can be helpfull in puzzle sections)
speaking of puzzles, they are not that difficult.most of them are relatively easy but they are still fun to solve
there is also a combat, which is the same as the combat from previous ones but more dynamic.your arsenal consists of two pistols, assault rifles, shotguns and grenade launchers.there are also bosses.not as memorable like in the original but still great
what suprised me the most is that this game has qte sections and they are not that bad. arrows show always in the middle of the screen so its always clear what are you supposed to push and give you enough time to react. Sure, they sometimes come out of nowhere, but they're not that frequent and still better than in some games (like RE 6 for example)
also Croft manor is back.you can train here, find more secrets and access dressing room, so theres more to do than in the original

11 years ago, I played Tomb Raider: Legend for the very first time, fell in love immediately when Lara dived into clouds, grabbed the edge of the cliff, rose elegantly with a floor exercise move from the cliff...Then I was brought to the wilds of Bolivia, so the journey began.
11 years later, for the affection I had with her, I enjoyed it once more to bring the nostalgia I had in Nepal. I knew I was seeking the long lost memory which still lying in the heart of mountain Himalayan sedately. As always, true love never fades, I remember you, Legend, so much about you...
In a word, Tomb Raider: Legend did absolutely her best for its time being. By evolving the weak points of previous vintage Tomb Raider games using next gen graphics at that time, puzzles now are more clear to notice, yet, not so obvious to sort out. It still takes time and efforts to figure out how they work for the first time play-through.
Despite the graphics might be revolutionary, the spirit of previous TR games had never been changed even so slightly. Unlike the direction of Tomb Raider 2013 or the Rise of Tomb Raider  have headed to which are questionable, Tomb Raider: Legend showed the respect of what made the franchise this far by standing where it was. Moreover, it seems had better understanding of how to carry the TR legacy that previous games had left.
If we take a close look about the content that Legend does offer, it is far more comprehensively constructed than any other TR games apart from trilogy itself. The game offers players variety of places to adventure across the world as the metaphor of previous series. Meanwhile, each stage separated from the other makes the whole story divided into several chapters that is neat for telling a long tale of adventure. The plot itself is captivating ever since the beginning and leaves a myth waiting for the players to witness it all by making progress till the end. The game also has countless collectables and hidden secrets to be discovered in each level of the stages and featuring Lara's costumes as the rewards to collect them. It was one of the brilliant creations for the first time among the entire franchise at that time. Furthermore, Legend has one last unique challenge called 'Time Trials' for hardcore players to conquer. Each stage has very limited short time for players to complete with unrivaled rewards to offer if succeed. The BGMs of each place of interests are epic. Main Theme is unforgettable top notched. There are some extra points below: the re-furnished Croft Manor is amazing to explore, thanks to the next-gen graphics, some scenery are fascinating...The list of Pros can go on and on.
In short, Tomb Raider: Legend has strengthened every angle that you can possibly think of from a previous TR game. But never cross the line to turn it into something against its origins. This is the future TR games suppose to continuously heading to. Therefore, CD stole the title and made the later games into something else, something I can hardly tell what are they.
Overall, despite the clunky control might be a bit out of time for new players to get use to and sometimes the odd camera angle could make Miss Croft do a fetal jump to the wrong direction and instantly killed herself, Legend is a perfect game in every way of her own charm.
My childhood had been filled up with the memories of Tomb Raider III Adventure of Lara Croft and TR IV the Last Revelation, Legend and Underworld are the only TR games I've appreciate that differ from the originals. Though, by turning TR a worldwide recognizable franchise using current trendy concept 'survival' made CD, Square Enix huge amount of profits and popularities, there is no deny that It is a backstab to the soul of what made TR games this far. Tomb Raiders are never popular games, they are treasured by a very small community for their hardness and horrfying moments that turns people away. This is mere one cruel fact among many of what TR games truly are. Just as much as Lara's coolness is way beyond her sexual appearance that made who she is rooted in our hearts.

If you aren't chasing long lost memories you should probably skip it.
Father Time has run amok on the Blue Hedgehog's Dreamcast flagship title. Its just a clunky game and there's no way to sugar coat it. An unofficial patch called BetterSADX (which can be found as the top rated "guide" in the community hub) does what it can to alleviate all the technical issues with running this game on the modern PC with full controller support. But the core game still is a bit messy.
The Dreamcast will always hold a place in my heart and a solid place in video game history. They pushed the limits of the era and were completely unafraid to experiment with gameplay. Sonic Adventure is no different in those regards. Interwoven character storylines, all of which you can play through. With each character being a wholly unique gameplay experience to boot. They toyed with open world and mini games. "Ahead of it's time!" or whatever. Call it what you will, but it just sadly doesn't come together cohesively. And as the years have worn on its become harder to forgive and enjoy. And while it features the iconic running from the whale scene and the first snowboarding sequence, it is otherwise very very lacking in the speed department. Sonic's main claim to fame is an afterthought to the experimental exploration, bad camera angles, and sloppy platforming.
I was one those chasing long lost Dreamcast memories though. While I seethed and spit in anger at the cameras of the last few Sonic levels and trudged through multiple glitch deaths fighting Egg Viper I still was reliving some memories. It'd take another level of dedication to appreciate all the characters, 100%'ing it, and/or Chaos mini-games that I simply do not have. But I still had fun.
Only recommended for those who want to play it again or somewhat decently hardcore Sonic fans. And just to reiterate, get the unofficial patch called BetterSADX if you are going to play. I cannot recommend it to anybody else remotely though. There's tons of better Sonic choices on Steam as this is arguably the worst.

In short, you "evert" between worlds when you pass certain spots in the level. Eversion is a simple platformer with a really happy and charming aesthetic, as the game's banner may imply. The gameplay is akin to the classic Super Mario games, and while it's mostly straightforward, the "eversion" game mechanic allows you to change the environment slightly at certain points in each level, which gives each stage more depth as it allows for some intricate puzzles and level design. Eversion's difficulty starts out quite low but rapidly accelerates into a challenging game as your progress.
The game does suffer from a couple of minor flaws. It's short - 7 levels short. However, there is a time attack mode with online highscores (with alternate versions of a couple levels), which gives the game a bit more replay value. There are also a couple areas where the hitboxes on the player make it difficult to maneuver through one-block gaps, but this only happens in a couple of areas.
Overall, Eversion is a cheerful and unique experience; it's something you and everyone you know should definitely play.

"The horror!"
A cheap little platformer, this might be one of the smallest games on Steam. I imagine anyone buying it just wanted it because it was cheap and looked cute.
How wrong you are.
Story
Something about the princess being taken is written on the store page. You won't really see much story once in the game, except for the ending.
Presentation
Cute graphics here, they are what drew me in to purchasing this game. Little did I know that would soon change to a nightmarish landscape rather quickly. While they are rather basic and obviously inspired by classic games, they still look nice.
The isn't a lot of music in the game, but it fits the setting. Simple sound effects that do the job as well. Not really much to say about them.
Controls
As the controls are rather simple, they work well on keyboard, but gamepads also have support if you prefer those. Movement, jumping, the Eversion ability (which shall be detailed below) and a pause button. You could play this with a NES clone controller if you own one.
Gameplay
Run, jump, bounce off enemy heads, collect the gems and reach the end of the level.  Sounds like any NES era platformer game, right? Well, since the game opens up with a Lovecraft quote, there is obviously going to be something creepy lurking in the shadows. And that is where the Eversion ability comes in. In each level, there are locations where the walls between realities are weak. If you can find them, you can shift to another reality, often darker than the one you were already in. This will have an effect on both the landscape and enemies. That bush will wither and die, only to be replaced by deadly vines. Enemies may lose the will to live, just standing there for you to end its life, or it may get faster and more dangerous. Switching realities is needed to get all the gems through the levels, and sometimes even to progress forward through what would otherwise block movement.
Lifespan
This game is short. Including the final level which requires you to find all the gems, you are unlikely to spend more than an hour or two doing the main game, including the different endings. Once you have seen the true ending, you do unlock a time attack mode with leader boards, which can add to the time spent on the game. There is also a level editor available, though I haven't played around with any of the community content myself.
While not a bad game, the short game length alone is a good enough reason to only get on sale or with a Steam discount coupon.
6 / 10

It plays well, looks great, the tone feels spot on for slasher tropes, and (the 2nd chapter especially): it keeps you tense without being obnoxious.  You will not win the first or tenth round, but you will keep learning and correcting, retinkering a plan until it works. Brute force rarely works and when it does, you have paid for it dearly.  The attention to detail in this game exceeds my expectation.  Two aspects I feel the developer did exceptionally well with are sound (particularly with auditory cues) and color (lighting and adherence to the appropriate color scheme.)  Compare the Friday 13th chapter to the Texas chainsaw massacre dizyingly sickening, washed out color scheme, for example.  Also, notice the transition of artificial light in the context of passing day/night.  These (both sound and color), I think are crucial components to recreating the tone and atmosphere of a slasher movie, and the developer executed it well.
