So, like a lot of people I was first interested in this when the kickstarter was announced - an XCOM remake in all but name? Take my money sir! And then Firaxis came along, announced their "reimagining" and release a truly brillian game in it's own right. It was X-COM, not quite XCOM but an excellent game. In the meantime Goldhawk (a little frustratingly at times) slowly got on with finishing their game and now it's been released.
So is it any good? This is the closest you are going to get to replaying XCOM again. OK so they can't use the same names or anything, they've set it in the 1970s (which, by the way was a minor stroke of genius) but works. It works sooo well. If you played and loved XCOM, then you can pick this up without even having to refer to an instruction manual. It does play a little differently yes  - the beefed up air combat being the main difference, something which I haven't really come to grips with so I'm heavily reliant on the "auto-resolve" button - but they flavour text accompanying the game is genuinely funny in places and very well written.
It lacks some of the creeping dread of XCOM on some of the missions (their Cryssalid replacement for example bears a remarkable resembalance to the Warhammer 40K Tyranid lictor) and suffers for it for some reason, and some of the models are maybe a little lacking. However the UFO design is excellent, and clearing them out a real tactical workout on occasion.
I've not "finished" it yet, but all I can say a couple of hours of playing this over development and now release is that it's pretty damned good. If you tried the Firaxis version and it didn't click for you, then believe me this will.  Well worth the purchase price for any XCOM fan.

Xenonauts is a worthy successor to the original X-Com. I played EU and Apocalypse as a kid and always thought that an update could really improve on the successes of those games while fixing their flaws. And Xenonauts delivers.

Good work Goldhawk, glad I spent my money on such a terrific game.

I was hoping to extend my XCOM 2012 experience with xenonauts....well, I was pretty wrong. Let's just tell about what's wrong :
1) LOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOONG " WAITING FOR I.A. " !! Seriously, the waiting at the end of each turn is much, much, much longer than the loading times !! and this " Hidden movement " artwork image is, after a while, worst than just looking at the map...
2) big map and lot enemies...it isn't a good thing ? well, no, most match, especially during the terror missions, will ends up with you searching for some single xeno running away...add this to the point 1) and...you'll know about those stolen and frustating 5-10 minutes !!!
3) despite the lore, even the aliens that should have a " worst vision than human " can still see you while you cannot, even when you're facing their direction e.g. you'll be shooted from nowhere and you can do few about this

Put up simply....
Notes:
-I played the whole game
-I still didn't play the multiplayer, though.
-I didn't use the Editor.
Pros:
-Great Level Design.
-Nice music
-Graphics pretty top notch for its time.
-Many guns.
-Beautiful Environments. (I guess it also counts as level design)
-Kinda makes you wanna come back for more.
-Almost everything is a trap. Even the +1 HPs thingies.
-Almost everything Sam says is worth being a famous quote.
-Very original.
-Fun shooting and controls are great.
Cons:
-Enemy are outstandingly and unbelievably overused. Specially the bulls, the horses and the robots.
-The same old formula is used over and over again. Go in a room, get item in the middle, fight many waves of enemies, get to next to room, same thing,.... etc.
-It has little to no music. But the music in it, specially at the last level of the game, is really nice and catchy.
-Quite frustrating when fighting certain types of enemies, like huge hords of bulls.
-When you come back for more, you, probably, get sick of it in less than 2 hours.
-The areas are too wide, and you're forced to walk too goddamn much from corner to corner.
-Almost everything is a trap. Even the +1 HPs thingies.
-Sam barely says anything, other than a line or two after the end of countless waves of enemies.
-So, do I recommend this game?
If it were a full priced game, even if it had nowadays graphics, I would not recommend.
But because the game is nice, when played from time to time, and holds historical value, and is cheap, I'd recommend.
Don't get me wrong, I like the game. It's just that it overuses pretty much everything it has, and gets repetitive quick.
I'm sure this game will be in your head for pretty much forever. It's a quite original and memorable game.
Personal review........ 7.5/10..... but it's originality leaves me thinking, so I'd add 0.5 more to that.
8/10. Would play again on different maps or multiplayer (which I still didn't try).

Xenonauts is basically a modern remake of the original Xcom, and it retains most of its original features.
-Uses TU(time units) which allows for a large diversity of actions to be taken during a turn, instead of the simplified scoot n shoot action system from Xcom:EU
-Destructible Terrain: you can destroy light cover, such as haybales and low barricades, to larger things such as entire walls
-Can have more than one base to operate from on the globe, and it can be placed in any exact location down to a pixel
-Base building: a 6 by 6 grid that can be outfitted with a variety of structures to win the war
-Base assault and defense: You can assault alien strongholds on earth and vice versa
-Medium size combat teams: You get to start off with 8 units, and you can increase that amount to 10 later on.
-No class restricting roles: You can equip any soldier with any item, and designate their roles as you deem fit.
-Soldier Inventory system: though slightly streamlined, (no more leg or shoulder slots, just hands, belt, and backpack.) you   can equip soldiers with as much as they can carry weight/space wise.

For those uninitiated into the wonder of the Xcom universe, the game basically plays as a world defense simulator. The earth gets attacked by aliens, and all of the worlds super powers are left bent over a table with their pants down. You, and your organization, the Xenonauts, are effectively the last defense we have left.
You start out by placing a base on the globe, and then monitor alien activity around you via radar dishes. While things are dark, you can research alien artifacts and technology,  build new military toys, and invest in both your base and its employees. Once a Ufo is spotted, you can choose to launch a fighter or interceptor to its location to try and shoot it down. If you succeed, you'll most likely be given the option to send a mop up crew to kill off any survivors and acquire whatever the ship had aboard it. Alternatively, you can also send in an airstrike in to obliterate the crash site, netting you a small amount of cast from the pieces left.
Once a crew of soldiers arrives at a crashsite or other battlefield, the game plays out in a turn based fashion. You move your soldiers around a battlefield, using various cover, weapons, and equipment to out position and destroy your foe. Whether that be by blowing a hole in the side of a building and running inside to flank an enemy, tossing a flash bang or smoke grenade to disorient and charge the enemy head on, or laying down supressive fire while a sniper gets into position and guns down an enemy. The choice is up to you.
While Xenonauts does however, have its own share of faults, (Playing the same levels over and over in combat missions, predictable enemies inside downed ufos, graphics ocassionally bugging out, etc.) they are few and far between, and the game can be modded to the point where most of these things are not an issue.
If you liked the original Xcom, I can almost assure you that you will love this game, and if you've never played one before, you should give it a shot.

You can skip dialogue but it skips it inaccurately and blows past most of the speech, but the speech bubbles aren't aligned properly anyway so you end up repeating the terrible dialogue. Serious Sam The First Encounter is a decent "old school" FPS.
You go around blasting various alien enemies with various guns. The game feel is good with Sam moving around. The weapons each have their own advantage against certain enemies. You won't be using the same gun the entire game. I was constantly switching weapons based on what was coming toward me.
The weapons I would say are pretty "standard". Pistol, shotgun, machine gun, rocket launcher, laser gun, etc. Each having their own advantages and disadvantages.
The amount of unique enemies is fairly small. You'll be seeing the same types of enemies over and over again. The design of them is nice though. Each enemy has a distinct audio clip that you will rely heavily on to quickly choose the right weapon for the job.
I think the graphics hold up quite well. I was able to get the game running in 2560x1440 and it was very sharp.
One thing that turned me off was the large difficulty spike toward the end of the game. It's a pet peeve of mine when games sharply increase the difficulty at the end. I had to use God mode to get past it.
-Good graphics for the time that still hold up today
-Good gameplay feel and hit detection
-Audio cues for enemies
-Each gun has advantages & disadvantages
-Quick save feature
-Stable. Never crashed on me (windows 8.1 64bit)
-Secret areas!
-Generally smooth 60FPS (has some slowdown here and there but didn't affect much)
-Lackluster story
-Repeating enemies
-Difficulty spike at the end
-Felt repetetive toward the end of the game
Good. Slightly above average

Entirely different gameplay than the previous two games, more reminiscent of a standard RPG.  Interesting class system but ultimately you'll just stick with the more obviously useful and easy to use ones.  Great music and story.

Zeboyd Games is pretty much my hero when it comes to the RPG genre as of late and I hope that if they can find the resources, they can move forward to create even better looking games. Do you honestly enjoy random encounters? Level grinding for hours? Having to save your best items for fights that may not happen? Zeboyd has you covered. Every battle in R-S 3 starts you out with full health and every item you have bought/collected at your disposal. At the end of the battle you get all of that back. You also get 1MP per turn (magic costing up to 9MP) which you can use freely without fear of having to save it for another battle. This creates actually enjoyable gameplay where every battle is a different experience (enemies are already put in groups at pre-set points in every map) that requires tactical planning prior and mid battle.
I loved the last two R-S games for being like the Mother/Earthbound games as delightully quirky and fun urban RPGs. R-S 3 manages to continue this trend while being double the length of the last two games (for the better!) and will ALWAYS surprise you. On top of that, you don't actually need to have any knowledge of the former games. Because of that, I actually recommend this game more than the games before it.
If you love RPGs you owe it to yourself to play this game. It's cheap, it's fun, and if you ♥♥♥♥♥ about it being too easy, play it on Insane and eat your level grinding heart out (level grinding is optional on easier difficulties!).

While I enjoyed Penny Arcade Episode I and II, III is by far the best. Zeboyd Games does it again! Each game of theirs has been better than the last and PA3 doesn't disappoint. The battle system is a familiar, albeit, unique system. The class system is close to what Final Fantasy has done before; each class learns different attacks, but you can assign 3 classes to a character (something Final Fantasy has never done). If you enjoyed Zeboyd's previous games: Breath of Death VII and Cthulu Saves The World, then you will most certainly enjoy PA3. Even if you aren't familiar with Penny Arcade or the previous games, you should still give it a try. I'm very excited to play PA4, and this Spring can't come soon enough! Always trust Zeboyd games if you love classic style RPGs, they'll never let you down.

Tomb Raider Legend is a story-driven platformer that is fun to play, but a near-game-breaking bug and some awkward mechanics  belittle the overall positive experience.
Installed size on hard drive: 7.3 GB
The story is decent, if a little disconnected. Lara is searching for an artifact that killed her mother years ago. A great excuse to send Lara to a variety of diverse locations, from a sleepy South American town to the frozen mountains of Nepal. Zip and Alistair provide some snarky commentary as she proceeds through the levels – some of it almost breaking the fourth wall. It helps keep the proceedings light-hearted and fun, even if what is happening is quite serious. Lara herself is keen, quick-witted, whip-smart, and always ready with a snappy come-back. TR: Legend was actress Keeley Hawes first time voicing Lara, and she does an absolutely fantastic job.
The platforming is well-executed and slick, with timed movements (move quickly before the platforms collapse) and required momentum (remember to HOLD the spacebar to jump in some places, or Lara won't jump far enough). Gun-play just feels odd; lock on to a target, use the arrow or WASD keys to switch the lockon from target to target. While doing this, Lara can run, jump and dodge. There is a free-aim mode, but once engaged Lara cannot move at all, so the lockon mode will be the one used most often. I rebound the keys to what I wanted, so there is that. There are no waypoints; not really an issue in a game this linear. The climbing puzzles are generally well done; remember to use Lara's binoculars first to scan an area for hints before trying to solve a puzzle. Some bosses can only be defeated with the help of the environment, so if a boss seems like it is taking no damage, start looking around for switches and levers (and things to grapple). Nothing is handed to you in this game, though once you figure out a puzzle or boss, it will be solved or defeated in a matter of seconds.
Now for the issues, and there are more of them than there should be. Lock-on would sometimes result in strange camera movements, and the camera doesn't immediately auto-rotate to the forward direction when riding a motorbike. The platforming direction controls aren't always intuitive. A similar issue plagues the QTEs; the onscreen arrows don't always indicate the correct direction, resulting in multiple fails until finding the right button-press. Disable Next Generation Content in the graphics settings; TR: Legend looks better with it, but this will eliminate nearly all crashes. And there is the near-game-breaking bug in the Nepal temple level. A cutscene, then Lara needs to run to a door, hit it (I won't say with what, because spoilers), the door will open, triggering another cutscene and a platforming section. But hitting the door doesn't always make it open, meaning progression through the game is blocked. Just keep re-loading a save until the game works the way it is supposed to (it took me seven tries the last time I played it). Ridiculous, but there it is.
The saving grace through all of this Lara Croft herself. Unlike more recent versions of Lara, this one has no lack of confidence. You never hear Lara telling herself, “I can do this.” She already knows she can, and can worry about other things. I still highly recommend Tomb Raider: Legend despite the game's issues, because there is nothing
game breaking, and this remains one of my favorite “older” versions of Lara. If story-driven platforming and puzzling is your preference, or you just want more Lara Croft, absolutely get this one.

If this is supposed to be the remastered version of an older game, then why is it so insufferably tedious to play? Everything screams rush job here. Some things are intentionally badly done (graphics notably), which is fine by me, but the UI is horrendous, some of the voice acting is painfully delivered through a faulty microphone, there's a crash at the baker shop (I managed to circumvent it by selling for $5 and then immediately leaving the shop), there is no save feature (all right, you can finish the game in less than 10 minutes but when you have to re-do it several times to get past that crash, it gets annoying), the inventory is ridiculous, and worst of all, you have to move with the arrow keys and bring up the inventory with the 'i' key, while the rest is done with the mouse... Sorry? You couldn't spend five minutes adding arrow icons to the left and right borders of the screen, and an Inventory icon in a corner?
I liked Tokyo Hosto and even recommended it, and I had a few laugh at the silly conversations in here too. But at this point, it's just a ridiculous scam attempt, a project that was destined from the start to be bundled so the guy could make a few easy bucks and not have to worry about people asking for refunds. This would be enough to make you lose faith in the indie scene...

This is UFO/XCOM of 1994 as a similar IP, the aliens are named and look somewhat different, but you're looking at a lovingly crafted tribute that far surpasses it's inspiration. If you didn't play XCOM 2012 because it was different and therefore dirty compared to your rose-tinted nostalgia goggled view of UFO/XCOM then this will certainly float your nostalgic boat.
Gameplay wise, believe me that the moment you research stun batons you want 3 dudes with high TU packing a baton and a riot shield. Storming a downed UFO is a cakewalk when you just stroll in and punch everybody in the face :D
I only have two possible critiques and they are that while the sprites are quite detailed, you really can't tell one soldier from another so it's hard to build the kind of bond you had with your troops in XCOM 2012 and secondly the fixed isometric veiw can sometimes cause you to leave a soldier in your dropship because you forgot him/her as you can only see the top of their helmet, that's happened a couple of times but isn't even a serious problem as you might guess.

A few scattered ideas to sum up my dissapointment, what's not mentioned here is probably good in the game, but not enough to recommend it:
Gameplay
The ground combat really kills it.
Seriously, the line of sight/fire issues are horrible. I like playing games like this without saving (I did so with JA2) but here, to me, it seems impossible. It's just not intuitive. If I have a soldier crouch in the center on a warehouse rooftop, he shouldn't be able to get shot by someone hugging the warehouse wall. Or all the times I've moved a heavy for a slightly better position, only to be informed I now have 0% chance to hit, or something silly like a windowpane blocking 50% of my shots and not enough TUs to get back to my original position and fire. Also, I think the entire MG spray hit chance is calculated when you fire, because I've tried firing through those silly waist high walls with screens on them that you get in UFOs, which give you 0% chance to hit your target, because I figured ok, 1 round blows them away and the rest spray the alien behind... well, no, they all randomly hit the air where the screen used to be. This stuff kind of breaks a tactics game. JA2 didn't have these issues and that was 15 years ago...
Also, you can't store extra gear in the dropship. I can't be the only one who used to go back to the ship to get the heavy explosives every now & again in a difficult mission. I miss that.
Mission variety:
There really isn't any. I know there wasn't that much in the original game either, but if there's one aspect where I think the game could've evolved, it's this one.
There was just so much wasted potential here, extraction missions, coming to enforce local forces battle lines (I think they promised a static tank emplacement at one point), pilot rescue missions, I don't know, anything?
Graphics
I don't mind the direction they took or the lack of female soldier models or lots of stuff that could've been. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised by the variety of local forces and civilians and stuff, but the game has next to no animations, the characters don't sway, don't move, they don't anything. Everything is frozen until you take an action and then it's all very mechanical.
Interface
No option to toggle off centering on selected soldiers starts giving you headaches when you have to move 10 of them through multiple levels like in a UFO or building.
You can't reorganize your squad order, which is a mindnumbing oversight. I can't have No. 1 be the shield, 2 & 3 be assault and so on. Was it so hard to let me drag the ground combat squaddie tabs around?
I would've preferred scroll up/down to change height levels instead of selected squaddies. I guess tab & tilda work well enough, though. You can change the key bindings but you can't bind them to scroll up/down. I guess you probably can if you  start tinkering with the game files but I shouldn't have to do that.
Xenopedia
I generally love the descriptions in games like this, even Aftermath caught my interest with their alien types and whatever, but here, it feels too... textbook. I read all the entries but they felt dry and the attempts at humor seemed forced. There was 1 funny joke somewhere in there, though.
Conclusion
In all, it's a real shame and it taught me a lesson about buying into this kind of stuff. Maybe that gives the pricetag some worth.

With the positive reviews came promises of realism, scares, and exciting co-op play. And ofcourse the warning signs of the game feeling buggy or unfinished. Believe me, all of these are true. Though the mechanics can feel almost unfinished at times (but not bad enough that it will ruin the game), melee combat without the proper weapons can feel half as bad as Elder Scrolls III at times, the inventory system is harsh on the player, and you'll encounter a few but LIMITED few "I call B.S." moments, none of these things ruin the games. I have not played very much blind online multiplayer, but I have played on my own and with a few friends from real life by hosting locked servers, and have had a blast so far. The idea of video game mechanics being like zombie movies where only headshots count and one bite infects you really makes this game standout, along with the realism that you won't find elsewhere. Believe me, killing a zombie feels so much more satisfying when you blow it's brains out! The scares felt genuine, based on maps being dark and eerie, a single running zombie being an intimidating and worthy adversary (believe me, you do not want those in your life),  and the sheer anticipation every time you turn around that a zombie (or 2, or 20) will be right behind you, ready to infect you with one bite, or end your life with a hundred bites. There are survival mode maps that borrow concepts from Killing Floor and Nazi Zombies, but provide a fresh spin on it. (you'll understand when you play) and there are objective based maps as well, that truly make you feel like you are desperately escaping a condemmned area.
Overall, I give this game an 8/10. It's not perfect, but it's close enough to keep you occupied, especially with a few friends (who hopefully know what they are doing). You can really have a blast with this if you can see past it's flaws. And it's free-to-play. You can never go wrong with a free game.

Oh man, this game sure is a controversial one in the Sonic community isn't it? I grew up playing this on the gamecube but I'll try to write this review without nostalgia goggles. Sonic Adventure was Sega's first real attempt to bring their mascot into 3D, and in my opinion it was a good try. There are 6 playable characters; Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy, E-102 Gamma and Big the Cat. I'm going to say 4 of these 6 are fun, 1 is decent and 1 is mediocre. Sonic and Tails have a very similar playstyle, speeding through action levels and fast paced platforming. Knuckles searches for lost shards of the master emerald in his treasure hunt levels. Amy is basically a slower and more boring version of Sonic. E-102 has a really interesting story arc and fun levels, and Big the Cat is.... Fishing, easily the worst gameplay style of the bunch. This game released in 1998, so clearly it hasn't exactly aged perfectly, but I think people tend to be overly hard on it. If you enjoy Sonic or 3D platformers in general this is worth checking out if you can handle the way it's aged (camera isn't the best, lip syncing is awful, story isn't anything special,) and tolerate Big the Cat then I reccomend this, it's a really fun game!
Side note, I highly reccomend you get the Better SADX mod, it just improves the game in a lot of different ways overall and it doesn't affect gameplay or the ability to earn achievements.
What can i say? It's Sonic Adventure, one of the last good Sonic games ever made! Buy it NOW! Hell, Buy TWO! And that's an order, Soldier!

The graphics resolution is 720p, quality ranges from bad Flash drawings to beaten-to-death-with-effects photographs. There are 18 backgrounds and 16 characters, but you'll only get to see about half of these because the game crashes as soon as you sell something to the baker. The voiceovers have amateur quality as well. I am calling this a visual novel because you can't really manipulate items in the environment; most of the gameplay is cutscenes and dialogue (but you do get a movable avatar in three scenes, animation is 4 frames).
One positive point: I can confirm that it will run (such as it can, seeing it crashes in the baker scene) on an old slow XP box.
It's a very incomplete amateur game. Don't pay money for this.

I love this game. It's got a cute and appealing art style that just makes you smile. This game is geat if you play it in small bursts, but after about 4 hours of game play, you've done just about everything there is to be done. I've played nearly 9 hours at the time of this review and I've spent maybe the last 1.5-2 hours just farming achievements because there's nothing else for me to do.
I've bought all the possible upgrades and I've gathered every available item thus far for v0.2.4 to the point where I have tens of thousands of the ingame money and nothing to spend it on. It's even gotten to the point where I've gone to islands that have nothing on them because they're still under construction. The opening screen has the Rad Slime on it, so I'm wondering why it's not in the game yet.
(Spoilers ahead)
Hell, I've even fed all three of the "boss(?)" slimes. I have a key to an area not available yet, so I'm wondering why I would get an item I can't use until the forseeable future. I know this is an early access game, but they shouldn't be giving players items that are unusable at the time of playing. This also includes the Slimeypedia that has ??? for things currently undiscovered that aren't in the game as of yet along with achievements that give spoilers (such as areas you can't get to yet). If you were to ask me, I'd say those should remain hidden/unseeable in the game until an update makes them accessible.
(End spoilers)
Overall, this is a good game but only for a limited time until you're just running around and feeding your slimes and collecting plorts for money you don't need. The price shouldn't be at $20 but rather $10 for the amount of things still missing from the game and how little time it takes the player to get as far in the game as they can. By all means though, get the game if you want something to do for 4-5 hours, but just keep in mind that there isn't much to do nor is there very much replay value thus far.

Having loved the first two Penny Arcade games; I sadly wrote off the series when it was first cancelled. So I had a hint of trepidation when it was revived with a new developer and a completely new art direction. Which I can say, were unfounded.
Much like the last two, its a turn based RPG with an impeccably surreal setting with some of the best, most characterised writing in games right now; and the new art direction perhaps better serves the style of comedy of Penny Arcade. Allowing the developers to dip deeper in Gabe and Tycho's twelve year reservoir of inside jokes and references. Its a little more linear than I remember from the last two, but that only results in a more indepth story and a harder, more engaging combat system.
And this game's fights are HAAAAAAAAARD. If you go into a big battle unprepared or without a plan, you will get the floor wiped with you. I personally attempted the second final boss at least ten times. You really have to work to find the right formula for each party member, the best equipment, the right classes and how they interact with the rest of the party. There's no infinite well of XP or money (unless you noticed the optional Colosseum), so you have to understand your characters moves and prioritise your every dollar. It can be difficult restarting a battle you thought you had clinched, but the tension only makes the combat more satisifying.
This is a fun game, a must play for the avid PA fan not to mention those that fondly love the roots of the RPG (but I'd still recommend playing the first two first). And I honestly hope Zeboyd Games run with this nostalgic aesthetic choice, perhaps make the fourth and final game in the series a callback to the late ninties Playstation RPG's, you all know what I'm referring too.

A few scattered ideas to sum up my dissapointment, what's not mentioned here is probably good in the game, but not enough to recommend it:
Gameplay
The ground combat really kills it.
Seriously, the line of sight/fire issues are horrible. I like playing games like this without saving (I did so with JA2) but here, to me, it seems impossible. It's just not intuitive. If I have a soldier crouch in the center on a warehouse rooftop, he shouldn't be able to get shot by someone hugging the warehouse wall. Or all the times I've moved a heavy for a slightly better position, only to be informed I now have 0% chance to hit, or something silly like a windowpane blocking 50% of my shots and not enough TUs to get back to my original position and fire. Also, I think the entire MG spray hit chance is calculated when you fire, because I've tried firing through those silly waist high walls with screens on them that you get in UFOs, which give you 0% chance to hit your target, because I figured ok, 1 round blows them away and the rest spray the alien behind... well, no, they all randomly hit the air where the screen used to be. This stuff kind of breaks a tactics game. JA2 didn't have these issues and that was 15 years ago...
Also, you can't store extra gear in the dropship. I can't be the only one who used to go back to the ship to get the heavy explosives every now & again in a difficult mission. I miss that.
Mission variety:
There really isn't any. I know there wasn't that much in the original game either, but if there's one aspect where I think the game could've evolved, it's this one.
There was just so much wasted potential here, extraction missions, coming to enforce local forces battle lines (I think they promised a static tank emplacement at one point), pilot rescue missions, I don't know, anything?
Graphics
I don't mind the direction they took or the lack of female soldier models or lots of stuff that could've been. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised by the variety of local forces and civilians and stuff, but the game has next to no animations, the characters don't sway, don't move, they don't anything. Everything is frozen until you take an action and then it's all very mechanical.
Interface
No option to toggle off centering on selected soldiers starts giving you headaches when you have to move 10 of them through multiple levels like in a UFO or building.
You can't reorganize your squad order, which is a mindnumbing oversight. I can't have No. 1 be the shield, 2 & 3 be assault and so on. Was it so hard to let me drag the ground combat squaddie tabs around?
I would've preferred scroll up/down to change height levels instead of selected squaddies. I guess tab & tilda work well enough, though. You can change the key bindings but you can't bind them to scroll up/down. I guess you probably can if you  start tinkering with the game files but I shouldn't have to do that.
Xenopedia
I generally love the descriptions in games like this, even Aftermath caught my interest with their alien types and whatever, but here, it feels too... textbook. I read all the entries but they felt dry and the attempts at humor seemed forced. There was 1 funny joke somewhere in there, though.
Conclusion
In all, it's a real shame and it taught me a lesson about buying into this kind of stuff. Maybe that gives the pricetag some worth.

Okay, so this is not a review so much as the ravings of a rabid fan boy.  This game is amazing. If you even remotely liked X-Com:UD and were saddened by Firaxis's approach to the reboot, give this a try.  The art style is great, the writing in the UFOpedia is well done, and the battles have a nice variety of tactical options if you use all the toys at your disposal. It is for all intents and purposes a clone of the parent game, but it is lovingly done and has enough new things to keep this one in my library for a long time.

Hey, remember X-COM: UFO Defense? Well, Xenonauts is like that. A lot like that, actually. If that sounds appealing, maybe you didn't care for Firaxis' modern interpretation of the series (I did, but eh, you can like what you like) or just want a well-made strategy game that is admittedly unambitious in its aims, then this is exactly what you want. That's not to say that Xenonauts doesn't tweak and modernize certain aspects of the 1994 original, but only in ways that make sense and throw a little more balance into the mix (i.e. no more broken mind control).
If you've never played UFO Defense but want something a little more complex than Enemy Unknown, then this wouldn't be a bad place to start. Same brutal taste, but with a little more player freedom and ability to mess around.

For fans of the original X-Com, this is a tasty treat. For fans of turn based tactical combat simulators, it's a must try.
4/5
This is quite literally what all the X-Com games up until this point wished they could be. Let me put it this way.. Xenonauts is to X-Com what Bioshock was to System Shock.

I had doubts about whether I would be able to enjoy this after playing Firaxis's XCOM, but boy was I wrong. If you've enjoyed the challenge the original Julian Gollop's X-COM provided, Xenonauts is going to delight your socks off.
The dev team behind it have come a long way and have learnt quite a few lessons from other X-COM spiritual successors released before it. This shows as a much more fine tuned balance between being able to micromanage while still feeling like the overall commander-in-charge of your organisation. The oppressive feeling of a world unsure of your ability to deliver its salvation adds to the atmosphere of urgency, uncertainty, dread and hope all at once. Planetary Defence Simulator indeed.
Highly recommended!

Serious Sam: The First Encounter is a very simple game: Shoot everything that moves. Literally. And while that is the beauty of the game (taking account the complexity and the realistic nature of modern day FPS's) it's also it's weak point. It's a lot of fun killing a ♥♥♥♥♥on of alien-enemies with your arsenal, but the problem is that the game has way too many gigantic choke points that are nearly impossible to pass. It can become extremely tedious to go through one segment of a level, and honestly, without the quick-save feature, I would have called it quits pretty soon. Not to mention how often you ran out of ammo and have to resort to using your pistols against really powerful enemies. The game also recycles the same type of enemies constantly, and it can get boring pretty fast. If you aren't familiar with old-school FPS games, don't go for this one.

Recommending this to the super-serious, look-at-me-I'm-such-a-badass-cos-I-play-VIDEO-GAMES-all-day league of uber-gamers is a bit of a no-brainer: it's long, it's hard, and it's positively RELENTLESS with the wave after wave after wave after wave (I'll stop there) of enemies that the game constantly throws at you.
Make no mistake, you'll kill a LOT of things in the course of this game. With a wide array of weapons, of course: the ultimate being the "cannon ball", my personal fave, which is a bit like ten-pin bowling, with the nasty big monsters filling in for the pins. And there's a nice variety and eccentricity to said monsters, what's more: headless kamikazes with bombs for hands, stampeding hordes of bull-like creatures that send you literally flying, wannabe Scorpion Kings with gattling guns...yup, it's a pretty crazy game. Serious Sam Classic: The First Encounter is a fast singleplayer action First Person Shooter.
Release date: 2001
Graphics:     8/10
For a 2001 game it actually has nice details. I like the egyptian flair and the textures. They even implemented real floor reflections and pseudo reflections on some weapons. The particle effects are good. The enemies are detailed enough.
Sound:     8/10
The game repeats some tracks relativeley often but the tracks themselves are awesome in my opinion. You always have some kind of slow ambient music in the background and fast music for the action scenes. The weapon shots sound really powerful and fitting. The double-barreled shotgun has the most remarkable shooting sound in the game. But the suicide bombers have the most famous sound. Quote: "AAAAAAAAAaaaaa yourself!!!!" (Serious Sam).
You can always hear which enemies you will face in the next room. Hearing the enemies will lead to finding a secret path sometimes (grunting behind a wall => secret room with enemy).
Gameplay/Handling/Equipment:     7/10
Serious Sam is a game series which is totally classic. And the controls are aswell. I never had problems. It's  a shooter with the easiest setting: Get a weapon, shoot enemies, go into the next room, do the same thing over and over. It may be a little bit rough to say it's a dumb concept but this is generally the only thing you are doing (besides solving easy riddles and jumping around). Every weapon has its unique and obvious application. Shotgun(s), pistol (infinite ammo), rocket launcher, minigun etc., and this makes the game great.
Level design:     6/10
The levels have a simple design: Long hallways, large areas, small areas, all mostly square shaped. Some areas are unique: completely dark, slippery floors, jumper floors and suchlike. But these areas are rather rare. You will mostly face the large flat areas.
Enemies/AI:     5/10
I will split this into "real AI" and "enemies in general". Let's start with the AI.
If I only rated the AI it would be a 0/10 because there is actually no AI. There are only 2 commands: Get in range and attack. Yeah, it's that simple. And no, there isn't something else.
But although the AI is so freaking simpleminded there are so many types of enemies that it doesn't really matter. You will face suicide bombers, guided flying big green slimeballs, "standard soldiers", rocketeers, charging bulls and more. And this diversity earned a 10/10. Which is a 5/10 when summed up.
Story:     2/10
To be honest: The game has not really a story. It's so simple and stereotyped that Terminator would have the worlds best storyline in comparison. But I will give 2 points for the funny quotes and ideas the developers had. Oh I forgot to mention the story: You are a superhero rescuing the world from invading aliens.
Critic summary:     6,3/10
Personal fun rating:     5/10     [mediocre game]
If you like it to shut down your brain and annihilate enemies then this is your game!!! It may be lowbrained but it's still a funny, simple shooter with a big dose of self-irony. I don't recommend this game for people who are fussy and who only like games with a high standard.

Serious Sam TFE displays what an arena shooter can pull off.
The storyline? It sets the mood, that's about it, and that's all it really needs to do.
You are sent into the past to kill off hundreds upon hundreds to even thousands of enemies from destroying the future. Simple enough?
Serious Sam introduces literally the most memorable foes in any video game I've ever encountered. I remember each name, and all the stats because the game throws them in your face in a way that actually satisfies. Two shots per beheaded soldier, a quick shotgun blast to male Gnaars, double shotgun for those damn Kleers, loaded cannon to the major Biomechs! The best part is that these enemies rarely appear in troops, but in groups! You'll have a Biomech on one side, an Arachnoid on the other, an Aludran Reptilioid on the roof... how will you choose to approach this? It's all up to you and your powerful arsenal!
Something also notable about Serious Sam is the stunning detail. Each enemy has a spot-on texture to make it feel like a true foe, and writings, paintings on the wall give for a total immersion into the mysterious landscape of Egypt. And how damn satisfying that is.
Running through factual lands to kill fictional beasts has never, EVER been so pleasing. With a unique arsenal and engaging gameplay, Serious Sam gives you an un-parallelled journey to the beautiful land of Egypt with true to history level design.
I could go on and on, but I can't do this all day. Basically, I find Serious Sam to exceed in almost everything it does, and what it does, just never fails to amaze me in all the probable 1000+ hours I've probably played it in my lifetime.
A closely followed community also backs up this game, giving you awesome access to mods, weapon models, gameplay tweaks, sound edits, and much more to make Serious Sam the game YOU choose it to be.

As I effortlessly freed my corneas and exposed Euro Truck Simulator 2's collection of rods and cones to the flowing rays of sunlight this ante meridiem, a simple proverb rippled throughout my central nervous system like a message in a bottle, lost at sea. "He who first votes for the noose is the first to deserve the noose." You might dismiss such a substantial epiphany as puerile or perhaps vacuous at best, but I must assure you that such a colloquialism sojourns itself at an opportune place and time, for these years that we live in, decades of strife and ceaseless antagonism, remind us of life's fleeting mortality. If there are consequences to be cultivated, one must assume that such a rich environment parents these delinquencies with the ease of an artist flicking his silver-haired brush upon canvas. But alas, such thoughts were not meant to be, and soon the modus operandi shifted throughout dissemination as if it were a field of broken glass.
I recall a time when I was a young boy of eight years, enjoying the simple life of youthful bliss. Although my mind grew with each influence of outside stimuli, its cells could not mature fleetingly sufficient to understand the commonwealth of mitigating factors beloved of mine outside universe. A tenet soon developed in my doughty sanctum declaring such vagaries would never become a fait accompli. I immediately proscribed these inimical anathemas which invariably led to such perfidy, knowing these actions would result in a much more grandiloquent and harmonious existence.
A wise man once said "he who first votes for the noose is the first to deserve the noose," but to an uninitiated shaveling, such advice falls upon deaf ears.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 (commonly abbreviated as ETS2) is a vehicle simulation game developed and published by SCS Software for Microsoft Windows, Linux and OS X and was initially released as open development on 19 October 2012. The game is a direct sequel to the 2008 game Euro Truck Simulator and it is the second video game in the Truck Simulator series. The player can drive one of a choice of articulated trucks across a depiction of Europe, picking up cargo from various locations and delivering it. As the game progresses, it is possible for the player to buy more vehicles, depots, and hire drivers to work.

An Excellent game with a strong community.
SCI have done a tremendous job to include as much of Europe as they have, with more content always being brought out. The game is consistently kept up to date and with a massive community following the workshop has something for everyone.
Graphically it's very strong, with varied terrain around the major roads and a considerable diversity beside even the smallest of country lanes. Of course the detail on the trucks is tremendous but don’t imagine that this is all gloss and no content.
On paper it can easily sound a bit boring, good graphics or not, after all, to many of us a driving sim is about speed, drifting, power, acceleration and competitive AI. However, this game is stunningly good fun without any of that.
To start with, before you have any money, you drive whatever truck goes with the job in hand. This gives you a chance to drive many different makes and configurations of truck, giving you an on going heads up about which truck you prefer, and which types of cargo are your favorite, and there and many, many different cargoes.
Since you choose delivery based on cash, truck, cargo, length of drive etc, you are fairly well versed in all of these before you get to buy your own truck, and then it's simply about making money while upgrading your truck and building your empire.
Once you start to employ other drivers you soon find the money rolling in, and it becomes entirely feasible to skip a delivery in order to simply drive to a different location, either to explore new areas or to find a cargo that you want to haul.
In any case, while driving you must consider multiple options because you will need to make sure you are routed to get fuel when needed and be able to take mandatory rest stops, and, if time allows, explore new routes, and careful driving is rewarded with no damage to truck or cargo and full payment for the job.
Overall I would struggle to find a problem with this game, and I would strongly advise anyone interested in driving simulations to buy it. Using a steering wheel would be the recommended method of control, but I have driven with an XBox controller and the keyboard and it responds very well.

Ok, I'll give this game credit where it's due. This game (the regular Sonic DX) certainly helped out the Sonic franchise back in the 90's when things were looking bad for the blue blur. It's fun to play as Sonic and run so fast through the levels. There might not be a wide array of enemies to face, but the varying level design more than makes up for that. Each level is a whole new experience for you to enjoy. The boss battles are pretty good, especially the finale with Perfect Chaos (although I wish they just used "Open Your Heart" throughout the entire battle rather than splitting it up into that orchestral piece on the second phase). Even after you beat the game, there are mini-games and mission modes for you to get into. Additionally, there is the Chao Garden for you to raise your own Chao. Needless to say, there's plenty for you to do here.
Unfortunately, there are some things that just aren't as fitting for a Sonic game. While it is fun to play as Tails and race against Sonic and Eggman, or roll through levels as E-102 and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, some of the characters don't have a very good gameplay style. When you play as Big the Cat, all you do in the stages is fish for Froggy. It takes a lot of getting used to, and the fishing game is more of a nerve-wrecking nuisance (definitely the worst of all the characters). Knuckles the Echidna is a scavenger hunt game; you go through non-linear stages searching for three hidden pieces of the Master Emerald, and you get a beeping sound whenever you're near one. In Amy's stages, you have to escape a robot who is constantly chasing you. She does not run very fast at all, which is a bit of a turn-off in a game franchise that prides itself on speed.
In all stories, some stages are recycled. While the experience is different and level design slightly different, you can't help but feel you're just getting a rehash of a stage you've already played through. Some bosses are EXACTLY the same for the characters; Chaos 4 will fight the same way for Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles. The Egg Hornet fights the same for Sonic and Tails. Some characters have boss battles unique to their own story (e.g. the Egg Viper for Sonic, Z.E.R.O. for Amy, etc.), which certainly makes up for it, and the way these bosses are done perfectly fits the gameplay style of the character.
There are also some nice easter eggs.
In addition to the six playable characters (seven if you count Super Sonic), in the DX version you can also play as Metal Sonic once you get all of the emblems (save for the emblems for his stages). Unfortunately, he plays nearly identical as Sonic, which is a bit of a let-down.
All in all, this is a decent Sonic game. I've heard all the praise about this game before I got it, but I just didn't find it as mind-boggling awesome as it was made out to be. It's still a great game, however, and for $7.99 it's definitely something you should buy.

Are you somewhat fond of crappy JRPGs from the eighties?  Random encounters, level grinding, changing equipment every new town, and other sins of a bygone era?  Than you'll likely get a kick out of this game.  Based loosely off the script Jerry Holkins posted a few years back, this game adds a pixelated flair while fusing together several ideas to keep the gameplay fresh.  Combat is based on rotation, the faster your character, the more often his or her turn.  MP is reset to zero and replenishes at a rate of one per round.  Health regenerates every battle, meaning that more emphasis is put on figuring out how to survive each encounter over throwing you a bunch of generic, easily dispatched enemies to deplete your resources.  Also, the fourth wall explodes violantly in a ray of scorching light every fifteen to twenty minutes, so, you may want to watch out for that.

A retro-styled RPG hearkening back to the likes of Dragon Warrior VII and Final Fantasy VI. It's not long nor grindy, and intentional measures have been taken to alleviate the frustrations of older RPGs: for instance, you don't have limited items, you have limited uses of each item per battle. They restock out of combat automatically. Thus, the retro-styled RPG. The real fun comes from the Class system: each character has a core class (Gabe is always a Brute, Tycho is always a Scholar, et cetera), but each character can have up to two swappable classes assigned to them as well, a la Final Fantasy Tactics. Find a combination that you like, steel your heart, and prepare to battle with evil gods from beyond mortal comprehension on the rain-slick precipice of darkness.

The game does not look anywhere near as good as the screenshots would imply.  It is an ugly, poorly animated game with very poor melee combat controls that don't provide the feedback or satisfication you'd expect.
Aside from its desperate lack of polish, the game is surprisingly well-designed.  Rounds are appropriately tense, with your seven co-survivors dwindling in number as they succumb to zombie bites or the resulting infections.  Infection doesn't immediately result in a player turning into a zombie, and death can be delayed rather reliably with pill bottles; however, upon death a player will turn into a runner, especially dangerous and fully capable of wiping out an unprepared team.  Any bite has a chance to infect.
This system is the fuel for the game's drama.  The group must constantly move forward and quickly complete objectives so that they can continue gathering the necessary pills to keep their infected alive just a little longer.  Running out means having to put down your friends, or more frustratingly it means idiotic or trolling teammates will start shooting everyone up "because they got bit!" resulting in a lost round.
Combat is appropriately balanced, despite melee's flaws.  With the scarcity of both weapons and amunition, it is often up to one or two players to be the group's "fighters" that protect the rest who are merely wielding claw hammers and crowbars.  Sneaking is often the only option for dealing with the sea of undead, selectively killing a few to make a path for the group to slip through.  Open combat often means death, and so the group is constantly running away from the horde.
Everything comes together to make a surprisingly dramatic multiplayer game.  Unfortunately, the game's lack of polish draws you out of the experience, and the limited randomization of objectives means success is a matter of memorizing the map.  Too easily does the game's map voting system and the like remind you that you're playing a rough Half-Life 2 mod.  Game bugs and crashes further degrade the experience into a frustrating mess.
You can't argue with free, though.  The game's modest filesize warrants trying at least a few rounds.

Slime Rancher has a wonderful foundation for a unique fusion of farm sim and sandbox adventure unlike anything you're currently familiar with.
The game is based around the husbandry of slimes, which are adorable, diverse, and quirky creatures that inhabit the wilds, and eventually your own ranch. Their AI is simple enough to be endearing, but complex enough to offer humorous, and sometimes dangerous, twists. It's easy to take interest in their care and behavior, and they do a nice job of keeping the momentum going in this otherwise unguided adventure.
The game world is fairly large for an early access title, and has pleasantly soft and bloomy style, with colorful views and interesting wildlife. Exploration is rewarding, and the world will happily greet you with interesting views and a barrage of new slimes. There are a few hidden surprises and areas that are easily missed on the first pass, and you'll find yourself needing to brave the wilds often to acquire resources.
Gameplay is heavily freedom oriented, and every player will find themselves doing things differently. The tools given are very functional and easy to use, and upgrades only continue to improve your abilities. The controls feel smooth and friendly, and are thoroughly satisfying.
The core elements of the game are excellent, and I believe, and hope, that the developers will build tremendously on this title, without limitation from faulty fundamentals. The overall concept is a very exciting one, and the early gameplay is very promising.
That being said, this release definitely has its problems. Of them, the most frustrating is the sharp lack of balanced spawn rates/resource distribution. It doesn't take long to notice as you traverse the wilds that there are a LOT of wild slimes. Catching and corralling them is surprisingly less rewarding when you realize you really don't have to. Wild slimes are as productive as captive ones, and when there's so many to be found you quickly learn that the wilds are utterly drenched with moneymaking slime byproducts; the very same that you're supposed to painstakingly farm for. This means that you can easily complete every current upgrade without ranching anything. That being said, it's not because the ranching isn't fun. It's very fun, it's just rendered obsolete by the tremendous number of wild slimes.
I also find the population problem taking away from the environments. I often rush through populous areas hoping to avoid the danger and overall bustle of the massive slime packs. It's only when I find the occasional sparse area that I can relax and enjoy the scenery. I find myself wishing there were more of a hunt for the rarer slimes. That I could put on a sharp eye and chase them down, as opposed to being utterly overwhelmed by groups so large they overtake my entire inventory. I wish I had reason to keep playing beyond the 4 hour mark.
My ultimate hope is that the devs see the benefit in stretching the goals and limiting the resources. Without the friction of difficulty, you glide through the game unrestrained. The large amount of features this title has already in early access could be days worth of content; but unfortunately you're allowed to fly right past them after just a glance. I fear future development will focus only on making the game bigger, and not on making it challenging. It really robs the player of the rewarding satisfaction of surmounting the task. I can see a wonderful framework here, and I want that potential to be realized.

I had bought this game in early access, when Greece was still located in Europe(and not in the Middle East) because I wanted to support the developers and help them finish what seemed like a game with amazing potential.
After that, I followed the development at the forums, I saw all good things about the game being "watered down".
I saw absurd concepts like "indestructible interceptors" being divined and adopted by the developers, despite of the abundance of *much better* ideas and propositions by the community in order to achieve the balance desired, without destroying immersion.
I saw the developers insisting that, after >4 years in development, the trajectory of grenades is not weird to be the same as projectiles(and be stopped on 60 cm walls or on a soldier just in front of you), because "it is not easy to program" :o.
I heard the most absurd excuses about why random maps "are impossible to implement", while the original X-COM had them so many years ago(one of them was "the better graphics" in this game :o ).
I witnessed the arrogance of the developers(threatening their early access clients with banishment from the forums because they did not agree with the turn the game was taking, disrespectful to straightforward insulting replies to criticism and more) and their complete indifference and disrespect to the type of game they were creating.
I was given as excuse for the placement of Greece with the middle east as being "difficult for the game code to handle it being with Europe, because there was no land connection". It does not seem that Scandinavia has such a problem, though, despite not being connected by land to the rest of Europe(or, should I say, Western Europe, since they peculiarly decided to pick the cold war era for their game?).
Realism and consistence with the time period set up was an excuse(whenever they bothered giving one) for the things people did not like as they were holding down game experience, but was never an issue when the decision was facilitating the "development" of the game.
The game was getting progressively worst, cool features removed, flat progression inserted, the development team was obvious that they did not care at all. All they wanted was to be done with it. Believe it or not, 1 1/2 year ago, the Goldhawk owner was asking for coders for another project since "Xenonauts was at the verge of completion" and wanted to share the resources with other projects for cost efficiency!!
This is the history of the making of the game as I witnessed it. Result?
A Broken Game!
The game is aspiring to have all cool features from X-COM, Jagged Alliance and various other great games of the past combined, but it fails in all accounts due to the laziness of the developers, the inexistent game design and the ridiculously high amount of bugs in the game.
This game has the most historically and topographically unrealistic "realistic strategic setup" ever made in a strategy game.
This game has the most lame balance ever in a strategy game I have ever played.
I feel I was cheated by Goldhawk and I can say for certain that I will *never* buy or recommend a title produced by this laughable excuse of a company and they are the reason I will never again buy an Early access game again.
I hope that this review will save some X-COM fans from throwing away their money, because the positive reviews of this game are greatly deceiving and misleading to anyone that reads them.

I've been following this title for ages and while I couldn't resist trying out the alpha demo about two years ago, mainly checking the looks and feels, I never really played the pre-release versions. I prefer having a complete experience, so I patiently waited for the magical 1.0.
And now it finally arrived. I am not disappointed.
I completed a playthrough on Normal not using Iron Man Mode in an 18 hour session, interrupted only by a short break to catch some Zs. I was pretty much hooked right from the start. The base building and overall beginning of the game is very XCOM-y. If it wasn't for the 2D geoscape you might as well be thinking you're playing the original. But there are certainly differences.
The mini game for this got made over quite a bit. You can manually move your jets around the battlefield and issue basic orders like 'evasive maneuvers', 'fire missile' and 'retreat'. I found it especially fun to fight bigger UFOs. Get one Jet to distract the enemy and another to get on the bogeys tail, hammering away on his butt. If you don't like this kind of gameplay you can just let the CPU auto-calculate the outcome for you, with the approximate winning chance displayed on the encounter screen.
Annoyances:
- The Corsair is way too strong, making alien air superiority fighters nothing more than a nuissance.
- The amount of UFOs appearing during end game can get quite the hassle. Not because they are dangerous, but because it ends in a neverending clickfest.
Awesome. Finally you can freely equip your soldiers again (unlike in Firaxis' XCOM, which had way too few options after my fancy). You can use a squad with different specialists or just stick to a jack-of-all-trades kind of team. I managed to work with the latter, but it was way more difficult and less fun at the same time. However I only played on normal difficulty, so I don't know how viable this is in harder modes. I'd definitely recommend going for specialized troops.
Aliens behave differently. There are smarter ones and dumber ones. Overall the AI is ok, but not breath taking. Yet the suspense IS there. Playing the game in a pitch black room, sweeping the area for hostiles while trying to keep your men and the civilians alive never ceases to be great and thrilling fun.
Movement and aiming hasn't changed much, but the newly included suppression system makes the combat feel way more alive. It counters reaction shots, so you can't just camp in a good position until the sun explodes. However this tactic is very often neglected by the AI. Would like to see them be more aggressive. Yet again, maybe that's the case in harder modes.
Also, you can now just bomb crash sites if you don't need anything in particular from it. This will yield no XP/loot but money. Really saves you from getting dizzy doing the 100th scout UFO ground mission for just some crap loot. Good thinking there.
Annoyances:
- Why no quicksave/-load? The hardcore crowd will play in Iron Man Mode anyway, so why not include this simple feature? If I just didn't see the button, shame on me.
- Sometimes maps repeat, I only ever had it happen twice I think, but it shouldn't happen during the same game at all.
- Alien Bases are too similair. I always found the base commander in the same corner of the base (I did 5 base assaults). Can this be randomized a little more?
- Why are there ALWAYS civilians? If a UFO crashes in no man's land, there shouldn't be any. Just a minor thing, but the occasional map without friendly NPCs would do for some randomization as well.
:
Uhh, well it's an indie game with a 2D engine. If you expect some fancy AAA effects and stuff you will be disappointed. But I have to admit the ingame sprites and art work in the game's encyclopedia are very good. The battlegrounds look great and especially the alien assets (and UFOs) look very nice.
Sound effects are nothing too special but meaty enough. The music during ground combat is awesome though and really helps create the creepy mood. Well done!
That pretty much sums it up. The geoscape gameplay is mostly the same as always. Research, build, expand, intercept. I wouldn't know what to drastically alter there and everything is well made, so it's fine for me.
All in all I am very impressed and would recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the old XCOM games or is looking to get into this kind of genre.

It's 1994 XCOM (AKA the best game ever made) with the gross UI fat stripped out and a few surprising new tweaks tossed in. If 2012's XCOM: Enemy Unknown was a reimagining of the classic original, this is the faithful sequel it never received. A must for any die-hard strategy fan.

Alot of people love this game because they didn't like xcom 2012 remake and prefered the original. Well I loved xcom 2012, It was my first xcom I didn't play the originals. So if my opinion as a non xcom hipster is revelant to you, read on.
To me xcom 2012 and xenonauts are two opposite approaches to a xcom remake.  Which means we have 2 very different games which are great in thier own right. In my mind both have strengths and weaknesses when compared. And if you are a big fan of this tiny genre, then both are worth sinking hours into.
The most immediate difference presentation and feel, both games evoke the original in different ways. xenonauts keeps the old school full 2d enviroments and sprites, but opts for more realistic and modern art design. While xcom 2012 goes full 3d modern high quality models and enviroments, and yet its art style is actually more reminiscant of the original, cartoony and a bit daft.
To me neither is superior. I prefer fully 3d presentation and destruction of xcom 2012, but prefer the more realistic and grounded art style which is more fitting to a serious game; I prefer xenonaut's chinook and m16s than the kitch skyranger and haircuts of xcom.
Xenonauts ground combat is much more similiar to the original, and it frankly just feels very aged and not as tight or fluid as xcom 2012. Having a much bigger squad means generally less need to employ tactics, as each individual is less important. The fire/cover/hunker system in xcom 2012 is genious, xenonauts doesn't require nearly as much decision making on the ground.
You mostly just line up all your guys and fire away, often relying on numbers rather than cover or flanking. One thing xenonaut's ground combat has is that enemies are spawned from the very start, which is miles better than xcom 2012 hugely flawed spawn on LoS system. Overall I have to give ground combat to xcom 2012, but it depends on your own preferences.
The place where xenoanuts really shines and becomes WAY superior to xcom 2012 is the geoscape. That is base building/management aswell as air battles. There is simply tons more depth and freedom and is the reason to buy the game. Once you play it makes xcom 2012's geoscape seem totally meaningless.
You can directly contoll air battles, your bases will be attacked and you get ground battles to defend them, you can build multiple bases. There is tons of decision making that xcom 2012 lacks, and it's a core part of the game not just a afterthought.
So it depends if you want a in depth planetary defense sim, buy xenonauts. If you have no interest in geoscape and only like turn based tactical combat, then stick to xcom 2012 or something else.

I don't see any "non-early-access" reviews of Xenonauts down below, so I figured I should put one up.  I don't review things normally, but I find this game interesting enough to do one regardless.  I won't arbitrarily assign number values, I'll should post my thoughts on a few areas.  My review is mostly based on comparisons with other games in the genre, so to speak.
To help you all learn what I am talking about, XCOM refers to the recent Firaxis game, while X-Com refers to the significantly older Microprose game that inspired both this and XCOM.
Looks:  I imagine that most people today might be taken back by the "cheap" 2d graphics and general lack of flashy-ness.  You need to realize that the simple ui and graphics really help make the game look clean for modern audiences, while maintaining the feel of the original X-Com.  The UI does a remarkably good job at allowing you to understand what is going on (which I think is the worst way that the original X-Com has aged).  The game also has a decent variety of environments to look at, which helps evoke the sense of a global war as you battle among the ruins of downed UFOs from Middle-Eastern deserts to downtown Edinburgh.  That said, the graphics often seemed underwhelming when compared to the action taking place (something that XCOM did a great job of fixing I think).  This is a minor gripe though, and the graphics in the game do a great job of letting you know what's going on while giving a good sense of the era the game takes place in.
Gameplay:  Being someone who has played a great deal of both X-Com and XCOM, Xenonauts does a great job of "fixing" a lot of the things that were broken about the original game.  One my biggest gripes while playing through XCOM is that while it was fun, I never really felt the same sense of horror that X-Com inspired.  Instead, I felt that I had a squad of colorful (literally) superheroes out of an action movie kicking alien♥♥♥♥♥  While that's a blast, it is quite different from the creepy atmosphere and balls-breaking difficult gameplay of the original (and yes, I have played XCOM on difficulty levels higher than Normal).  For me, Xenonauts captured the utter feeling of terror that the original had in the tactical game.  It also fixes a lot of the dumb micromanaging of the original (like having to re-equip soldiers for each mission), as well as making certain tactics unnecessary (you no longer have to send suicide rookies through doors because you can open them finally!).  They also added in a second victory option on the tactical map, where you only need to hold a UFO for a certain amount of time before winning, which eliminates the need to go on those time consuming hunts for the lone alien cowering in a corner somewhere (which you can still do if you really want to).  Xenonauts also brings back X-Com's basebuilding and geoscape game, as well as (I found at least), vastly improving the interceptions.  Finally, they added in the very nice option of simply authorizing airstrikes against downed UFOs instead of sending in the grunts, which makes the game feel much less dumb at moments.  If you are a fan of X-Com, be warned about a number of changes they made though.  In order to make you reliant on council funding, they removed the efficiency with which you could produce and sell items for cash.  I believe they also removed many of the end-game options that make enemies irrelevant (such as blaster-bombs), although I could be wrong since I have not played this enough to say for certain.  If you are neither of those groups and this is just something on the front page of steam, this game uses an adjustable speed real-time global strategy map where you plop down new bases and send interceptors and strike squads as you try to save the earth from a massive alien invasion in the 1970's.  When intercepting UFOs, your fighters can either autoresolve the battle or you can command a quick realtime interception minigame.  When you send choppers full of your troopers to take downed UFOs, the game switches to being a squad-based, turn-based tactics game.  The goal initially is to just find out about the aliens and get the weapons that can take them down, all while surviving the invasion, and the gameplay does a pretty good job of making you feel that.  If you haven't played any game related to this one, you might find it difficult to figure out what everything means and how to play, but I might put a total noob's guide or something soon to help those in that boat.
Price:  I know many of are looking at that price and saying that the game can't possibly be worth it.  $25 for a 2d game that is basically a clone of a game that has already been cloned?  MADNESS!  If you are on of those types of people, I imagine you also seldom buy any game that doesn't seem like a sweet deal to grab, so just wait for a sale if it seems to strike your fancy.  If you like XCOM or X-Com, this game is different or better (respectively) enough for you to probably enjoy it.  If you don't mind throwing down the dosh for the game right now, I can tell you that as a fan and owner of both X-Com and XCOM, this game is a great addition to the collection.  Since it changes a lot of issues that X-Com has while remaining in its style, it feels nicely different from XCOM and just superior to X-Com.  If you own neither of those games, this is still a great game in its own right.  It's also one of the few games in recent memory that hasn't hit me with buyer's remorse.
Conclusion:  Xenonauts is really different from XCOM, since it plays much more like X-Com.  At the same time, it really improves on the old X-Com formula, making it worthwhile that way.  It might look a little weird, and if you aren't used to it, it will likely feel incomprehensible, but it isn't impossible to figure out what is going on.  If youa re interested in the premise, I think it does a great job of executing on that front (much more so than X-Com ever did).  If you don't normally buy games at full price, wait for a sale to hit like you always do anyways, but if you don't mind it, this game is worth the full price in my book.

A very cute and fun game. The kind of game that makes you lose track of time. Fun for anyone who would like to collect cute slimes and chickens and upgrade your ranch, and of course fight off the hordes of evil glob slimes when it gets dark.

I can see a lot of potential in this. The graphics are cartoony and the controls are very simple and easy to pick up. You run around an area collecting various slimes and foods to give them then corral them and combine them with another slime's "Plort" which is what you're aiming to collect. The resulting slime has traits from both slime types used to create it including what its favorite foods are, what kinds of foods it will and won't eat, and if there are any special characteristics those would get passed along as well.
However, my main issue is that the game isn't great at it's own automation. You can buy an upgrade for the corrals that allows you to throw food into it and the corral will automatically feed the slimes at a set interval which seems to be about every 3-5 minutes i would guess. The issue with that is a lot of the time when you just want to throw a ton of food in so you can forget about that corral for a while to go do things, it'll continue to pump out food even if there is already food laying there on the ground the slimes didn't already eat. So you run into a situation where most of the food is spoiling on the ground where it could just be sitting idle in the food tank waiting until the slimes are actually hungry so you're better off just manually feeding the slimes unless you really want to go exploring or have to be away from your ranch for an extended period of time.
So in short:
Pros:
-Cutesy, cartoony slimes to play with
-lots of types of slimes to breed and experiment with
-Easy to pick up controls
Cons:
-Automation leaves a lot to be desired

Lakeview Cabin is best known for the flash game that has been circulating the internet for a while, portraying a peaceful scenario, where you seemingly have the freedom to do whatever you want without a guideline up until the point where everything turns gruesome as you are hunted down by a monster.
The current episode released (Lakeview Cabin III) goes by that same formula, except with 4 characters that can be played to make survival possible (Or you let everyone hide and only one person does all the work).
This game gives you a setting and basicly allows you to re-enact scenarios reminiscent of 80's slasher fics, where you decide on how to dispatch/survive your pursuers and wether or not your friends live or die (by the murderer's hands or even your own) and giving you a sense of freedom to set up your own horror movie.
+Simple, yet pleasing graphics
+Random spawning time for the murderers (they seem to either spawn early or late or depending on what you do)
+Many ways to dispatch/hinder/distract your pursuers
+Gruesome deaths and in some cases the corpses get strung up by the murderer after switching away from the corpse
+Get drunk, get high and have a bisexual foursome

On a personal note: This is one of the few horror games I've played lately where I've actually been afraid, so I have taken quite a bit of enjoyment out of it so far and look forward to further episodes. Keep on doing what you're doing, dev. It's great and my money has been well spent !
