The Rescue Team games are among the best ‘casual strategy’ games. Don’t be fooled by my almost none play time as I played them previously outside of Steam. There has been a chain of disasters and you manage a team of rescuers (Duh!). There’s a ton of levels to play and a variety of actions to do like building houses, rescuing locals, putting out fires, exploding stuff, repairing buildings etc. Each game has 60 levels spread out in three parts. Each part has a different theme and setup, like having a port and a rescue boat, rain and thunder, different background etc.  The graphics are cute, sound is okay and music is non-intrusive. PA's OtRSPoD 3 continues the story of the previous games, with three main differences: first, the look of the game has completely changed to that of a 16-bit style RPG; second, the combat (while grounded in the 16-bit RPG style) is based on an all new system involving "pins", which are basically different classes with specific abilities that can be applied to characters; and finally, there is no longer an option to create your own character to join Gabe and Tycho's party (also note: nothing from the prior games is imported at all). The writing is the same as it was (perhaps even better), but if you're not a fan of Jerry Holkins' style, this game probably won't change that. As a fan of these types of RPGs in my youth, this game brought a lot of nostalgia to the table, and I enjoyed it for that alone. It's not perfect, but Zeboyd Games and Penny Arcade have put together a nice little retro package at a fair price. If you're a fan of retro RPGs and/or Penny Arcade, give it a look.

Serious Sam The First Encounter can easily be taken as a tribute to Duke Nukem with a similar style of both gameplay and storytelling. That is not to say that it isn't a game that can stand on it's own though as a solid dose of juvenile shooter action.
The premise of Serious Sam is simple enough, you are the most badass dude on on earth and you have to kill a bunch of aliens in order to save humanity. The game knows that it's story is not important and makes no effort to hide the fact that the only purpose of the few tidbits of writing you get every once in a while are simply there to make sure you know it's a single player game. What Serious Sam is about however, is the shooting.
Much like Duke the main character, Sam, is no power armored pansy. He doesn't need cover systems, regenerating health or turrets to kill his way to the alien overlords. The weapons are many and varied although the lack of anything equal to the shrinker makes me a little sad though. The combat is fast and furious your only protection against the multitude of projectiles being thrown at you is your skills at dodging, and of course, you ability to kill stuff so it stops shooting at you. The levels are huge seemingly unending at times and the game throws legions of enemies at you at a time making for some of the most hectic action I've experienced in recent years. Similar to Duke the levels are also littered with secrets and shortcuts that rewards the attentive players among us.
Graphically the game looks good without impressing too much, a good enemy variety and a decent amount of detail in the level design ensures that the graphics only add to the experience. The music is somewhat bland but the sound effects are of a decent quality and Sam's one liners are well delivered.
All in all Serious Sam The First Encounter gives you a great first person shooter experience the way it's meant to be played, fast, hard and hectic. At a good price point even on release this should be a must own for every serious FPS'er.

Seriously, the future of the species is in good hands!

Tomb Raider Legend. My Rating: 7 / 10
The Reboot of 2006 where the controls are different in comparison to it's simplistic father. I heard this game is practically good though it's kind of short and linear in comparison to the previous games; However this game has a lot more things to offer; Like bonus costumes, cheats, puzzle and plenty of things more. Sadly the unlockables as there are more to gain than it is to experience during in game. I beaten both the console and PC version so it's safe to say that the PC versions need some more fixes than the Console versions [oddly enough]
Why the PC version needs fixes? 1. The texture glitches are still there so you may be able to see through the maps unintentionally, 2. I had random crashes during the game before, 3. One of the cutscenes had the objects mission so carrying invisible things can be a slight problem.
Right. The gameplay is pretty good; it's not too hard to get used to unlike Angel of Darkness; The difficulties can be off the balance especially during motorcycle segments where you can take massive damage from the shotgun that can kill you 2 or 3 shots on Normal Difficulty, The machine gun damage received is fine. Music

Disclosure - the original SA occupies a special place in my childhood as it was the first time we got a new game on a new console, so it has a lot of the warm fuzzies in it. I've tried to be as objective as possible here though.
Sonic Adventure is a ****ing weird game.
It's a combination action/platformer/racer/pinball/fishing/arcade shooter/puzzle/snowboard game, and it really does seem like Sega were just throwing♥♥♥♥♥♥at the wall to see what sticks. And, to be honest, most of it actually does. Yes, even the fishing. It doesn't really belond in the game, but as fishing mechanics go it's FINE. Not amazing, not awful, but FINE.
The plot is eh, but I really like the way it's told - I'm a sucker for multithreaded plots experienced from different angles (ask me about Arrested Development Season 4!), and would love to see it used in more games. That said, having to do a big chunk of Sonic's stuff with Tails is rather dull and doesn't add anything aside from new ways to approach boss battles.
Runs very well for a 13-year-old port of a 17-year-old game, didn't have to fiddle with configs or anything to get it going, it just went! Camera's god-awful, mind, and they try to handwave this away by having a boy by the pool in Station Square tell you to "just deal with it". I guess it was made for a controller that lacked a secondary analog stick, mind.
Overall, not a bad game, holds up surprisingly well, give it a go!

This game brings back memories of when I was young. Oh boy, what a game to come back to!
After the success of the classic Sonic games, Sonic goes on a new adventure. The good thing about it is that it's 3D! It's the first 3D Sonic game to ever be released, and with it introduces new characters within the story. Some characters being important, and some characters being... there... (we'll get to that certain individual in a bit).
Sonic Adventure DX introduces 6 playable characters. This being: Sonic, Tales, Knuckles, Amy, Big, and E-102 Gamma. As expected, they will have different play styles, whether it's Sonic running fast through the level, or Knuckles looking for the Master Emeralds. Play Styles:
Sonic - Like in the classics, Sonic will run through a level as fast as possible, getting past enemies and obstacles along the way.
Tales - Each level, Tales have a race against somebody to get to the destinations. Tales can fly, which makes it easier to win.
Knuckles - Knuckles runs around each level looking for 3 Master Emeralds. He can glide, climb, and dig through dirt to find the Master Emeralds.
Amy - Amy gets chased by a robot, and has to escape from it in each level. She uses a hammer to destroy enemies along the way.
Big - Big fishes his pet frog in each level. This is the one play style that I despise because it's absolutely boring! Like, seriously. That's all you do. You fish for a frog. Unless you're a fan of fishing, I have no idea how you can enjoy playing as Big personally.
E-102 Gamma - Because E-102 Gamma is a robot, he shoots enemies with his missile launcher to progress through the level.
In each story, you can get upgrades to further enhance the play style, like E-102 Gamma gliding, for example. If I were to voice my opinion on which story was the best or worst, I'd say Sonic's story is the best, whilst the worst being Big's story (I seriously hate him at this point). I've left out their part in the whole entire story so that you can link the story together. Once you complete all stories, you get a surprise in the end. It's worth it.
I found the action stages to be memorable. I will remember playing through Emerald Coast as the first action stage, and also going through the Lost World. Personally, my favourite is the Lost World, just because of how unique it is compared to other action stages.
As for the soundtrack, they're great. Once you go through the Ice Cap action stage, you'll understand what I mean. There is another feature in the game known as the 'Chao Garden', where you take care of your chaos, and you... feed them to animals that you find in actions stages and then... take part of their body... (I have no idea). Another thing that does is improve in the stats of each Chao, which helps you race in the mini-game that's available. If you get bored of playing each story, you can always pop in the Chao Garden to see how they're doing.
Despite problems with the lip-syncing, it's a classic game that you can get hooked to. Although Sonic Adventure DX is my favourite Sonic game within the series, I say that only because of nostalgia, plus I haven't played much Sonic games other than Sonic Adventure 2 and Sonic Heroes.
Is it the best Sonic game in the series? Most likely not. But it is quite a fun experience. I highly recommend you play this game so you can get into the story, and how everything makes sense.

Beginning with the conclusion: If you enjoyed the original XCOM, buy this game immediately. It is a faithful modern remake.
It is not precisely the same--and every single change I have noticed is for the better. It provides additional control over some matters (such as UFO interception) that used to be purely automatic. Conversely, it automates some matters that used to be purely tedious, e.g., you are afforded an infinite supply of conventional infantry equipment. Like the third game, Apocalypse, you can view soldier stats prior to hiring. Like the original, soldiers are likely to die in one hit before you develop new armor, while aliens are noticeably resistant to less than concentrated fire. An "airstrike" option lets you deal with crashed UFOs when you cannot afford to send in the ground troops, and still nets a minor gain.
Comparing it to the AAA title is more difficult, as it has virtually nothing in common with that that it does not have with the original. The graphics are modern and pleasing but most resemble higher-resolution versions of Apocalypse's sprites, maintaining a mildly retro feeling.  While soldiers have "roles," these are less classes and more changeable, customizable equipment loadouts, allowing you to quickly change equipment according to any established preference. Soldiers gain stats with experience, but do not gain unique skills.

Do I like Xenonauts? Yes.
Do I recomend Xenonauts? If you've played XCom: UFO Defense/UFO: Enemy Unknown, Jagged Alliance 2, Breach and Clear, Silent Storm, or the new Xcom, and enjoyed it- you'll like Xenonauts.
Every update adds not only features I'm used to, but new features that streamline and improve the experience.
At the time of this writing, I'd say that the game is probably a year off being pretty much complete, but the current level of development is impressive. I'm looking forward to the final product, and have absolute belief that it's going to be one of the deepest and most compelling games on the market.
EDIT: Final product review, 07.OCT.14.
Xenonauts has turned out to be everything I'd hoped for.
This is the true spiritual successor to Julian Gollop's genre-defining UFO: Enemy Unknown (AKA XCOM: UFO defense). There were only two games that ever perfectly demonstrated the potential of the turn-based tactical genre- Jagged Alliance 2 and UFO: Enemy Unknown. These two pillars of the genre are now joined by Xenonauts.
The grand strategy? It's there. The micromanagement? It's there. The research and development? It's there. The tactical challenges of storming a crashed UFO full of very hacked-off aliens with plasma weapons? Oh, yeah, it's there.
If you're a 'thinking' gamer rather than a twitching gamer, this is a game that lets you sink into the role of planetary defence coordinator. Hours can slip by as you arrange UFO interceptions, juggle base creation against reserach and development, and weigh up airstrikes on a crashed UFO against sending in recovery teams.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough to the grognard-type gamer who wants a deep gaming experience without interface complications. I honestly place Xenonauts in my top ten games of all time- and I've been playing computer games for thirty-five years.
Bravo, Goldhawk. Bravo.
Here's hoping you make enough money from Xenonauts to buy the rights to the Jagged Allliance IP and treat it better than the last mob of semi-competents.
The last feedback I can give is to comment that it's a little jarring to have female special forces soldiers in a game set in the 70's/80's, but I'll take a little Sarkeesian-mollifying Social Justice Warrior history revisionism if it means I get to play a game this good.

A new era of shoot and loot is about to begin. Play as one of four new vault hunters facing off against a massive new world of creatures, psychos and the evil mastermind, Handsome Jack. Make new friends, arm them with a bazillion weapons and fight alongside them in 4 player co-op on a relentless quest for revenge and redemption across the undiscovered and unpredictable living planet.
Key Features:
All-New Characters and All-New Classes: Four all new playable classes including the Siren, the Commando, the Gunzerker and the Assassin. Step into the role of the Gunzerker, whose highly deadly skills allow him to dual-wield any two weapons found in the game. Not only that, you will build on that skill to do more things with two guns than you ever imagined possible. Dual machine guns? Cool. Dual rocket launchers? Of course! Dual Sniper Rifles? Sure, if that’s your thing! Want to try other styles? More tactical perhaps? There are multiple classes to choose from!
Dynamic Co-op online, and LAN: Share your adventures with friends both online and via LAN. Borderlands 2 features a seamless system enabling you to drop in and drop out of a campaign without ever having to restart the game. On top of that you can even take your new gear from any game to any other!
World Connected Story: Find yourself left for dead in the frozen tundra of Pandora as you begin your quest of revenge and redemption. Expose the evil surrounding the Hyperion Corporation and take on the perpetrator of a universe-wide grand deception -- the nefarious Hyperion CEO, Handsome Jack. 87 Bazillion...Everything: In addition to the new gun system, you will lust after procedurally generated shields, grenades, Relics, class mods and much, much more. And you thought the original Borderlands had a ton of loot!
Brand new environments on Pandora: Hunt through entirely brand new areas of Pandora that are more alive than ever! From the arctic tundra, through the dangerous grasslands, past the mysterious corrosive caverns to beyond, you’ll be surprised by the unpredictable world of Pandora at every turn!
Brand new enemies: A whole slew of new enemies are out there to kill you in Borderlands 2. Hulking, gorilla-like Bullymongs, vicious predatory Stalkers and the Hyperion mechanical army, run by Handsome Jack, are just some of the new enemies in Borderlands 2.

Many people reivewed this game talking about how this was a childhood favorite of theirs. My childhood, however, was largely a PS2-involved one, and any sonic games I did play were either the old 2D ones on the Mega Collection, or the ones on my older brother's old Genesis. Now years later (and after playing duds like Sonic and the Secret Rings) I finally get to play the game that forever changed Sonic the Hedgehog as we know him. After playing Sonic Adventure DX, I'm pleased to say that it is quite an enjoyable game, however, it definately shows its age in some spots.
-GAMEPLAY-
------------------------
The gameplay is interesting because each of the six main characters (Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy, Big, and Gamma) have their own campaign that once unlocked can be completed at the player's own pace. Having trouble finding emeralds as Knuckles? Play with Sonic for a bit and come back to the echidna later. Not feeling up for Big fishing? Go shoot things with Gamma and deal with him later.
Sonic, Tails, and Amy relatively have the same mission structure, and that is to run to the end of the stage quickly, only while sonic's stages follow that description to a T, Tails is more about racing a computer opponent through the level to prove he's faster, and Amy, armed with a hammer, is much slower, more focused on traditional platforming, and must also avoid an indestructible robot persuer. These stages are the traditional fare for the game, and are possibly my favorite stage types for the game (especially Sonic's levels.) Sonic's first few stages might have a type of "go straight to win" feeling to them, with Emerald Coast possibly being one of the easiest to glitch levels (at least without trying), but if you give the game more of a chance beyond the first two action stagees then you will find that there's some pretty neat platforming and speed in Sonic Adventure.
Knuckles, Gamma, and Big, are the most divergent of the game's campaigns. Knuckles' campaign involves finding three emerald shards to clear the stage. I'm not really too interested in these segments, but they're relatively interesting enough to keep a sense of variety in the game. Gamma the robot is mainly a shooting game. Defecting from Eggman, you go though Sonic's stages as your mission is to shoot down all the robots to free your fellow enslaved animals and keep up your timer, with a boss battle usually at the end of a stage. Out of all the gimmicky stages, I enjoyed Gamma's the most, as they provide a unique spin on the standard stages, and manage to retain the speed-oriented spirit of sonic. Big the Cat's much-groaned-over stages involve.... Fishing for some frog. These stages feel very odd and tacked on; the game definately could have lived without these levels, but don't worry; Big's campaign is the shortest. You can spread his levels out with the other characters.
What connects the action levels together is the field stage. You have three feilds to explore and each one is big and adds a nice exploration element to the game, something I wish the more streamlined later games would have kept. There's also lots of items for each character to collect to enhance their skills for more exploration, provding a nice sense of progression. Some may complain that it is easy to get lost, but as long as you refer to the glowing orb of light located in any area then you should be able to figure it out on your own.
-STORY-
-----------------
Before the 3D Sonic titles became known for their needlessly convoluted plotlines involving ancient prophecies and edgy rivals, Sonic Adventure 1 suprisingly stays relatively grounded under the surface and feels like the typical Sonic plot you'd expect. Eggman's trying to rule the world with the chaos emeralds again, only this time he's awakened the ancient diety Chaos, and is feeding it the emeralds to power it up. The game follows Sonic and the other protagonists on their various journeys to either stop Eggman or go on their own personal adventure. Each character has their own story arc that's simple enough to follow and doesn't get too melodramatic. The graphics and voice acting, however, give things a very campy feel, but if you enjoyed games such as the original Resident Evil for their good gameplay with cheesy, terrible voice acting, then you should find yourself enjoying SADX as much as you're laughing at how silly it gets. This game's story is not going to win any awards, but it at least doesn't try too hard to be something greater than it really is.
-PRESENTATION-
----------------------------
The music is very memorable and has plenty of great stage themes. The character themes with lyrics, however, are typical 90's SEGA cheese. You'll either hate them or find them to be a guilty pleasure. The level songs, however, feel very much like old school sonic tracks (some of them are even recycled from older games!), and fit nicely with the levels they're in.
The graphics are possibly my biggest complaint for this game. The game's visuals do not do it justice and have aged pretty badly. It gives the game a sort of unfinished feel and makes it seem almost like a joke at some points. Don't even get me started on the facial expressions of the characters. they're just hilarious. I feel the game's graphics and bugs are possibly what is most likely to detract people from this game the most, and what could cause people to prefer SA2 over SA1 (or older Sonic games over SA1&2 in general) Also for some reason this port doesn't come in widescreen. You always have this border around the screen at all times, which is quite annoying since SA2's pc port doesn't do this.
-OVERALL-
------------------------
I found Sonic Adventure to be very true to the spirit of the Sonic franchise. It plays very different from what you'd expect from a Sonic game (especially if you're used to the 2D games), but like Mario 64, playing signifficantly different from your 2D games actually works in its benefit, since SADX adapted for the 3D gaming environment, and while it isn't perfect, it managed to be an enjoyable game while staying true to the Sonic feel that also provides a variety of gameplay modes to keep things interesting. I almost wish sega tried improving upon the model laid by Sonic Adventure 1 and polished it to make more neat exploration/action hybrid Sonic titles. Heck, they don't need to have multiple characters; having a game where sonic himself explores fields for items and goes into action stages would be fine by me!
So basically, you'll like Sonic Adventure if:
-You like 3D platformers like Mario 64
-You like games with an exploration aspect
-You like games with cheesy voice acting
-You want games with multiple characters with different abilities and story paths that you can tackle at your own leisure
-You're open to try a Sonic game that tries to do something different.
-You're willing to give the game time and not judge the game based on its wonky first action stage
-You're willing to tolerate a few (thankfully short) fishing minigames.
You probably won't like Sonic Adventure if:
-You aren't really that much into platformers
-If you can't really stand a game that looks really funky graphic-wise
-If a few weird glitches deter you from enjoying the game
-You're looking for an amazing storyline
Overall I'd totally recommend this game!

GTA: SA has been a long time favorite game of mine. Compared to previous open-world games, the landscape for this title was HUGE. It still feels pretty huge to this day. It is chock full of interesting characters, missions, story, and gameplay. It almost feels like it goes on a little too long with the main story side-tracking, but ultimately reels it in quickly at the end. Back when I first played this game like 10 years ago, I probably easily put 30-40 hours into the main missions and doing all the extras (trying to 100%). This most recent playthrough, I feel like I definitely put another 20-30 hours into the main missions and fewer extra missions. If you are the type of person to 100% games, this one will keep you busy for a while. The bang for your buck with this game is incredible, especially if you were to get it during a sale for like $3 or less.
As much as I gush about the gameplay and how fun this game is for the most part, I would be remiss to mention the final part of the final mission is still garbage to this day. Rockstar had and, I think in a couple of cases with recent GTAs, has a problem with making the final mission so grandiose it breaks the game. Needing to catch people falling off of transports with cryptic instructions and uncertain landing zones is garbage, most particularly when the price is having to repeat the same 2-3 minutes of easy gameplay to try the obnoxious 10 second part over again. I've had this character you need to catch bounce out of my car, fly over it, you name it. Considering this is the conclusion to an otherwise amazingly fun game, it really leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Not enough that I wouldn't recommend the game - just so that you know when you get to it, you are not alone in quitting early and just looking up the ending on YouTube. It's so badly executed it seems bugged (and maybe was patched out in later versions that are kind of broken/unmoddable now....).

Rescue Team is a casual time and resource management game(RTS lite) by Buka Entertainment. A storm has ravaged Greenfield Island and has left the island(and your property) greatly damaged. Your goal is to earn enough money to fully restore your ravaged property. To earn money you must restore Greenfield island section by section by controlling  a team of workers and pilots . Completing each island section (or level) in the least amount of time can earn you cash bonuses(and gold or bronze trophies).
Tough decisions are the hallmark of good strategy games and Rescue Team has plenty of those - Do you restore lumber mills(wood) or delis(food) first to generate resources ? or do you rescue workers to increase  your manpower ? how soon do you restore the helipad to get the helicopter and begin rescuing people ? should you restore the bridge to gain access to more areas or do you remove debris to gain resources and clear more road ? Clever level design compliments the sound strategy to create a satisfying experience.
It took me about 10 hours to complete the game with gold trophies for every level - but I am no RTS genius - so there is probably 7-8 hours of gameplay for the RTS inclined - more if you take it casual or are a novice to the genre. The game has decent graphics and a competent soundtrack but does lack option to adjust the resolution.
If you want a good casual RTS with solid gameplay and intelligent level at an affordable price then Rescue Team may be the game for you - easy to recommend (this game would be worth twice the price if it included a level editor)

Rescue Team is a casual time management game where the premise is you're overseeing a group of workers coming in to rebuild after a natural disaster. You play through 60 levels where you manage a crew appointing them to do various tasks within a short time frame, about 3-5 minutes.
There are two awards you can get for finishing a level. The silver is for finishing around 5 minutes and is quite easy to get while the gold you get for finishing around 3 minutes and is often trickier. If you want to play low stress you can easily do that just aiming for the silver medals and playing through the game. Getting the gold is completely optional and is a bit hectic but there's also more strategy involve since you will often need to figure out the best order to complete tasks in so that you can complete the level in a shorter time frame.
Personally I found that I often got silver on the first try, then once I got to know the level I'd go back and play for gold.
Visually the game looks quite nice. The 2D graphics are done well and everything is crisp and clear with no blur or pixelation like you may see on some older or low res casual games.
Another aspect of the game is you get a wrecked house to refurbish and slowly do that over time by earning money through completing missions. This gives you a sort of progress meter for how you're coming along in the game though I did wish a bit for more to that feature such as managing a rebuilt town. Perhaps in a future game.
I quite enjoyed Rescue Team and found it to be a well made game for the casual genre that has a nice balance between relaxing and some strategy. It can perhaps get a bit repetitive at times however it's a game that can easily be played in short bursts and come back to later so helps mitigate that. I did like that I could pick it up, play a few rounds and then just come back to it later.
For anyone who's a fan of casual games and light strategy I'd recommend Rescue Team as a fun, relaxing change of pace.

Rescue Team is a casual action puzzle game with a time attack element.  Your home gets wrecked by an unfortunate extreme weather event and it will cost a fortune to restore your domicile to it's former glorious stature.  You are required to assist with rescue and repair missions across the islands in order to generate income to pay the repair bills on your home.  Along the way you will rescue workers to assist you.  Rebuild hotdog stands, gold mines, sawmills and municipal landmarks.
There are helicopter missions to rescue stranded villagers, and to douse raging fires.  You will rebuild bridges, repair roads and remove rubble.  You also get to collect resources generated by buildings you have repaired.  Last but not least you get to find and recover shiny sparkling gems.
The art style is cartoon like and has a cute factor.  The game plays perfectly at full HD 1080p resolutions.
The music is cheerfull and bouncy calypso/reggae chip sound midi which is a nostalgia trip to the good old Atari ST and Commodore Amiga days.  The tunes are catchy and pleasant easy listening.  In game sounds are not too disimilar to the modern gambling casino machines :)
Gameplay is fun and simple and gradually eases the player into more complex puzzle scenarios.  Players can reselect any previously completed stage should they feel they could improve on their score or time performance.  For some strange reason completing all the objectives except one and ignoring the time restraint, the player can leave the game running passively in the background to generate additional resource income and boost score for a round.
This game will appeal to young children and to adults who enjoy casual games.  There is no violence and so the game is extremely family friendly.  This game and "The Promised Land" would both be great first additions to a young players game library.
Rescue Team will provide many hours of stress free casual gaming and leave the player feeling relaxed and happy.  The game is extremely well thought out and appears to be bug free (unlike some disappointing AAA titles).
The biggest benefit of this game is the diminutive file size (under 40Mb) which is small even compared to patches or updates of other games.  So if you are one of the corporate laptop casual gamers pressed for space this is the game for you!
This game is less complex and less demanding than "The Promised Land" but is fun to play.
Rescue Team automatically tracks progress of each player name registered and so there is no need for a Game Save feature.  This is a great benefit as a player can easily resume from where they were the next time they open the game without having to remember to save.

Rescue Team is a cool little time management game in which you are tasked with cleaning up after a disaster on a tropical island. During each level, you are given a certain number of workers -- plus the potential of freeing others by removing debris. Your workers will then rebuild the town by repairing structures, collecting resources, rescuing villagers, and putting out fires. As you progress through the levels, you earn money that can be used to repair your personal villa, which has also sustained damage during the disaster.
Completing each level awards cash and statues in three ranks, with bonuses given for completing the levels faster. Achieving gold statues on each is a challenge, but just playing through the missions is pretty easy -- making Rescue Team appropriate for young kids or anyone who enjoys relaxing with casual game time that doesn't require a lot of brainpower. In each level, you have to determine in what order to perform each of several tasks so that you can keep your workers busy and complete all the tasks as quickly as possible. It's much more addictive than it sounds, and a lot of fun. It's quite a few hours of gameplay for a really low price, and the replayability comes in trying to beat the levels fast enough to achieve gold times.
Rescue Team is really similar to another game from the same developers called
. In fact, it's pretty much the same game, except with a tropical disaster setting instead of heroes and wizards and other fantasy elements. So, if you enjoyed that one, you will probably love Rescue Team (and vice versa).
I do wish that the game included Steam Achievements (it does have trading cards though), but the in-game achievements available do at least add an additional level of play for goal-oriented gamers.  Graphics settings are limited to full screen and windowed mode, and playing fullscreen at widescreen resolutions will add a background rather than expand the play area. However, as someone who tends to prefer casual gaming in a window, I didn't find it to be an issue.

Rescue Team:
~~~~~~~~~~~
Rescue Team is a  strategy / simulation game.
After devastating weather hits Greenfield Island with full force and is well reported on the news, you are sent to the Island to be part of the rescue effort.
At the start of the game, you will see a map with 3 islands. You will have to achieve all goals per level as fast as you can. Goals can vary from building houses, repairing restaurants, rescuing people (with a boat or helicopter) and getting gems. On some levels you will start with only one worker but do not worry too much because you will be able to add more workers to your team by removing obstacles like trees, rocks or repairing bridges that block their path. It becomes quite challenging when you have several workers to manage.
You will need logs of wood, money and food to be able to remove obstacles or repair buildings and bridges.
If you manage to beat the clock, you will be rewarded with a golden trophy which is worth $10,000. You also have silver and bronze rewards but the money reward is very minimal. Why is it important to get the golden reward, you might ask? Well, you have a mini game in which you repair your own house, and it costs a fair few pesetas to rebuild it.
This game reminds me a little of the first Settler game; just the way it looks.
The graphics are decent.
If you like playing against the clock and figuring out which way is best to achieve a golden trophy and have fun, then give this a game a go!

So, as you can see, I've played a fair bit of this game. Anyone who is into simulators and trucks can see why.
I like to take games like these serious, as if I was actually behind the wheel of that beast of a truck, hauling that heavy trailer with important cargo on it that just HAS to arrive in time, while also making sure to keep to the speed limits and not hit anything or anyone!
Here are the basic rules:
Yes, yes. I know, I know. But it's a simulator, right? It's meant to simulate, as best as possible, what it's like to do this for real? Well, I like to really immerse myself in these types of games. So, of course I'm going to worry about causing an accident! I don't want to ruin people's days, or♥♥♥♥♥♥off the client. Or spend half that money I just made from this job to repair my truck because I was too careless!
Well no, not quite. It's not really too expensive. Even less so when you get more experienced, level up your skills and therefore earn more money for a job, considering you're a more valuable driver. However, the prices can get high if you're stupid enough to race at around 90 mph down the motorway, and think you can take the turn-off at around 70-80. At that point, you're likely to crash into the barriers several times, and maybe even flip your truck. Even if you're lucky enough to not flip, your engine will malfunction. You'll be cruising along, at a cosy 60 mph, all of a sudden your engine shuts down, an error message pops up on your dash and your truck basically does an emergency stop.
. So, after a crash that caused quite a bit of damage, you can choose to risk your engine constantly going off, or you can call a tow truck that will take you to the nearest town/city. Obviously that will cost you, both money and time! So do be careful when you drive  around, especially with an urgent and important delivery!
Having said all that, sometimes it's kinda fun to just mess around. Who doesn't like to find out what it's like to drive through town at 70 mph?! If you have enough cash, and are willing to waste some, go right ahead and see just how fast that new truck you just bought can really go!
Of course, you can also upgrade and customize your truck. There are Service Stations in every city (that I'm aware of). There, you can make repairs to your truck, like replacing your tires that are starting to wear out. Go to a Service Station, select "Service" and a list will come up on the right side. It will list all the parts of your truck, what their damage is, and what it costs to repair it. All of the parts are automatically selected for repair, however you can pick and choose what you want to repair. Just note, whenever something has suffered too much damage, it will cause you problems. Just like in the real world! If your tires wear out too much, it will be more difficult to control your truck, since you won't have the traction that shiny new tires do. If you don't repair your engine, it will malfunction at random times and shut down. That can be several times in 1 minute, or happen once every 10 minutes. I'm not sure what will happen with the other parts, but I can guess that it's not going to make for a very comfortable and enjoyable drive...
To upgrade and customize your truck, go to a Service Station, and select Upgrade Shop. This will bring you to another screen where you can select a new Cab, Chassis, Engine, Transmission, Left or Right Steering Wheel, Paint, Outside Accessories and Inside Accessories. When you select either of the Accessories, some gray dots will appear on certain parts of your truck. Clicking on one will display parts on the list to the left. Hovering over a part will show you what it will look like on your truck. Clicking on it will install it.
Once you're finished, confirm your order at the bottom of the list and all the changes you've made will be saved. If, however you want to remove something from your order, just click on "See Changes", and select the part/s you want to remove, or just clear your order.
Once you've confirmed your order, you can leave the menu and see that beautiful new truck you've just spent the last hour creating! Why not take a screenshot and share it?
Another thing you can do is connect your profile to World of Trucks. You will have the option to sign into your account, or make a new one in-game. Once you've done that, you can go to the World of Trucks website. There you can set up your profile, see your truck stats for both ETS2 and ATS, as long as they are both connected to your account. You will also be able to change your licence plate number, for both games. Choose which Country/State the plate is from, then enter whatever you like. If you take pictures of your truck in-game through the Picture Mode, you will be able to see them in the Picture Manager in-game. There you can select which pictures to upload to your WoT account, and which one you'd like to set as a profile picture (the picture for that game, where you will see the truck stats). Whenever you upload a picture, anyone will be able to see it. Logged in users will also be able to like, favourite and comment on your picture, so remember to keep your pants on and smile before you take a selfie!
Once you've explored the game enough, you have your company set up, several garages and people working for you, bringing in so much cash you can basically move to Hawaii and retire. Or you've just got the hang of the controls of the game, but you don't like the idea of playing this awesome game all by yourself, then you can try and find a multiplayer mod for this. Personally, I use TruckersMP. You can use it with both American Truck Simulator, and Euro Truck Simulator 2. It uses your save game, so you will have everything you do in the single player version, but in multiplayer!
Of course you can also use mods through the Steam Workshop. Personally, I use mods that remove traffic, and I also got a mod that gives me a lot of XP. That way I will have all the parts unlocked in the Upgrade Shop and spend the next 2 hours going through all the new parts and paint jobs, and then try to make a truck that I'm proud to drive around the EU.
Just note that TruckersMP has some rules around mods, so any mods that are through the Steam Workshop will be disabled when launching the game with TruckersMP!

I can't remember the last time I've been this excited for an early access game. I started playing Slime Rancher right as it began gaining traction on the game circuit and I was hooked from the get-go. The art style in the game is great, the slimes are super cute and it's all around a very pleasant experience that you can easily pick up, play for a few minutes, then go about your day without skipping a beat.
The game itself plays a lot like a harvest moon game in the sense that your ranch also doubles as a farm, you grow food for your slimes, you raise chickens, and manage your multiple corrals full of slimes. For being so early in development, there's a lot to keep you occupied: catching slimes, collecting their favorite foods, surviving threats out in the wild (looking at you tarrs), exploring, and upgrading your ranch.
All that being said, the $20 price tag is a bit hefty for what you get at this stage in development. Not to say that it's not worth it, but some people may be a bit let down when their investment only returns a dozen or so hours of entertainment before they start to run out of new things to do. I very much recommend this game, but if you're interested in the long-term vision of the game, you may want to wait a little bit on this one.
TL;DR: Super cute, super fun and about as close as you can get to being able to buy happiness. Definitely recommended if you're looking for a game to pick up for a few minutes (or hours...) and unwind. End-game content is currently lacking, but is looking to be very promising as development goes on.

Upon finishing TR anniversary for the second time around, I decided to finally play Legend. Turns out that Legend, Anniversary and Underworld form something of a trilogy or at least Legend and Underworld form a story and Anniversary gives a little more background story.
As for Legend, I enjoyed it more than Anniversary. There is more of a focus on action and "doing stuff" rather than collecting ammo and finding secrets. The story is where it's at though, that's also a main focus in this game.
Graphically, for a game that's nearly 10 years old, it's nothing to write home about, 10 years ago though, it would have been pretty nice looking. They've enhanced it for PC, turn on the "next gen" features and the game looks pretty ok, with some nice lighting, water and shadow effects, makes the game almost pretty decent to look at. There are the occasional annoying graphical glitches.
Sound, guns pack a punch, voice work isn't tacky but it can be pretty grating some times. The one liners from the cast are lame....sometimes you think to yourself " I KNEW they were going to say that" .
Gameplay, puzzles are almost too easy, so easy you don't think of the most obvious solution because you're expecting something a bit harder from the TR series. The gunplay can be quite fun if you mix it up with more than just shooting stuff. Oh also, you don't have much of a choice in weapons.
One thing that carries over to Anniversary also is the annoying "trajectory" jumping issue. You THINK you are lined up properly for a jump, there's no way you could possibly miss the target or jumping from one ledge to another, make the jump and fall to your death. Then once you attempt the same jump, all of the sudden it works. It's frustrating and annoying thinking to yourself " BUT I JUST JUMPED DIRECTLY TOWARDS THE FREAKING LEDGE!!! " Dark souls eat your heart out. Using either a keyboard and mouse or controller won't make a difference either.
You can bust through this in only 10-12 hours if you're only doing the story and not the rewards. All in all, it's a good addition to the series and I'd personally recommend playing this alongside Anniversary and Underworld seeing as the stories are related.

This is my first foray into the franchise after II and III, and I must say I am severely underwhelmed. Yes, the graphics are pretty, I dig Lara's more realistic look, and the controls are fairly nice and intuitive. But other than that, the game's just too flimsy to stand up well.
The levels are extremely short and extremely linear. The locations, though pretty and nicely varied, never confer a sense of amazement. Again, because there's just too little of them, and exploration is almost non-existent. The result is that you just breeze through the locations, and never really get that epic feel that few other games could create. Even the secret rewards aren't really secret. You practically stumble over the bronze and silver, and the gold usually isn't all that hard to find either.
The puzzles are almost insultingly simple, and that's without the blatant hand-holding by the sidekicks and the solve-everything goggles. In platforming sections, the correct and only path might as well be highlighted in neon colors. The only challenge usually comes from the stupid interaction between camera angles and movement keys. The vehicle sections are phoned in as well, simplistic and boring, a disgrace for this day and age.
The most I can say about the combat is that it's there. If you weave and dodge a bit, almost none of the mooks will hit you, and all go down with relative ease even if you stick to the pistols. The boss fights are equally simple and rarely take more than one or two tries to get right. And the taunting gets old quick. The only interesting, and dare I say epic, fight was the one against the sea serpent, which nevertheless was quite simple and would have been over even quicker if the grapple lock-on wouldn't have been confused by the multiple targets. It also left me with a bitter aftertaste, since I pretty much waltzed into its lair and then killed it for defending its territory.
The story is nothing but a ham-fisted cliché storm, which I could excuse if the characters weren't so flat and unlikable. Lara is an absolute mess. On the one hand, she's supposed to be this snarky, tough-as-nails action girl, and on the other hand her entire motivation for the game is the quest to find her lost mommy. The writers mash together these two halves of the character without anything even approaching finesse. I find Lara's flagrant, even gleeful disregard for her own life and that of others deeply disturbing, especially in the context of said mommy-issues. The villains are simply boring and cliché, the evil magic vamp, the corrupt playboy and the generic yakuza (nice tats, though). After having read much vitriol about the sidekicks, I found myself enjoying their banter quite a bit. I felt they complemented each other well, and were significantly more sane and well adjusted than their sociopathic boss. By and large the most interesting character was Nishimura, the extremely rich and extremely ripped Japanese dude in badass white tux. Why couldn't the game have been about him?
As a whole,
is extremely forgettable. It has some good points, but they are lost in a sea of meh. At the end of the day, there's just too little to this game, both length- and content-wise to make it compelling.

Xenonauts has been heralded as the classic X-COM games spiritual successor.  It's been compared to both new and old X-COM and it's still making quite a bit of noise.  The game is very playable and very enjoyable in it's current state but the devs are still hammering out little issues, doing balance and stability updates and trying to get Xenonauts perfect.  If you liked the old OR new X-COM games then you should very much like Xenonauts.  I could spend hours talking about the similarities between the two games, but you can read that virtually anywhere.  So, I will try to explain the game for those of you who have never played it before.
Xenonauts is considered a Strategic Planetary Defense Simulator.  It's around the time of the cold war in the late 70's and aliens have invaded the Earth.  You are the commander/leader of the Xenonauts and your goal is to basically do battle with the aliens and save the world.  You are "graded" each month by the nations of the world and based on how much you helped them, you will break even, gain or lose monetary support from the nations.  You have a lot of responsibility and control on how everything pans out or works.  You control where you want to set up your bases, what to build in the bases, which aliens ships to shoot down, what to research, what to engineer, what roles your soldiers have, which soldiers to hire, and even which crash sites/missions to take.  There's a ton to do and it can be overwhelming at first.  I'll try to break it down a bit more.
Your base is pretty much the very start of the game.  You have to place your base so you have decent satellite coverage over land.  The more individual nations you can cover, the more likely you are to please them when the end of the month comes.  Anytime you shoot down an alien ship or send troops to deal with a crashsite or landed alien vessel you gain a sort of "reputation points" with the nation.  The more you deal with aliens in their nation, the more they will fund you.  Likewise if you do not have coverage and alien activity occurs in other places or you ignore it, you will lose those "rep points" and funding.  Base placement is important as is what to build in your base.  It might take some experimenting to find the perfect build.  Xenonauts does have a quick start guide to help you and one of the good things is, it does not overkill you with a tutorial phase.  :)
The air combat is a pretty cool feature.  There is a mini-game you can do for the air combat when you send your interceptors after the alien ships.  It's well done and enjoyable but one of the really cool features is that the autoresolve is actually really really good.  So if you don't care to do the air to air mini-game, you generally can autoresolve it and skip it.  To explain the mini-game briefly, you can pause or unpause at any point and your ship(s) and the alien ship(s) will close with one another.  Then any weapons you have active at the time will fire on the aliens.  The aliens will fire back and you have the ability to do evasive manuevers as well as retreating.  The aliens also can avoid your missle fire, so you have to plan accordingly.  It's all sort of RTS-ish with the ability to tactically pause.
The bulk of the game is spent in the ground missions.  It's what makes or breaks this type of game.  You have a roster of soldiers.  Hopefully you outfitted a decent variety.  There are preset classes as well as the ability to make your own.  It doesn't CHANGE the soldiers in anyway, it's more to ease you gearing up people.  The classes are: Assault, Sniper, Shield, Heavy, Rifleman, Scout & Rocketeer(and of course the ability to create your own).  So basically you click and assign your soldier to assault, outfit it with whatever you want, then save the gear configuration.  Then anyone you make an assault class will automatically get that gear.  They have different icons in certain places so it makes it easier for you to tell what role they play.
All that being said, you chose your soldiers, and deploy them in a drop ship.  Send the dropship to an alien landed craft or a crashsite and the ground battle begins.  It's a throw back to classic squad turn based strategy combat.  It's your turn and you can use any of your soldiers in any order.  You can move each and every one of your soldiers before you end your turn, then it's the aliens turn.  You move cover to cover and with the implementation of the shield units, you even have mobile cover!  All your moves/shots/actions are based on TU's (Time Units).  So any time you move out, turn, crouch, throw a grenade, or shoot, you use up a certain amount of TU's.  You can conserve TU's to make sure you can still shoot and move, or have enough for reactionary fire (taking a shot at an alien if it moves past you or shoots at you).  The entire ground combat system is done extremely well and once you get the hang of it, it's amazing.
Those are the big things to cover most of the game.  A few other things worthy of mentioning is the fact that you can rename your soldiers, aircraft, and I'm pretty sure vehicles as well.  Naming your soldiers generally makes you care more about them and is a nice tool.  Your soldiers DO level up, they climb in ranks, the lowest being Private and the highest being Commander.  Each time you go on a mission with your soldiers they have a chance to not only earn a promotion(i.e. level up) they also have a chance of increasing their stats.  The longer your soldiers survive combat and the more they do in the missions the better they become.  So it pays to play it safe and keep your people alive.
There's a ton to this game and I like virtually all of it.  I don't think I could explain each and every part of the game as there is simply SOO much.  I'll give a word of caution about some stuff and those are kind of my "things I don't like", or "what's bad" in Xenonauts.
Two things I'd say to be cautious of are:
1.  At the current point in the game, the devs are still hammering out issues here and there.  I have literally only run into one major issue at this point and that was my ironman game got stuck in permanent "Alien's Turn - Hidden Movement Screen".  They had planned to take the game out of early access at the end of May, but decided it's not quite ready.  My word of caution is to NOT use Ironman mode until the game is out of early access.
2.  Money is a bit of a challenge in this game.  Spending enough to keep everyone happy and getting good coverage but not so much as to over extend your funds and end up negative is a big challenge.  A LOT of people are having the issue of balancing what they need and what they can afford.  I know Goldhawk Interactive is still doing balancing, so it's something they are trying to tweak.  It's just something to be cautious of.
All in all, Xenonauts is an amazing game and I highly recommend it.  The UI is great, the graphics are nice, the music fits the game perfectly.  It's well worth the investment of time and money, it draws you in, it's challenging, and rewarding when you pull off a perfect plan.  Grab it now and support the Devs!

Review based on V1.01
Most of what is good in this game has to do with the fact that for the most part its gameplay is copied directly from the original (1994) XCOM. XCOM is easily one of the best designed games ever, so a faithful remake can't be too bad by definition, and this one is not bad at all.
Where Xenonauts tries to diverge from XCOM it does that with mixed results. For example, the alien races are quite a bit more diverse. One of the starting races is tough, has innate regeneration, but poor eyesight and is best dealt with from a distance. The starting weapons are great - the classic pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle and machine gun differ not only in stats (as in the original), but in their tactical values. Shotguns are deadly close-up, machines guns dish out tons of damage and can easily punch through obstacles, sniper rifles are amazingly accurate from a distance.
Advancing the weapon tech is, unfortunately, quite boring. It is the same set of classic weapon archetypes all over again, only gradually more powerful. This is exactly the same as in the original game, but after seeing the initial diversity of ballistic weapons this was very disappointing. I had the same issue with the Firaxis XCOM - a "laser shotgun" just has to be one of the silliest sci-fi weapon concepts. The more interesting parts of the original tech tree, like the mind probe, the motion scanner, the psi technology and the blaster launcher are no longer in the game.
The UFO activity seems to be much more involved, later in the game the aliens will start defending their missions with aggressive fighter wings that will bring down your dropship or fighters returning from a mission if you are not careful. The aerial terror missions are also a nice touch.
On the other hand, the interception mini-game is highly repetitive, and very slow-paced - I have been using autoresolve most of the time because it gets very tedious after just a few interceptions, and the game will usually swarm you with UFOs because of how the economy works.
I really didn't like the change where the engineers can no longer build items for profit - that option made a lot of sense in the original game (though was  probably too good to the point of Xenonauts' authors calling the feature an "exploit"). In Xenonauts your engineers are just wasted resources unless you need something built immediately, which you don't always do, so they have to be fired / re-hired as needed to save money.
The funding provided by the nations is just about enough to run 2 bases and fund two workshops. The only source of income for further expansion are the UFO raids, which are (relatively) less profitable than in the original, and therefore have to be more frequent. There is even an option to earn about 33% of the downed UFO's worth by bombing the crash site in order to avoid losing money when the ground squad is not available. Still, the income is quite low. For instance, the cost of a new base is $1M. Medium-sized UFOs that are prevalent in the mid game are worth about $50-75K if you raid them and $25K if you bomb them, minus the combat losses that can be VERY painful (a basic scout vehicle costs $60K to produce, and they are easy to lose). This means that in order to get a new base you need to raid about 15 UFOs with near perfect performance, and that is not considering the cost of buildings, staff and maintenance.
Ground combat is pretty much the same as in the original game, except for the cover system that can sometimes be frustrating because it is not at all obvious how it calculates the lines of fire, and the game won't show you the cover calculations unless you are aiming at something.
The game's performance is frankly embarrassing at times. The Geoscape scrolling is very laggy, visibility calculations cause obvious frame rate drops on larger maps, and the animations seem not to load until they are played for the first time, so the first time a new animation is shown it is basically dropped frames. This is simply unacceptable for a 2D game that is not particularly more complex than a 20 year old game that ran fine on computers compared to which your today's phone is a freaking alien planetary mainframe.
Overall, the game does not really add that much to the original XCOM experience, however it recreates it quite successfully. I am finding myself returning to play just a couple more missions all the time.

Rescue Team is a fun little Time Management game developed by the same folk who gave us the Treasures of Montezuma series.  The premise is simple, disaster has struck three small islands and you must send workers to rescue stranded residents and repair the damage.  Sounds good to me.
Time management games generally aren't my forte, but this little gem is a lot more fun and engaging than I was expecting.  Gameplay consists of completing various objectives (rescue residents, rebuild homes, etc.) before time runs out.  You're only given so much time and resources to complete each level and earning a gold trophy often takes you right up to the wire.
Despite the casual tag, earning gold is anything but casual and will require pushing your multi-tasking skills to the limit.  At times you'll be pulling out your hair, trying over and over again with different strategies to eek out those precious few seconds.  But once you FINALLY squeak in on time, that feeling of accomplishment will fuel you to continue on to the next level.  Addictive gameplay is an understatement.  Sitting down for 10 minutes to complete a level or two just doesn't happen.  That drive for perfection will often have you tied to your seat twice as long as you were planning, but I regret nothing!
There's quite a bit of strategy involved here.  Determining the order to rebuild to increase output of cash and materials while also managing buffs to get the most out of speed boosts requires careful planning and timing.  Any lulls in action often means failure, so moving as quickly and efficiently as possible while keeping all workers busy at all times is a must.  Once you get the hang of things, though, it's just a matter of execution.
With 60 progressively harder levels, there's plenty to keep you busy.  Each completed stage earns you cash to rebuild your destroyed home.  It's a small touch that adds something extra to the game, although I think the gameplay stands up just fine without it.
My only gripe is the lack of Steam Achievements which I find a little boggling as they add quite a bit of value to games like these.  And there are indeed in-game achievements to be earned (and reward bonus money), however the achievement gallery is currently broken and links to the House Restoration screen instead.  Once that is fixed and perhaps Steam Achievements added, there's not much I can complain about here.
All said, Rescue Team is a lot more enjoyable than I was expecting, especially for the price.  If you're a fan of the genre, you'll definitely want to check this one out especially if you're looking for a bit of challenge.  I see myself going for Gold on all 60 levels, and with achievement fixes (and added Steam integration please), will find myself back in the midst of multi-tasking craziness for hours to come!
Bottom Line: 7/10 (8 with achievement fixes)

I'm having a hard time classifying Rescue Team into a single genre. It's got city builder elements, with its resource management and buildings. It's got puzzle elements, with you figuring out how to clear the island in the proper path, and it's a whole lot of casual. But that's okay, as it's a whole lot of fun! I did not expect this game to be much, but it genuinely surprised me.
Rescue Team has the player tasked with clearing a series of stages set on an island that's been ravaged by natural disasters such as fires and hurricanes. It doesn't really show these disasters, but it does show the damage that's been caused! It's yoru job to clean things up and get everythign back in working order. To do so, you take command of a set of workers who can be ordered around each stage. Starting from the "Base", you can click on a pile of debris or a resource and your worker will rush out, do what he's been ordered, then run back once finished. For example, each level is littered with piles of woods, branches, etc. Click on one and a worker will rush out to clear the pile. While working on the task, a bar will appear over his head to indicate his progress. Once the bar fills up, his task is complete and he will run back to base with any gathered materials. It's very simple gameplay, but it quickly becomes more challenging. Before you start each stage it gives you time to lok over things and plan out your first few moves. Once you click something, the timer starts. Worry not, the timer only influences your final rating on the stage.
As you progress, you will gain access to some buildings that generate resources for you, at a rate of 10 per tick (tick = a minute or so, sometimes it seemed faster than that). Sometimes the buildings will drop an extra pile of resources next to them for you to have your workers grab. There are 3 resources: Food, Wood, and Gold. Food supplies your workers with nourishment, and is also part of the cost of some actions. Wood is the resource needed for most repairs, such as fixing bridges and buildings. Last, Gold is used as a cost for some actions, much like food. For example, fixing a bridge costs 50 food and 50 wood. Sometimes a stock of resources is stashed behind obstacles, such as a pile of rubble or beyond a broken highway. Accumulating the required amount to get past the obstacles is sometimes a puzzle in itself, as you need to manage your resources properly (especially if you do not have the buildings that generate them for you), as you can hit a dead end, requiring you to restart the stage via the menu. Cleared stages get you money in your bank account. Money in your bank account is used to fix your own house, piece by piece. This will take you quite some time, so don't expect it to be done in a short period!
The graphics are simple, as well as the animations, but they are full of charm. Rescue Team is a very cute game. Everything is very well defined and crisp. I did not notice any graphically glitches (or any glitches for that matter) during my time playing. The music is also simple, but it's very catchy. As for length, the game appears to be pretty long. You have an "overworld" type of screen, spanning a few islands, and each level is represented by a safety cone. As you clear each stage, the cone is replaced with a colored statue representing your score (bronze, silver, gold).
Very good game <3

Tomb Raider: Legend has the sole honour of being a game that I've bought three times now, on three different platforms, and 100%'d three different times. I've yet to regret it.
Legend remains largely unchanged from it's original incarnation on the sixth generation, a fact which contributes to just what a fantastically optimized port it is. Honestly, stunning. 1 Ghz compatible? Other developers could take notes. Ran suberbly on my 1.8 Ghz toaster of a laptop, though for obvious reason it did mean having to forgo the visual changes added as the game was ported to seventh generation consoles - which range from relatively minor lighting adjustment to complete foliage overhauls. It's menu-toggled.
There were more than a few glitches - ranging from moderately amusing (floating rocks in Nepal) to moderately annoying (Lara refusing to grab ropes, plummeting to her death as she phases through them), and the game isn't lying when it says Partial Controller Support, but on the whole the experience was seamless.
Tomb Raider has you control Lara Croft in her quest for some contrived MacGuffin, spurred on by some event in the past and important because they say so, damn it. It's not the most compelling plot, and lacks the spectacle or involvement you'd get from an Indiana Jones or Librarian film.
That the antagonists; Rutland, Amanda, and Takamoto, are barely given any screentime to banter with Lara before being unceremoniously killed off doesn't help. Of more note are the support characters, Alistair and Zip, and Lara herself, all of whom give wonderfully entertaining performances. In one case their brilliant spurious dialogue alone manages to elevate an otherwise okay level to one of the best in the game.
Variety-wise, the levels are all incredibly distinct from one another, while the enemies are unfortunately not as much. The platforming mechanics are serviceable, and for the most part responsive, but incredibly underused; the best platforming level remains Croft Manor, a completely optional area. Likewise, the combat mechanics with the various kicks, bullet-time triggers, and grapples are all well and good, but almost completely unused in combat. It's a sad waste of potential.
Of note are the bosses, that take advantage of the mechanics to some degree instead of pretending that the game is something it's not. They're not particularly memorable, but none are less than on par.
It's a short game, incredibly short - if you haven't got a head for puzzles expect a good 7 hours, otherwise expect something closer to 5. Perhaps preferable to overstaying its welcome, but completely understaying it isn't fantastic either. The one billion unlockables they've managed to fit into the game help to counteract that - from concept art to outfits (hearkens to a day when they weren't just DLC, ey?) to model viewers and cheat codes, there's plenty there to play with.
Best puzzles are all saved for completely optional content - that is, grabbing the gold tokens. These legitimately involving puzzles (unless it's Nepal in which case it's hidden under some unremarkable ledge. Gorramn Nepal), which often require breaking previous puzzles, are all infinitely gratifying, and would be more so if the game didn't expect you to have a near-psychic amount of knowledge as to where they are before you even begin messing around to get to them.
Seriously, don't be ashamed to look up a hintbook or something to get even a vague idea of where they are. It's ridiculous.
With all this fairly good, there's some inexcusable bad. The QTEs are bad. The "developer hints"; the frustratingly slow camera cuts to completely obvious platforming sections in completely linear levels that every sixth generation platformer had, are bad. The physics puzzles that expect you ignore how physics work - in one case assuming that a 90 pound girl like Lara can send deliriously heavy metal cubes rocketing into the sky with the help of a medieval see-saw - are bad.
But overall, Legend's saving grace is that it's extremely easy to play.
Everything from the writing, to the combat to the puzzles is designed solely for you to enjoy it and have fun. If you're up for a completely undemanding fun ride, to be completed with rocketing ease and satisfaction, then Tomb Raider: Legend is a game to look into.

Turn-based strategy is one of my favorite genres, I grew up on stuff like Fire Emblem and Advance Wars.
Xenonauts is much more hardcore and simulator-esque than those games are, but it does so in a way that's extremely rewarding and fun. All the little decisions you can make (like those regarding the minutia of each unit's equipment) genuinely mean something and impact the game, I never once felt like the detailed interface or combat systems held me back, rather they allowed me more tactical freedom and room to be clever.
If you want to play super aggro with flashbangs and aggressive shotgun units, you can. If you want to play super careful with extreme range snipers, shielded scouts and rocketeers to demolish cover, you can. Otherwise this remake of X-COM is extemely close to original, even in its awful, really awful interface and slow uneventful combat system. Seriously: Time Units suck, especially when interface doesn't help you much to predict whether you have enough of them to complete your plan. Soldiers can't look behind a corner! They need to WALK behind a corner, then TURN - take a REACTION shot from an enemy - then maybe SHOOT, then WALK back. WTF. Cover system is very obscure. You cannot tell at first glance how much protection a cover offers and where you should place your soldier to use it effectively.
New air combat is unnecessarily hardcore though it can have an appeal of its own. I struggled to fight against light scouts losing a fighter after a fighter, while autocombat offered me a 100% victory. It's not impossible to master, but well, it's hardcore. I warned you.
Back to ground missions. Maps are extremely similar to each other. I found myself playing on the same map three times in a row, only differences being my starting place and UFO type!
Xenonauts could be a much better game if they dared to shred some X-COM's obsolete features like TU's and interface micromanagement, but well, we have Firaxis XCOM with Long War mod for that.
Great games for all the fans of the original X-COM, and could also be fun for those who like the remake and want a deeper strategical experience.

DISCLAIMER: Review based on early access and on current V1.03 build.  At this time the game is pretty much ready and should be set for official launch in the next few weeks.  Still working on finishing V1.03 build so review will be updated and finalised by official launch.
Summary: For all intents and purposes Xenonauts is a modern remake of the ORIGINAL X-COM from 1994.  Where as the modern X-COM Enemy Unknown changed alot from the original, making it more of a action tactical combat game (one that I enjoyed alot) it strayed from the original.  Many a vetran from the original game (including myself) have been clamoring for a remake of the original and, now, I can say, that has happened.
Xenonauts remains true to the original and as a player of the old game I was right at home with the controls and mechanics.  To summarise, the game puts you in charge of an organization charged with defending against and alien invasion.  Your main strategic view is the Geoscape, a full map of earth.  You start out by placing your first base whereever you wish.  You must make considerations for how much coverage it will give you and to which funding nations.  You will be able to develope your base, building new buildings, hiring new staff, training new soliders, researching new tech and building new gadgets.  You will outfit your troops and aircraft for battle and eventually build additional bases to increase your coverage.
Soon your first UFO's will arrive.  You will need to intercept them with your aircraft.  This can either be handled via auto-resolve for via an Aerial battle minigame which is surprisingly involved.  Once the UFO is downed (over land) you will send in your troops to retrieve the wreckage and elimate any surviving aliens.
From here, the game turns to the Turn Based Tactical map.  Your troops will start in your dropship, and you will have to move them about the map.  This portion uses a turn based system.  Each unit has X amount of time units which they use to perform any action, being it move, shoot, crouch, etc.  Shooting can take up more time units if you want to improve accuracy.  Once you have used up all your time units for all your units, you can end the turn.  Then the aliens will take their move, and it will then go to your turn etc.
Fans of the original and of old school Turn Based will be at home here.  It allows for fine control of each unit and as unit get more experiened, they will get more time units and their other stats such as accuracy, health, reactions etc will also improve.
The aim of the game is to defend against the aliens, tech up to be able to match them more evenly and eventuallly defeat the alien menance once and for all.
Pros: Playing the game, I felt like I was playing the original...I cannot think of higher praise.  For all intents and purposes this is  the original, given a face lift and brought into the modern world.  It streamlines things a bit, for example, no longer do you have to manufactor basic weapons, nor do you have to manufactor items such as grenades, flairs, and ammo.  This was tedious micromanagement in the original which has thankfully been streamlined now.  Instead, you focus on building weapons, armor, vehicles, planes etc.  Grenades, ammo etc are auto-crafted.
Also, now you have the option of calling in an airstike against a downed UFO instead of sending your combat team.  I remember in the original, during end game it was quite annoying having to deal with smaller UFO's that I shot down, so this is a welcome addition for when you don't want to have to deal with them.  You get a small amount of money doing this, but you gain much more if you send in your assault team.  It's nice to have options.
Now you have a wider array of weapons and equipment including Pistols, Shotguns, Shields, Rifles, Machine guns, Sniper Rifles and rocket launchers.  There is a "class" system, but basically this is just a set of pre-determined equipment.  You can assign any solider any class.  It is useful for quickly giving units gear and you can set what gear each class gives.
The graphics are beautiful 2d graphics and the interface works well now with modern conventions.
Cons:  Alas, all cannot be perfect.  The most pressing issue at the moment is bugs.  Even at V1.03 there are some bugs still left to be addressed, but the dev team is aware of them and looking to fix.  Right now, for me, I get crashes when new gear is made and I go to equip my troops.  Since I save alot, and am now aware of this, it is not more than an annoyance.  I have spoken to the dev's and they are activly trying to fix this.
Maps - While the game has some random placement within maps, it still uses an existing pool.  As such, before long you will be replaying the same maps over again.  The community has already published a map pack to increase the number of maps available.  However, this will always be a problem when not using auto-generated maps.
Weapons - A personal issue, but each generation of weapons is literally a more powerful version of the former.  I.e, laser weapons handle exactly the same as the ballistic versions, just more powerful and different ammo counts.  Not an issue, but would be nice to get some more exotic weaponry that differentiates itself a bit more.
In Closing
If you like or are interested in Turn Based games with a strong strategic and tactical element you should give this game a try.  As I said before, when I played this, it was like playing the original X-Com, and I cannot give higher praise than that.
9/10
