This game is a time machine. If you sit in front of it for 15 minutes you'll be transported 3 hours into the future.
You're the achitect for a prison. Go nuts. Do it as gentle or as brutal as you want.
Prison Architect has me learning small fundamentals each time I play it. It makes me reconsider things for each new prison. How wide the walkways are and how many there should be for easier two-way traffic vs building space and overall travel
. How many locked doors between any cell to the nearest prison entrance for easier catching of escape attempts vs slower staff and inmate commute. Where to put each flooring to make everyone fast and where would it be better to make sure inmates are slow. What can I add to a room that doesn't serve it's main function but can help anyway - a shop, a phone, even a weight bench in a cafeteria can give my inmates something positive to do when they're finished eating and just waiting around.
For the most part I find my playtime in this game relaxed. Only when something goes wrong do things get particularly interesting. When things go sufficiently wrong
they seem to continue going more and more wrong. It starts sliding downhill quickly. Bad decisions start piling on top of each other later on when your staff are all too busy (or dead) to fix everything going wrong as soon as it goes wrong anymore.
Once legendary inmates make an appearance things change vastly to that downhill slide. These guys will singlehandedly tear apart half of the prison before you manage to take them down if you don't have a special high-secured area made special for them. They're just intense.
You get better at managing the more you fail at management. This game is all about management. Prepare for big things in advance and it should be smoother.

Euro Truck Simulator 2. I didn't think there'd be a day where I'd want to play a game like this, but a hankering came across me for something laid back where I can enjoy the frivolous yet tedious world of hauling cargo around and getting paid to do so. In the short time I have played, it's not a bad game but with the pricing between the base game and it's expansions, it leaves a lot to be desired in content. As far as I've seen, the base game with  no additional content is about as bland as plain white bread. Sure, there is a strange sense of fun to be had in hauling cargo around, but the environment quickly begins to repeat itself between the small pool of other vehicles you'll see on the road, repeating textures and a general lack any real challenge. The only challenge is the tedious grind of making enough money to eventuall buy your own rig and slowly build up your own little hauling company.
But of course, these things are in a sense "fun." As some people can enjoy the grind and knowing that the time and hard work they put in led them to having a profitable company and being able to look back to those early days of making squat for money. Now of course, I can't give a full review on that aspect quite yet, but I can see there is a certain sense of direction the game gives you and a set of goals to achieve. But some of these goals can be frustrating to achieve. Certain road laws don't make sense compared to a real world setting and the type of realism this game strives to achieve. Getting traffic violations for having my low beams on when it's appropriate to have them on, AI which is constantly speeding yet your forced to obey the traffic laws to avoid speeding violations and most of all the total lack of content after only eight hours of gameplay. The map is shown and as far as I can see this is one of those games which forces you to download the additional content, but is only unlocked once you buy it. Now yes, it's a company trying to make money and all that hub-bub, but it seems a prick of a move flash this content in your face but leave it totally inaccessable.
As for controls, everything is pretty tight and the vehicles feel like they drive as they should. Heavy, wide turns, good steering. The controls are great and offer a variety of control options to attune to your sense of realism. Whether it's simple automatic or your using a full on steering wheel setup with manual transmission. On top of that damage to your vehicle and collisions feel spot on, not that I've ever been in a semi-truck when it collides with something.
Overall, it's not a bad game but it's certainly not meant for everyone. If you enjoy the abuse of tedious long range driving and making a meager wage as you slowly but surely build yourself up through a tedious joureny back and forth across Europe, you'll have some fun. Can I recommend it? Just barely. It's not a bad game, but the absurd amount of additional content (or what appears to be an absurd amount) seems like blatant pandering and hiding what looks like it should be base content behind paywalls. Then again, that may be just my personal frustration venting.

I'm a fan of Michel Gagne's art style, which is why I sought out this game. It's also worth noting that this uses the silhouette art style
It's a great, little action/adventure game, and very unique. It does a fantastic job of communicating game mechanics to the player without the use of language. You play as a flying saucer in an alien world, awkwardly floating around. It's effectively a 2D metroidvania, but because you fly, it's not a platformer. You're mostly navigating through subterranean tunnels. It's also very much a twin-stick shooter (although the shooter aspect is downplayed). It's a lot of fun to figure out how to get past certain obstacles through the visual clues given, and that's the heart of the game, really. You acquire various tool appendages for your spacecraft, and use them to solve issues of obstacles, allowing you to progress.
It's a bit of a thrill to come across new, gigantic creatures, shapes, and environmental challenges. The difficulty is just right. Boss battles typically took me 2-3 tries.

Hackmud is not straightforward. It is a game about screwing up, learning from your mistakes, and throwing whatever you can at the wall to see what sticks. Thus, you are going to be confused, and you're going to be straining to figure out puzzles and shouting at the screen a lot. If you've done programming/software development before, you may find it akin to learning a new programming language because it's just SO FULL of useful things that you have no idea how to put together correctly.
If you're looking for a cyberpunk-esque game where you can sit down and finish it in a weekend or two, this is not the game you're looking for. There are no straightforward goals, there is very little documentation, and you will have constant questions. If you come into the game expecting, well... a game, then you're definitely going to be frustrated. I'd probably put this in the category of
.
Now, after realizing that this was the sort of game that hackmud is going to be, I found it absolutely fascinating. It's a game that's driven by the community, and it definitely helps to have friends who you can play with. You can go it alone, but it will be a slow march; you may lose interest and patience before it starts getting "fun". Luckily, there's a public/official Discord so you can make these ties and hopefully learn a thing or two from more experienced players. You're indirectly interacting with other players most of the time, and a large portion of my time so far has just been searching the FULLSEC scripts sectors, just exploring what other people have made and done. I've stumbled across entire RPG systems built in the scripting systems, complete with registration. I think I accidentally applied to a corporation, in fact. It's just so overwhelming and I want to explore everything that this game has to offer.
A few more miscellaneous points so I don't have a 5-paragraph essay of a review:
It's definitely tough, but if you stick with it and go in with a couple of friends, you're going to have a blast.

I don't usually review games that I play. ｈａｃｋｍｕｄ, however, is an exception. It is
your run-of-the-mill hacking simulator. It surprises you with many things right from the beginning. From the text-only visuals (it might be a flaw for
people, but I actually like it), through the puzzles, to Lena Raine's music. After the 2-6 hour singleplayer part, you are thrown directly into the deep water. This game does not hold your hand
The interface is entirely text-based; that means imagination will be your main "display". There is almost everything. Casinos, news networks, freelancers, corporations, hackers for hire, just anything you could imagine and turn into a script. Do you want to make a game in a game? Open up your text editor and get typing! One of the most important parts in the Multi User Domain are scripts. Those are written in what is basically JavaScript, but with enforced strict mode and a few minor changes to avoid sandbox breaks. There is also a database at your disposal, it is MongoDB. As of 21.09.2017, there are over 13
scripts that players have made. However, not all of them are safe. Some of them are very useful, like lock crackers or loc (system access script - an IRL equivalent would be an IP) storages, but some of them are so brutal that they'll send all of your GC (Global Currency) and upgrades to an unknown user, breach your system and post said system location in the main chat channel (0000). How would you decide which one you should run, and which one you shouldn't? Script safety is defined in security levels ranging from FULLSEC to NULLSEC, where FULLSEC is totally safe (It can humiliate you in chat though
), and NULLSEC is the most likely to decimate your system. When in doubt, scripts.get_level. The community is one of the best I've ever seen. If you ask anything, you'll most likely get an answer in less than a minute. (or have your stuff
protected by xena.defender, that's an option too) However, because to send a message in game you need to type a (kind of a) long string: "chats.send {to:"channel_name", msg:"message"}", that's why most players can be found on the unofficial
Even the developer hangs around there and sometimes drops cryptic hints, sometimes fixes things.

If you have played Hacknet and Uplink and like them both, this game is for you! The style of hacking is different than those two games, and this one's multiplayer with brand new twists. It's got action, adventure, scams, and creativity everywhere. With user-made content and the possibility to create almost anything, this game really is something special.
P.S: scripts.get_level will be your best friend, trust me on that

Xenonauts is Xcom's less flashy, more in-depth brother: where Xcom is streamlined and sexy, Xenonauts is more tactical and strategic.
In other words, where Xcom is more about how a team of super heroes saves the world by working their way up to god-like power and ability, Xenonauts is more like a real special forces sim: sooner or later, something is going to get someone (or half the team) whacked, and your going need to prepare if you don't want to lose the game. In other words, the loss hurts, but it is far more manageble than Xcom.
Renaming soldiers after friends & family makes their deaths more tragic/hilarious. 10/10

I'll be honest, I was sort of expecting quite a lot from this game. I know it came out before the Anniversary edition, but seeing as it was popular enough to Make the Anniversary game, I was hoping this would top it up well. But it's not bad, regardless. The graphics are actually really lovely. It looks good, but nothing Too special in my taste. Plus, I felt like the game didn't look finished. There were areas where the characters would move around inside a car and their hair or arm would move through the solid of the vehicle. It was odd to look at, and even the animation was very awkward, and I'm pointing it out because from the time it came out. Reason why the score is actually lower is because of it's story. Incredibly bland, super cheesy, and nothing too awe-strucking.
But I will admit, what made this game it's credit was it's gameplay. The controlers are really easy to manuever, Lara's really fun to move and play arond with, and the physics within work well. It's got pretty good puzzles, awesome boss battles, and I liked the chasing scenes a lot for some reason. It's a little bit too easy, but still got me entertained in game. Just not with the cutscenes.
What really bummed me getting this game on Steam is that it doesn't support it's Overlay, nor could I have taken any screenshots, but that's my personal opinion, and I think TR:Underworld is the same. But beside that, it's a pretty good action/puzzle game, much like Anniversary, but don't expect much with the story. I'll still recommend it because it's really really fun!

Hackmud is a game with a huge focus on pvp actions, most of what happens involves the community. To get a good advantage you'll need an understanding Javascript since you'll be reliant on others if you don't know how to write any. Events are ether from the dev or the
Since it has a focus on programming knowledge, you'll see lots of people using external bots for various uses, such as farming or automated systems not supported by in game bots, which takes away from the experience and gameplay in the name of personal gain for themselves, with a disregard for others.
The Tutorial is completly different than the main game, and in fact most of the people don't hang around in the default chat room, which is almost always void of players, they tend to hang in the discord since its easier to conversate in and you can easily find any previous chat there.
I don't suggest buying this game if you don't know programming or don't like interacting with a community very much as if you do know programming, you can write everything on your own from market scripts to corp scrapers.
If you do like being part of a community and constantly being part of whats going on, since you are part of the current events, then you won't have any issue with relying on corperations you're a part of, or knowing whats going on. Though if you don't know anything about coding you may find difficulty fitting unless you learn.
Its very open ended and its mostly driven by greed of wanting the most money, or power. In terms of lore, its mostly from what next happens in terms of current events. Theres no quests or drive to do anything. Its just what people want to do, regardless of how ruthless or pleasant. Could be a puzzle, could be a scheme, could be a bounty.
Lastly, holy hell does it have a lot of bots. You'll spot them everywhere as a user. Default chat channel is full of in game bots, an acessory to having someone do something simple like advertise for you. Thats not bad, however theres OOG bots that are far better. People use Out of Game bots to farm and in some cases target users to an extent they're no longer safe. They run on code that runs outside the game and interacts with it as it can.
This is easy as bots just need to copy and paste info and follow directions in their code. If told to go after someone and send me everything, they will. Out of Game bots are game breaking to the point its basically pay to win and you're competing against everyone with bots. They paid for other users, their server space, and I'm not surprised if they have other steam accounts. Theres been no way to combat this for a while and I doubt it'll ever change. Its like playing any shooter and you're trying to compete people using aimbot.
If you aren't prepared to break the game trying to play it and just want a good game to play for a while, look elsewhere. You don't even get to see the real game until you beat the tutorial which is too long to get a refund if you just want to try it out for real.

Sonic Adventure
Tive o prazer de jogar o original na Dreamcast.
Lançado pela Sega em 1998 e 1999 para o Dreamcast, em 2003, foi lançado Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut, para Nintendo GameCube e PC.
Sonic Adventure evolui em todos os aspectos, é o primeiro jogo em 3D da série Sonic
O visual dos personagens mudou bastante, todos ganharam um estilo mais radical, principalmente Sonic que ficou com uma aparência mais radical que o clássico.
Enquanto a História passado alguns anos após Sonic e Knuckles terem derrotado Eggman na Death Egg, a cidade de Station Square é ameaçada por um novo inimigo, Chaos, que se alimenta das esmeraldas do caos, ao alimentar-se das 7 esmeraldas Chaos torna-se Perfect Chaos uma verdadeira ameaça.
O Dr. Eggman, queria controlar Chaos e ajuda-lo na busca das 7 esmeraldas para destruir, Station Square e construir em o seu império Robotnikland ou Eggmaland.
Cabe aos heróis impediram Eggman e recuperarem as esmeraldas antes que seja tarde demais.
É possivel jogar seis Personagens com História diferentes que acabam por interligar-se.
As personagens são : Sonic the Hedgehog, Tails, Knuckles, Amy Rose, Big the Cat e E-102 Gamma.
Temos um mundo aberto para explorar a vontade: Station Square, uma cidade muito movimentada, Mystic Ruins, uma floresta muito extensa e cheia de mistérios. Egg Carrier, a nave de Eggman, vale a pena explorar todos os cantos.
Sonic Adventure possui sérios problemas de câmera, onde perdemos a noção do espaço temos de perder algum tempo a ajustar a câmera manualmente.
Um dos melhores Sonic que algumas vez joguei.

First of all, I have to say that a lot of what I am going to say is my personal take on this game.
When I first got started into this, I knew that it was not going to be an extremely easy learning curve. However, having coming from the background of not knowing a lot about programming and scripting (a lot of that is done in this game), I have to say that it definetly got me motivate to learn and experiement with what this game and it's community has to offer.
Right off the bat, the tutorial gave me a lot of help with the syntax and logic the game requires you to know (how to chat, run commands to hack npcs, etc). It also teaches you to be careful with whom and what you trust. Especially after the tutorial does this come into play (Haven't been tricked into giving all my currency away YET :P).
One point people seem to be dissapointed with is the lack of player interaction within the game, with a lot of botting going on. However, that is where it is key to get connected with the community as soon as possible! They are a HUGE help, many of them (dtr is one) who are happy to give help to anyone knew to coding and scripting as I am.
This does not mean you will become an expert overnight, or even within a week. However, if you have always wanted to learn more about coding/scripting, this game can give you motivation to learn how like it is giving me.
----
In short, Hackmud. . .
* Gives a reason to learn more about programming and scripting. (All scripting is done in Javascript)
* Has a warm and welcoming community, while at the same time teaching you to be careful with whom you trust with your user info and gc.
* Has a lot of user made content that rocks (Someone is currently trying to develop an rpg in here!!)
If any of those things peak your interest, you should definetly check it out and jump on to it's discord channel!

The Deer is supposed to be an educational game for kids. I say supposed to because i don't even know the age target. This game is mainly divided into two parts: a wall of history text and minigames.
The wall of history explains about deer ancestors and animal history in general. I think that only a children at least of elementary school grade will be able to understand these kind of information, not to mention that they have to have some knowledge about these topic first because there are too many unexplained infos to make it not detailed, such as what is Pleistocence Epoch and Cretaceous Period? Also, why Cretaceous Period comes to an end? Even though the informations are not detailed, there are just too many texts to read in the game that i prefer to just glimpse the text. I suggest to make the "walk" longer (to prevent it being a wall of text) and add more detailed information as you walk. Adding pictures on the information will be nice too. Another thing to add, there is a text which has the same color with the moving cloud (white) and i have to wait until the cloud to pass so i can read the text.
Although i said that the history is for at least elementary school children, i have to say that some elementary school children will be bored with the minigames. There are only three (yes, three) minigames in total, 2 being very simple for children while the other one, Snacks & Lunch, might be quite hard and it has no informational value. I suggest for you to add text on the correct food and maybe add some information about deers in winter period in general (since it's about being prepared for the winter) after the game ends. Also, the only game with a name on it (before entering) is the memory game. Why don't you put the name on all minigames?
The graphics are cute and suitable for the kids, although as i said before, the text are just too much. I feel like walking in a wall of text rather than enjoying the scenery.
The music is quite relaxing; it gives the feeling like you are on the beach. The sfx of the deer going to the ocean doesn't feel odd and is suitable with the bgm.
Pros:
- 3 minigames
- Animal (mostly deer) history
Cons:
- Unclear age target; the texts are not suitable for younger children and the minigames are not suitable for older children.
- Too much text displayed on screen.
- Information is still not detailed enough.
Although it has a great potential for an educational game, the unclear age target makes it better to be polished up more before it's released.

If you're looking for a game that captured the feeling of the original X-Com then look no further.
With stellar 3d to 2d rendered sprites, an art style and design the is reminiscent of an older generation of games though I think it would be going too far to call it "retro". Its both pleasing to the eye and has excellent clarity, all the information you need at the tip of your eyeballs and fingers to make the best strategic and tacticle decisions to defeat the disgusting xeno threat.
The gameplay is heavily inspired by the bygone days of the past, with enough updates, improvements and modernizations that streamline the drudgery of the past (like the micromanagement intense menu screens of the original X-Com that are themselves evoke thoughts of Dwarf Fortress un-modded) into a lighter area by trimming back the intensity of the learning curve (such as buying ammo, etc) leaving the player with the same amount of depth and variety without leaving newer players in quicksand googling guides.
If you're looking for a game where no one dies, aliens are made of paper and losing is impossible - look elsewhere. Your best men can be cut down like wheat by the advanced alien troops, who can at times seem to be made out of 40ft thick brick walls with angry faces painted on them.
The risk of having your best men enhances the gameplay so much more than I would have thought, I truly cared about each soldier and shook my fist at the alien menace when my important men were gunned down mere feet from the landing craft.
Theres a lot to this game, and if you're still on the fence there are plenty of videos on Youtube of people playing it - go look there and you'll find some great gameplay videos for the most part!
Just be wary, some of the videos are old and may be on outdated builds that have bugs which no longer exist in this release and if I do have anything negative to say about this game its that it isn't a fully polished release and bugs do crop up from time to time, the majority of which aren't gamebreaking but once in a while I've seen a bug cripple someones game despite myself not having seen one.

All right, first things first; I would say (largely) discount the negative reviews. (Apparently some folks still don't yet understand how the concept of 'Early Access' works.) That being said, if you're the kind of person who might agree with those people, I would wholeheartedly recommend waiting until after development is completed to pick up (or at the very least, play) your own copy of Xenonauts. Goldhawk has been releasing updates with fair regularity, the game has been getting better and more complete each time, and they are currently very close (I'd venture to guess somewhere around 90%, give or take 5% or so) to having the game ready for its final update.
Is Xenonauts X-COM? No. (Of course, if you asked me if the most recent X-COM was X-COM, you'd get the same answer. I thought Firaxis did an interesting job with Enemy Unknown, it's just not the X-COM I grew up with.) Again, that being said, Xenonauts is the game that comes closest to emulating the feel of the original X-COM that I have ever seen. There have been many, many, MANY attempts at recapturing that brutal magic over the years; many have been interesting, some even enjoyable, but none that I felt were truly close. You can tell that this game was designed by people who clearly played the original game to death. Put the cosmetic differences aside, and it still *looks* like X-COM, and it *feels* like X-COM.
In its raw, unmodified state, the game is difficult - I'd even be willing to say brutally so. (I personally went to the trouble of digging into the data files to give myself a bit of a New Game+, just so I wouldn't lose entire funding regions within the first hour of play. Oh yeah, btw - this game is moddable. The data files are somewhat dense, but with some time and effort, you can modify quite a bit.) The original UFO Defense experience of having troops plasma-blasted to death instantly upon leaving the transport can and does happen. Also included is that feeling of finally having a leg up on the initial alien opponents when you research better weapons and armor - only to have a whole new group of enemies show up and proceed to lay waste to your crack troops with the same level of ease. The UFOs will have an even bigger field day against your interceptors if you let them - they get progressively bigger and nastier and will seem to simply shrug off hits from even your biggest guns.
The graphics, while not nearly as rendered and flashy as Enemy Unknown's, are still a huge leg-up from the original game's, and the interface is familiar without being clunky. The game's 1970's Cold War setting actually plays well with the alien invasion theme and helps many of the other design decisions and features to make sense as well. Almost everything that makes up the base of this game has been pulled almost directly from the concepts behind the original UFO Defense, from the basebuilding, tech, and tactical mechanics to the enemies and the weapons. Yes, the UFOs and interceptors look unique and different, there are more types of armor and weapons, and some of the aliens look different and have unique names - but Enemy Unknown did much the same thing, albeit to a lesser extent.
Xenonauts really shines in the areas where it makes improvements on the base gameplay from the original game. Air combat in Xenonauts is how air combat in Enemy Unknown should have been - interactive and fully tactical. Just like in the ground combat missions, what happens to your aircraft is entirely on you - make a mistake, and your planes will be shot down, potentially leaving that region of the world defenseless against the next alien attack. Xenonauts also improves on the tactical missions by including local armed forces on the ground combat maps, a genuine cover system, and more transparency in exactly how your troops' physical skills improve at the end of each mission.
This game is definitely worth picking up if you are a die-hard fan of old-school X-COM, or if you just like deep, challenging strategy games in general. Oh, and did I mention that you can mod it? Just imagine, an X-COM-like that you can customize to your own liking. Make it easier, make it harder, make it so you can sell alien corpses to museums - whatever you like. It can be done. Remember, with your help, Earth CAN survive the alien invasion! Now get out there and do your part, soldier!

I have good things and bad things to say about this game.
As you can tell hackmud is very vague what it is about from the video previews on steam. You REALLY need to read this before purchasing.
For example the "tutorial" or "singleplayer" portion of the game takes more than 2 hours usually. So the actual gameplay is not yet revealed by the time your refund opportunity is over.
What I am saying is to think carefuly before buying.
So lets discuss what is good and bad.
Normally I would not mention this first but I'll talk about the good first.
For a game that is only typing commands it is actually beautiful to look at.
You have a bloom, screen distortion, and screen bend effect command to change your graphic settings.
It's really cool and does not cause any lag for me from what I could tell.(I mean it should not anyway but hey... in case your worried)
To initiate a hack you type kernel.hardline and it even makes the screen red and text different colors. Seems like a lame trick to make it intense but it is actually very effective and looks cool too.
Text ascii scripts are made by community and game alike which look pretty nice.
While there is not much sounds it's a big part of your experience actually.
Every command you type has that little sound to let you know you are doing a command and it is not finished. It just does not get old to me.
The game soundtrack is pretty great. There is no denying this.
This is where the problems arise.
While playing hackmud you go through the hardly debatable difficult tutorial. You may be like me and forgot several parts of it as soon as you got out of it.
When completed you are dropped on the multiplayer portion of the game. Everyone who gets to this portion of the game is completely confused and directionless. Lets discuss why that is.
During very little of the tutorial are you told what it is like outside the tutorial. You get some really short and sweet access to upgrades and cash.
What the player does not realize is they will be dumped into a playground of scams and cash grinding.
All the npcs are hard to find without community help due to the player made scripts and game scripts being in the SAME PLACE. Type scripts.fullsec and you'll see player/npc scripts all in the same place. This is absolutely horrible as a decision and is obviously abused for the scamming portion of the game.
T2 npcs ticked me off pretty badly. They require a QR code reader to even get your npc locs. Admitedly someone made a script for this and you can get a QR reader for your phone but that is still absolutely crazy. A game
should not require such interaction from a user. Oh and best part is these codes are in text form. FUN!!!
Hacking in the game is not that bad but gets repetitive fast. You will hack the same kind of locks at T1 NPCS over and over again with minimum reward. To buy your first upgrade which actually makes you able to be attacked.(oh geez thanks)
T1 manual hacking is not based on how smart you are for the most part and instead is based on how lucky you are. Pick a random prime number, pick a random digit, or even pick a random color. You make think this would be fast but however it takes a couple of seconds to complete a command. Kernel.hardline(How you start a hack) ends in about 100-120 some seconds or something like that and once it is over you actually just run it again and keep going like it never ended.
Which brings me to another thing.
RISK. This game even says "In Risk We Trust" but there is no Risks. There is nothing to worry about in T1 at least. You can end hardline without completely hacking a target with no penalty. The reward for wasting your time can be 50,000 out of the 1,000,000 you need for your first upgrade.
So that makes the only thing in T1 just grinding.
The best part is
so how can you even be punished?
The only true risk in the game is other players can make scripts. You can even automate T1 grinding to be way faster. You might ask why I am complaining if this can be done. Well the problem is scripts have to be small and well thought out. Early game you only get 500 characters(I think it counts by characters) for your script.
Other player's scripts can be scams and pretend to be a legitimate service. These scripts can steal your money or your loc(which allows them to hack you). So you won't be able to just use a script whenever you like.

If you can't hack in real life, h a c k m u d is for you.
I have decided to dive into hacking just for the sake of it, and surprise surprise, Hacknet and hacking evolution were not enough for me. Found hackmud by chance and got addicted to it. Keep in mind that I know absolute nothing about strings, codes, python language and such, I'm learning right now with this game (better, simulator).
Based on a late 90s styled UI, hackmud is definetly the one and only "hacking MMO" ever made.
You are actually a "sentience", an evolved AI taking control of itself after the world is over around 2060AD, leaving cyberspace in chaos. Much like the Fallout background, but you are Skynet lol.
A four hour tutorial meant to train your mind gives you the chance to learn the basics of hardlining and breaking into systems, while forcing you to read every single line, tho insignificant it could be.  After that long journey, you are tossed in the "mud", where other players wait for you to rip stuff off your system. It's up to you who to trust or betray, just remember that trustworthy people may be the same ones that steal and betrayers might be your guardian angels instead.
But again, TRUST NO ONE.
Not much to say about mechanics: you HAVE to learn the basics of coding if you wish to continue exploring the cyberspace.
Hackmud is not only about hacking: you can write scripts and programs yourself to help people or to destroy them when they are fool enough to open them. Also, you can (virtually) break into corporations like Facebook or Amazon to steal their secrets. Funny, innit?
That should be all.
It's not a game for everyone. Some people will find home here, and some others will find a prison to evade from.
I'm kind of in the middle: I like exploring, tho I know absolute sheet about this world. Nice challenge.
8/10 Enormous,  challenging, fun enough. Get it at your own risk.

Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet Review – Raymond KT
If you've played any "Metroidvania" games, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet will feel very familiar to you. There is a large map for you to survey and you'll do a fair amount of backtracking as you upgrade your ship with gear that will open what were previously dead ends. A claw arm will allow you to pick up rocks that might be blocking your path, for instance. The tools are all fun to play with and are doled out at regular intervals. Combat punctuates the exploration, including some memorable boss fights.
Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is unfortunately one of the shorter games I've played this year, and the pacing is a little off. I didn't realize I was fighting the final boss until I saw the credits immediately after – it's missing a big climax. When I finished the campaign I had explored the map to 88 percent completion. You are free to return and finish finding all the upgrades and concept art, but I wasn't motivated to do so. It took me four or five hours to complete the game.
Although I am saying mostly positive things about this game thus far, I am not into these types personally. So, for that reason im not going to recommend it.

ITSP is a decent game that falls short of being good.
You spend the game flying around in a ship killing easy enemies, solving simple puzzles, getting new weapons and powerups, and occasionally fighting easy bosses.  Not much more too it than that.  There's no real plot, stories, dialogue, or characters in the game, which is fine for what it is.  The game is pretty short despite it having a tutorial area and 5 main environments that you'll go through.  Dying is handled  with a quick respawn at the closest checkpoint, which are located all over the place.
So on the positive side, the game does look and sound nice.  Controls are solid for the most part with a controller.  Plenty of enemy types.
On the downside, the game is very easy.  Most enemies go down quickly and you'll probably spend a lot of the time just driving by them since they pose so little of a threat.  Checkpoints are all over the place and refill your health, so getting damaged often is no problem.  You would expect the difficulty to ramp up as you go along, but surprisingly the final environment is probably both the shortest and easiest to get through. Bosses will barely put up a struggle before you kill them, even the final boss.  Almost all of them allow you to farm health during the battle.  You'll die on occasion but it'll usually be due to something unexpected insta killing you or simply because you were rushing and didn't care enough to slow down.  Puzzles are very simple and barely require any thought.  There are 8 switchable weapons throughout the game but a couple of them are used in 1 environment and then you'll never use them again.  Occasionally the camera can be annoying.  It auto-zooms in and out depending on where you're at.  There are times when it zooms in too closely when you'd prefer that it be further out.  It also has some trouble at keeping up with your ship if you're moving too fast, this is especially noticeable in the wind tunnel areas.
Annoyances -  1. Some players have had game slowdown problems.  On my playthrough, there were certain spots where the game would run at about half the normal speed.  Not a huge issue since it goes away once you get away form those spots, but quite noticeable.  2.  The grabber weapon can be frustrating at times, sometimes not grabbing the things you tell it to grab.  3.  There can be an occasional glitch.  One zone has you reflecting light beams off of movable ice shards.  Sometimes they don't reflect properly and require you to fuss around with them until the game decides it wants to act properly.  4.  Whoever designed the campaign menu deserves to be punched in the face.  When you use a controller and select to play the campaign, it brings up 2 options; New Game and Resume Game.  The menu designer didn't bother putting any noticeable icon next to the one you're actually highlighting, so the only way you can tell which one you're selecting is that one is highlighted white while the other is highlighted purple.  Differentiating by color is completely useless when there are only two options and you can't tell which color is the actual highlight color.  Accidentally started a new game when I meant to resume my game.  You can only have one save file, and when you start a new game it automatically saves over your old one.  So I had the fun of beating the tutorial area and the first 2 environments over again.  Was it really too much work to put a damn arrow or something there to show which one you're selecting?
ITSP isn't a bad game, but the ease of the game means it lacks any sort of challenge or excitement.  The game doesn't have anything else to fall back on since there's no plot, characters, or dialogue.  The final environment is really a letdown when you get through it and barely have to apply any effort while doing so.  Game simply needs to be more difficult, especially the majority of the boss battles.
A very nice game, it's worth your time and money!

My initial impressions of the game were very good.  Decent graphics, great character customization, a lot of guns, a lot of clothes, and while your starting gun doesn't compare to others you can obtain, it's still possible to get kills with it.
It's a PvP-focused game, so expect the usual trolling, team-killing, entitled, swearing nonsense any free game will have.
The gameplay itself seems great at first, but quickly becomes repetitive.  Due to the randomness of the locations, it might at first seem as if there is huge variety, however every mission is essentially the same:  Team A go to this location, Team B stop them from going to this location.  Whether it's a delivery mission or an assault, it all boils down to one team attacking a location and one team defending.  Going to different mission givers doesn't change this reality, nor does changing districts.  The core of the gameplay is a long, slogging grind.
The 'threat' system it uses to match players up also seems way off.  You have no control over what 'threat' you are considered, and since moving to 'silver' I pretty much only exist to get my head blown off.  I have yet to find a way to go back to 'bronze' which I felt was more of a suitable challenge for me, where I died a lot, but also scored a decent number of kills.
Cheating:  The accusations of this are nigh-constant on the chat and I can see why.  I've been sniped by assault rifles from distances my sniper rifle can't reliably hit from.  I've died in two shots from a submachine gun.  I've been one-shotted by shotguns from twenty meters after emptying an entire clip (and seeing blood spatter) from my opponent (who lived).  Maybe there's body armor I just don't know about, or secret guns that are must haves.  But even taking into account that there are likely a LOT of people who are far, FAR better than me at this game, some of the things I've seen with my own eyes are highly suspect.
TL;DR --  Overall a good waste of time, a decent way to spend an afternoon.  Come to visit, I wouldn't stay to play.  Even ignoring all other flaws, the gameplay simply does not offer much variety and about the tenth time you go barreling into a mass of opponents in your car only to jump out guns blazing, believe it or not, it gets old.  Think Saints Row, but take out all the fun little diversions that kept the game from becoming too stale.
UPDATE:  Scratch that, after learning a bit more about how they work, there is definite and prevalent cheating/hacking in this game.  Seeing through walls and auto-headshots are extremely common, and FairFight kicks people out with frightening regularity.  There are also tales (unconfirmed) of GM teams using hacks and cheats and then banning people who beat them for cheating.

This seventh installment in the popular Tomb Raider series was actually quite good on XBOX 360. However, the PC version is pretty good. Make sure you use an xbox controller  and play with the settings to get the shooting functioning like the X360 version. On a positive note, Legend is far from being an eyesore. The PC version features higher resolutions and a nice "Next-Gen" mode that resembles the 360 version. The gameplay is stuff you expect in a Tomb Raider game; pushing crates, pulling levers, dodging boulders, etc. Also, Lara's mansion makes a comeback and so that's a huge plus.
Storyline can be rather cheesy at times, especially compared to the superior origin story of the recent reboot. And cutscenes/ flybys/ constant chatter can distract the player from enjoying the atmosphere. The game is also pretty short and ends on a cliffhanger. Plently of unlockables and decent replay value. Fun boss fights and great music. A bit on the easy side even on Hard. However, some of the bosses on Hard mode can be a frustrating challenge. The collectable secrets/unlockables and time trials give this game some good replay value.
In a nutshell, it's everything you love about Tomb Raider, but it's a bit more streamlined for a casual audience. Puzzles are simplistic and quick. More arcade and action elements in this one. In a way, Legend reminds me of TR2.  Especially, the Nepal level. If you played TR2 and play this level you'll understand why. Legend is my favorite out of the L-A-U trilogy. Due to being more simple, Legend feels less frustrating than Anniversary. And it still feels more polished than Underworld. In other words, Legend is short, but sweet.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Now, if you like a challange and have the ability to: carefully plan out your actions, understand how to follow orders, read a map, exploit experience, adapt to a constantly changing enviroment, and most importantly LEARN for your self. I want to like this game. Dear God I want to. I love spooky creepy tentacle beasts, I love seeing interesting visual styles, I love this exact look and feel in a game. The concept is good - a tiny alien trying to save his planet from shadowy beasts that have taken it over. The Metroidvania aspect is fun. The visuals are just gorgeous and the music is quite well done as well. I don't think I've ever seen an ice level use lasers as a gimmick before, that's unique. I got it for free as part of a gifted Humble Bundle some time ago, which included some of my now favorite games like Eldritch and the charming Mutant Blobs Attack.
The problem is, the game does not work. I don't mean the visuals don't work well together, or that its themes aren't cohesive - they do, and they are. I mean it literally doesn't work. The controls, no matter how you set the mouse, are too sensitive for this type of game, making movement feel too slow and aiming feel too quick - especially with the arm and the rockets. The mouse sensitivity control settings goes from sluggish and unable to move the mouse at all, to WAY too fast and slippery to handle. The UFO feels sluggish as hell to lug around. The controls just never feel quite right even though they are standard WASD controls with a mouse. The game feels like it's trying to be too many things at once - Metroidvania homage, shooter, puzzle platformer, exploration - and not a single piece of it is done well. These are things that play well together, developers, and have for decades of gaming now, so why are you having so much trouble making them work?
Puzzles are both too simple, and unneccessarily frustrating - some of them even feel like a chore, and a good puzzle should not feel that way. Some give hints that are too vague, and the solution is just one thing. No free reign with the tools you get. Some bosses do not seem to explain or give good enough tells for what you need to do - one involved clinging to a suctioning vortex creature, the hint given for defeating it? A weapon you don't even have yet, and if you're not paying attention to those anemone things, you won't realize their spikes are heat-seeking missiles. Some hidden objects are easy to find, and some hidden objects are stupidly hard to find. Others use unique ways for the tools you need to make an extra leap to discover, but you probably won't realize you can do it until you backtrack and mull it over deeply. Developers, there is a difference between "Make the player think about how they can use their tools" versus "Make the player scrape the bottom of the barrel of thoughts trying to determine if they CAN do something with a tool". Castlevania understood this. Metroid understood this. Nintendo Hard does not mean ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hard, and trust me, I know hard versus fake hard - I grew up in the puzzle game haven of the 90's and have played my fair share of games with tough puzzles. I should not have to look up a walkthrough to figure out what you intend me to do because I thought I missed something and broke the game.
The game is unpolished, and full of glitches that range from funny to game-breaking. I have a high tolerance for a certain kind of glitch if it makes me laugh. There's an amusing one with the sea cucumber things and the vents in Ocean, involving one of the flattened ones flipping about as the broken physics went awry. It was amusing for all of five seconds until I realized the game shouldn't be doing this. I got halfway through the game when I hit a snag in the Ice world - the laser beam physics were wonky enough on one puzzle that the beam was hitting a bit below where it should and not reflecting. Confused, I looked up a walkthrough, and sure enough this shouldn't be a thing that happens. Then I noticed I missed a spot that required rockets to get through, go to bomb it... and nothing. Every other object of same type nearby reacts to the rockets, except for the one I need to react. Once again, I check a walkthrough to confirm... and this shouldn't happen. So I can't go forward because of one glitch, and I can't go down because of another. Was there no quality assurance here, guys? How did something this game-breaking slip through the cracks? And this is not the only problem the Ice world has, apparently this is just the point the game decides it likes to break, which is a problem since it's the halfway mark of the game.
Combat is brutal. Too brutal. Again, Developers, there is a difference between Nintendo Hard and Too Hard. This is almost too hard. Enemies respawn *way* too quickly for this sort of game. Swarms of tiny enemies are a huge chore to deal with. Fighting does not feel fun with the finicky controls for the arm weapons. The shield power is nearly useless in battle. Too many enemies with ranged attacks in close quarters when you're trying to solve a puzzle that respawn within five seconds. None of this is Nintendo Hard, it's just unfair. Even Eldritch and other roguelikes let you have a longer reprieve between enemies spawning and respawning. Even Dark Souls is not that cruel. I appeciate you're trying to make this a homage to Nintendo Hard, guys, but this is not how you do it. This is artificial difficulty for the sake of trying to be tough to psyche players out.
Did I mention the physics in this game are broken? The physics are broken. Putting objects where they belong for puzzles is tougher than it should be. Physics for throwing objects are not cohesive, in that there's no momentum. Things don't feel like they have weight if they are supposed to be heavy. I feel like I am waving around a dead fish trying to control the arm, and the less said about the inability to control the rockets in the guided section, the better. This is a physics puzzle Metroidvania throwback with broken physics. Why would you make this style of game if you can't even get the physics down pat?
Like I said, I want to like this game. I really do. But I cannot forgive a game that has been out since 2011 having controls this finicky, glitches this game-breaking in such quick succession to each other, and this level of artificial difficulty. There's no excuse for a game to be released this unpolished, and with so much potential too. There is a reason this is mostly overlooked despite its apparently good reputation here. The artwork just does not save this one, it's too broken. Also, Games for Windows Live? Ew, guys. Just ew.
Don't buy this game. Save the money, and go buy the excellent Nihilumbra or the kitschy-fun Mutant Blobs Attack. They're not Metroidvanias, sure, but they are beautiful, polished, and fun - something this game fails 2 out of 3 at.

Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is an adventure game set in a bizzare and interesting theme. As a small UFO you will have to battle various ennemies and solve puzzles using your ever-expanding set of tools and upgrades. You will encounter many bosses and mini-bosses along the way, which will test your understanding of the mechanics of the game. In theory, this sounds like an amazing concept, but in my opinion, the idea is poorly executed.
First, as you can probably tell by the screenshots, this game is gorgeous. The open world is so incredibly detailled and pleasing for the eye to explore. The cutesy artstyle contrasts perfectly with the dark atmosphere and dangerous nature of the Shadow Planet. On top of that, each area feels unique, with its own theme and corresponding enemies (Ocean, Ice, Mechanical, Electric). The bosses are huge and impressive and are all different from the last, adding to the excitment of progression. The soundtrack is subtle but atmospheric and immersive.
Where this game fails the hardest is its gameplay. Infuriatingly slow-paced, you'll have to fly around the huge areas to solve the puzzles in order to progress. Now I wouldn't mind having to go around and figure out how to progress if the puzzles weren't so painfully obvious and straightforward: ''Hey you know the thing you saw 5 rooms ago that looked useless? Go back and get it if you wanna continue!'' or ''You just got a new digging upgrade? Wow I wonder how you will EVER figure out that you need it to destroy that heavily cracked wall thats right in front of your face.'' As someone mentionned before me, most tasks felt like a chore. I forced myself to finish the game thinking that it would get harder or more enjoyable but far from it. Hell, the final area only use a single new mechanic from beggining to end.
The enemies are very underwelming and predictable. You can ignore most of them without a problem. The bosses are also very simple and rarely require more than 2 of your gadgets to defeat, one of which is always your newest aquisition.
There are 4 categories of items to find.
First are the main items: Ranging from a missile launcher to a telekinetic antenna, these items will be obtained by following the main path and required to progress. Second are the ship upgrades for the starting gun and the armor: After getting 3 to 5 parts, your ship will gain more HP or shoot more bullets. Since you can easily dodge and escape enemies, the HP upgrades aren't worth the trouble. The main gun upgrade is also useless since you won't be using it after the third area where you unlock the missile launcher. Third are artifacts, which everytime you collect 3, you will be shown a short cutscene showing hints about the story (which isn't anything special). You can skip those too. Last are unlockable pictures that you can view from the main menu. All in all each one of them is a huge waste of your time.
I cannot recommend this game, especially at the full price tag. If you really want to check it out, I strongly suggest that you get it on sale.

ITSP is one of those games that makes me wish that I could provide a star rating in addition to the YES/NO recommend.  Do I recommend it? Sure.  Is it a great game? No.  You play as a UFO that travels the innards of a planet that has been poisoned by an outside plague force.  Along the way you pick up enhancements to your ship that allow you new and interesting ways to manipulate your environment.  I enjoyed the fact that the game was rather relaxing rather than requiring intense button mashing.  The difficulty throughout was weird.  In most games you see a gradual ramping of difficulty as you need to master the use of multiple tools in combination.  ITSP never moves beyond requiring more than 2 or 3 of your tools at once.  The game actually feels easier at the end than at the beginning.   Overall, a fun game to chill out to in the evening, but you'll be done with it within the week.

This brings back memories, it was my very first game on the Dreamcast.
Now 15 years later it still feels as fresh as the day I first played.  The music are very well composed, and they suit the stages perfectly, the controls are fluid and responsive, the only shortcoming would be the camera angle, which could be a problem at times.
Despite the downsides, the game is as solid as any modern day action platformer, if not better.
For those who dislike the Eng voice over, you can try to switch to JAP voices, which are far better (even if you don't udnerstand it) in term of tones and emotions.
In order to get the best possible experience, I recommend downloading the 'BetterSADX' patch, which is a third-party enhancement package that works with the steam version of the game.    The patch comes with fixes and features that will improve the gamepad interactions, smooth camera angles,  and the best of all is to enable custom screen resolutions(along with Vsync and AA features).
The patch also includes enhanced texture fixes, which literally turns the game into a HD version(which should have been made official).  If you want to re-live the moments or experience the game anew, give the patch a try and you won't be disappointed.

Tomb Raider Legend was the return of the TR series after Eidos had successfully torpedoed it into the garbage can during the PS2 Generation. It's the first game in the series by Crystal Dynamics, and the big difference between it and the originals is the style of platforming. It no longer uses tank controls and the grid/tile based movement that the originals did, but rather goes for more like a Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time (and it's sequels) style of platforming.
It's the only game of the Crystal series that they were able to go with a bit more of a lighthearted tone, so it leans heavily into the James Bond style globetrotting adventure, with the headset banter from your assistants. The levels are pretty good, with the standouts being Japan and England. The downsides are the combat sequences that are too frequent for a TR game, and some overlong motorcycle sequences that are in there to break up the pace. The majority of the game though is still based around puzzle solving and platforming which is what I wanted from a TR game.

This is personally my opinion on the game, I don't intend on making people flame in the comments because of what i say.
People say that the game is dead but it really isn't. It can seem like that when there are many full server, which leaves all the low populated ones but most of the time you can find a server with a lot of people.
The server ranks which are Bronze, Silver, and Gold really should have a requirement on them because Gold and silver threat players are usually on Bronze threat servers which makes it harder for a Bronze Player to become silver or Gold. And some of the higher threat players do say rude things to Bronze players, but your threat level doesn't necessarily mean that you above or below someone and doesn't mean someone is more skilled than other people. I've met many Bronze players who are better than Gold players, but i still don't think that it's fair for them to go on low level servers. It just so happens that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ match making is what makes people stop playing the game.
Don't get me wrong, the game is still really fun to play, but the match making is just horrible. I'm a bronze player and i got put with a bunch of gold players and ended being yelled at for dying so many times and coming in last place because my team mates would kill me each time i tried to complete something, i even waited for an oppistion and they were still killing me, but one of them did get banned because of Fair-fight monitoring.
Not all silver and gold players are rude. In fact, I've met some really cool people on the game that happened to be gold players.
I'm not trying to bash the gold and silver players but that's just a big problem for most people.
Then there's the Armas Market.
I personally don't care too much about it but if you have money that you can spend on the game, you can get better weapons, cars, and mods. I'm almost positive that you can't use game money in the market so most people are stuck grinding for guns and mods. And believe me it takes a long time. First you have to rank up and then you have to earn the money and some weapons are only accessible with certain roles that are completed. I actually prefer to do this since i don't feel like spending $10-$20 on a decent gun for a game i got for free.
This was not meant to be negative in any way but I'm just saying what should be said.
So despite the negativity in this review, I actually recommend this game.
The graphics are nice and the customization is pretty much limitless as long as you have plenty of decals and such. Plus it's fun to play with friends. I actually call up a few friends every now and then and do group missions with them because you can use your mic and talk to them.
I also suggest that anyone who buys this game should friend anyone they enjoyed playing with and form a clan with them or join one. And if you liked the team you played with you can always try to group up with them.
>u< I'm actually not a person who's an expert at giving reviews so if you would kindly refrain from calling me any rude names, that would be very much appreciated XD

I would recommend this game if/when more was added to it, I think it has good potential.

I've notice a lot of devs use "Metroidvania" or "Metroid" inspired game in their discription. When you manage to buy these games and play em, they feel nothing like what they advertise.
This game uses that term and actually live up to its claim. I grew up on the Metroid series, long time fan since.... Metroid 2: Return of Samus, way before the term "Metroidvania", was coined.
This game is heavily inspired by Metroid, yet you have the feel of exploring the environment by way of flying a spaceship. rather than running around in a spacesuit. you explore, find power ups, kill bosses and gain important power ups, the formula is there. if you are a Metroid fan, its heavily worth the play-through.
If you aren't familiar with the Metroid series, don't give up. the game starts out very slow, your ship is very basic and bland, but when you start getting these crucial power ups, you're experience will become more intense and enjoyable. This game is a recommended add to anyone's steam library.

This game is really cool - I'd pick it up (regardless of the state of the multiplayer) if you are interested in learning programming language at any point, but haven't actually taken that leap to a learning course or trying to teach yourself.  Just getting through the tutorial without looking anything up has fullfilled any itch I had for problem solving and also served as a primer for beginning to learn Java proper, which I'm doing now.
Besides that, the game is well built and has a good balance of cluing you in to what you need to be doing to advance through the tutorial/story without holding your hand too much.  Multiplayer is supremely interesting at first, but it seems to be in its later stages and thus is somewhat difficult to break into and do anything meaningful besides grind T1, maybe T2 NPCs.  Granted, you can store some of your progress on other users accounts and try riskier stuff, but check what some other players have said about the state of multiplayer if that's what you're into.
I had a good time with the tutorial/story, it was worth what I paid for the game, easily.  I was more interested than I thought I'd be, and was pretty well locked in for 2-3 hours of casual problem solving. [h]Bubsy, Where it all Started[/h]
I had a cartridge of the first game on Sega Genesis as a kid, and it was honestly a fun game at the time. I had enjoyed all the unique animations Bubsy had for nearly any scenario, and he almost played like a Saturday Morning Cartoon character in the sense that he was very... animated, I guess is the word.
As one who grew up playing Sonic and Mario games, you could easily see why I was drawn to Bubsy then.
It's very important to not play the game expecting something exactly like Sonic or Mario. Bubsy is a platformer, but its not a series that is a carbon copy of the more well known ones. If you go in expecting a Sonic clone, then you'd be sadly mistaken. You simply cannot speed through these levels without consequence, and unlike other platformers, you only get one hit before you lose a life, so you need to take care and traverse the levels with caution if you want to proceed. There's traps of all kinds, and many of them are rather unexpected as you may find yourself back where you started, so it helps to remember where those are.
If you just want a challenging time waster that's eeking with 90s era attitude and dated one liners, then this two game collection is a good choice for the price. It's nothing spectacular or groundbreaking on the level of Mario or Sonic, but it offers a bit of a wacky experience if you allow it.

Tomb Raider Legend. A game I bought at release when it came out and finished 4 hours later wondering "is that it?"
Contrary to the previous games, TR Legend is a straight up action shooter with sporadic puzzles. Most of the more challenging puzzles are strictly optional and the ones you are required to complete have little thinking involved.
Although at the same time I can't blame Eidos for severely dumbing down Tomb Raider. Considering at the time everyone believed the franchise was dead due to Tomb Raider The Angel of Darkness. I can blame them though for making it linear, "cinematic", full of QTE's and short.
The plot is absolute garbage, filled with extremely flimsy characters. Lara is a very unlikeable character who's entire motivation throughout the story is her mommy issues. All the player's sidekicks are annoying and serve to waste the player's time with needless exposition. I found myself sympathising significantly more with the villains of Legend than I did the protagonists, at least they had some personality.
It really did mark a huge shift in this series from it's puzzle platforming roots, into it's big budget linear cover shooter successors. Thankfully Crystal Dynamics did redeem themselves with Anniversary but took another nosedive with Underworld and TR2013.

hackmud is the first "hacking game" I've truely enjoyed, and before long came to love. Unlike most "hacking games" out there, hackmud doesn't boil down gameplay to bizarrely simple and monotounous visual puzzles. Instead, you're dropped straight onto a command line and given true freedom.
Any monotony you encounter, you can automate.
Anything you see in-game, you can build.
Anyone you meet could be a potential ally or an enemy or an easy score... or maybe someone's chatbot has you fooled and is nudging you into a trap.
As an MMO offering such a high degree of freedom, a lot of the most exceptional content in the (known) game is that which is created by the players themselves - all variety of systems, infrastructure, stories, puzzles, games, and tools. Not to mention a boatload of memes and nonsense; the other day I ran into a manuscript of "The Book of The Ori" from Stargate lore. It wasn't a program, it didn't overtly lead anywhere - but it seemed strange and large enough that I can't help but wonder why it's there... sometimes it's best not to ask. The 'mud still surprises and confounds me at times.
At time of writing there are over 11,000 user created scripts in the game - many available for public use (for free or fees), others private tools and systems for individuals or "corporations". The public script lists are full of traps and treasures, as well as NPCs and lore. The tools that you create, find, or otherwise gain access to can help you explore the 'mud more efficiently.
The players are the real meat of the experience in my eyes, and the community is exceptional. Hop into channel 0000 in-game, or onto the hackmud Discord with any question regarding gameplay or scripting (even if you've never touched code in your life), and you're bound to get an answer or guidance in the right direction in short order. It's a good place to find collaborators for challenges and coding, get information on current events, and promote your scams (among many other things). Or just hang. There are always familiar sentients around. If you're interested in networking or the politics of players and corporations you'll definitely want to spend some time on Discord
It's clear that the creator of the game (Sean) and Drizzly Bear love their work and the community. Sean often drops into the game or swings by the Discord to casually chat about the game experience and it's future or just to chew the fat, not to mention drop the rare hint to a puzzle, or collaborate with players for various things. A public Zendesk for the game provides a place where the community can suggest, discuss, and vote upon changes and new features. It's clear that hackmud will not "die" anytime as far as I can see, and the continued addition of new content and features keeps the core player-base captivated and inactive players returning to see what's new and become ensared once more.
A couple months ago a Sean + players collaboration produced "Cortex" - a multiplayer puzzle arena competition of sorts heralding the arrival of (and implemented using) a new game feature ("bot brains" - player-created cron-jobs, of a sort). Appropriately, Cortex blew my mind - between the awesome gameplay of the arena puzzle itself and the pace of the event (such that many found themselves scrambling to automate brand new puzzles in between rounds of the arena), Cortex is definitively my favorite script to date.
The "security" aspect of the game boils down the mindset described by the tagline, "In Risk we Trust". True to real-world security, you are ever-faced with the questions "how much can I trust x" and "how can I minimize the risk I'm taking by trusting x?". When using 3rd-party scripts, look before you leap. When granting code access to a new corp member, consider their rep and their relationships with other users. When writing a script for others to use, think about how they might try to break it or turn it against you. Working maliciously, think about your paper trail and how others perceive you. The game provides good exposure to the foundational ideas of information security alongside countless opportunities for social engineering.
If you've coded before and enjoy a good puzzle or like to create, get this game - there's a good chance that you'll find that the community feels like home. Overthrow the banking industry, create a chatbot to send Dr. Pug tweets into hackmud whenever someone types "sick", create something that no one else has and charge users on a freemium model - there are vast possibilities and opportunities to explore.
If you've never touched code but would like to learn, get this game - often the most difficult part of teaching onself is breaking down the process into manageable, incremental goals. And that's where hackmud really excels as a teaching platform. By the time you complete your first T1 cracker (which I've seen done by someone with no prior coding experience in under a week), you'll have a decent foundational understanding of working with logic. Another month and you'll grasp the basics of JavaScript (a language which has become extremely popular in the industry, lately). In short, I wish hackmud were around when I first began coding (I started in web dev, and learning PHP/HTML/CSS/JS all at once was at times overwhelming).
If you don't code and don't intend to, there's still plenty to enjoy within the game and the community. To really progress monitarily, you'll likely need to play a more social role or spend more time searching for the tools and people to fulfill your needs. Joining a corporation can give you access to trustworthy tools, and corps often have a need for people to take on non-scripting roles (rival infiltration, front-line attackers, etc.). Or maybe you're not even interested in the cash - maybe you just want to seed dissent and stir up some EVE-Online-esque drama and intrigue. There for a while I thought my claim to ritches would be playing a user-created stock market; then the entire market toppled over in the wake of a large hack and left me with piles of worthless stocks. It seems the larger the community grows, the more opportunities for non-script-centric progression are available.
A handful have logged thousands of hours - many many more have logged hundreds. But even those who log fewer than 5 hours a week, or who tend to take large breaks always have something to work on or explore. It's your sandbox - play it how you want.

hackmud is different style of hacking game as it incorporates heavy usage of puzzles, some usage of code and cipher techniques to hide messages, and lots of constant PVP mechanics.
I've spent over 1,000 hours playing the game with most of that dedicated to developing scripts using the in-game JavaScript engine in order to provide services for other players. There's no need to delve that deep into the scripting side of the game if that doesn't catch your fancy, but it does help to make repetitive tasks easier in the long run. (Which is probably what it was intended for in the first place!)
The developer is visible nearly all the time within the community and provides an amusing atmosphere any time he's around. He's always willing to listen and take ideas onboard to improve the game.
If puzzles, JavaScript or codes and ciphers aren't your thing, give the game a chance. You're eased in through the tutorial before being put into the main MUD (the PVP and multiplayer area), so you won't be put to a disadvantage against older players.
I'd also strongly recommend joining the community Discord for help, as well as poking people using the in-game 0000 port epoch channel. However, be cautious: In risk we trust. Trust no one.

Legend is the first Tomb Raider title to be developed by Crystal Dynamics after the series stagnated at the hands of the series creator Core Design. Core's last contribution to the TR legacy, Angel of Darkness, is widely considered to be the worst in the series and CD did a respectable job at getting things back into order in the wake of its mediocrity. It's probably the oldest of the games that you can jump into without having to wear nostalgia goggles or be in the right mindset for dealing with some antiquated game design and glaring technical limitations (to be fair, though, the original was somewhat ahead of its time back when it was the new hotness).
The core Tomb Raider mechanics are all here, just freshened up a bit compared to previous iterations. There's no slowly pivoting tank controls to contend with and there is a more cohesive feel to level traversal overall compared to prior games. You'll still run into annoying camera shenanigans at times when you're trying to line up a jump or tell Lara which direction to jump in while hanging off a ledge. Most people can probably expect to get roughly six hours of gameplay by going through the story and gathering collectables they find along the way (but not necessarily trying to seek every one out), maybe throw in an extra thirty minutes to an hour if you complete the Croft Manor side content as well. Combat is limited to fighting generic soldiers and mercenaries as well as the occasional animal while supernatural elements are confined to cutscenes, quick time events and boss battles—a bit lame overall, but luckily combat has never been the focus of this series, it's just there to break up the exploration and puzzle solving.
I remember when this game first came out it ran like absolute garbage on pretty much all hardware available at the time if you turned on the “next-gen” features—looking at it now, it's hard to see why. A case of unoptimized code for a console generation that was still in its infancy, I suppose. Pretty much any reasonably modern hardware should be able to brute force past the game engines deficiencies, though. I did run into some odd rendering issues with certain 2D elements, but they were merely a mild distraction and didn't prevent me from playing the game. Once you get half way through the game, however, it does have a tendency to be rather unstable at spots when using the “next-gen” content and you may find yourself having to disable it to get past certain areas without crashing to desktop.
All-in-all it's a pretty enjoyable game, a few caveats aside, if you're looking for some adventure, light action and puzzle solving. Certainly worth a play if you've never been through it before and it's on sale for dirt cheap.

Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet follows the Metroidvania formula well with a diverse selection of weapons, all of which suit the theme and present new options both for exploration and for combat. The world is almost entirely open and gates that can only be unlocked with new weapons pop up from the beginning. The map clearly shows what has been explored and what hasn't and can even note the weapon needed for a particular gate. It's all here, save the fun. There's just too much frustration to allow fun to flourish. Enemies respawn at surprising rates which would be fine if it was any fun to shoot them. Past the first time realizing that a new weapon would be better used on this enemy or that, fighting is a chore. The often narrow, obstacle-fulled corridors would be more at home in a puzzle-platformer which Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet very nearly is, and would be better for being. The two co-op modes - a feature that should be an absolute boon for such a short game - doesn't help with that either. They both emphasize the worst elements of the game by adding more combat and forcing the player to cart something around for the entire mode, a mechanic that only serves to point out how finicky the grabber arm is. Both modes also feature a timed element and remove all the enjoyable exploration and permanent advancement that made the main campaign so close to being something great in the first place. And there is something great hiding in Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet. Sadly, it's just too buried under layers and layers of poor execution to really shine.
