For a game that was released for the SEGA Dreamcast and then ported to the Nintendo Gamecube, this game doesn't look half bad... but DAMN those cutscnes are horrible!!! The voice acting is terrible, but i'll give the actors credit... it's the first time Sonic and his friends ever got a voice in a game (cartoons don't count cause AOSTH-That's just buggs bunny dressed up as sonic Underground-HE HAS A BAND? SatAM-NGHNGHNGHGNGFFFFFFFFFF) but i can't come up with an excuse for the terrible movement: the characters move like they have a clever up their a** and the lip synching... I hope you didn't plan on sleeping the day you bought this game.
2-SOUNDTRACK
So, as many of you know, Sonic games usually have an amazing soundtrack... and this one being no exception, seriously: Emerald coast has such a catchy theme, and Speed Highway is really pumped... every track fits the level perfectly in it's theme, no disapointments there... except one thing... but this is kind of a nitpick... IceCap Zone is returning from Sonic 3... It had one of the best tracks in the game... in Sonic Adventure... it's the only zone with a bad theme... what the hell, SEGA... couldn't we get a remix or something?
3-GAMEPLAY
This game is divided in 6 types of gameplay, with the characters being Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy, Gamma and Big...
Sonic is... well... he's sonic... take something from the classic games and i'll guarantee you will find it in it's 3D form here: amazing level design, Running through loops, collecting rings, killing robots and saving animals, it's all here.
Tails is basically the same thing as Sonic, except you're racing someone to the finish of the stage... but don't be afraid... this is really easy...
Knuckles has treasure hunting stages, where you search for 3 pieces of the master emerald with the help of Tikal and a trustworthy radar
Amy is basically sonic... only a bit slower... you're also runing away from this robot thing eggman created
Gamma is basically Amy with a blaster and a jetpack... you blow sh*t up... so... go blow sh*t up... i'ts fun
Big the cat is a F*CKING TRAINWRECK THAT'S WHAT HE IS!!!!!!!!!!! *sigh* with Biggie over here, you're best friend froggy escaped and you have to fish for him... yep, that's right, FISHING IN A SONIC GAME, WHO THE HELL WOULD WANT TO GO FAST IF YOU CAN FISH FOR A F*CKING FROG RIGHT?!?!?!?!?!?!?! ok sry
4-CONCLUSION
The game is good, DAMN good... It hasn't aged very well, in these days... well... it might as well be sh*t, but i'll be damned if this isn't the best, most fun piece of sh*t there is, so i give Sonic Adventure DX:Director's Cut...

Been playing off and on since October 2001. I pop back in every few years to see if the game has improved. They add things here and there, but the gameplay is still wonky. Animations are strange, netcode is bizarre, people will fall dead 2 seconds after you've shot them.
Mouse seems to suffer from some sort of irreparable acceleration which causes your iron sights/optics to jump several pixels at a time, killing any sort of precision shooting that's found in every AAA title for the past 15 years. I made a post on the official forums about 10 years ago, lots of young competitive gamers notice it, but the older devs and veterans don't seem to care.
If you aren't playing during peak hours, it can be pretty dull. Yeah, the map is huge, but that is also a drawback, especially considering 98% of it is just barren landscape littered with shrubs and trees. I popped in to check out the Steam release on a new account just to find that the largest battle happening was maybe 25vs25, and it was taking place over a large town. Massive game in scale, but not when it gets down to the fighting. You could find that size of a battle in pretty much any shooter on the market nowadays, with modern mechanics and graphics, without paying a subscription.
There is an unskippable tutorial at the beginning which the dev claims, "Anyone who wouldn't go through it would be instantly lost in the game." Yeah, the tutorial is literally showing you how to walk, crouch, go prone, fire your weapon, throw grenades, and chat on the radio. These are all instantly familiar controls to anyone who has ever played an FPS on PC. This game seems to be developed and aimed at people who are in the 45-60 age bracket.
Air combat is probably the only decent thing about WWII Online; the flight models are fine, and it is pretty fun strafing infantry on the ground and divebombing tanks. Air to air combat is satisfying enough, even if the entirety of it feels incredibly dated (because it is). If you are strictly about air simulation though, there are plenty of better titles on the market for cheap or for free (War Thunder, IL-2, DCS).
The most egregious thing about WWII Online is their subscription model. If you want to experience the whole game, be prepared to pay $18 a month. Free to play accounts are restricted to Riflemen only. Most modern gamers would find this incredibly dull and boring, but again, I think this game is mostly now aimed at a senior demographic.
Should you play this game?
Back in the day when there were actually massive battles, you could look past all the glaring issues, and it was a good time. But now it's on life support, and somebody should pull the plug.

If you've ever wanted what could be considered the purest form of a platformer, Super Meat Boy comes pretty close. Very tight level design, a bunch of unlockable characters that completely break said level design in a number of interesting ways, and a level designer that allows people to try and one-up the actual level designers at their own job. Admittedly, the wall-jumping could be a little better, as Meat Boy is curiously sticky, and can have trouble detaching from a wall if you touch it. This is especially apparent when you need to do precision vertical movement through chutes of death (which happens quite often)
Otherwise, it's a meaty challenge that'll keep you playing for hours, provided you're not the type of person that frustrates easily.

I found out about this game through my "random links" method on Youtube (I click mindlessly untill something of interest pops up). It was a video made by a guy called Rapid99 titled "A Day of Impromptu Traffic Collisions"
which showed a bunch of moments from their so-called "street racing" with some pretty sweet cars and some pretty sweet clothes and stuff. At first I thought "Wow those cars and clothes look so cool" and "I can't think about the amount of work the devs put into those designs". Literally 5 minutes later I was marvelling at sped-up car customizations and "How-to" videos on the game's HUUUUUUGE amount of content. I mean, this game has the best customization options ever, and I doubt you can get anywhere this amout of content for FREE.
A few days later, I was documenting myself on every single aspect of the game, so that I can get a head start when I will begin playing. In this time I also looked at some Steam reviews on this game, and everybody there was either saying "BEST GAME EVER" or "MOST UNBALANCED GAME EVER".
Then I got the game.
At first, I was enjoying myself with the carelessness of a newbie, that feeling before getting to know the ins and outs of the game and getting competitive. I was driving about and testing the gun mechanics, getting the feel of the interfaces, the control layout, everything. As I started playing more and more I came to realise that I was better off playing the game for a few days.
This game is gonna be REALLY hard on a new player. Having to deal with veterans, pay to plays and the occasional hacker, smurf and griefer will put off most new players. But at the same time, it offers so much that it makes you come back and play: unlockable backstory emails with detailed narration, the occasional Armas daily events which grant you cool stuff, the unique combat mechanics like switching from left-handed aim to right-handed on the spot to lean over cover, learning how to use all the different weapons in the game (I think the number of unique weapons passed 50 a long time ago) and grenade cooking, the amount of cars, the map and all the tricks to gain positional advantage over the enemy team and the ground-breaking customization.
In APB Reloaded, customization ranges from your car to your character to your gun. You can make a Domino's Pizza van or a street racer's dream car, you can make your character look like a sharp-suited professional or like a total fool and you can add skins to your guns, you can make your own death themes and logos and you can add perks to everything: make your car take less impact damage or make it self-destruct, make your character agile and weak or slow and resistant to damage and you can make your rifle reload and shoot really fast or make it really accurate with ammo to spare. The way you want to play is really up to you, and the game lets you do just about everything to help accomplish that.
The missions are a bit underwhelming. You are most of the time given some reason why Enforcer faction X wants to ♥♥♥♥ with Criminal faction Y (or vice-versa) and you are sent to spray a wall, break some doors or steal some car, or defend and not let any of those events occur in the first place. You either progress until your team wins or you let the timer run out to win. There are also the events that can take place in free roam: bad guy A ram-raids some stores, steals some cars or mugs a bunch of pedestrians so he can take the stolen items to make some dirty money from a contact that he after has to turn into real money by taking it to the laundry. If cop guy B steps into action and witnesses the man doing those crimes, they can engage in a side mission where the cop has to take the dirty money to a police storage locker to get payed for the retrieved goods or the bad guy has to take the goods to another storage locker to get payed for the retrieved goods. The winner gets the dirty money multiplied based on a multiplayer determined by player Prestige (if Enforcer) or Notoriety (if Criminal): increasing your Prestige as a cop means taking out bad guys or stunning and arresting them, which increases your Presige a whole lot more, and it gets decreased by running over pedestrians and crashing your car into other pedestrian-driven cars, mailboxes, etc. Criminals increase Notoriety by running over people and crashing into stuff, killing Enforcers and it gets decreased by doing nothing.
Now the game doesn't seem so bad after all, does it? All those traits SURELY have to compensate for the community's short-comings, right?
No, they don't.
There STILL are veterans, hackers, pay to plays, griefers and smurfs. And you will get virtually beaten into depression unless you stop playing or start joining them, or you get friends to play such a notorious game. Whichever path you choose, you will have a hard time coping with the circumstances. Not playing means losing out on a really awesome game, joining the ranks of the latter 4 means losing your honor and becoming a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ while becoming a veteran means enjoying the game at the expense of others since you will become a god at it, and finding friends to play outside of APB is REALLY hard and it will anger and sadden you while finding friends from inside the APB community means you get to spend less time with your IRL friends.
In conclusion, this is a game which you have to dedicate yourself to if you want to enjoy it to its fullest, or you hate it and you never come back to playing it. There is no grey area, and it really is a shame, because this game really is one of the best sandbox games ever, and I look past the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ community and devs and see the true and overlooked value.
EDIT: There is an absolutely vocal majority of veteran players who are claiming that they're getting banned for no reason or getting locked out of their accounts for buying some shady CD key from god knows how long ago, with the devs holding up the latter players' accounts for ransom until they pay again for the CD keys. This seems like a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ move from the devs, and some people have spent huge amounts of money on the game. While I can't really imagine why you should pay money for this game when you can get some really good weapons with in-game currency (OCA 626 Silverado, I'm looking at you), getting cheated out of your money for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reason really is scummy. Nonetheless, I don't see the game evolving at all. It's in limbo, with no major updates that add new weapons, the playerbase is not growing but not dying and ARMAS seems useless in my opinion. The Youtubers who play this game have really obscure channels and the only guy to actually get succesful with APB, Rapid99, has stopped uploading anything on his channel, not even other games. And even though this game is not dying, I think it should actually die, get the game sold to another company again or get hit with something absolutely major, like ripping the Free 2 Play status off of it, ripping ARMAS off of it and giving it the price of like, I dunno, 12.99$? 9.99$? But if that would happen, atleast the devs should give back some money to the players or some huge bonus or whatnot. It sounds really stupid, but it's a move the devs should have to pull off at some moment in the game's lifespan.

A turn-based strategy game that mimics the original XCOM games that started the genre in the mid-90s, Xenonauts is one of the better indie games currently in development. You start with a ragtag group of soldiers with the best technology humankind has to offer, which isn't much. Aliens invade with their own weapons in great force, striking against ships and towns, and it's up to you to shoot down their UFOs, aqcuire their technology, and use it against them before they turn human forces against you.
Much like the originals, you never really have the upper-hand. As the game progresses and you learn the secrets of alien technology, the invasion ramps in difficulty with larger UFOs and more intelligent aliens armed with even stronger weaponry.  You must rely on your own planning and a bit of luck to pull through. The game can be brutally difficult and is not ideal for people new to turn-based strategy.

This review is taking into account this is an early access game on release day 1, and that I've only spent an hour with it, just getting acquainted with the controls and mechanics of the game.  Here are my first impressions:
Pros:
The game is visually stunning right of of the gate.  It has a real sense of "atmosphere" to it.
The music is peaceful and I can't imagine it will become offensive to listen to for long periods of time.
The controls are fairly intuitive if a bit "clunky".  I imagine these will only get better.
There is a good but small set of initial stuff you can craft which really shows off the potential of where this game will go as more content gets added.
The monsters you can transform into all appear to have unique powers.
Cons:
Camera control seems too "fluid".  It makes camera movement really smooth, but feels like your cameraman is slipping on ice at times.  There doesn't appear to be ways to customize this yet.
Monster spawns appear random and not tied to particual biomes or anything.  I could be mistaken on this one.
Building placement is somewhat difficult because of the viewing angle, and figuring out how to move things once you've placed them is not obvious (if possible)
Customization/decoration is pretty limited at this point.
As you can see, considering this is day 1 of early access with limited playtime, my gripes are pretty minor.  I can see having a lot of fun with this game.  I haven't tried multiplayer, but I'll probably pick up copies and play this with my family once it gets a little more filled out with content and stuff to do.
Edit:  Forgot to give a final TLDR - If you like picking up cool indie early access titles that appear to be "going somewhere", give this game a shot!

Part 1:
I remember a long time ago, after i played Angel Of Darkness and was heavily sad with the bankrupicy of Core Design. Damn, those were rougue times. Luckily, Crystal Dynamics came to save the day and brought us Tomb Raider: Legend.
I was a bit anxyous, to be honest. Tomb Raider changing hands into another developer, will they bring us the same essence again?
As screenshots from the game were showed and when it appeared on the E3 of 2006, i was ready to say YES!
When i played the demo, i desperately needed to play the full version. And so i did. Back theses days, i bought my PS2. Witch got me not only Tomb Raider Legend, but also Anniversary some time later (Witch i will talk in other review). I played it with no clues of secrets or other things, din't even bothered reading the manual. IT WAS FUN. I mean, really fun. I remember, one of my first things that i've done after i first finished the story mode: Going out of my house and buying me a gamer magazine (Woah, those were the times...) to be able to finish it 100%. And so i did. I was so happy when i did.
First thing: The graphics. Even on PS2, they were beutiful. They are even better on PC. The ambients are pretty detailed and the immersion is great. I loved the art design of this game. It made me remember Tomb Raider 3. Moutains, temples and militar base. The snow part was my favorite, specially because of the change of gameplay.
Gameplay: Lara is like 450% more flexible than on Tomb Raider 6 and can do even more moves than the other 6 games. But it had a reason for it. As you go though stages, you will see that not you can climb, but also, run on walls (Like Prince Of Persia). I actually liked this featured and i think that it could've been more explored.  Besides that, you can roll and do a lot of acrobatic moves with it. As i said, Lara is way more flexible than in other games. It feel MUCH MORE pleasurable to play with her. Other changes to gameplay are: Quick time events. There are two types of them. One is the common one, where you have to push a certain button to not fail and die. Since there's always a checkpoint before these events, it will not give you any trouble. The second one is what i call "Quick Action And Reaction". When a "Lara's icon" appears on the bottom right of the screen, you will have a limited time to get to safety. You will have to run and jump, and react real quick to anything that is happening. An example: In the end of the first stage of the game, a chopper will come and start to blow up the bridge that you're on. You have to get to the other side if you want to make it alive. But the chopper's shoots will always vary. Sometimes they will hit a little bit forward, so you have to keep attention where you are stepping or else you will fall to death. I also had no problems with this event. I actually found it pretty cool, if you ask me. I preffer then more than common quick time events (I would love so much if Castlevania: Lord Of Shadows was more like that). The reason is because i think it's more skill based than "pressing the right button" based. Am i right?
Okay, next on the list of gameplay is vehicles. Sometimes, Lara will ride a vehicle. I personaly had no problem with them. Expect for two things. I swear to god, the physics of this game in these parts are rather strange sometimes. What i'm trying to say is: Don't hit walls many times. Seriously, don't. And the other thing is: Gunplay while driving. It's quite obvious that you can't fire both weapons, right? Okay, so what do you expect? Enemies with less life, right? WRONG! Enemies will take 7-9 shoots to die. I mean, SERIOUSLY. Couldn't they low it a bit, so it din't got THAT repetitive? Here's a tip: Try always to fire explosive barrels and explode their bikes, it's MUCH FASTER.
Also, this is another things. Explosive barrels are back. And with them another "interactive destructables". What i mean is: To either explorer a barrel (That's marked with a "!") or an "interactive destructable" (Also marked with "!"), you have to press the action button (On PC: "E", can't remember right now witch one it is on Gamepad). And Lara will shoot into these places and take out more enemies (Or take ou heavy enemies with less challenge). You also can use manual aim on them (Tough i din't used manual aim in the ENTIRE game, so). These are cool. And thanks to them, some destruction is possible in this game. And, again, that could've been MUCH MORE explored. Damn, this game had a lot of potential. And may be the game where the devs took out most of the ideas and put on Tomb Raider 2013.
Sound: I really liked the sound of the game. I really loved the song from intro, menu, ending, mission ending and the Tokyo mission theme. It's a memorable soundtrack and does it job. Lara's voice is quite good and i think it combines with her new visual in this game. Zip is back and...Tough he is not annoying, i preffered SOOOOOO MUCH his voice from Tomb Raider 5. He sounded so much cool there, what happened? If i can say one character that annoys the ♥♥♥♥ out of me is Allister. JESUS ♥♥♥♥ING CHRIST. SHUT UP ALREADY! AND I MEAN IT THIS TIME!
.
The Story...Oh boy. I think i will need to put these into parts. I will begin. With the failure of making a trilogy of the Angel Of Darkness, Crystal Dynamics tried to make their own trilogy (Witch was never a Trilogy BTW). At least they started it right. They tried to erase TRAOD from canon (Since we don't know anything that happened after the ending of it) and create their own story. Not only for the exploration part of the game (Myths, artifacts, etc), but also for Lara. That's right, this was the first game since Tomb Raider 4 (Witch only did a bit of this on the first two levels of it) that tried to explore Lara's past. As you can remember, nothing was ever said about Lara's dad and mother. The only thing you know is that they aren't showed and Lara is rich as hell. That's it. And that's where the devs tried to explored, creating a whole new story of it, introducing new characters like Amanda and Anaya. Anaya is just friends with Lara, and doesn't have much impact on plot. She just helped her to locate some things and was rescued by Lara later on the game. Amanda is the big fish in the new characters here. She's now the main antagonist. And i really mean it. She was best friends with Lara, since an accident happened and Lara had to leave her. More of this is revealed during a part of the game. And now, she's back, with hew own plan to gain infinity powers and become immortal (Well, that excalated quickly). And Lara has to defeat her by collecting all the parts of...Excalibur.
...
I know what you're thinking right now: "LOL, that was the best they could do?!". It has a connection. Not only Excalibur is the only thing capable of hurting Amanda, but also, Lara's mother disappeareance had something to do with her getting to another known as "Avalon". Now, with this, you know what mythology this game is about, right? Okay. Through it doesn't really happen a lot on plot (I mean, only things about Lara's past are revealed and there's the fight with Amanda and a little recounter with Lara's mother), it isn't bad. Each piece will be somewhere in the world, and that's will be a new mission. So location variety is back and this time, at least, it's good. Remember when i said i like the Tokyo mission soundtrack? It was also one of my favorite stages. I liked how they got a closed space and transformed it into a open exploration space. I just really think that the enemy of this mission in particular isn't that memorable. I can't even remember his name if you ask me.
But that's the most of the story.
Now, we are going to talk about two major things in this game that completes theirselves: Exploration and unlockables.

It makes me very sad to see Lara given a group of men to work with. Since when did she need anyone to hold her hand? still, at least they were assistants back at the manor rather than adventuring buddies.
The game was as much fun as every Tomb Raider game is, really. A nice little platformer with the odd fight thrown in. They tossed in a few quicktime events as well, which is sad. I always find it more fun to do the cool things yourself rather than watch a cut scene and occasionally press a button during it. The story was very predictable too. But even with predictability holding it back, it was enough to hold my attention.
While it was fun, and quite enjoyable, I don't think it holds any replay value. The story's been told, after all. Tomb Raider, for me, has always been on the same level in my mind as Indiana Jones, though. Light, fun fluff. In spite of the negatives, it was fun

This game is not only a breakthrough, but also the one of the easiest games I ever played. On this note, if you've never played a Tomb Raider game before, and even if you have, I highly recommend reading a walkthrough as you play through it.
In Tomb Raider Legend, we are once again reunited with our beloved friend and heroine Lara Croft who has been 'looking for certain artifacts for some time'.
Unlike in the previous Tomb Raider Games (Tomb Raider I through Tomb Raider Angel of Darkness) in Tomb Raider Legend, we see a HUGE update in graphics with Lara looking spectacular and 'better than ever', according to the official Review from Toonami.
And she is not alone either! Joining her on her quest for the thrill of discovery and adventure are a few of her good friends, one of them already being familiar to us. I won't provide any spoilers, but you'll be sure to remember at least one of the people she encounters from the start.
The combat system is new and improved, although the one disappointment of this game is not being able to carry more than two different weapons at a time (Your standard pistols a secondary weapon). In spite of this however, you can still have Lara kick people's♥♥♥♥♥with seriously awesome results! I guarantee it.
On the flip side however, this adds to the realism of Lara's world as in the real world, people would be limited as to the number of weapons he or she could carry around. In addition to this, there are plenty of rewards to be had, including upgrades, lots of outfits, and other such rewards.
Another annoyance is the way the game runs (Or fails to run) sometimes, resulting in help needed if the game crashes. I am usually able to keep it up and running, although I have had problems with it running in the past. The game is rather short and straightforward and unlike in some earlier Tomb Raider Games, you are not able to return to the exact same location after having finished it with the exception of one location.
Overall, this game has a few challenges here and there, and a lot of the dialogue is witty with some of it being dramatic and a little melancholy. However, I must say, this is by far the easiest Tomb Raider Game I ever played.
Try the demo and see if you like it and then if you like it, buy the full version!

TL;DR: Great game, but not a $30 one, pick it up on sale for $25 or $20.
It's an amazing game, it's not worth $30 (should be $20 or $25), but it's still great. I wouldn't buy it if it wasn't on sale, but if it is and you like games that involve designing and building complexes, as well as managing people and resources (games like Stardew Valley, Rimworld, Sim City/City: Skylines, etc) then definitely get it.
So, why isn't it worth $30 (also the price of Fallout 4)? Just because of some bugs and a few minor issues, its nothing gamebreaking, but it's something that needs to be addressed before a game can reasonably be priced above $25. First off, the AI is a bit wonky at times, mainly the workmen are the most inefficient group of people ever, and the prisoners are a bit odd at times. There are also a few bugs that should be fixed that, from me looking up fixes for them, have been around for more than six months. Bugs such as the staffroom saying there aren't any prisoners to use this canteen. Also, the games micromanagement tab is amazing, but could use some functions to make the game feel more realistic, like adding a way to stop certain staff memebers and prisoners from using certain doors, so that they will stop treating my visitation center as a front gate.
All of the cons aside, Prison Architect is an incredibly fun and addicting game with a decent amount of replayability and an amazing little 5-15 hour campaign that introduces the game very well, while still leaving enough for you to explore and build.

Xenonauts is a UFO:EU-inspired turn-based tactical strategy game set during the Cold War.
The game begins in 1979, when the player is tasked with leading a joint NATO/USSR task force formed in response to a mysterious alien threat. The player is responsible for managing every level of the organization, from constructing bases and researching new technology, to deploying and commanding fighters, to directing individual soldiers on the battlefield in turn-based combat.
Aesthetically, the game has a unique, classy visual identity, great sound design, and a superb soundtrack.
Gameplay-wise, the game is of course similar to its inspiration, X-COM (or UFO: Enemy Unknown), but with rebalanced combat, a vastly superior interface, added mechanics (such as suppression), and real-time air combat.
If you're a new player who was at some point intimidated by the original X-COM's initial lack of direction and micromanagement, or a fan of Firaxis' XCOM looking for a different experience, definitely give Xenonauts a try. It has all the depth and fun of the original X-COM but with almost all of the micromanagement stripped out and a clearer, more presentable interface.
If you're a UFO:EU vet, you'll find something new here. For instance, unlike in UFO, combat armor is extremely valuable, but also heavy, so if you want to follow the tried and true strategy of blowing everything up with C4 you'll have to pay for it in either survivability or mobility. Running out of ammunition can be a very real concern. Suppression and improved alien AI moves the gameplay away from massed reaction fire toward more dynamic "fire and maneuver"-style gameplay.
The best thing about Xenonauts is its ability to remain "faithful" to UFO:EU without feeling like a nostalgia-driven fan remake of an older game. Xenonauts is not afraid to make changes to the formula if they benefit the overall game, nor is it trying to "recapture" the greatness of its idol. Xenonauts wants to forge its own identity as a bleak, uncompromising, tense, occasionally terrifying strategy game. And it largely succeeds.
Very much recommended.

I'm not completely sure whether or not to recommend this game, because of the flaws it has, several of which are actually quite frustrating. But on the other hand I did finish it, so while they annoyed me, I still did enjoy the game and kept playing, so from that point of view, the good parts outweighed the issues.
This is the first Tomb Raider game I've played, so I don't have any "Tomb Raider Standards" set in place. Keep that in mind.
So, before we get into what the issues are, let's look at the basics. Tomb Raider: Legend is an action platformer, with some mild puzzles in it. When I say mild puzzles, it's because while there's quite a few puzzles scattered around, they're really simple to do, and you're often told how to do them just to make matters worse. It's like, you come to place you can't reach and the game just outright goes "Hm, if only I could find something to stand on to get up there"; before you even give it a try yourself. You have a pair of binoculars that can go into a special mode, where you can focus on certain highlighted objects (the important ones) and know whether they can be pushed, are mechanisms, are fragile, or such. You hardly need to though, because it doesn't take an expert to guess that a box can be pushed and moved around. The game even sometimes tell you that "Hey, I bet I can push this". So yea, very mild puzzling.
The action parts are mainly gun combat and twice in the game, a stage where you're on a motorcycle. Seems pretty standard, and the motorcycle would add some variety to the gameplay. That's what you'd think, right ?
We'll get more into that later.
Thirdly, and most importantly, is the platforming. Platforming is pretty much the core of the game. With ledges to grab on to, a grappling hook to fly around with, ropes to climb and jump from, and such. It's pretty fun once you get a hang of it, and it's probably the main attraction, alongside exploring tombs and other interesting locations, and sometimes dodging traps while you're at it.
The controls though, can be a little weird at times. I highly suggest rebinding the keys if playing with a keyboard, because you do not want to play with default controls. They're so weirdly configured, it's like they were chosen by a randomizer, even going as far as using "k" as the grenade button. Yea, "k". Rebind them first chance you get, trust me. It makes it more enjoyable, when you know you're able to actually do things.
That all being said, let's look at the issues mentioned earlier. First issue, is sadly, the platforming. Not all of it, most of it is pretty solid. The ropes more specifically, are what we're looking at here. Oh god, the ropes. I have died so many times because Lara refused to grab onto the rope I jumped at. Sometimes they work, other times they just don't feel like it and you'll phase through them. Doesn't help the game uses a checkpoint based save system, so if you go through a bunch of stuff, and then fail at a rope, you'll have to do it all again. The checkpoints are fairly generous though, so it's not that big of a deal. Personally, it only affected me once or twice, but man, having to redo the same part over and over, just because Lara refuses to use the rope, is infuriating.
Next up is the camera. Being that this a 3D platforming game, there's bound to be issues with the camera. It's just a rule, seemingly. You control the camera with your mouse, and for the most part, that works just fine believe it or not. It's quite responsive and you can look at what you want. Unfortunately, sometimes the camera just decides to turn 180 on you, and if you don't notice then whoops, down that platform you go.
On the bright side, the game does have an auto-grab feature with ledges, where you for the most part will catch on, so it won't kill you... Much... Just annoy you a little.
Thirdly is the aforementioned motorcycle stages. Oh boy, where do I begin with these? These parts are so, so boring. The terrain is basically the same bits that just keeps looping for seemingly forever (most noticable in the second one) and they just keep going and going. Sometimes, once you reach certain "key points", something new will appear and you'll think "oh thank you, is it finally over?" But alas, no, it keeps going after it for a while too. You'll also be fighting a bunch of badguys on motorcycles of their own here, but you just spam your gun at them till they flail all over the ground and leave you be.
Really, these stages really dragged down the overall enjoyment of the game for me, just because they were so boring, repetitive, and just kept on going and going. Worst part about them, they're really stingy about checkpoints, so if you screw up (you're bound to out of boredom) you'll have to redo it. FUN!
The camera also sometimes messes up here, and it's really slow at turning, so if it does, you're in trouble.
Thankfully, there's only two of them, and only one of them really drags on. The first one isn't as bad, but it's not really good either.
And finally, the grappling hook. Yup, there's issues with this thing too. Not really too many, just one. The fact that if you, while on it, touch ANY wall, you'll instantly detach. That there, is something I do not understand, and it WILL get you killed if you think you're on it, but touch the floor (yup) and detach and keep moving forward. Goodbye life, hello spike pit.
In order to move up and down on it, you press up (w) and the use key (e by default). If you do this quick enough, you wont crash into the floor you just stood on, but that's really dumb that you have to do that. If you use it while swinging from stuff, it's perfectly fine.
Just, don't touch any walls. Ever. It's very shy.
The last thing to discuss is the gunplay and combat. It's pretty bland. The AI isn't amazing; they just shoot at you, throw a grenade now and then, and maybe hide behind cover. Sometimes they move around, other times they just stare at you from the open. The way it works, is that you enter a "lock on" mode (g by default), where the game will lock you onto a target (closest target) and then you just press the trigger, or hold it down. It'll auto swap to another target if the current one dies and you hover over a new one (or if you aim too far away). It's pretty simple, pretty generic and pretty easy.
You can free aim if you want, but you're unable to move while doing so, for whatever reason. Good thing is though, you can move around and roll around in combat, without losing the lock on, so even tho it's pretty easy, you can still look like a badass while shooting people and rolling around all over the place. The shooting isn't the game's strongpoint, by any means.
The boss battles are also pretty straight forward.
There is hidden stuff to collect scattered around the levels, and getting to it can actually be quite fun. There's also a time trial mode, where you'll race the levels, to see how fast you can beat them. So there is replayability, if you're into those kinds of things.
So overall, it's an okay platformer, with some generic shooting in it, a couple of issues and some boring looping stages. It's still fun tho, if you like platformers. Just, don't expect to need to think too deeply over puzzles.
I'd recommend it if you got the money to spare and want an overall pretty enjoyable platforming experience, with some tomb exploration, trap dodging and item gathering. Else, you probably wont be missing out on much by skipping it. There's also a story in there, but I wouldn't say it's something writing home about. I personally got it for sale and had my fun with it, so that might be a factor to consider.
It does have some nice scenic views for you to look at, so if that's something you're into, that's another plus for you.

hackmud is different from any other game I've played so far. It's not just about being good in the game, it's about learning to exploit game mechanics. Over 130 hours into the hackmud now, I did not expect to become addicted. I learned a lot about Javascript and mongoDB, and after reaching tier 4 the PvP part gains more importance - whether you focus on offense (hacking other players) or defense (farming NPCs to get good locks as drops which you must equip to secure yourself), both elements will play a major role. NPCs, while very easy at tier 1 and tier 2, can become quite difficult even for experienced players, and not just fighting them, but also finding them in the first place, which is done by solving randomized puzzles - but if you're eager, all of this can be optimized by scripts. And since external scripts are also allowed - as long as they don't break the sandbox - you may run into learning autohotkey or something similar too.
You write javascript code in an external editor, upload the file inside the game (character limit and script slots etc are determined by what upgrades (NPC drops) are equipped) and choose whether you want it to be private or public. There are bots which execute your script in intervals at a certain cost per run, there are scripts that act as banks, wikis, scams, games, puzzles, lotteries, ... well, everything. It's an MMO where players decide the rules.
The game starts off with a tutorial, which is basically the single player part. After finishing that, you are thrown into a vast world of both good and evil, and you will be confused what to do next. But there are helpful ingame wikis and a Discord server with an awesome and very nice community.
It would be wrong to not point out what I do not like about hackmud (at the time of writing this):
The performance and the lack of telnet (or any other method to play this in a real terminal environment).
This is a text based game, and - in my opinion - graphics are not needed and the usage of the Unity engine may be the wrong decision here. Colors, sure, they are important, but shaders and scanlines and bloom are not. They can be disabled with an ingame script, but still it requires a reasonably good computer to be able to run hackmud in windowed mode while editing code. Custom clients are a thing on the developer's to-do list though, so we can expect that to become an option.
Another thing is the font size. Try playing this in windowed mode on a Microsoft Surface or any monitor with a similar DPI - it's impossible. I'm sure the developer is aware of this, too, and may add an option for that, too.

I've always been a big fan of hacking simulation games, but this one comes to closest to actual, real-world hacking by far. In fact, calling it a hacking simulation is not doing it justice, it's a sandbox. This isn't "Press X to hack", hacking npcs or players takes some work and can be challenging to figure out at times. And getting them takes work too, you'll have to search through the blogs and websites of corporations, finding passwords and project IDs to finally get to the addresses of your targets to begin with.
The game is also great for people who want to learn to program, or are already familiar with programming to begin with. The game has a build-in JavaScript engine that allows you to do basically anything you can think of. Want to keep track of what your competitor is doing? Want to sort your upgrades, or automatically transfer money to another account? Want to write a script to get past that tricky lock? Maybe program a game to play for yourself or other players? Only a handful of things are locked down for security reasons, but you have nearly all of the power and flexibility of the JavaScript language to do things for you.
Then there's the Mud part of the game, where you can explore the huge amount of public player scripts, that can be anything from games, to providing banking services. Recently one of the veteran players even created a wiki from scratch, complete with community editing tools. And there's public tools out there made by experienced players that you can use if you don't want or know how to write them yourselves.
I almost forgot about the amazing community. There's a (unofficial) Discord server run by veteran players that has players from all over the world. There's lots of channels, for anything from general chatting, scripting help, a Noob Tips channel, etc. The community will always embrace new players with open arms an there are always passionate people with more experience that will be happy to share their knowledge and experise with you. The game can have a bit of a steep learning curve, but the ability to ask experienced players anything really smoothes that learning process. I would fully recommend the Discord to anyone playing this game.
I'll end this with something that I've heard a lot of people say: you'll either hate the game or love it, and when I say love it I meant LOVE it. I played for almost 80 hours in just my first two weeks of playing. If any of what I just said sounded interesting to you, go give the game a shot. I can guarantee you won't be dissapointed.

For the time, the game had purrfectly acceptable level design; it just didn't age well in the face of the relatively homogenized (milk pun? Sure, let's go with that), and, honestly, much betfur ubiquitious one-lane, always-move-right standard we have today.
So, think the level design is bad? Keep dying on the first stage? I can actually get to stage 7 with all nine lives, at this point, and I'll tell you how.
Think of every level as having 4+ "planes", none of which necessarily intfuract with one another well. There's sometimes a "dungeon" plane, there's the ground, there's the roof-plane, and there are usually 2-3 regions above the roofs.
Jumping to a higher plane is dangfurous! The combination of the game's camera + Bubsy's ridiculously high jump (sorry, Bubsy, you can't jump out of your own game :( ) makes jumping an arduous endeavfur, but...
You have to be /extremefurly/ carefur about jumping UP to a higher plane, but, the game is immeownsely generous when heading downwards. So, stake out a place without enemies, jump upwards for a while, and then glide downwards. You can clear 20-40% of the level this way per leap, and, while gliding, the zoom and controls actually opfurate in a manfur that makes the game feel /fair/. Bubsy will almost never die while gliding (unless you get as unlucky as Bubsy's career), and, by staying either within your "plane" or only heading downwards at high speeds, the game suddenly turns into the Mario/Sonic fusion it's sometimes accused of trying to be.
So, uh, yeah. I like puns, I love the way this game plays like an interactive cartoon, and, hopefully, by assuaging some of people's completely justified rage about the level design, more people can see the pawsitives inherent. Just climb to a meowntain and glide.
Also, it's still better than No Man's Sky.

Sonic Adventure DX is a trip down memory lane for me. I never got in touch with the Dreamcast version and only experienced the DX Version every time i played this game. Back then, i didn't really mind this port/version, despite it's reputation, and i still think to this day it is not too bad. The entire gameplay is rather solid (except for Big and Amy most of the time), story wise it is one of the better ones in the entire modern Sonic Franchise with the most character development.
But this PC port is giving me a really tough time. Here, the downsides the DX version brought are even worse here, with bugs left and right, extremely bad camera issues, very weird controller mapping, audio errors and so on. I even had the problem at one boss fight that the entire fight got glitched and i couldn't finish the boss. After installing the fanmade Patch (which didn't work for me sadly) and uninstalling it, the fight suddenly went without problems. Needless to say, this whole thing still costed me 1-2 hours of my time and it was rather annoying.
When the game works, it's the same enjoyable game i remember from back then, with usually short and very nice stages usually lasting 2-3 minutes. Every story is usually fairly short and you only have to endure Bigs lame fishing games and Amys slow as molases platforming for a short while.
Also the game offers a lot to do even after, but nowhere as deep or exciting as Sonic Adventure 2.
Speaking of said title, i can highly recommend the second game to this one hands down. The gameplay is better, the story and presentation are better even if it has more plotholes, it has tons more content and the challenge level is also higher. And for people who only play for the Chao Garden anyway, get SA2, the Garden is a way more enjoyable experience.
In Conclusion, i am not completely sure if i can recommend this or not. The normal game i can recommend without a doubt, it's still a pretty good entry in the Sonic Series even with it's downsides. But the Steam version is so unbelieveable broken at parts it really discouraged me to play further sometimes.
Get it when it's on sale.

I've played and beaten Sonic 2, 3 & Knuckles, CD, Adventure 1 & 2, Heroes, Shadow the Hedgehog, Sonic 2006, 4 Episode 1 & 2, the DS version of Colors, Generations (including the Unleashed levels mod), and nearly finished Lost World, and I have to say... Slowly eroding nostalgia and stockholm syndrome are the only things that keep me playing his 3D outings.
You probably already know whether or not you're going to buy Sonic Adventure before you read a review of it. You most likely played it when you were younger, or are a fan of later Sonic games curious about his past. Reading this might not change your mind, but I can assure you of one thing: This game has not aged well.
In 1999 a platforming game with 6 playable characters and a Tamagotchi-style side game was a big deal. When the DX version of Adventure was released in 2003, the novelty had worn off, and its many, many flaws were much harder to ignore. Every re-release brings lower and lower review scores from critics, and if you're playing for the first time you'll see why.
Sonic Adventure tells the stories of Sonic and his friends Tails, Knuckles, Amy, and newcomers Big the Cat and E-102 "Gamma". Sonic and Tails are trying to stop the evil Doctor Robotnik/Eggman's latest scheme to dominate the world. Knuckles is trying to gather the scattered pieces of his treasured Master Emerald, which the doctor shattered to release an ancient evil. Amy is trying to reunite a bird that escaped the doctor's robot factory with its family. Big is just after his pet frog. And my personal favorite, Gamma - a robot created by Eggman who eventualy rebels against his creator and sets out to free the animals enslaved by his former master.
The story overall is actually ok, about on par with a saturday morning cartoon plot (and was actually adapted into a story arc in the Sonic X anime). The dialog is rarely groan worthy, though the acting is hit and miss. Sonic and Eggman are pretty good, Tails is awful. The technical presentation of the cutscenes is terrible. Lip synching is all over the place. Animations between props and actors don't sync up correctly. Sometimes characters continue to walk or gesture after they should've stopped. All these small errors set the stage perfectly for the much larger errors you'll experience during actual gameplay.
Sonic, Tails, Amy and Gamma all go through action stages linearly in standard platforming fashion, occasionally solving minor puzzles or making tricky jumps. Tails races Sonic to the end, Amy runs away from a persuing robot, and Gamma uses a gun to shoot enemies. Knuckles' stages are more open, and involve him searching for 3 Master Emerald pieces. He has a display on the bottom of the screen showing how close you are to each piece; blue for cold, red for hot. And Big fishes. Yep, just fishes.
I'm going to focus on Sonic's gameplay, but all my comments are applicable to the others in varying degrees. This game introduced his homing attack, and when it works, it's a cool trick. You press the jump button again in mid-air to rush towards and defeat the nearest enemy. They can be chained together to cover gaps you wouldn't normaly be able to cross. The problem is, you don't have a reticule showing what you're aiming at. If there are multiple targets in view, it's all down to luck what you'll go for, and it WILL cause accidental deaths, many of them.
Running fast is fun. The problem is, the level design actively discourages this by having narrow paths that are hard to navigate at speed. The controls are incredibly twitchy, and even a slight deviation from straight will send you straight into a wall. This game also started the tradition of having Sonic auto-pilot through certain sections. During these, which you have to learn the location of by trial and error, you simply hold forward and hope he makes the right twists and turns. He will twitch and shudder, as the game's physics try to pull him off the scripted path. Sometimes he will just give up and fall during a loop, or shoot off in a random direction at full speed. Also, using a spin dash during these sections makes him stop following his path. Actively playing the game is dangerous.
The camera does not help this either. Though it has two modes, free and auto, both will actively sabotage your attempts at basic navigation. Auto constantly swings the camera around when you go to change direction or jump, and "free" does not always let you rotate it, though it will lock in an unusable angle for you. The camera also frequently gets stuck in level geometry. And this is all just in normal gameplay. Woe betide you if you should try for a "clever" shortcut over a long gap - The camera will do a 180 at just the wrong time and you will fall to your death.
Once you learn the levels and try to finish them faster, the fun really begins. The camera becomes your mortal enemy as you try to short cut your way through paths the developers didn't seem to intend. You WILL sometimes fall through the floor, especially where it meets walls. Dash pads will fling you straight off cliffs. Springs will propel you blindly into the sky and you just have to hope you'll land safely. The spin dash in particular will cause all sorts of weird behavoir, especially during loops or scripted sections. Even navigating normally will get you into trouble. Try just walking near a wall or slight elevation change and watch your character spasm uncontrollably. It's not as bad as Sonic 06, but you'll see how that game was considered acceptable for release given the state Adventure is in.
There's also the Chao garden, which I never cared much for. Defeating enemies in levels releases animals that you can use to power up little creatures, Chao, in one of several statistics, like power, swimming, flying, etc. After you power them up enough, you can pit them against other Chao in races that are require almost no imput from the player. Occasionally your Chao will get a sparkle around them and you can cheer them to run faster, but it's completely random, and doesn't always happen to your Chao either. The Chao garden has a somewhat complex internal logic, with several life stages the Chao can go though, including mating, and even death by old age. Some people even ignore the main game and just play with their Chao, although I was never one of those people. I'm neutral on it - Its presence in the game doesn't detract from anything, and it's a neat little diversion.
Upsides? Some of the music was pretty good, although your age will probably dictate if you find late 90's rock appealing or not. I still like Open Your Heart, the main vocal theme, and some of the character's vocal themes are guilty pleasures. The stage music fits the environments well. I like Gamma's last boss music outside of its gameplay context. The final boss fight, where you play as Super Sonic, is pretty cool. Discovering short cuts is fun when they work right. If you manage to get a glitch free run of a level, you can see how the game could've been fun if it had been worked on for longer.
You probably know already whether or not you're going to buy this game. Personally, I don't know what keeps me playing Sonic. I love the 2D games (mostly), and I even liked Generations (again, mostly). Every once in awhile, everything clicks. I make all the right jumps, find all the right routes, and get through a level faster than I thought I could. And it feels great. Then I try again, and some glitch flings me through a wall, causes my homing attack to target the wrong thing, or I reach a piece of level design that makes me question whether the game was actually even played before it was released. I suppose I am a true Sonic fan. I stick with him through the bad times. Because with the nostalgia glasses off, it's hard to see many good ones.

Bubsy Two-Fur is the moves of a company daring to use an emulator as their base and hardly giving the owners much to enjoy.
Bubsy Two-Fur is a combo set of two games for the SNES. The first game, "Bubsy in: Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind," sees you saving the world's yarn supply from a group of alien bandits, the "Woolies." The second game, simply titled "Bubsy II," has you running through space and time.
On the surface, it's a good way to bring attention to a long-lost character. This is despite him being rather infamous for his poor resemblances to Sonic the Hedgehog. Within, of course, it's a bit of a struggle. Gameplay is pretty straight forward, as Bubsy will jump about, run fast, and glide through the many levels. The level design hardly seems to benefit the bobcat, however.
Further in, we note the legacy this particular rendition has. It was previously being attacked due to its use of an emulator to basically run two ROMs of the games. Where those results have gone, is a good question.
My somewhat dated analysis of Bubsy Two-Fur, from its launch, can be viewed
The game appears to have had some consistent updates, so I suppose the developers are at least attempting to make sure it's up to snuff.
If you want to experience one of the most infamous attempts to copy a popular system mascot, Bubsy will do just fine. If you have some history with Bubsy, this could either be the perfect purchase, or a plague to you. Personally, I can't recommend it to anyone looking for a worthwhile game, much less one that isn't simply inside an emulator the way it's been done.

Xenonauts started development before XCOM: Enemy Unknown was even announced to the public. It aimed to be a modern day remake of the original 'XCOM: UFO Defense', also know as 'UFO: Enemy Unknown' in Europe.
Xenonauts has stayed true to the original, plus expanded on it. Everything that was great about the original XCOM is here and even better. The UI is very nice and clean, Air and Ground Combat both feel great, and base/research/production management is very fun as well.
Now that the game is released, I can finish this review. From when I first made this review, there's been quite a few changes and much balancing, which made an already fun TBS even more so. My only real complaint is that the soldiers stat generation has had its minimum lowered, so when starting a new game or recruiting a new soldier, you often get soldiers with annoyingly low Time Units(TU for short).
The only saving grace is that they changed how much TU's shooting costs. Instead of a flat number, it's a percentage of their max TU's. This means that no matter how few TU's you have, you can still rally off as many shots as a high TU character. However, movement TU cost is still a flat number, so low TU will greatly restrict how far you can go, and if you want to shoot and move, you'll have a hard time with low TU's.
They also nerfed some of the armor and the shield. The shield is the biggest in my opinion. I used to love having two soldiers with shields, but with its small nerf, they start to become a liability far sooner than before. There IS a shield upgrade, but you get that option LONG after the first shield becomes a liability. Doesn't help that they nerfed the pistol pretty hard too.
With the release version I tend to drop the shield pretty quickly, and I rarely use the pistol due to its poor accuracy and range.
Anyway, enough with complaining. Despite the whining, this game is still incredible. If you like XCOM and/or Turn Based Strategy games, then this is definitely a game you'll need to pick up.

TL/DR - A much better Planet Side 2 (for those that aren't familiar with this game having come first.)
This is the only tactical FPS / flight sim / tank sim game out there where the battles matter. This is not an arena shooter. This is not a fast paced action game. This is the type of game where you may sit around guarding something for say 20 minutes with no action, and then suddenly get plunged into 15 minutes or more of pure carnage.
The best feature of the game is the absolutely massive map. Seriously these guys put every other FPS out there to shame with that.
Some of the downsides are that the learning curve is straight up vertical especially in the seat of a fighter plane. Everyone mentions the graphics being bad, but honestly they aren't that bad. They wont be winning any awards for it, but it does its job well.
There's so many good stories that come out of this game, as you battle it out for a hard fought victory across the map. Once a map is completed it resets again, and technology advances as the time of the current campaign does.
Being a free to play player allows you to play with weapons that are slightly out dated. Now a lot of folks may see this as a disadvantage but it's truly not. In certain match ups maybe, like a tiger vs a matilda mk 2 perhaps, but you shouldn't try to engage a tiger with a matty 2 anyway lol.
This is the only game I have played where it felt truly awesome to win a map, or even to lose one for that matter. I feel that now that it is on steam and has a wider audience the game will only get better.

Having played the most recent Tomb Raider reboot, I had low expectations for its aged predecessor. Quite honestly, I was suprised, if you can get past the dated graphics, which I very rarely have a  problem with, TR Legend is an addicting, solid game that willl keep you engaged throughout its lengthy story. The story takes you across a number of very interesting environments, to name a few, you have to navigate frozen rivers, climb through a Japanese city, and slide down dunes in the desert. It never sticks to one single mechanic or setting for too long, before it becomes boring, you are whisked away to another section of the earth, which is usually coupled with a new gadget, type of puzzle, or platforming element that expands on the game. Minor complaints include a generally jerky camera, which will sometimes force you to complete jumps you really can't see, and some puzzles which can require you to run to google to find the answers (I had to do that once, I'm afraid). Occasional boss fights can be frustrating, but are rewarding when you finally expose their weakness and kill them. Combat isn't anything to recomend, it involves locking onto a character and circle strafing constantly while occasionally jumping to throw them off, but the developers were aware of this and made the platforming and puzzle solving the highlight of the game. Fortunately, these two features are executed perfectly, and make this game a must-buy even with its differences from the reboot. If you find it on sale, which I did for less than 2 dollars, you have virtually no execuse. Do it.

Blockwick 2 is a game about moving blocks around until all blocks of the same color make contact with each other. Sounds easy but I assure you it's much more complicated than that. Some of the blocks are bolted down and can’t move while others are forced to move when moving a different block. This type of puzzle is not the kind that you end up getting frustrated at when you can’t solve it since the game lets you progress to the next level if you can find the hidden pear in every level. The soundtrack is very nice and goes with the game very well and can even be purchased on Bandcamp if you wish.
I found this in my discovery queue and was instantly reminded of the original Blockwick that I played on iOS a long time ago. Kieffer Bros. has another game on iOS called Aqueduct and that’s how I found out about them. Since I was very familiar with this developer I decided to give this game on steam a try and I think you should to. And if you decide you don’t love this beautiful masterpiece of a game you can always return it if you want, that is if you haven’t played it for too long.
Also really hoping that even though Aqueduct was made natively for iOS and Android I hope that the devs decide to port it over to steam.

A great puzzle game about sliding block in  tight spots to group by color.
Where the old Klotski could get repetitive, Blockwick never repeats the same configuration and introduces special blocks to keep things interesting.
Each level has the chance of being solved or illuminated. Even if a level is hard, you can move to the next level if you find a hidden pearl. If you find a hard level you can at least move on and come back later.
The set of Basic levels added after the initial release is easier than the normal levels but they are still some extra fun.
Very recommended if you're the thinker type.
Small cons:
* Undo is limited to one movement. After that there's only the option to restart the level. And even then, this is not too bad since when you're stuck, trying a new fresh solution can be the best idea.
* Music is pleasant but the tracks are short and it will get repetitive. Easy to silence, of course.

Well-designed metroidvania game with a striking aesthetic and a some unique puzzles. Each area has a distinct feel, and all of the items obtained throughout the game are powerful and have a few different uses. Sound design is very well done, and adds to the feel of the game world immensely. The world is easy to navigate, although I feel there could have been a few more shortcuts to connect the various areas together. Backtracking is mostly optional, and is not tedious since there are doors to open with newfound abilities. Boss design is solid, and the last two bosses especially were a lot of fun. Enemy design is a bit less inspired, but is diverse enough to avoid getting stale.

I love unique art direction in games. A couple that come to mind are Limbo and the recent Rayman games. I still need solid mechanics, but a unique sense of style can elevate an otherwise solid but unexceptional game to something special. Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is a perfect example. It's a solid ​Metroidvania game with a decent-size map, a nice variety of tools and weapons, and some clever puzzles and boss fights. The movement of the ship and the physics of the environment are also exceptionally well implemented. None of it is groundbreaking, but not every game has to be revolutionary. It does what it does very well, and with flawless design in both UI design and art direction.

I am editing this review for the released verson of the game. Okay so my initial impressions of this game was that it was the first true original xcom successor, and if you felt enemy unknown released in 2011 was too simple or just not enough like the original, you'll find all of that here and more. From watching this game very early on in development to full release, I can full heartedly say that it has come a long way, and the devs have certainly done a wonderful job making the game into all it could be. Some things in the game are still a little wonky, however it all has to do with the RNG of shooting which is to be expected in any pecentage based strategy game so I can't fault it for that as the original even had it. This game has a very wide enemy variety, and a fully interactive dogfighting minigame when shooting down enemy space ships of also wide varieties. Also this game captures my personal favorite part of the original xcom, which the 2011 verson didn't even come close to, and that is the dynamics of the game. In this game everything you do effects the way the game plays, if you don't go to certain missions or let certian abductions, bombings, etc happen, the enemies will gain the upper hand. And if they gain the upper hand instead of having a linear, boring experience like the 2011 game, you will have a very replayable strategy game that will keep you coming back to see your friends and loved ones get blown to pieces by plasma blasts. All in all this game is truly an example of what an early accsess game should be like, and has lived up to all my expectations for an xcom like successor.
FINAL VERDICT:

If you enjoy complex strategy games, I definitely recommend this title, however if you are looking for an easier stategy game to casually play, you won't find it here as even the normal difficulies can be extremely punishing for even experienced players. I personally love this game and hope to see its added modding community only produce more content for it.

The Deer is a static diorama type of a display, where you walk left and right with your deer and read dry encyclopedic facts about Pleistocene. You can also mouse over some object in order to read some more facts. There are 3 ultra short & easy minigames that vaguely align with the game's theme. Going back and forth through the entire length, reading everything on display, clicking through "minigames", reading instructions and whole curiosities section in menu - it all takes a little under 10 minutes.
The artstyle is nice to look at, but that's the only positive thing I can say about it. I have no idea who the target audience is - not adults that's for sure. As for children - they would need to be old & knowledgeable enough to read English (there are no other languages), exhibit high tolerance for boring random tidbits of knowledge and be ok with no other elements to entertain them (just get your kid some nicely illustrated and well edited children's book on this topic instead).
The only gameplay there is (pressing A & D to walk left & right) is clunky - it takes several presses to switch direction, and The Deer will often continue walking in the previous direction for a while, even when the opposite button used. Sometimes it will get stuck going in one direction and if you want to walk another way you need to restart the game... Clicking often misses it's mark (most apparent in the "find 5 right foods" minigame - what gets marked is usually somewhere around the cursor, not under it, sometimes you need to click a couple of times for the game to register). Oh and those issues persist even in the correct resolution. What resolution is that? Well apparently anything 16:9 - if you pick different ratio (windowed/ fullscreen - no difference), then the sides will be cut off (which is apparent by things like half a home button in the curiosities section or half of the deer head stamp you receive after solving a minigame).
Basically what little gameplay they had in there, they couldn't even make that right.

This is one of my favorite games I've ever played.  It's hard to explain exactly what the draw is in a concise way, so be prepared for a little reading.
It's easy to say that I love it for the scripting, which is my primary focus, but the reason I love it is so much more than that.  The atmosphere really clicks for me, where the lore is presented "Dark Souls style", which takes some digging to reveal - and what it shows you makes you want to know more.  The npcs in this game talk from time to time, and as you see what they have to say you may start to realize they are not just making jokes, spamming weather reports, and adding to the lore, but they also hint at secrets that players can find.
Exploring content in this game is one of the most interesting things I've found to do when I'm not scripting.  A lot of reviews I've seen on the store are posted from 2016 - and I can say without a doubt that the game has had a lot more content added, and is constantly getting minor updates interspersed with periodic larger ones.  There's the obvious things - finding NPCs to hack, learning how to hack them, maybe even writing your own scripts to hack them (and other players).  That's only scratching the surface - there's hidden content everywhere, much of it undiscovered or unsolved.  Unique chat channels with interesting messages, information and buried in NPC corporations only available to those who look carefully and dig deep, and unsolved (and likely undiscovered) puzzles and solutions still waiting to be found.
PvP and hacking is something I specialize in when playing this game.  It is a constant arms race for attackers and defenders, usually an exciting (if sometimes imbalanced) one.  The PvP aspect of hacking is still being balanced and tweaked constantly.  I'm not going to gloss over it and say "it's fine" - there is definitely work to be done here.  As someone who writes scripts primarily focused on releiving others of their assets (and dignity), I find this to be interesting more than frustrating the majority of the time.  By spending time to learn and use game mechanics to your advantage, you can excel far beyond your peers.  There's multiple layers of competition - not just how much "stuff" you have, but also the tools and scripts people write, the strategies and plans people come up with, and how well you can leverage mechanics to help your cause.
The community also is a large contribution to why I have spent so much time playing.  It's not the largest community ever - but one common theme I've seen is that people are passionate about this game.  You don't have much middle ground where people say "this game is fine" - my guess is you'll likely either love it or hate it.  Having so many people who are passionate about the game makes the community much more interesting than other larger games that I've played, and there's usually people around who are happy to help with questions you may have.
Time for some cons, as it would be misleading to leave them out.
- The ingame chat experience is not great.  It's currently a work in progress and there is a chat API and an open source webchat project that can be contributed to, but chatting in the game itself still needs work.
- It has a steep learning curve.  You will likely run into scams, get hacked, and/or need to retire your user.  This is all normal and expected, and is part of the gameplay, but it can be off-putting to some players.
- The community is present nearly always, but not always visible.  There's often a lot going on, but it's not publicly visible, making the game seem quieter than it really is.
- There is a fairly heavy community driven focus on scripting.  This is a problem not with the game so much as with the way the community approaches the game.  This is a sandbox game, and most things can be done without scripting even if people try to claim otherwise.  We are also given the tools to make our own content that
be scripted - but as things are today that mentality is a bit lacking.
Given all of that, I can only say that you should give this game a try.  It pulled me in and I'm guessing it could do the same for you as well, if you stick with it and are willing to take on the learning curve.

Hackmud features an excellent single-player campaign. My reccomendation is to not use any of the guides available online and just go at it with your own wits since it is, in essence, a puzzle game. The development team has obviously spent a great deal of time working the single player mode which is a tutorial for the MUD part. Buy this, but don't try to rush through the single player mode since half of the tutorial content's goal is developing your intuition.
CASE IN POINT: My first experience with the MUD aspect of the game was to enter the global chatroom with one player and one bot active. The player had evidently just escaped the single-player mode as I had, and we talked a bit about what to do next since there didn't appear to be any pointers on where to go. The bot kept posting a script and announcing  how much fun you could have running this script (it's a game within a game, RPG system, leveling, multiplayer,etc). Anyhow... Then the other newbie goes quiet for a while. When he starts posting again, he's saying the exact same things the bot was. Word for word. Then he quits the game. I guess he missed the part of the tutorial where you learn the hard way not to run unidentified scripts...
