We exploded aliens, solved puzzles, and, in generally, kicked♥♥♥♥♥ What more is there to say? Let’s get into the review.
I – Story [6/10]
Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is a  2-D action/adventure from Shadow Planet Productions. The story is simple: you (an alien) are tasked with exploring an incredibly hostile planet; making your way steadily to the center in the hopes that you can save your home world by destroying an alien infestation at it’s source. Like I said, simple. But, it was well done all the same.
II – UI [8/10]
The user interface in ITSP is intuitive and easy to master. HUD is almost non-existent, forcing you to really on visuals to assess your level of health. There is no reticle for aiming (which I wasn’t the biggest fan of, but whatever). The map was very user friendly, but can become cumbersome as there is no mini-map on screen. When you receive a new objective, a directional bubble points you in the right direction and off you go.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
There are three modes of play in ITSP. Firstly, there was the campaign. As I explained above, the story line is simple and there are no real side quests to speak of. You make your journey deeper and deeper into the hostile planet until you have accomplished your ultimate goal.
One of my favorite aspects of the game was the research tool that your space craft is equipped with. You will use this tool the entire game to figure out how things work and to assist you in solving various puzzles. You point it at what needs scanning, scan it, and then pick the right tool for the job. I personally thought that this was a novel way of learning as you go and getting through the game.
Combat is simple; just point and shoot (or saw, in a lot of cases). Each enemy has a certain weapon that is best against it, though you don’t strictly have to use that one weapon if you don’t want to. Why blow something up with a rocket when you can melt it with a laser beam or cut it in half with a gigantic saw blade? My thoughts exactly.
The second game mode is called “Lantern Run”. While all the game modes are co-op, this one was definitely designed to be played co-op rather than alone. In this mode of play the player(s) have to drag a lantern (or multiple lanterns) as far into a cavern as they can go. All the while they are being chased by a huge alien monster. Every so far into the cavern, the player(s) must stop in an arena and fight respawning enemies until the big one catches up and breaks through the next wall for you. If all of the lanterns break, it’s game over.
The third game mode is called “Shadow Hunters”. Again, this is another one that was designed for co-op. The player(s) must drag a bomb through a cavern that is teeming with enemies. The bomb has a timer that is always counting down, though it can be recharged at bomb recharge stations. If the bomb takes damage, the timer goes down faster. Every so far down the cavern, the player(s) will again be stopping in caverns to fight both regular enemies and boss enemies (hence the bomb you’re carrying).
While all the modes of play were pretty fun, I particularly enjoyed the campaign best. Though, I didn’t have the chance to get much co-op time in.
IV – Content [6/10]
For as big of an in-game map as ITSP has, I was a bit disappointed by the amount of content. There are several tools that you’ll zoom around the planet collecting, but only one is upgradeable. In addition to this, while your hull armor is also upgradeable, there is no way to change what your craft looks like (even though other space crafts are selectable in the Shadow Hunters game mode).
There were a lot of different enemy types though, although a seemed to be the same enemy with a new theme for each biome of the planet. The boss battles were all pretty fun, blending combat and puzzle solving into a chaotic good time.
V – Visuals [10/10]
The visuals of Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet were splendid. It had a creepy, Tim Burton-esque feel and was almost endearing in a way. While the enemies were fascinating enough, it was the environments of the planet that were truly breathtaking and made exploring the hostile underground a real treat.
VI – Audio [10/10]
The music of ITSP was fantastic and always seem to kick in right when it would boost the immersion the most. The ambiance throughout the game was great and all the sound effects fit in to the game world perfectly.
VII – Overall [8.3/10]
Overall, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is a genuinely fun game and is easily worth the full price tag. If you can get it on sale, great, if not, you won’t be disappointed anyway.

So I feel like I can finally review this game. I have been with Prison Architect since almost Day 1 of release back in Early Access and to see how far it has come is really amazing.
This game is the type of game you can sit down, relax, enjoy yourself and just let the hours fly by. It's not a riot simulator or a action movie simulator, it's a creative blank slate. Make your prison what you want it to be. You can control everything about your prison from what walls are made out, what time lunch is, who gets how much free time, if it's a for profit or a balanced prison, happiness, and much more. Each prisoner is unique including some with unique backstories, appearance, gang affilitation, crimes, characteristics and even some legendary prisoners who will be a handful to say the least.
This game hasn't gotten old even after 223 hours. Now hold on, 223 hours doesn't seem much, right? Well 200 of those hours were spent on ONE PRISON. The same one I have been working on. I downloaded a basic setup from the Steam workshop and went with it, expanding and modifying it to meet the ever-changing needs of the prison. This game holds up and continues to be fun.
Lets get down to business.
Goods:
Good developers who put out helpful videos with updates and genuinely care about the player. Hard to find these days.
Customization options
Replay value is sky high
A touchy subject handled well
Tutorial campaign is genuinely helpful and well executed (pun)
So much detail put into how the prison works
Steam Workshop is amazing with this game
Escape mode is fun
Bads:
Bugs, including some involving particularly violent prisoners who will not stop fighting ever.
NPC's moving through walls occassionally
Some issues with task prioritization (sending a guard to a fight and having them not notice it and leave for example)
Overall: 9/10 Will continue playing and recommending. Perfect casual game. Love it.

This game is MINDBLOWING. Anyone who says this game is only about passwords or codes or something like that clearly hasn't delved deep enough into this game, they haven't even begun to scratch the surface. The deeper you go, the more complex and "dangerous" it gets. The stuff that you can do, can have happen to you, and what comes out of this game is absolutely INSANE. Good if you're patient and willing to learn about how this game
works, bad if you're like some of the other reviewers who say that all they got to do was guess passwords and talk to NPCs. That's not what the game is AT ALL.

While a background in coding certainly helps, it is not necessary to enjoy this game. You'll finish the single-player portion in probably 4-8 hours depending on how hard a time you have (maybe quicker than 4, it really varies). I would compare the multiplayer portion to a MUD version of something like, say, Castle Doctrine or maybe countering a clever redstone trap/lock in Minecraft. You will be solving puzzles and employing commands you learned in singleplayer to hack into NPC accounts and even player accounts. Be careful not to fall for tricks in which players can get into your accounts, such as using a script they created that's currently Full Sec, for them to switch it later and it become something that hacks your account. Social engineering is a big part of multiplayer. You can form/join corporations (guilds) and there are many different paths to take as a member of the multiplayer community (not just coding scripts and hacking accounts).
This is a pretty fast and simplified synopsis of the game, but many have said everything I would want to say already. I would give this game an 8.5/10, with my only complains being the lack of word wrapping (command lines can stretch beyond the width of the screen) and the sometimes problematic scratch pad (window you can write and copy/paste text into). This is a must have for gamers that code or those that enjoy puzzles or anything in the realm of cyberpunk/hacking culture.

Charming graphics, haunting audio and simple yet satisfying gameplay: what more could you want from a space-exploration title?
Your task may be simple: explore your planet and collect valuable resources so you can build up your stores in order to take to the skies and explore a new planet - all in the name of making money - but this simple drive to collect resources to fuel your next exploratory adventure is something that is wholly intoxicating and well worth the price tag.
While the title may be a simple survival-grind title it really plays like something so much more and, with more features being added regularly (including the four-player co-op feature that was added after I had already begun my adventure), I really do see Astroneer being one of my favourite games to come out of 2016/2017.
Featuring a simple concept, equally simple but beautiful and charming graphics (as well as a haunting soundtrack that really immerses you in the game), Astroneer plays like the space exploration title we were looking for before the whole No Man’s Sky incident and I for one am extremely excited to see more of this highly addictive title (though I am tempted to say that this title is probably receiving more love that it would have had it been released before Hello Games’ now highly patched offering).

A lot of people compare this game to No Mans Sky but honestly I don't see the relation. The games are completely different.
Astroneer is pretty fun at first. Everything is fairly intuitive and it's not long before you gather the items you need to get started.
I love the mining mechanic, it's pretty cool how you can just remove or restore huge amounts of land. It makes it really easy to dig caves.
Unfortunately it didn't take long for all the game breaking bugs to show their face and I ended up getting a refund.
I will definitely buy the game again when it comes out of early access (hah!) because it was fun while it lasted!

I think this is an awsome game

It isnt a shoebox shooter, the game varies constantly from day to day from battle to battle even from one minute to the next.
Sometimes you spawn in and barely have time to breath before someone is shooting at you, other times you have plenty of time to get situated and figure out what you want to do.
There is no hard and fast rule about where you have to be and what you have to do.
If fighting in town is not for you, you can venture out into the countryside and scout out a location to ambush enemy units at they make their way to town, or you can decide to go assault and destroy their field position.
The game is hard, there are no helpers. no assisted aiming, no units that are normalized to be less than what they might have been in real life, so some things are very difficult to kill, and when you first start out you die a lot until you start getting the hang of things, but the players will help you learn anything and you will get it sorted and you wont die near as much. At least not all the time :)
It isn't the kind of game you can make much judgement about in an hour or two because you are still trying to figure everything out, and there is lots to figure.  Its all human beings, no bots, so you can never quite predict anything.
You might die 10 times in a row, but on your 11th try capture a choke point and kill 8 guys while defending it.
The graphics are simplified, but then in other games you dont have to see and track potentially 100+ players just in your area all running around on one single map that is 1/4th real scale.
I cant think of any other game where i have looked up to see 40 human enemy players parachuting from the sky, while 20 human operated enemy tanks are trying to crush me from the east, and an uncountable number of human operated enemy ground soldiers are running at me across a field trying to shoot me to pieces with everything from rifles to light machine guns to mortars while a dozen enemy aircraft try to strafe or bomb me to death.
Try the game, give it a week before you make up your mind on it.

Steam doesn't reflect this, but I've been playing this game...an ungodly amount of time, on and off for over 10 years now. In that time I've seen WW2 Online go through massive changes and population flux's, and I've always come back for more. There's simply nothing else like it out there, bar none. There's admittedly a big learning curve to it, but the Squads in game are more than welcoming and eager to teach newbies the tricks of the game. Of all my greatest memories in gaming I've got a dozen just from this game alone, and hundreds of screenshots, from giant armor clashes, massive paradrops, to thick dogfighting furballs above contested towns. The last few years have seen the pop slowly wane away, but with Steam the battles are back to what I remember, just the other day I was part of a para drop on Luxembourg with 100 other Fallshirmjager. While in the end we didn't take the town, it was crazy to see the chutes blocking out the sky, as I ran around with 2 other green tags helping them capture control points.
I love this game, but I'm ready to admit it's faults, the biggest being graphics. But again, this game is older than some of the people playing it, and the devs are working to fix this. It should also be noted that this is a small Dev team who are totally devoted to the game, and you'll often see them running around in the game themselves. I can't tell you the joy it would bring me to shoot down Doc. They're passionate about the game and aren't in this for the money, they're working to keep the game and studio alive to keep the community together, running and having fun.
If you can look past the graphics you've got the perfect blend of simulation with action, and though it can be incredibly frustrating it's also insanely satisfying. When you're the sole anti-tank gun in Huy holding back a horde of Sherman’s from pouring across the bridge and cutting off the army base. Watching destroyers fight it out in the Zee's while you're up a bush line to get to a CP. Taking off far in the back of the map to interdict Allied pilots heading for Axis factories. After a campaign, you'll look back on the map and remember hard fought battles around Amsterdam as you're invading England.
I'm a lifetime Axis player, and more than happy to help and train anyone who's looking to learn more about the game. I'm KaisrJoe and you'll find me in the air, ground and sea. Feel free to message me.

But if you want to see a person describe a game with broken english then continue reading.
The gameplay:
if you played gta game before you know how it plays you can drive cars, shoot at people, etc. But some of the things that stand out in this game are car customization, buying property like houses and bussineses and the small things like races, arcade games, girlfriends and all that stuff. Car customization is pretty good you can add nitro, change colorscar faster and all that stuff. Buying property gives you things like more money and new save points. All of the small things are just some things to get you more money or to just to do something when you don't have anthing to do.
The story:
It does the job of introducing you to new gameplay mechanics that i mentioned above. The story starts out pretty good and ends with what i think is a pretty good ending. You play as Carl Johnson aka CJ whose mother just died and you come back to Los Santos based off Los Angeles to pay your respects and visit your family and friends. Also you are gangsters forgot to mention that.
The world:
It's a open world game that gives you more of the world after you complete enough missions. You start out at Los Santos which is based of Los Angeles as i said above. The you move on to the forest area can't remember it's name but there are a lot of small towns, farms and forests there it can be a bit creppy at times. Then we have San Fierro based of San Fracisco. Seriously though, the best thing to come out of this were the backgrounds and other Bubsy related steam items that I now decorate my profile with.

Honestly, I think Bubsy 1 is an all right game. Not amazing, but all right. The level design is built in such a way where each level has multiple ways to get from the beginning to the end, oftentimes with ways to avoid most enemies pretty easily (once you've found these alternate paths, that is. Some are hard to find). Its also pretty easy to speed through levels the way its made. You can find a lot of these alternate paths on accident just by running and jumping as fast as you can to get to the end of the level. You run at Sonic level speeds in this game, and I like that.
The music is catchy, but you hear too much of the same music for too long. Bubsy himself is a fun character though, from the poses he makes to the pop culture quotes and puns he makes at the beginning of each level.
People like to complain about the game having falling damage, but the thing is is that to avoid falling damage all you have to do is glide. And gliding is encouraged since it slows down how quickly you fall, allowing you to get farther while in the air, which is extremely useful when you're trying to fly over levels from higher points in them.
Is it perfect? No. My biggest qualm with it is that getting touched kills you. Its unbelievably unforgiving, and considering  you don't have a whole  lot of screen to see enemies and obstacles as you move, this can be an issue. Thankfully, because this game runs in an emulator,  you have save states, so this helps alleviate said problems.
As for Bubsy 2....Its terrible. It fixed Bubsy's biggest problem (the 1 touch death thing) since you can actually touch enemies in it without immediately dying, but the music and level design took a nosedive as a result.

UPDATE:
The game was finally patched so Bubsy 2 no longer constantly crashes but the update also completely broke controller  support for me. I used to be able to play the first game fine using either a PS3 or 360 controller, now none of them work even if I reinstall the game. Also, the function keys for quick loading do absolutely nothing.
As it is, the first Bubsy is a classic and the eponymous character really does stand out as a great character design. The game however is poorly balanced, unfair and at times completely  unwieldy. It tries real hard to be like the classic Sonic games, but what you get is a Sonic-wannabe who dies from fall damage and running into walls too fast.
There are some very cool ideas for stages and gimmicks, such as the multi-part desert/train stages and the black shirt power-up - but no matter how good they are, the assets are recycled ad-nauseum and get repetitive real fast.
The sequel, Bubsy 2, fixes some of the problems from Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind - you no longer instantly die from taking any sort of hit and the enemy designs and stages are much better and much more varied with added gimmicks like shooter segments and mini games. You also have a choice in which order you want to tackle the stages which certainly makes the game less punishing in the long term. The game does suffer from inconsistent frame rates however can be really sluggish but I can't tell if it's due to poor emulation or if this was really what the original was like.
Either way, it’s Bubsy and if you’re here looking to buy, then you’re probably either getting it out of pure nostalgia - in which case this review won’t matter - or you’re a glutton for punishment like me. But with all of the technical issues of this port, I can’t recommend it for either of those groups at this time. It’s one thing to be schooled by old-school Nintendo-hard games, and another thing entirely to get stuck trying to find workarounds for controls that are completely broken.
Joy2Key does work but can be a pain to set up.

A Steam port of Bubsy 1 and 2...
WHAT COULD POSSIBLY GO WROOONG?!
Everything, actually. Both the port, AND the games. The reason I even own this game is because I got it as a joke gift, which says a lot about the actual games.
First off, let me explain this "port". It's literally Bubsy 1 and Bubsy 2 lazily slapped onto an emulator, with a price of $5.49. Now that we got that out of the way...
Let's start with the first game!
Bubsy is the pinnacle of bad game design. It tries to go fast like a Sonic game, but you immediately end up dying because of running into an enemy you can't even see until it's right in front of you and have half a second to react. Then, the game tries to be like a platformer. The problem is, the game's areas are barely even designed to suit high-speed platforming, which this game seems to aim for. Honestly, I have no clue what this game was aiming for. It's all over the place.
ALSO WHEN YOU DIE YOU HAVE TO START AAAALLL OVER.
I gotta hand it to Accolade though, I really like the charm Bubsy packs. Especially with some of his death animations. Not so much what he says. Bubsy's actually pretty annoying.
Now for the second game!
It's better than the first, that's for sure! Yet, it still suffers from the same lack of good level design and a few of the same flaws the first game had.
I've literally only played this game for fifteen minutes and these are my first impressions.
In all honesty, I think the reason people green lighted this port to begin with was a joke. And it's pretty funny.
Die in a fire, Bubsy. And bring your cat puns with you.

Unlike others I do really enjoy this game. I find it a fun and challenging platformer, and the animations, especially death animations, are funny. Plus Bubsy is cute. :3
That being said. I do have some negative points. Never a good thing I know.
NO LIFE SYSTEM
Mario Bros. was challenging, but fair thanks to a life system, same for Sonic. But in Bubsy you don't get that. Everything kills you in one hit. This creates a strong sense of frustration that games shouldn't cause.
TOO MANY DEATH TRAPS
I know there are bound to be spikes, and pitfalls, but good god. They are all over the later levels. I can't take more than two steps with running into, or nearly running into some sort of death trap. Plus enemies are all over the place, and yep you die in one hit so that adds to the frustration.
A nice save system included in the emulation is nice, but the game would still be fun if I didn't die in one hit making me constantly use the quick load function.
I would certainly like to see Bubsy make a come back in some new games, and I hope you guys, Retroism, could provide that. And that is why I bought this to help support. It's only five dollars, not an arm and leg. :)

Note: This review is for Sonic Adventure DX using the BetterSADX mod pack, because otherwise the game is an optimized mess that's nearly unplayable and SEGA hasn't bothered to properly fix it yet. BetterSADX is absolutely mandatory here.
This was the first truly 3D Sonic game, launched alongside the Dreamcast. Back then, it was a blast to play, but perphaps because that's what we had back then. To me, this game hasn't aged well, but it's still a good Sonic game for the most part. You can play as 6 characters with different playstyles. Thankfully, playing as Sonic is easily the best part, with speedy stages and a longer story. Tails is also cool to play, using it's flying ability to shortcut through the stages. Too bad that it's story is short. Knuckles is all about exploring, and he can glide and climb walls. It isn't too bad, but his stages aren't based on speed. Amy stages feel more like a traditional platformer, and they aren't too bad either. E-102 Gamma style is similar to Amy, but with a shooting mechanic. And Big the Cat sucks. Fishing is terrible, and shouldn't be in a Sonic game. Overall, the game is fun to play, especially the Sonic stages. The rest is okay, except for Big the Cat. Connecting all the stages there's a hub world, but honestly i didn't like it. It breaks the pace of going from stage to stage. There's also a Chao raising garden that was a good distraction back then, but today i just skipped it. I won't spoil the story, but it basically sucks, alongside the voice acting. However, the soundtrack is awesome. After collecting 130 emblems you unlock Metal Sonic, but it's just a skin of Sonic. But if you have the BetterSADX, you also unlock some classic Game Gear Sonic titles, which are a nice distraction. To sum it up, i recommend this game on sale and with BetterSADX installed, even if today the game isn't really that great.

A game of nearly 17 years despite its dated graphics, aesthetics, and aged subscription plan has managed to grasp the air, land, and sea of World War 2 in a highly immersive and in-depth video game. Coming from a non-vet and first timer through steam I have quite enjoyed this game, and this is very much thanks to various veterans and a friendly community who were more than willing to show me the ropes (ADVICE FOR NEW PLAYERS: Go out there on the battlefield and ask questions as you go. It will be a much better experience than trying to learn everything in one go!).
While the graphics can be an eye-sore to some, it was outshined by the massive depth and complexity of the war mechanics of the game. Being able to capture towns through great teamwork and careful planning is highly rewarding. Many games fail to offer the big picture and consequeces of a player's actions in the world, but WWII Online has definitely delivered in this aspect. I cannot shake off the experience of what started as a defence against a German armoured attack at Verdun to finally taking back Bastogne the next day after much bloodshed.
For many f2p players however, in this day and age the subscription business model is one that does not cater to a majority of gamers today as it doesn't with me. While the f2p access offers a good sample of how good WWII Online is, it is not compelling enough to put in a monthly subscription investment towards further development of the game. Albeit, I will still continue playing this game as a f2p player and hope a better business model can be offered!
P.S. Check my topic on a potential business model that will help f2p players enjoy the game and keep playing!

I was looking forward to this game's steam release. I'd been hoping I could find something else to scratch that Planetside 2 itch. But when I finally got ahold of it, oh boy.
First, the interface is incredibly user unfriendly. It took me a while to figure out how to spawn somewhere because I didn't realize that I am obligated to join a mission or a brigade to do so. There is no crosshair on anti-air guns and the fire is just enough off-center that you can't use your normal FPS instincts to aim.
Second, the open world is certainly massive, but it doesn't seem to add anything. Maybe it's one of those things where you need to be a pilot to enjoy it, but as infantry the open world is almost a downside. There are huge gaps in between the smallest fights followed by even bigger gaps which puts the pacing in this game into a death spiral. So I'm left wondering, why open world? What does it add? If it adds nothing, why is it there?
Third, the controls are really flaky and I can't find an option to adjust my mouse sensitivity. The running feels so weird in this game as well, like I'm in a perpetual ice level straight out of mario. When you let go of the key is not necessarily when you stop moving. It's not just an inch or two trying to simulate inertia either, it's like my character's sliding or running for a good 2 feet past where I want to stop.
Fourth, this game has a habit of not telling you♥♥♥♥♥♥ Did you know that you have to press Z to go into fire mode with your AA gun? I certainly didn't, I had to figure it out through trial, error, and a google search. Did you know that snipers are locked away until rank 7, which apparently takes quite some play time? I didn't, and if I did then I may not have bothered with this game in the first place. In fact, I'm starting to wonder if the developers intentionally locked it like that so you'd have to subscribe for a while before you get to try and and see if you like it or not.

Well, this game certainly hit me out of nowhere.

I had grabbed Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet as the next title to play through on my ever-expanding list of “Games I Must Play,” and was very pleasantly surprised. The controls are tight, the visuals are very striking, and the sound design is very fitting. Overall, this is a very complete package, good for a few hours of fun.

I’ve found that I greatly enjoy “Metroidvania” titles, and this game fits that descriptor perfectly. You progress linearly from point A to point B, collect a new power-up and defeat a boss, then use said power-up to continue on to the next area that was previously blocked. The game map is relatively small, and the game can be powered through in roughly four or five hours, but forward progression happens at a steady rate and you never feel slowed or frustrated with any given puzzle.

There really isn’t much of a storyline – there’s no voice acting, and any story is relayed through orchestrated cutscenes that give you the bare-bones minimum that you need to know: you’re an alien, and your planet has been attacked by some type of strange mechano-orgranic virus that corrupts the environment’s flora and fauna against you. Your little alien character decides to do something about this, and from that point, you’re off and running.

I had only expected to play this game for one quick playthrough, but the more I completed the story the more that I saw that I would be coming back to this title again in the future. Secret areas hide in plain sight and wait patiently for you to uncover the correct ability to retrieve them.

The only gripe that I may have with this game is the fact that it is somewhat hard to backtrack to previously explored areas once you have traveled through them. This became an issue once I had defeated a boss, then accidentally progressed forward without picking up the power-up that they had left behind. Thankfully, it wound up not making a difference to the storyline for future puzzles, but it felt strange completing the game and having a gap in my ability wheel.

At any rate, this game is recommended to anyone – the price point during sales is very cheap, and the show you get for the price of admission is a steal. Any fan of “Metroidvania” titles deserve to pick this game up without hesitation, as it’s a title that you’ll probably find yourself going back to a few more times just for kicks.

Tank brawl is a top down tank shooter. It’s a fun shooter with plenty to offer. It’s ‘inspired’ from NES classic “Battle city”, even though it’s different it still has elements from that game. It has some RPG elements too in which you can upgrade certain things in your tank. These upgrades really do matter and can be used strategically to win a certain level you’re unable to beat. Power-ups, hard levels and bosses will keep you coming back for more and more. Game can also be played in co-op mode locally
The game looks gorgeous and colorful. Different stages have different themes like Jungle, Sahara etc. The game is based on Unreal engine. There’s not many graphic options to configure, only ones available are post processing (includes anti-aliasing and depth of field toggles), resolution and fog. Considering this is a top down shooter that’s not really a problem.
The sound is average in this game, the soundtrack wasn’t too amazing but it was not boring by any means as well. The sounds for explosions and hitting enemy are spot on. Overall not too bad sound though lack of sound adjustment sliders is not good. You only have the option to turn the music on or off, there is no slider to adjust volume which can be a pain as I had to alt-tab out and lower volume from windows.
There are 23 total levels In the game and they get harder as the game progresses. Later levels can be really challenging but not too hard as to discourage players. Each level you beat earns you a point which you can use to improve your tank. There’s 5 upgrades in total which are tank speed, damage, bullet speed, life and point rewards. The life and point rewards become useful when you hit a certain number of upgrades invested into them e.g the life upgrade will give you an extra life when you have 5 points invested into this tree. Same with Rewards if you invest 5 points you’ll gain 2 points instead of 1. The other upgrades however can be incremental in each point. Though they still have perks or reaching a certain number of points in the damage, speed and fast bullet upgrades. If you upgrade speed with 10 points you gain a frontal crusher. If you upgrade damage with 7 points you will gain explosive ammo and if you upgrade fast bullets with 7 points you will gain a rechargeable beam-like power shot.
You can customize this upgrade tree at anytime and this is where the strategy part comes in. Being able to adjust your tank for each level you can easily customize your tank according to that specific level. Boss too fast? Just upgrade your tank speed for that level, Boss is a bullet sponge? Simply upgrade damage or bullet speed. These upgrades come very handy for later tougher level.
Each level requires you to kill off all enemy tanks and in some levels you have a base which you must protect. If the enemy destroys your little base you’ll have to restart the level. In my opinion those levels can get annoying as later game can become a bullet hell with lots of tanks shooting at you. You have to protect yourself and your base which can sometimes cause frustration. The levels also have destructible environments, these blocks can be destroyed and a path can be made, enemy fire also breaks these blocks. There’s also a death meter which tells you how many times you have died.
There’s many types of enemy tanks, your good’ol pawn tank which can be killed with one bullet, the stronger armored tanks, the speedy tanks and faster bullet tanks, super fast tanks with spikes etc. As the levels progress these tanks also get stronger and require more damage to be killed. The bosses are also interesting and require you to be patient and make a strategy to kill them.
There are in-game power-ups and weapons. One such power-up is bombs which can be picked up and thrown and can be exploded on demand. Although when you have placed a bomb you cannot shoot as the bomb explode button is the same as your shoot button so when you press the shoot button the bomb will explode and then you can shoot normally. Another power-up is these tiny friendly tanks which can tag along you once you run over them. They follow your tank and shoot randomly in any direction they want. Sometimes they can also get you killed as they open up these destructible blocks where you intended it not to be opened. There are also pick-ups, one of these pick-ups is the bullet time effect where time slows down for the enemies but you carry on your usual speed. Another one is the shield. These run out within a few seconds.
Very fun arcade-type tank shooter. It has some RPG elements and overall a very fun experience. Fans of Battle City on NES should like this, it’s sort of a different approach to the genre but very fun nonetheless.

This game is incredibly fun and challenging. Dont' let the trailer fool you, though. This game is not quite like Left 4 Dead 2, in that ammo is INCREDIBLY scarce and varied. Not all the ammo you come accross will work with the gun you're holding, and coupled with the inventory system, you have to carefully plan out what you take with you. There are tons of campaigns where you try to make it to a certain point while completing mini-objectives, and there are also survival campaigns where you hold out against waves upon waves of the undead, with supply drops from FEMA half way through to assist you. You are also prone to infection and bleeding, both of which will kill you if left untreated. WARNING: This game has no health bar that you can see when living. There's also stamina for running, jumping, and swinging melee weapons, so be careful.

This past year has left me incredibly skeptical of the game industry for this year of 2017. Between false promises, the constant pushing of microtransactions in already paid games, developers blaitant disregard of the consumers opinions, and just outright bad games have made 2016 a miserable year in the great industry. HOWEVER... After picking up this early access title, it gives me hope. thus far in this title i have had more enjoyment over the last couple hours than i have with other triple A titles of last year. For being a pre-Aplha build and a $20 asking price, this game is what big name publishers and developers should look at and take notes. For only being a pre-Alpha this game has plenty of things to do and allows the player to make their own goals and achieve the at their own pace. It does not shove a tutorial down your throat, but neither does it leave you completely in the dark on what to do. It's a fun learning experience in resource management, use of space, exploration, and a tiny bit of real science if you think about it hard enough. The game is well worth the asking price even at this point. I know plenty of people have said it before but, this is what No Mans Sky should have been, and i also see myself putting in MANY more hours into this game than i did with No Mans Sky. Keep up the good work devs, your making an example for other games in early access, as well as the industry as a whole.

ITSP is a very concise game. It might not be long, but it's always moving; you're always getting new equipment and doing new things. You're always solving puzzles that are mechanically different from the last. It is nearly devoid of filler unless you actually want to get all of the concept art unlocks, and this is a path that I prefer developers take. I want short games that don't endlessly repeat over long ones that feel like a chore.
The puzzles aren't the most difficult out there, but they're imaginative and are very appealing in visuals/effects. The entire game, in fact, is one of the most visually appealing games I've ever played. The world itself is alive and squirming around you. The animation and kinematics are extremely smooth. The camera fluidly zooms in and out to frame the environment around you; for boss battles this means you are a very tiny ship in front of a monster taking up half of your screen. Areas have distinct color palettes with parallax backgrounds (also with animated squirmy things moving around in the distance), but the palettes are always limited in nature and most feature the distinct black silhouetted foreground that probably caught your eye to begin with.
I have a few dislikes about the game. The first is that it feels like it straddles the border between explicitly telling a story and leaving the story to the gameplay. It has these confusing cutscenes that don't really assemble into much of anything I care about. Honestly, I am fine if you just show me the planet/sun being corrupted by a dark force, allow me to infer that I need to stop it, and leave me be for the rest of the game; let the gameplay tell the story. This plot is not on the scale of Mass Effect or The Witcher where you'd need anything else explained in any other way.
Secondly, despite the quasi-storytelling, it doesn't properly build up to an ending; there is nearly nothing to suggest that you're nearing your ultimate goal of cleansing the planet and no real signifier that the last boss is... well, the last boss. Yes, it's really big, but so are the other bosses, it doesn't strike you as particularly end-guy'ish, so you beat it, pat yourself on the back, and then realize the game is over. For how fascinating the game was and how often it "ups itself" with something even more neat, I was hoping for an ending a bit more dramatic/climactic, something like an end-guy with a mind-exploding size that you have to beat in pieces at a time, or the throbbing core of the planet itself.
Despite a somewhat deflating end, ITSP is fascinating and entertaining. It's a game that makes you laugh because of how awesome its bits are, be those items you collected, the visuals of an environment you just entered, the very clever effects and how they integrate with the puzzles you are solving, or just how big everything around you is. It packs a lot into the several hours it takes to beat and makes them very worthwhile. If the main flaws above were fixed I feel like it could be one of my top favorite games - the potential is there but it got a bit muddled up - but the game as it turned out must settle for "just" being really good.

The Deer is a Indie "Education" game developed by Fabio Ferrara, and published by Chubby Pixel December 2015. You control which direction a deer walks, read text message popups, and play a couple little kid minigames.
Story: The story? You play as Alfred the Deer, what's that? his name isn't Alfred? Well it's Alfred now, you join him on his deer story of coming to grips with depression of the loss of Dinosaurs.
Not really, There's no story for the game.
Game Play: Hello reader, have you looked at the store page for this game? Because after reading the store page there's no real point to playing the game. "Did you know there are no Dinosaurs in the ice age?" Yep. "Did you know that the Megalodon's are extinct?" Yup. "Did you know the Ice Age is called the Pleistocene?" Ye.....wait, what? "Can you pronounce that word, Atratzu?" Now you're just being sassy.
I'm definitely not the age demographic for this game, and chances are, if you're reading my review: YOU AREN'T EITHER! This Game is probably geared for little kids who know how to read, or for you to read to your little kid while he or she hammers on your right and left keys or matches acorns and pollen.
Really, the best use WOULD be to spend time with your little kid and let them play this, treat it like a bed time story book.
Features: 2 mini-games ("A matching game", and "put the skeleton back together!"), hub world where you walk around and "learn" about the ice age or "Pleistocene".
Achievements: There are no steam achievements, but I wish there was one that said "You're a full grown adult and played through this game while streaming it on twitch", but I guess that's too specific to apply to many other people.
Price: The stand alone price is $0.99, You can play through it in minutes, the longest I could drag it out on stream was 20 minutes.
Conclusion: If you're over the age of.... 7, this isn't going to hold your attention, also if you're under the age of 7, wow you're an active reader if you look at my reviews, kudos kiddos!
Now the real hard part... do I thumbs up or thumbs down? It's not a "bad game" it hardly feels like a game though, I'm going to thumbs it down because Steam really isn't the medium for this type of game, in my opinion.
Thanks for reading!

Sonic Adventure DX is easily one of the funnest Sonic games I've ever played! There's a great story, and astonishingly good music, but the gameplay depends on which character you are.
With Sonic's stages, GOTTA GO FAST will be screaming in your mind. It's a simple yet adrenaline-pumping "get to the goal" objective!
With Tails' stages, you always have to be moving forward, whether it be on the ground or in the air, because if Sonic beats you to the goal, it's game over! Luckily, your ability to fly grants you access to shortcuts in the levels, and something about flying over a bottomless abyss is really exciting.
With Amy's stages, you always gotta be on the move like Tails, as there is a relentless killer robot chasing after you! Smash your way through the stages and beat up the robots with the awesome Piko Piko Hammer!
With Knuckles' stages, things are usually a bit more calm. Because you aren't constantly doing loop-de-loops or running from a killer robot, but instead searching for the shards of the Master Emerald!
With Gamma's stages, you shoot your way through the level as quickly as you can! You have taken control of an E series robot and must either please or fight against Eggman, before time runs out!
With Duke Nuke-- I mean Big's stages, you just fish for a stupid frog. Nothing exciting here, stay away from this unless you want to 100% the game. Which I assume you do.
Then, there is the Chao Garden! You can take care of adorable creatures known as Chao, and enter them in fun racing events!
I reccommend this game! 8/10! Play Sonic Adventure DX, or you are missing out on a great game!

Let me preface everything I say here with this: I grew up with Sonic games. Sonic the Hedgehog on the SEGA Genesis was the first video game I ever remember playing. I've played nearly every Sonic game to date, both the good and bad. However, I will try to detail the workings of this specific game without the bias of nostalgia.
Sonic Adventure has really not aged well. It is wracked with glitches, some "guide-dang-it" moments, hard to learn controls, and character animations that really show their age. Taking that in mind, however, you should be aware that this was the first true three-dimensional Sonic platformer. But that does not excuse anything bad with the game.
Let me start with the visuals. While the models and environments look good for games of the era, the animations are what really bring the games visuals down. The characters look very rubbery, and stretch in ways that look very unnatural, even for a cartoon styled game. However, this is only apparent during cutscenes, and most of the animations during the actual gameplay hold up well enough over the years.
The audio is pretty awful, to be frank. While the music still holds certain charm, the voice acting and sound effects really show their age in the worst possible way. While I understand that the game was essentially the first of it's kind, it's lip-syncing looks as though no one even tried. Honestly, the only redeemable part of the audible experience is certian music pieces. Open Your Heart, Sonic's Theme, and a few stage themes to be specific.
The gameplay suffers from age the worst in my opinion. I look back fondly to the gameplay during my childhood. Running with Sonic, flying with Tails, and exploring with Knuckles were highlights specifically. However, they do not hold up to the same degree. While the three I stated still have fun to be had, once you can learn the quirks of the control, the other three characters do not fall in the same boat. Amy is just awful to play as. She's slow and completely unfun. Big is frustrating beyond belief. Gamma, however, controls simply okay. Nothing stands out as awful, but just feels very out of place. The glitches associated with gameplay are very apparent. Falling through floors, and moving through walls are things many players can plan on experiencing.
The story is nothing too special. While Tikal and Chaos are vaguely interesting, every other character falls short. Sonic and Tails' stories are rather boring, and don't engross the player. Knuckles has a slightly more interesting story, but it feels as though it losing speed rather quickly. Amy and Big's feel laughably absent, as their individual stories impact basically nothing. Gamma's, while self contained, is actually the best of the game in my opinion. The final story is somewhat cool, but is over very quickly.
So, overall, would I recommend this game? Honestly, while I do not feel like it has aged well, I still consider most of it a decent game, especially of your a fan of the series. Even the gameplay has it's moments of pure fun.

Short version:
I strongly recommend this game! It's cute, colorful, whimsical, and will give you many hours of caring for and managing large amounts of chaotic little slimes. The Devs have done wonderful work with the mechanics, and keeping in theme with the game's chaotic nature. Even in Early Access, I feel the game is worth every penny spent, and every bit helps the Devs improve and progress the game further!
Long Version:
A lot of reviewers will say that the game doesn't have enough content in the state to be worth the price tag, but I really would beg to differ, just primarily on the feeling of the game. The game isn't about content, but the thrill of experimentation, exploration, and developing bonds with your slimes. There really can be a huge set of emotions there when you play the game if you're the kind of person who really enjoys pets (especially extremely cute ones)!
The major fun of it is experimenting with the slime largos and learning what they do, and what efficient methods you can use to keep them all at their happiest. I've personally found favorite with the Phospher Tabby slimes.
I'm proud to have put $20 into the game's development fund-pool, because I have strong confidence that Monomi Park will add so much more. They even have a roadmap to what they may add in the next couple of updates, to show they are committed to this project.
On a closing note, I will point out that this game is Early Access. People can complain there is little content, but you have to remember, it's not about the quantity of the content that gets added, but the quality of the content in the game already.
If I compare this game to other management games, such as the early Sims Games, (which were sold full price, more expensive than this game at full versions in retail stores) they had a large number of content in those games that gave them an appearance of looking big, but in reality the content was dull and unexciting after a short while... (not to mention EA-Games CHARGES you to buy extra content that should've already been in the game, or should've been free downloads since the game already had price tags of $40-50.)
So please take into consideration, this game is Early Access with great content already in it, and promising greater content in the future. Ultimately it's up to the player whether they find the content appealing, but from this satisfied player's standpoint, I give the game in it's early form: 11/10! I look forward to the game's future updates and progression.

I was looking forward to play a polished management/building game/anthill, but was very disappointed. With Prison Architect being heralded as an Early Access poster child or Early Access "done right" expectations were high. But since I'm pretty much immune to overly high expectations due to hype the game had a fair chance. And let's not forget I played it two years after release.
I started with the campaign and it turns out to be the tutorial of the game. It does a decent job to explain the basics, but lacks to really teach more advanced mechanics of the game. At that point I and I bet many other players, start to look online for answers. I don't like that the game relies on the internet as an information source. There should be more info in the game. I found answers for most issues, but sometimes they aren't easy to find, despite the age of the game. One problem is that a great deal of info is outdated since the game was updated in the meantime. And as always, some online tips are plain wrong.
So, I soon saw that the initial campaign I started is pretty short and coming to an end. It was fun though and after finishing it, I thought there is maybe another campaign or some scenarios, but no. The tutorial/campaign is all you get.
What else is there? The sandbox mode.
I'm not the greatest fan of sandbox modes, but gave it a try. It has some more optional features that aren't explained in the tutorial. Pretty soon I ran into various problems.
The game has several bugs and issues, some of which you even notice in the campaign. But only in the sandbox mode, you get really impacted by them. Some of them can be solved by reloading the game. One I fixed with a mod. And at the end I had one with doesn't seem fixable. A cell wasn't "enclosed" anymore and nothing fixed this.
The optional features seem to be unfinished and not fully thought through.
When you search for answer for your problems you will soon find posts about how the devs abandoned the game, how the game was released unfinished, how bugs haven't been fixed in a long time etc. etc. And I can only support these opinions. The game feels unfinished. It looks polished superficially, but underneath it lacks polish. I also feel like it lacks "meat". The game should have at least some interesting scenarios or a proper campaign.
In the end this game is just another example of how Early Access is bad for the quality of a game. I bet it was fun to play this during the development since they added more and more features, but a player who didn't do this, you get an unfinished game that is simply abandoned, because the player base drops down after reaching a peak during Early Access. The devs just seem to have released the game to get out of Early Access, not because it was really finished. Now that the media coverage of the game is gone, they don't have an incentive to improve it anymore. Anyone who really was interested in it, has bought it by now.
Not recommended unless you know what you are getting. Might be more enjoyable for people who like playing with mods.
Certainly not worth the full price of currently 28€.

My nostalgia goggles are probably on for this review so bear with me.
I've owned this game since my mum bought it for me in a book club catalogue in primary school - I'm in university now. I never finished it as a kid because I was too scared of the temple segment. I finished it today in under 4 hours.
The game itself is a point and click adventure game like other games in the Nancy Drew series. Nancy Drew is a detective so you solve puzzles and mysteries in the case. The premise of this game was that Nancy had just begun her internship at Beech Hill museum in Washington DC when a prized carving of King Pacal is stolen from a display case in the museum. The thief leaves behind a scarlet hand print. All the action of the game takes place in the museum as well as a metro system which can take you to two offices, a hotel and a hospital. This is not a big game. It isn't as big as other Nancy Drew games I've played.
The game isn't scary in hindsight. Some other Nancy Drew games are beyond creepy but this game is an escape from creepiness.
The Mayan history is very interesting but it is tedious when you have to remember facts about certain people for the quizzes in the temple.
Graphics and gameplay: the graphics are quite atrocious but it doesn't hamper gameplay. This game was made before they gave Nancy a cellphone; so to read the journal for hints or phone someone you must return to the hotel which is tedious.
This game isn't the best Nancy Drew game. But it was the first that I played and that counts for something. Pick this up cheap on Steam if you want a nostalgia kick or a fun and challenging short game.

Astroneer has a unique visual style and is enjoyable earlier moments.
However, you very quickly get through the research tree. Once you have access to all the blue prints, exploring the world and placing tethers or expanding your base will slowly sap the game's overall performance. Without maxing any of my hardware resources, the game slowed to a crawl to the point of being nearly unplayable. Interesting little game. As the screenshots show, this game has a sort of cartoony dark sci-fi horror theme going, which is easily its best point. But the world design and the myriad of puzzles and enemies are great as well. Especially boss fights are well rounded out: not too easy nor too hard, making use of a mechanic you've learned previously and usually rewarding you with a new toy to play with.
The controls took some getting used to (especially guiding rockets), and I found swapping the controller for a keyboard and mouse to make things MUCH easier (this is probably me, though).
As for the story: take it for good or for bad, but there is no dialogue. At all. No cutscene text, no voice-overs, no tutorials (in the literal sense...level design is set to make you acquainted with new weapons), no nothing.  So you can only take a guess at things like why you're there or even what the weapons are called, but it doesn't distract much. This is a game that should be played...not watched or read.

Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is a "metroidvania" twin-stick shooter with an emphasis on environmental puzzles.  The game looks great and has a ambient, foreboding soundtrack that sets the mood well.  Simply getting around the environment is fun and the level design is quite good; there's enough variation in the tunnels you're going through that it's easy to develop a map in your head, but never so difficult you get lost or hung up frequently.  The several zones all have a very distinct look and feel and offer unique challenges.
The game is fun; it's a little short – I beat the game 100% in a little under 6 hours – but for the right price is a good deal for the money.  I do wish the bosses were a little bit harder...the only reason I died on them was simply because I didn't know what to do; as soon as I did they almost became pushovers.
For the size and scope it's aiming for, ITSP executes very well. Other than one zone that has you fumbling around in the dark (for all of about 5 minutes), I never got frustrated and enjoyed pushing forward, exploring and seeing what's around the next corner.
Word of advice, though: if you're aiming to get all the collectables, scour as you go.  There's no way of seeing their location on the map, so it can be quite difficult to find things later on when the whole map is uncovered and you don't remember where you did or didn't pick them up.  I don't think it would work well to put the locations of them on the map, but it would have been nice if the developer added icons for the ones you had picked up so you would know where not to look.
Anyways, all around a good, quick and fun game.

All Points bulletin: Reloaded was a game created by Realtime Worlds until they went under in 2010, and bought by Gamersfirst in 2011.  It has very many pros, yet cons that are very hard to look over. Let's review some of the bigger ones.
Pros:
1 Very user friendly, doesnt try and complicate things more than it should. Shoot bad guys, do objectives, make money.
2 INCREDIBLE amount of customization, it never stops amazing me the boundless amounts of effort you can put into the customization system, and the spectacular things these people create.
3 It's very addictive. Once you start getting involved in this game, you really dont want to stop, it is a very rewarding game, saving up for that seventy thousand dollar car, then running over people without a care in it, is one of the many things that let you work hard, and feel good about it.
4 The story is so well thought out. The universe of San Paro is a deep one, that you can spend hours reading along all the things the characters have to say to you, or all the lore about the city, and it's workings. No part of the story feels silly, or pointless. It's all very real in a sense.
5 The way it pits you against players is very fine tuned, and well thought out. Seamlessly going from open world cruising to intense battles, and being able to see other players taking part in their own little missions.
6 The banning system. You get banned if you break the code of conduct, and then it broadcasts to the entire game, to every single server, district, and player, that you've been banned, your name, and the server you play on. It's very nice seeing the occasional cheater get booted.

Give the graphics a pass because it's the gameplay that is the true star. This is a game where consequences matter. You can feel proud for each kill you get knowing you've denied the enemy access to that vehicle for a short while. You're also more careful with equipment because you know that if you die then you've wasted that vehicle. So if you're flying Close Air Support or a Combat Air Patrol and take a bit of damage, you want to nurse that plane back to base so you can respawn a fresh one. No longer is a game incentivizing you to just kill yourself so you can respawn quicker.
It is so satisfying to be in an aircraft and strafe a truck full of infantry or towing an AT/AA gun. Or driving a tank to the edge of a hill and going hull down to snipe enemy tanks from a distance. Or running around a town as infantry listening for tank engines so you can flank around them at the next building hoping to get a satchel charge on one of their weak points. The highs this game gives you is unparalleled because of the environment they've set up and cannot be reached in any other game.
You'll want to join a squad and get on voice coms to get the full experience. Give this game a chance and you'll be hooked. If you do not have the patience for this type of game that's understandable. Know that maybe this game isn't tailored for you but thanks for giving it a try. I do know there is a large community out there dying for a game just like this and for those of you that have been waiting for it, you won't be disappointed.

We like Trucking... We like trucking... We like Trucking and we like to Truck!
The immortal words of the "Not the Nine O'Clock News" team rung loud in my ear as I was given a copy of this game wth the intention of using the Multiplayer mod to establish a freight empire with friends however in order to get into the game I first had to attempt to play a single player run a few times.
Now, theres absolutely zero story obviously, as is the case with these kinds of simulator games, however quite how Jeff Bridges ended up running a haulage firm out of Trafford (in the Rock 'n Roll metropolis that is Greater Manchester) is actually a story I wouldn't mind hearing (yes, one of the in-game avatars bizarrely resembles the famous hollywood actor) but I digress, the closest you get to a story is you own a start-up haulage firm in europe, you deliver stuff for other people whilst building up your own empire, hiring new drivers and buying your own trucks. Theres not really much to comment on on that score, it's largely just completing haulage runs, makign enough money to expand your business and keeping yourself in the red like 90% of most of these Simulator-type games. In terms of gameplay it's your bog-standard quasi realistic simulator (thankfully days-long drives are condensed down into hour long chunks or so) so if you just fancy a reaxing cargo run you can do so as opposed to grinding your way to Eddie Stobart levels of Haulage Godhood.
Graphically it's what you'd expect, not that much in terms of assests or design but it gets the job done and the trucks look nice enough also Kudos to the team for recreating the Humber bridge as I mostly remember it, the country roads are nice enough but the drive does get a little repetitive. As for controls the game handles well enough, it does handle better through the keyboard but the wheel option still works. As for music the inclusion of DAB radio stations is a nice feature, as is the option to include your own Trucking Tunes mixtape (which I loaded with a few classics, including the legendary Convoy theme song) which does aid in breaking the monotony a little but not by much. Of course you could just see how badly you can crash your might rig, in one case I somehow Peppied and did a barrel roll, but paying the game as intended is fine in short bursts.
So, in conclusion Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a fun enough game but, unless you have a serious love of trucks, is best played in short doses. It can still be fun but it might wear you down if played in those prolonged sessions. Reccommended, especially with mods.

Prison Architect is the kind of Game that just speaks to me, as I like economics in my Games. It's really fun to play around at the start, just building stuff without having any idea of what you're actually doing. In the beginning the menu's all can seem a little intimidating, but once you started figuring out how to navigate them and started experimenting on your first two prison's what works and what doesn't, you're finally ready to really play the game. Or just play the Campaign ... as far as I remember they have some introduction, but I couldn't really bother with that.
I wanted to start my own prison as soon as possible and started out. The game offers you different approaches to how you can handle your prison. Just by adjusting some sliders you can make a low security prison, a medium or high one. Considering which type of prisoner you take in. While a low security prison doesn't take as much to maintain and there's no real danger in them rioting at some point, you don't get as much money to keep those prisoners around as you would with more violent ones.
So if you wanna make the big bucks you either have to take in the really evil ones or make a ridiculously large complex. As the latter one isn't something I was really into I was doing a mixed prison on the basis "Let everyone come in". Only to notice I don't get as much, but still need extreme security measures for the dangerous ones or appease them with comforts of daily life. A bigger cell, a TV, Books, Free time, Good meals ... but those suckers would always riot anyways and it would cost more money than smaller cells anyways.
Now you come to the question if they riot anyways, why bother? So I just set up a prison that didn't appease to them anyways and just put a lot of guards around with a lot of tazers, body armour and whatnot. Shaking them down for tools, checking on them and making their lives miserable, which basically led to a daily riot, offering me the perfect excuse for putting them in solitary. So if you go for that run, make sure you have at least one solitary cell for each prisoner waiting, as they will be visiting often.
This game clearly gets a recommendation! Especially if you think about the ♥♥♥♥ed up implications your actions would have in the real world.

Apart from the sad fact that nobody took this as an opprotunity to update the game to 2010's standards, this game still holds up to the test of time. While this is arguably Sonic's first successful transition into the 3D realm, it didn't come without some flaws, but overall it was a promise for a better future--which was (for the most part) delivered in it's sequel. ...and then squandered (in my personal opinion) in more recent years.
While keeping in mind that this game is well over a decade old, this game is a must play for anyone who wants to know why the Sonic fanbase is notably so divided--this is the game that sparked a new play style and managed to pull it off quite successfully, essentially dividing the fanbase between the "Adventure" lovers and the "Old School" lovers. It is a different experience than the old Sonic 2D-side scrolling styles, but it brings it's own unique pros and cons to the table as well. It's--in short--just a different experience.
Pros:
-This game (at the time) created a new buzz for Sonic with a brand new play style
-This game kept the feeling of speed throughout most of its major sections
-This game allows for some freedom with hub maps
-This game includes the well-loved (and entirely optional) Chao minigames
-This game introduced the ability to play from different character's perspectives, each of which had slightly differing play styles
-This game does offer a large amount of playtime, especially for completionists like myself
-This game offers Metal Sonic as an unlockable character, like in the Gamecube release
-100% completion of this game is notably challenging, but the regular playthrough has a nice medium difficulty
-This PC version offers a fan-made high-resolution texture pack for the Chao Gardens, as well as some other more haphazardly-made mods
Cons:
-This game does not contain the unlockable past Sonic games like the Gamecube release did
-This game still contains some bugs in certain areas of the levels, as well as a new texture bug in the Chao garden
-Big the Cat's play style is widely disliked due to it's slow pace and generally boring gameplay (it isn't optional either)
-The storyline is a bit hard to grasp, although getting the general idea isn't too hard
-The better Adventure game (it's sequel) is also available on Steam and doesn't require you to have any knowledge from this game (so it might be a better buy on a tight budget)
-The graphics were not updated from their original form
-Many of the Gamecube release bugs were not fixed, leading to some (unfortunate) player deaths every once in a while
I would recommend grabbing this game in a sale if you haven't played it before or if you're just looking for some nostalgia. Notably, it is regularly put on sale in the Humble Bundle store. Any Sonic fan who hasn't played this installment or it's sequel should also give this game a go in order to get a better grasp on the divide within the community.

This game defined some of my childhood; back when I was around 10/11 years old.
I remember playing this game on the gamcube version and I absolutely loved it.
Looking back at this game and playing it now, there is A LOT of flaws in the physics of the game, and there are plenty of glitched to go around. Not to mention... the voice acting and lip syncing. Good god.
Though, in all honesty, the moment when the physics break, or when the voice acting is horendous, it makes the game a little more enjoyable. I tend to get a good laugh out of it, rather than being frustrated at it. Though maybe there are times where if the game breaks at a dire situation, I would call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Other than that, the main positives I can give this game is the story, and (obviously) the chao garden. I remember spending countless hours on the chao garden just taking care of those cute little creatures and it was really relaxin; like I was taking a little break from so much action from the game. The story was interesting too, and at moments it got quite tear jerking. (Especially with E-102 GAMMA, but I wont spoil it here). Big the Cat's missions were kind of slow, but playing it now, I kind of like the slow pace of fishing. Like the chao garden, it gives you a sort of break from the rest of the story; and I guess maybe that's what the developers were kind of going for.
Overall I would give the game a 8/10. Though there are major flaws, they can really just be either overlooked, or just make the game a little more enjoyable at times. :)

Really love this game. It's Super Metroid in a flying saucer with physics puzzles and beatiful 2D visuals somewhere in between Limbo, World of Goo, and Tim Burton. Every collectible is fun to acquire, every weapon/item is useful and fun to use, and the gating of areas is almost always tied to inventive use of your items and is never a glorified lock and key ala Metroid's weapon-specific doors. In order to progress from area to area you will do things like ride currents through twisty underwater tunnels, reflect laser beams off of ice crystals, and drill passageways through rock walls. The boss fights are exciting and well designed, requiring you to make interesting uses of the tools you have acquired (similar to Zelda boss fights except more intricate). Music is wonderful, usually just ambient themes to set the mood of each region, with occasional uptempo moments reminscent of the most exciting parts of older Danny Elfman movie scores.
Control is very good with the mouse and keyboard, though if you have a twin analogue stick controller, I suspect the game will play even better this way. You move your ship in 8 directions with the keyboard, and aim your weapons/items in 360 degrees with the mouse. You switch between items with a radial menu brought up by bolding the right mouse button.
Combat is a relatively small part of the game, but well done. Enemies are varied and require different tactics to take down. Most enemies are perticularly vulnerable to a specific weapon, but all of them can be tackled in more than one way. There is considerable overlap between enemies/items/environmental elements, and oftentimes you will solve puzzles by manipulating enemies. There are many things which can kill you, but very few cheap deaths. There are ample checkpoints throughout the game so you are never set too far back when you die.
Exploration is a healthy balance of backtracking and unlocking new areas. There are optional side paths to explore which lead to upgrades and other collectibles. Each area has a distinct look, which makes it easier to keep track of where you are going. There is an auto-map feature which fills in as you explore new areas, and a red blinking objective is marked on the map at all times, indicating where you should go next in order to progress.
Your ship is equipped with a scanner ala metroid prime, which can be used to get information on enemies' weaknesses, as well as indicating which item is needed to break through obstacles or activate certain objects. The great thing about this is that once you scan an obstacle, your map will be updated with an icon indicating which item is needed to proceed. This way you can easily find your way back to the same spot when you have the item you need. By the time you acquire each new item, you will already have marked several places on the map where it is needed, which means you'll immediately have a list of places to return to and try out your new items.
I completed Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet in about 7 hours, with most of the collectibles and upgrades, so it's not the longest game. However I think it's worth noting that there are no "filler" sections in this game, nor is there a lot of busywork or gratuitious backtracking like you find in most open-world exploration games. A major reason that the game goes by so quickly is because of the aforementioned excellent map system and easily identifiable zones. The persistent "objective" marker combined with the fact that the map notes all of the obstacles you encounter with icons indicating which tool you need to pass them, is another reason why you can complete this game so quickly. In short, the game is very well designed and respects your time, which means you will get through the content much faster than in a less thoughtfully designed adventure.
MAC USERS: I had a lot of performance issues with this game. There were frequent periods of intense slowdown, and the game crashed or froze many times. Tweaking the graphical settings did not seem to have any effect on the framerate. The only thing that made any difference was to quit the game when the framerate started to drop, and then start it back up again. Most of the time the game ran better when it was first started up, and would start to perform worse and worse as time went on.

Also, this game is REALLY hard, but REALLY fun. Oh, and if you're also a frequenter of Newgrounds, were a fan of platformers from the 80's, and/or have played other Indie platformers, you're in for a real treat because this game is LOADED with references and secrets. Play it and see!
