THE RAVEN: Legacy of a Master Thief has a strong start, but a somewhat meandering finish for a point and click adventure game.  While it tries to homage Agatha Christie’s work it can only produce a rather crude imitation.  Despite that, the game still deserves a recommendation, but only just.
The Raven is a 3D point and click adventure done by the same team behind The Book of Unwritten Tales.  Oddly though, the rigging and animations feel extremely rushed. A few characters have obvious issues with their faces. One rig seems to be jutting out a character’s teeth while another (main) character has a frozen expression.  There is a valiant effort put forth for animations, but it really falls short many times.  It seems like the team was aiming high, but could not get past prototyping quality of work.  That said there are still a lot of nice things to be said about the visuals.  Character designs are distinct and fit.  While there are only a few maps, they are all well designed and thought out.  There is clearly a lot of work put into the visuals, but either time or money limited the overall quality.
Voice acting is pretty good as well. Most of the characters fit their voices with the exceptions of Adil. Kerry Shale is voicing him and he sounds exactly like Rufus from Deponia with almost no distinction at all.  Adil is supposed to be Middle Eastern and grew up in Europe, but he does not have any European accent at all. That just makes character stand out as odd. Shale is an excellent actor, so I can only imagine this is a failure in direction. Still all the acting is pretty good, and even though Shale sounds out of place, he still does a good job. Audio engineering has some problems as the game continues on.  There first chapter is solid, but by the third sound effects and music scores sometimes disappear or feel lacking.
In the first half of the game you solve the mystery while the second half you figure out how to commit the crime. It is an interesting idea, but it does not pan out to well. The crime solving is actually quite fun, you are not sure what is going on so you need to figure it out.  But committing the crime is different. You are told exactly what needs to happen so you just have to click randomly till it happens.  The primary mystery is solved at the half way point, but you still have to play through more game to find out the conclusion.  And since you are a stealthy criminal in the second half of the game, you do not interact with many people. The story fails apart and becomes uninteresting.
The story is the biggest failing of the game. It starts well enough. The game draws some clear comparisons to Agatha Christie’s “Mystery on the Orient Express” and “And Then There Were None”.  But the plot has holes and non-sequiturs, which is much more pronounced in a mystery.  The plot is at best forced.  Even the story telling demands the audience to be inattentive and forgetful. While the ending was rather predictable, the contradictions that denied said ending where not satisfyingly resolved. The first half of the game is well done and endearing even, but the second half just is not and it complicates the ending.
Overall, despite significant criticisms, the game still deserves a recommendation for adventure fans. While the first half enthralling, the second half falls flat.

There are other games out there that scratch the itch this game is aiming at in a much more satisfying way.  This is a planning/workers build my plans type of game in the same category as Dwarf Fortress or Rimworld.  It has decent graphics, a decent campaign, and is pretty polished in terms of UI and being able to figure out what's going on/why something happened/what to do next.
Unfortunately, the biggest problem is that you finish the campaign in about 10 hours (with all the optional objectives complete), then you start up a sandbox game.  That's when you realize the sandbox is just the last level of the campaign, but with a larger building area.  Once you've built all the different types of rooms and seen how the different types of prisoners interact, the only thing left is just to build a bigger prison, which you could do by literally just sectioning off a new part of the map and repeating what you just did.
I had literally no connection to any of the guards or inmates in my prison.  A guard gets killed, fine.  Hire a new one, put the shanker in solitary, put the shankee in the morgue.  Done.  No emotion.  There's a riot?  Hire some nameless riot guards to subdue everyone, stick the rioters in solitary.  Done.  Totally emotionless.  I will grant that the campaign tried to create emotional attachment to the characters, but then those characters aren't actually impactful on your prison play experience at all.  For example, there's a story involving a mob boss, which is cool, but when you actually play the game, it makes no real difference which prisoner in your prison is that mob boss.
My recommendation is to go buy Rimworld instead.  When I play that, there's a sense of progression, attachment to my colonists, and a sense of fear and challenge of what the game might throw at me next.
If I'm looking for a resource management and supply chain game, go buy Factorio.  But then, I'm addicted to that game and am probably going to go play it right now.

I used to play GTA SA all the time back in the day on my friends PS2, and then again when I got it for my orginal Xbox. So for me, on top of everything great about this game, there's a little nostalgia mixed in as well. How does it stack up as a GTA game? Best ever. Why? Well compared to GTA 5, which is a great game by the way, it has many more detailed upgrades(and even downgrades, like obesity) for your charater to level up abd aesthtic customation is on par with games released today. It also has a variety of story and side missions that are also on par with GTA 5, and some honestly being a hell of a lot more fun and unique. It has a pretty big array of weapons to choose from, all with skill levels for each gun type. As for vehicles...for the time of realease it was impressive, now compared to newer titles it feels lacking(no suprise here though). Along with the vehicles, the customization is there, but seems like a last minute thrown in feature that really is only worth it if you're trying to throw some cash away. The map feels still very big today, and with new areas opening as you progress through the story, it really feels ever exspansive at times. However, what really makes this game amazing, and one of Rockstars best works, is the story and progression, and the characters and their development.  If you haven't played this game you're in for a ride. How the charaters build of each others morals and decisions, really makes this story play out like a movie. And somehow makes you feel family with these gangster friends, and see that it really isn't all about drugs, money, and kills. I think the story is really the only factor that makes GTA: SA better than GTA 5, that alone is saying a lot. GTA 5 is amazing the story is astounding and all in all I really have no issues with the game, I love it. However, once you play SA you'll understand why it is usually hailed king, because it's never a dull moment. It's a must own. So if you haven't yet, try it out.

This is a neutral recommendation. The gameplay is solid, metroidvania-style spaceship shoot'em up. The puzzles and fighting can get rather difficult at times, but never unfair. If you fail a few times you will recognise patterns and you'll eventually get it.
You end up getting about 10 different weapons to play with, but the ones you get near th end of the game end up being just utility/physics in a very few niche situations. It just seems to work that way with these type of shooters, and it doesn't really change gameplay dramatically enough for any refreshing changes. One thing I like to see in metroidvania games are mobility abilities and this game lacks them.
The game tries convey a story through very short cutscenes and gameplay and while it works at getting the story through, it didn't work well at making a compelling narrative. I would have preferred some dialog but I can see why they choose this style. It just didn't jive with me. Same goes for the art style. It works well for the game and is unique without being 16-bit pixel indie game graphics, but I would have preferred more colors than black in every scene, even though you are on a "shadow planet". Just personal preference, I guess.

To be honest, 9.5/10 people who try to play APB are going to be slavering at the jaws with rage within 15 minutes of entering their first server. The game is heavilly PvP orientated... Unfortunately, the PvP is weighted heavilly in favor of anyone who pays exorbant sums of money for the best gear. Not to mention the highly experienced, well-geared high levels that come to the starting areas to murder new players.
In terms of concept and general gameplay, APB is a wonderful game. Imagine an MMO version of Saints Row or GTA, with players being both criminals and cops. That's the general idea behind APB Reloaded. Unfortunately, as mentioned before, the player versus player that is cventral to the concept is horribly unbalanced. To give you an example, a fresh player with reasonable third person shooter experience can pick up a weapon off the real money market and dominate matches just like that. Now imagine an experienced player with that same weapon. It's one of those cases of a free-to-player attacking a paying player and the paying player essentially going "Lol, stop it, it tickles! Here, have some bullets!"
I've touched on the subject a bit already... The game's community. To be frank, APB's community is utterly terrible, filled with asshats, trolls, and plenty of children who think they're MLG level hot stuff. Combine this with that pay-to win imbalance... Yeah, a ten year old with his daddy's credit card will kick your♥♥♥♥♥more times than you'd care to admit. And both children and adults will announce their pro skills and taunt each other and whine about Haxoorz in the chat. Oh yeah. Hackers. They're there. Not as much as a lot of the people in the game would tell you they are (Every time they die) but they're definately there and a force to be reckoned with.
Did I mention the customization?
I didn't mention that, did I? silly me.
The level of customization you can apply to your character and vehicle is... Mind-boggling. Simply glorious. It's the main strength of the game, in my opinion, but unfortunately it's subscribed to that same Pay-to-win philosophy as the rest of the game... Less so, however. Put enough time into it, and you, as a free to player, can potentially look just as cool as that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who sunk 2000 bucks into his kit. He may be able to one-shot you with his god-pistol from a mile away, but hey, at least you'll leave a cool-looking corpse!
My advice for playing this game? Avoid actually playing the game like you're supposed to. Don't play the PvP, you're bound only for frustration and rage. Do side activities, They award more cash faster and, while they can get a bit monotonous, there's plenty of ways to stay entertained. Remember what I said about the demolition derby? Actually happened. There's plenty of people in the game that are just as bored as you. Oh, yeah, there are decent people, it's just that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are pretty loud. Criminals can make cash a lot faster than Enforcers, simply because their activities are largely dependant on the envirionment- mugging, robbing stores, jacking cars, you get the picture- whereas most of the Enforcer's income is largely dependant on criminals. And that PvP. You want cash as an enforcer? Gotta engage criminals in PvP to get it. Which is probably why the beginner areas are always swamped with high-level Enforcers. They want some easy cash.
Honestly most of this game's problems can be traced back to the Pay-to-Win PvP and the Enforcer's lack of quick cash income. THe only way to really have any fun with this game is to♥♥♥♥♥♥around. As a free-to-player, attempting to take the game seriously will only end in your frustration.

Update: Might as well give some real impressions on the game so far.
I recommend this with some caveats:
1. You need to know how to code to fully take advantage of everything in the game
2. If you don't know how to code, you can still enjoy yourself with the game, but it'll get really repetitive really quickly if you don't do some learning
3. If you don't learn how to code and continue to play the game, you'll think it's bad.
Basically, learn how to code.
That being said, hackmud is a wonderful little sandbox that really gives you a lot of room to learn and challenge yourself. Your success is only limited by your imagination and some basic Javascript constraints. The game uses a strange progression system in which you earn things like more script slots, larger character counts, special in-game functionality, etc. You start out with one measly private script slot, a 500 character count limit (not a lot if you want to follow basic coding conventions), no money, and very little help. The tutorial is pretty long, took me probably an hour and a half to get through it, but once you're through that it just dumps you into channel 0000 and throws you to the wolves, and if you don't immediately put into practice the things you learned in the tutorial and figure out some stuff for yourself this game will eat you alive and spit you back out the other end. There are malicious scripts that take all your money, including ones linked in completely safe scripts (looking at you, info.scripting) meant to help you. People can take your account location and completely bone you for money and upgrades going into the foreseeable future, forcing you to retire the account and start fresh with nothing except your previously editted scripts which probably don't fit beginner constraints. Basically, get good or get ♥♥♥♥ed. And I wouldn't have it any other way.

For the record, I've followed this game since I was probably eleven or twelve years old after seeing an article in a 99-00 issue of PC Gamer. My PC at the time couldn't handle something of this magnitude, so I stuck with playing my MUDs and such. A few years down the road I took the opportunity to play this game, on and off, but I was always amazed and addicted by what the game offered. The one problem I had, though, was I worked the night shift... so playing TZ3 would absolutely suck for me as there was no one to really play with or against.
I stuck with it for a while, ended up buying a ton of flight gear (expensive VKB stuff) and a cockpit and such and even later on tossing money for a lifetime account in the game. Quickly, I knew that this wasn't going to work as it simply wasn't any fun for me at the times that I could play.
I'm very lukewarm about the game, in a sense this game does a lot of things that modern era games still have't been able to emulate. Like running a concurrent land/air/naval war on a huge map, though it seems to be buckling under the pressure of the steam release adding some 400 odd players, though I can't say I didn't see this coming with the amateur team that is running the game now.
There are two large detractors that stop me from recommending this game. One is the subscription cost, even for someone where money isn't an object, it's not conducive to throw money at this project that was largely finished 16 years ago with no new features until recently. There are free games out there that exist solely off microtransactions that have a much better business model and are more worth your time.
The biggest detractor to me is the amount of hacking that occurs in this game. Due to the age of the game, it's quite easy for someone to use an openGL injector and create an undetectable chams/aimbot, and that sucked all the fun out of me after I ran into some seedy individuals in the community that were running these sort of things and saw them for myself. The air game, nor the ground game was no longer competitive for me... but that's only the way PC gaming is going... down the tubes with the hackers.
When the staff wisen up and make this game entirely free to play and fix their server issues, it might be worth it... but right now? Play Heroes and Generals or Warthunder or something, you'd have a lot more fun in the short run until some real heavy hitting titles come out.

I hope that this review provides a comprehensive overview of the game. There seems to be some misunderstandings about the game, and there are also some perhaps overly-favorable reviews out there that don't really communicate the strengths and weaknesses of the game.
So, first off. I began playing this game about 6-7 years ago, and had a Free Trial account (that went through many different evolutions and devolutions as the devs tried to hammer out what they wanted as far as a Free to Play trial account went) until late last year, after I subscribed to the game.
I have played a LOT of games, of many different genres. Most of these are WW2-related, including the first real computer games I ever played: the Close Combat series. The originals, not the re-releases.
This game is a WW2 Massively Multiplayer First Person Shooter/Tanker/Pilot/Sailor Historical Accuracy Simulator game. This is not an Arcade shooter, like you might see, for example, in titles such as Call of Duty, Heroes & Generals, Planetside 2, Squad, etc. There are no medics to magically heal you up to perfect, there are no mechanics that can magically repair vehicles. There are no crosshairs allowing you to accurately fire from the hip. The flight mechanics are not arcade flight mechanics. It is very unlikely that you'll be able to even attempt to fly with keyboard & mouse controls, because there is just too much fine control required to actually pilot a plane. There is bullet drop, even from large-caliber guns.
Given that the game is a Historical Accuracy Simulator, there is definitely some Asymmetical Warfare going on. The different guns and equipment of either side are NOT carbon copies of things on the other. There is no equivalent to an 88mm Flak gun on the Allied side, and no equivalent to a Matilda on the Axis (at least not at the time that the Matilda is used). Fighter planes and bombers are not identical to each other, and have very different flight models. However, it is still a game, so sides are roughly balanced with the types and amounts of equipment they can bring to bear in the game.
The game is also absolutely massive. It uses a 1/2 scale map of Western Europe based on satellite data. It is the largest MMO world map, period. It's also completely open: you can spawn in at one end of the map and fly to the other; this actually happens when players organize bombing runs on enemy production factories. Keep in mind, however, that means it can take literal minutes when initially setting up an attack on a town, because players have to drive out, set up mobile spawn points, etc. Walking from one town to another, or even from a forward base to a town, can definitely take 10+ minutes.
There are 2 layers to the game: Fighting as soldiers/tanks/planes/ships, and moving around Divisions and Brigades on the world map as well as coordinating attack and defense objectives. Only High Command players have access to moving supply around the map, and HC accept applications from individuals and train them up on how to use the game tools to move around supply, and when it's a good idea to do so. As for fighting on the ground, in the air, or on the seas, players spawn in, using up supply from said divisions and brigades, in order to achieve objectives. These objectives can be attacking or defending towns, blowing or repairing bridges, blowing or defending forward bases, etc. When players are killed, despawn without being in a "Return to Base" area, or are sufficently wounded/damaged, then that supply doesn't go back to the division or brigade it came from. Supply trickles in based on the production rates of a side's factories.
Additionally, it can be said that there are two different ways to play the game in terms of fighting in the actual game world: tactically and strategically. Tactical play is basically anything that's fun and exciting: attacking a hotly contested area, defending a hotly contested area, assaulting defensive positions, shooting down planes, bombing towns, etc. Strategic play is basically anything that your side really needs you to do that's NOT fun or exciting: defending critical control points from sneaky enemies infiltrating behind enemy lines, defending forward bases from intermittent attack, etc. It's VERY LIKELY that some newer players will happen upon these strategic missions, and may mistake the lack of action that's due to the strategic importance of a given mission for the game being boring. In this case, newer players should leave that mission and go to one that's more immediately satisfying, so they can get a feel of the actual meat of the game, which is that wonderful tactical play.
At the present time, there is no integrated voice chat. You will have to rely on the third-party application Discord. However, Discord is a very solid application to use in the mean time while the developers work on integrated natively supported voice communication in the game.
The in-game groups are known as "squads" - these are basically the same thing as "clans" or "gaming clubs" that you might see in other games. Playing this game solo is like playing a single individual soldier who knows no one around them while fighting in an actual war. You're going to die A LOT. Everyone does, even 16-year veterans to the game. Doing that over and over, without being a part of a group, is going to wear you down. You're just not going to enjoy the gameplay, because it's not going to feel personal. You're not going to be able to know what's happening around you. You're not going to be able to coordinate movements or attacks while playing if you're not in a squad or if you're not on voice comms. I implore new players to use Discord whether or not they're in a squad, and to immediately try using Discord. Almost all of the current players have been trying to do everything they can to help the new players coming in, and that includes helping them out on voice comms.
The biggest thing I have been seeing is that there are complaints about the Free to Play accounts. There are accusations of hiding content behind a pay wall. There is a lot of disgruntlement over just what and how much Free to Play accounts should get access to. The reality of the situation is that World War II Online uses a PAY TO PLAY business model. This is the same business models that MMOS up to and prior to World of Warcraft use, in that to actually play the game, you need to pay. However, your account is still left ACTIVE after the initial trial period. This is meant to allow you to continue to see what the game has to offer, in the hopes that you eventually subscribe. Therefore, once an account loses its premium status, it is HEAVILY RESTRICTED. You get access to the mainstay of the infantry, which is the standard bolt-action rifles everyone, including premium players, use. This is because weapons are tied to supply, and there could be hundreds of bolt-action rifles to spawn with, but only a few dozen sub-machine guns. You also get access to early sub-machine guns, trucks, and perhaps some other early equipment. You can, and this is the HUGE one, create your own missions, and run out and make your own mobile spawn points. That allows you to not only play at the tactical level, but also on the strategic level, so you can contribute meaningfully to the side that you play on. Considering that the game is Pay to Play, in my personal opinion, the Free to Play accounts have enough content, because they're meant to keep you around if you're interested but can't afford it or aren't sure until you can afford it or until you're sure whether or not it's worth it for you.
Lastly, there is simply nothing else like this game. I mean that very seriously. A lot of people have been throwing out "Heroes & Generals", but that's not close. A better comparison is a combination of Foxhole and Planetside 2, but with the mechanics of a Red Orchestra game. Still, none of those, on their own, offer what this game does.

I’ve got a soft spot for puzzle games, and the indie scene is a fantastic place to find games presenting puzzles in new and innovative ways.
However,
truly surprised me, not only for its remarkable difficulty, but also its brilliant design. What appears to be a strange version of color match with a pulsing electronic soundtrack quickly reveals itself to be a test of coordination, memory, perspective and reflexes, all at the same time.
has an incredibly simple premise: You have to match the color and position of a number of squares in a short amount of time. As you progress, more colors are added. The game ends when time runs out on the clock. Sounds easy, right?
It isn’t.
The perspective you’re given of the solution is just slightly off enough to require a little bit of adjustment, and you’re given a remarkably small amount of time to complete the puzzle. As you progress, more and more colors are added, and you’ll need to cycle through them in the right order while moving to match things up. Make a mistake? Suddenly those spots have disappeared. Get the next puzzle correct and they’ll return, but fail too many times and you’ll be working with a very small playing area.
The mechanics of
may be simple, but they’re executed so precisely and accurately that they cannot help but be compelling. It took me quite a few tries before I figured things out, and it felt frustrating before then, but once things clicked, I was entranced, driven even, to keep playing.
is entirely fair. all the rules are laid out to you, and its as clear as…well, colors on a white board… what you need to do. And while you may fail and fail and fail again, you can feel yourself making new connections, learning tricks on how to look at specific orientations, your fingers getting ever so faster. That sense of improvement and learning is infectious and breeds a competitive spirit to improve.
's absolutely amazing soundtrack, and only helps to keep you driven. The pulsing electronic beats urge you to move faster and faster, pushing yourself to get the combinations of color and position correct. It puts you into a frantic, trance-like state. Time seems to slow slightly, and you’ll feel yourself putting up blinders to the rest of the world, concentrating completely on lining up the fluorescent blocks creeping towards you.
has two game modes, an arcade and a classic mode . Mechanically, there’s not a tons of difference. Arcade will see you going for as high a score as possible, while classic mode is more of a last as long/get as far kind of affair. Personally, I found the competitive spirit taking over and arcade move claimed most of my time, and the end screen does a fantastic job of showing you how you got your score, and how far away from the next ranking you were.
is challenging, and addictive. With bright, clear visuals and an amazing soundtrack, it’s a game that puzzle fans should absolutely check out, particularly if they’ve got a competitive streak.

though…

Sonic Adventure is a tricky game to judge. When it was first released back in 2001, it was loved by almost all. I myself have fond memories of playing it on the Gamecube. But some games just do not age well, and unfortunately, Sonic Adventure is one of them.
The game's camera often has a difficult time focusing on the characters and actions, thus making even the simplest of jumps an annoyance to be repeated again and again. The controls are also frequently difficult to work with, epsecially in situations requiring accuracy and a bit of finess. The story which is told from the perspective of several different characters is a boring and cliche-ridden droll, complete with events that often don't sync up. But it is admirable that it at least trys to present some character development and lore.
The game's highlights are its level design, which can truly be a joy to traverse through every so often, and to a lesser extent, its music. But neither of these traits are enough to make an enjoyable experience.
Overall Sonic Adventure is a clunky and boring game that only has a few inklings of entertainment sprinkled thoughout its entirety. Unless you're a dedicated Sonic fan or just want to experience the character's first true foray into the third dimension, I wouldn't play this game.

Sonic Adventure was a magnificent 3D plateformer who had just as many gameplay types as it had characters (6, to be precise), some focusing on speed, others on exploration, and all ultimately providing a unique experience enjoyable by all.
Emphasis on "was". The more time passes, the more Sonic Adventure's flaws appear obvious, such as collision glitches and bugs, terrible voice acting, subpar animations and graphics that in general haven't aged well. All of which make the game terrible. Which in turns makes the game great. Kinda like Tommy Wiseau's The Room, you know?
But I can't just dismiss this game as bad. It does have a lot of good moments. The Sonic levels, for the most part, are genuinely good, with a heavy focus on speed... for the most part. Some of those levels require some puzzle-solving, which tends to slow down the otherwise rapid pace of those levels. The Tails levels are similar, dropping the slower moments of each levels and focusing even moreso on speed and finding shortcuts to achieve your objectives. The Knuckles levels are exclusively focusing on exploration, which can get a little tedious in larger levels. The Amy levels are pretty unequal but most just represent classic 3D plateforming. Big the Cat's levels are an overglorified fishing minigame and honestly the worst part of the game. Gamma's levels are timed 3D plateforming sections where you need to eliminate adversaries to get more time, which can become rather stressful and annoying, but the story behind those levels was enough for me to forgive its obvious flaws.
The story branches out between each character and is generally somewhat classic of Sonic games... with a little twist on it. Each character also has a secondary story which they fulfill throughout their own adventure, but aside from Gamma's, it's nothing to write much about. It's just silly enough to be likeable.
Overall, Sonic Adventure is a deeply flawed, yet incredibly fun, experience that anyone should try out, be they Sonic fans or not.

"Not just a social commentary, a damn good game."
This game will change how you think of society, prison, and people, in all likelihood - and you'll have a lot of fun doing it, especially as it lets you set your own pace and truly make your own decisions in solving one of the toughest problems mankind has ever faced: criminality.
I've played many sim-management style games over the years, but this one is hands-down one of the deepest, most thoughtful, and most entertaining. Where most sim-management games develop complexity in terms of how systems interact (like managing how multiple businesses or large groups of people conflict), Prison Architect keeps things personal; inside of every prisoner, there is a mixture of traits and issues you need to address on an individual scale. You're not just managing a prison; you have to manage individual prisoners, and do your best to reform them.
The game essentially lets the player scale their own difficulty by choosing whether to run a minimum, medium, or maximum security prison (male/female options and death row are also possibilities). Every choice has its own complications to learn; maximum-security prisoners are far more likely to be illiterate, drug-addicted, violent, and so on.
But at the same time, they stay in your prison much longer. A cynical warden could choose to use that trait to force them to work longer, making more money off of their expertise in the factory, but the game never encourages cynicism (not optimism) in any direct fashion. Your goal, as laid out very early on, is to get your recidivism rate to 0% (reoffending rate, in other words, no prisoners leave and go on to commit new crimes), or as close to it as you can. Speaking as someone who has run a max-security prison with a recidivism rate that went between 0 and 2%, this is a great challenge, and will make you engage with the mechanics in all sorts of ways.
But the game offers no particular reward for doing this. You aren't penalized for having a high recidivism rate; you can feel free to be as cynical and money-grubbing as you wish. To get your re-offense chance to 0, you need to both punish the prisoners enough that they do not wish to return to prison, and prepare them enough for a career (purge them of addiction, teach them job skills, etc.,) to get them ready for their release. Health, criminality, addiction, and violence must all be managed, as well as educational and spiritual needs.
I'd recommend this to virtually any gamer. It's not just a social commentary, it's a damn good game.

But there's more, the character walks slow, talks slow and talks about everything at a pace that would make the pope rage.   It's just a VERY slow plodding pace and the game never picks up, at least for the first chapter.
Worse there's scenes that are just annoying, the game doesn't have a brightness setting, so you're fumbling around, pixel hunting in pitch black rooms.    And it's not clever or funny like Monkey's island situations.  These are just annoying.
There's also the navigation between rooms that just doesn't work and is uninititive, quite often you'll want to go between two views of the same room.  So you figure "I'll go walk towards the other side of the room and the camera will switch like when I walked over here.
It doesn't work, in fact you'll keep trying this before getting frustrated, then you'll walk to the a random point about halfway up the screen on the right side, and the screen will switch.  There's no indicator you're in the right spot, you'll just magically switch screens.   And that's assuming you have the mouse.
If on the other hand you're using the controller... well good luck looking for clues.  Unless you're standing in the right spot in the right director, and the random number god nod towards you you're able to completely miss clues.    Use a mouse, that's the best thing I can say.
Eventually you'll get annoyed so you'll grab a guide, ok. I don't fault a fan for that.    Except the game only seems to slow down then.  When you're not solving the "puzzles" you realize how ungodly slow the dialogue and situations evolve.  Dull and slow.
Then there's achievements, interesting but even those are a bit broken such as one to look at all the evidence in a room.  Even with a guide, the achievement might not (probably won't ) pop the first time....
Finally you get to a puzzle, a REAL puzzle, not just exposition, and you realize how utterly weak this game is.  You're supposed to lock pick a door, ok that's an interesting concepts a lot of games have done, but they find the worst possible system to do it.  Rather than give you any help you have to be pixel perfect to unlock it and there's a LOT of possible ways to set it up.   This is after a painfully slow game, you now have a tiddly puzzle that you're going to get frustrated at.
At that point I gave up on this game,  I once played this game for an 2 hours, now I played this game for another 3 hours, and honestly, I can say I haven't had any enjoyment from it.   Don't buy this game, if you like adventure games, go play Machinarium, Monkey's Island, or newly released, Full Throttle, but what ever you do, don't play The Raven unless you have 11-12 hours to kill and want to kill them in the worst way possible.

I was hoping this would be a multiplayer successor to Uplink, but unfortunately, it isn't.
It doesn't even have consistent gameplay.  It feels very unfinished, or rather, taped together.
The singleplayer part of it is frustrating on its own - with conflicting information in tutorials, and a long drawn out campaign.
Then you get into the MUD part of it, and you find out: the tutorial you spent hours in is useless in context to multiplayer almost entirely.
All the low level NPC's that new players need access to are constantly farmed out. All the game is, is random scripts. "Word.word."  "Thiscould.beanything."  So you spend hours just typing mush into the terminal, and doing the same tasks over and over again.
For comparison sake, its still crazy to compare this game to Uplink. Uplink, while based in the dial up days, still has a crap ton more features, is non-linear, has a competent tutorial, and has a full story.  I realize it may have had a bigger team, and it lacks the multiplayer component, but it's still the premiere hacking game. Dev's of this genre would do well to pay attention to it.  You can rob banks, falsify ID's, steal files, all while repainting the logs to make it look like someone else did it... THAT IS HACKING.
Hackmud just has a long way to go. Right now its just a ball of mush. It has no composition. If the dev can't keep up with the demand, they should open it up to mods, or user created content. I'm not sure what they were going for with this "hacking simulator."  It's a Run CMD simulator - thats about it.

This game is quite simply amazing. There are a few unique things that really make this game great because they have really thought about does and doesn't make good play experiences, and then made the game to make sure there are no bad experiences.
First example is the item system. There are no menus and no inventory. Every item is a physical object. You can only carry one at a time, you have phsyical slots on your back pack to attach them, and you physically seem them all taking up room. You can store things on rovers, spaceships, bases, or just throw them on the ground. It all involves physically moving every item in the world. No boring menus/investory to manipulate, no 'stacking'. It really makes the game immersive because you feel like you are part of a more 'real' world having to gather resources. Infact most of the game is based around how you will physically carry things back to your base (hence the need for trucks and rovers etc.).
Secondly the crafting is simple. The formulas are never more than one item, and they are shown to you at various crafting stations that you build (like 3D Printer, Vehicle Bay). So you don't have to go hunting for various things at the same time, and you always know what you need. It may sound overly simple, but its actually liberating because it makes mining and exploration more fun and goal driven.
Another amazing system is the idea of teathering. To get air (And power if needed) you need to tether to a supply. You can drop teathers every 10m or so. Its a vantastic idea because it not only serves as a good limiting mechanism for air/power, but it also doubles as a way to mark your path. Plus the tethers look quite simply amazing especially as you start to make tether lines to various mines etc.
The game also has a sort of module system in which you build things and attach them to each other in various ways. For example you can make a rover, then attach things to it like a seat, a storage shelf, solar panel for power, etc. Its all done extremely simply and intuitively, yet it allows amazing flexibility.
The world is very well chosen for scale. It currently has a solar system of about 5 planets and a moon. They planets are big, yet at the same time small (you can probably drive around one in 30minutes or so). The solar system really behaves like a real one, with planets orbiting the sun, and planets rotating for day night cycle.
Overall, I only review this on the current content. I don't care if its supposidly 'pre alpha'. There maybe on only about 10 hours of actual play, but it is great and makes you want to start again for new experiences several times over.

A short, but funny little game. There are a few minigames to go through, but it's more of an interactive visualization about the Pleistocene epoch rather than a game. As you walk in either direction you will discover text bubbles consisting of facts related to the wildlife, plants, and what in general characterizes this era in particular. With this in mind, I am giving this a positive review for it's purpose and the idea behind this game.
As a game I did find it a bit lacking, but if you play it for what it is I think you can look past those faults. The game is a bit buggy, and gives me kind of a feeling of being incomplete. I feel that it could easily have been built upon to give the player a bigger area to walk through, more minigames, more info, even more ways to interact with the environment around you. The Deer has several friends that are mentioned, but I feel everyone else is a bit left out. Maybe adding some minigames where you help them out of a bind, or could play different parts of the game as another animal (changing characters) could be one way to do this.
To conclude: It's a short learning experience, but a bit lacking as a game. The idea is nice, and I definitely see both it's potential as well as recognize it's uniqueness compared to other titles at Steam. It's relaxing to play, and definitely something to show to the kids. I'll give it 7/10 and let's hope for a solid sequel or new game expanding upon the potential that is here already ^^

Well, let's review it.
Hackmud is a great game in my opinion.
It does have some flaws BUT it is as far as I know a One-Man-Project and to create such a game alone is probably quite hard.
I do have some experience with Linux + Coding in general, so the start was a bit easier for as it may be for others.
E.g. my buddy bought this game for both of us, i do have experience, he doesn't.
It is way harder for him to learn or understand some things in this game but he tries to learn and improve himself.
That showed me that this game is not only for people who know some stuff and more, but also for someone who does not give up and tries to learn more and more.
It may be way harder but you got to start somewhere.
It's like the Dark Souls of Coding.
You have to be careful who you trust and which script you run.
(But you can trust dtr, he is a really nice and supportive guy.
He even made an email-Account just for this game and you can mail him.
Can't really say much about the others but be careful that v doesn't fools you.)
I also read some reviews and 1 negative review was quite interesting.
He/She said that you can only write 1 line in your small scratch"book".
Well He/She didn't know that you can write more lines.
Just hit STRG+Return/CTRL+Retunr/CMD+Return while you're "writing" inside of it and boom you have a new line.
I also don't know much about server issues.
Since I got the game it runs fluently and i never got a unwanted dc.
But I do have a really big issue: It is veeeery hard to get some GC (Money) once you're out of the prologue.
Almost every low-tier NPC is already hacked and henceworth you can't get money to init your system.
That way you can't upload any public scripts and more.
I put about 4-5 hours into the game just to find some existing NPCs just to get the message that they are already hacked.
All in all it is a solid game, even though it is very hard to get some money.
I like it, i will play it for a while and if you're interested in such games and you're not scared to learn and put many hours into a game than this might be something for you.
Just be cautious, don't get fooled, try to learn and be patient.
Encourages horrible coding habits; all of your progress can be wiped out by a one-character typo.

Well, there ya go. My first review ever. And that is because I want to show my appreciation for this one man's endevour.
Personally I always enjoyed hacking styled games since I was a kid. That is why this might be a little bit biased but nontheless I will try to keep it as objective as possible:
WARNING. THIS IS FROM A T2 PERSPECTIVE. CORRECT ME IF I AM WRONG.
This game (properly) integrates older, similar hacking games into our beautiful world wide web, with gameplay features that feel authentic yet familiar. There is a player economy, channels, corps, you name it. On top of this Sean integrated JavaScript (some coders will shout, I understand, but it is the best for this and you know it!) with a few limits (for understandable gameplay reasons), but otherwise completely free to use how you wish. This feels amazing, and even if you have little to no understanding in coding this community will teach you in no time.
A few things I want to talk about:
The hacking is done by cracking a set of t1 or t2 locks, that all have a particular set of actions that you will have to perform in order to unlock them. First, you have to find NPC corporations that leave crumbles of information on how to get dead npc accounts, commonly referred to as npc.locactions. Once you have said location you can start hacking it and cracking the different locks. This is done by engaging a kernel hardline, which gives you a limited amount of time before beeing disconnected. You can only get information from the locks within that given time before you have to reinitialise the hardline (which consists of typing in a random ip number after a nice animation).
Once you break all the locs you will gain the fruits of that dead npc account. PVP is another aspect but I am still learning the ropes so more on that later. A lot of aspect are the same but finding the player.loc is done differently and harder.
Overall the hacking feels genuinely exciting, especially when you are dealing with players. Also optimizing it is fun and keeps your mind on the highest setting.
Scripts all have a -SEC level, ranging from NullSec to FullSec. FullSec is safe in the sense that it cannot screw around with your systems or account. If you run MidSec scripts however you run the chance of getting robbed of your money, or worse, in LowSec it can even send your own location to other people, which leaves you open for attacks. The minefields one treads in is vast, one misspelled word and the autocomplete (just loose it, dont use it, ever...) will finish you off. It has happened to me twice, without even trying... You can check all security levels on all scripts, which is nice.
You can also create your own scripts, ranging from thieving, people angering steal-scripts to gracious, general information scripts like dtr. or ada. (users that create user friendly scripts). The freedom allowed in these scripts is pretty great, and although I have not seen this on the level of actually creating your own locks (not sure if this is possible, I am still T2 so correct me if I am wrong), some of the scripts and minds out there are freaking mind boggeling.
The last thing that I want to talk about before I summorise my review, is the awesome but dangerous community. Information (especially player.locations) is key, and some people take it very seriously. The Discord on the other hand is mostly friendly, there a different channels where you can ask the correct questions, less information hungry vibe (pseudos!!!). Scripting fanatics will help you on your way in no time, go check it out:
- Does not hold your hand, at all. Even after the tutorial you feel lost and not sure on what to do. This leaves you feeding on all bits and pieces of information you can find on what to do next, on how to become a h4x0rz. I find it an enjoyable hunt.
- Mistakes are your own, and they are brutal. It will set you back a few mils on T2, and I am still not sure how much information you leave after your main is breached and had transactions with your alt. We will see.
Wrote down kernal.hardline instead of the correct kernel.hardline? Tough luck, all money gone and your location is known. <3
- Good overall vibe / graphics / sounds. I would like to see a bit more diversity in the sounds, and especially in the music (I turned it off. Not the worst but quickly becomes repetitive). The sound of gaining credits feels... <3 so gud
- Freaking multiplayer, with an player based economy. < Good. I would like to see some more features in the sense of community though, mayby admin capabilities on channels (correct me if I am wrong but I have not found these) or the likes, more ways to interact.
- Complete JavaScript integration with the correct limits in place to not ruin the game. Or atleast, lets hope so ;)
- A real challange regarding the locks, and even more so on creating your own scrips on how to auto-unlock them. I dont know if new locks are introduced on T3, I would like to see some more variations. But this might be done on purpose so the scriptors can be within a set amount of chars each tier, I dunno, yet to explore T3.
- Selection of text is horrible sometimes. Especially when its busy in your channels. A shortcut to stop the shell from moving would be great!
- Multiline support on the scratch, useless now, hit enter and you screw the whole thing up. Spacing it up is annoying.
- I probably have not thought of all ramifications but it would be nice if your player.loc would rotate each week or so, or each month... or... I dunno. Some more information in general would be appreciated on the so called shadow.loc and player.loc, the difference between them and what you leave as a trace when you breach a breached npc, or a player. I had to learn that you will leave your .loc if you even try to breach someone, the hardest way.
All in all a very enjoyable experience, peaks my mind, and I feel like I am only half way there (Not gonna lie, I have done some heavy T2 cracking (mostly manual with some helper scripts, but no lock breaking scripts), and I am now on the top users list within 3 days of exploring this game. And I am not great coder. Whats going on here? Everyone blowing credits on corps? I will buy mine very soon, that is for sure, with some great individuals. Be wary! Or... wait, no, be Kind! :D
